A GUIDE TO REALITY

The Universe,

*Actually*

*What humanity currently understands*

*about reality*

Lothar J. Musiol

A guide to what is known

# <a id="fm_note"></a>A Note on This Book

This book is written for the reader of the great one-volume guides to science: an intelligent person who is not a specialist, and who would rather be told what is known than be flattered with wonder.

The model is a classic one-volume guide to science from the 1980s, together with the shorter guides to physics, chemistry, and biology that preceded it. Those books offered a single account of the natural sciences, updated as the account changed. The present book follows that ambition in two ascending arcs. The first runs from the rules of motion and the quantum world through particles and atoms to space and time, planets, stars, galaxies and the universe as a whole. The second runs from the first living chemistry through the body and mind and the living planet to technology and the way knowledge itself is made.

Compared with a guide finished in the 1980s, entire subjects had to be added. CRISPR and gene editing. mRNA medicine. The human microbiome. Gravitational waves as something heard, not merely predicted. Exoplanets as a catalog. Dark energy. Quantum information. Artificial intelligence in the form of learned systems. Climate science as a body of measurement. Synthetic biology. Those chapters are here because a guide that omitted them would no longer be a guide to the present.

The voice of the opening pages is kept throughout. Short claims. The evidence named. The uncertainty named beside it. Nothing in this book is offered as a final truth. It is offered as the picture a careful reader can hold in 2026, actually.

# <a id="fm_preface"></a>Preface

Every child is born a scientist.

The evidence for this is plain enough. Children ask questions with a persistence that adults often find exhausting. Why is the sky blue? Why does rain fall? Why do people age? Why do stars shine? Why is there a Moon?

The questions arise naturally.

The answers do not.

Human history can be viewed as a series of attempts to answer such questions. Some answers were beautiful. Some were clever. Many were comforting.

Most were wrong.

This should not be taken as a criticism of our ancestors. The universe was under no obligation to make itself easy to understand. A species that evolved on a small world around an ordinary star could scarcely expect to discover the workings of atoms, galaxies, life, and time itself.

Yet that is exactly what happened.

Slowly, over thousands of years, humanity assembled a picture of reality.

The Earth was shown to be a planet. The stars were shown to be suns. Life was shown to evolve. Matter was shown to consist of atoms. Space and time themselves were shown to be parts of a larger structure called spacetime.

Each discovery displaced an older certainty. Each expanded the horizon of ignorance. For every mystery solved, ten new mysteries appeared.

Today we know more than all previous generations combined. We know the age of the universe to remarkable precision. We can watch galaxies billions of light-years away. We can read the genetic instructions that build living organisms. We can alter those instructions. We have observed black holes. We have detected gravitational waves. We have constructed machines capable of performing tasks once believed to require uniquely human intelligence.

And yet.

We do not know what dark matter is. We do not know what dark energy is. We do not know how life began. We do not know how consciousness arises. We do not know whether we are alone.

Science is not a monument of certainty. It is a process of reducing uncertainty.

The purpose of this book is therefore not to present final truths. No such book can be written.

Its purpose is simpler. To describe, as clearly as possible, what humanity currently understands about reality.

Actually.

# <a id="bm_intro"></a>Introduction: Why Any of This Matters

You are a collection of atoms that has become temporarily organized enough to ask what atoms are. The atoms themselves are indifferent. They were forged in stars that died before the Sun existed, scattered, and later gathered into a planet where, after several billion years of chemistry, some of them began to copy themselves. Those copies eventually produced a nervous system capable of noticing the copying.

The noticing is recent. Written records cover a few thousand years. Science, as a systematic method, is younger still. In that short interval the same atoms have measured the age of the universe, the size of the electron, and the sequence of bases in their own genome. They have also built devices that can destroy the biosphere that sustains them and devices that can leave the planet. Both facts are consequences of the same understanding.

Nothing in the laws requires that understanding to continue. The laws are compatible with a universe that never produces observers, or with observers that appear and then vanish. The present moment is one in which observers exist and have begun to reconstruct the history that produced them. How long that reconstruction continues is not written in the equations. It is written, if anywhere, in what those observers choose to do with the knowledge they have acquired.

The chapters that follow are the current state of that reconstruction. They are incomplete. They will be revised. They are nevertheless the most reliable map yet drawn of the territory in which any such choice must be made.

### What the Sky Is Doing While You Read This

While you read this sentence the Earth has moved roughly 30 kilometers in its orbit. The Solar System has moved roughly 220 kilometers around the Galactic center. The Galaxy has moved several hundred kilometers relative to the cosmic microwave background. None of these motions is felt. All of them are real.

The photons striking your retina left their sources long ago. Some left the Sun eight minutes ago. Some left distant galaxies when the Earth was young. A few, if you are looking at the microwave background, left when the universe was 380 000 years old. Their journey does not pause while you turn the page.

The calculations that describe these motions and these journeys are the same calculations that describe the fall of an apple and the swing of a pendulum. The scales differ. The laws do not. The recognition is ordinary once it is made. It is still capable of producing a slight shift in the way the next sentence is read.

### A Brief Interlude on Scales

Consider a bacterium. It is roughly a micrometer across. Enlarge it ten thousand times, to the size of a grape, and its genome, a single loop of DNA, would unspool to more than ten meters, packed inside that grape. The bacterium copies all of it before every division, as its ancestors have done for several billion years.

Now consider the opposite direction. The observable universe is about 10<sup>27</sup> meters across. Shrink it to the size of the Earth, and the Earth itself would end up less than a hundredth of the width of an atom. On a globe of that universe, everything humans have ever built is a speck far below the reach of any microscope. The speck is recent, local and, so far, unique.

Both comparisons are accurate. Neither is especially comforting. They do, however, explain why the same physical laws can feel remote when written as equations and intimate when written as the difference between a bacterium and a person. This book follows that range in order, from the rules of motion and the quantum world, through particles and atoms, up to planets, stars and the universe as a whole. It then climbs a second ladder, from the first cells through bodies, minds and the living planet to technology and the way we know anything at all. The laws do not change. The number of zeros does.

![Two horizontal powers-of-ten scales in meters. First arc, Parts I to VI: quark (below 10^-18 m), proton (10^-15 m), atom (10^-10 m), molecule, a person (1 m), Earth (10^7 m), Solar System (10^13 m), galaxy (10^21 m), observable universe (10^27 m). Second arc, Parts VII to XI: DNA (2 nm wide), cell (10^-6 to 10^-4 m), brain (0.15 m), body (1.7 m), forest or reef, the living planet (10^7 m), technology reaching other worlds.](scripts/rev16/figures/fig1_two_arcs.png)

### The Cosmic Calendar

Compress the 13.8 billion years since the Big Bang into a single calendar year, as Carl Sagan did in his television series [*Cosmos*](#bib_40), and the proportions become vivid. The Big Bang is midnight on 1 January. Galaxies begin to assemble within weeks. Our Sun and its planets do not form until the first day of September, and the earliest life on Earth appears in the last days of that month.

Oxygen builds up in the air in late October. Animals with hard parts arrive in the middle of December, and the dinosaurs vanish on the morning of 30 December. Our species appears about eleven minutes before the year ends. All of written history occupies the last twelve seconds or so, and the four centuries since Galileo turned a telescope on Jupiter take less than a second.

The calendar is a device, not a measurement, and its dates move as the science improves. Its use is the sense of scale it gives. Almost everything in this book happened before there was anyone to notice it, and almost everything we know about it was learned in the final sliver of the last day.

### A Remark on Numbers

Large numbers are best approached with caution. A billion is a thousand million. A trillion is a thousand billion. The difference is the difference between a modest public building and the annual budget of a medium-sized country. Both are finite. Neither is easy to visualize.

The same caution applies in the opposite direction. A nanometer is a billionth of a meter. A femtometer is a millionth of a nanometer. Atoms are measured in the former. Atomic nuclei in the latter. The fact that both can be manipulated with instruments built by people who occasionally lose their car keys is one of the more surprising achievements of the species. The achievement does not make the numbers less large or less small. It merely shows that careful counting can be done even by creatures whose native range is meters and years.

# <a id="part_1"></a>Part I: The Rules of Motion and Energy

*The everyday laws of motion, heat, waves and fields that every later part relies on*

## <a id="ch_1"></a>1. Motion, Force and Energy

### Motion and Newton’s Laws

Aristotle held that every kind of matter has a natural place. Earthy things seek the center. Fire seeks the heights. An object out of its place moves toward it. Heavier objects, being more eager, fall faster. Forced motion requires a continuous push. Rest is the natural state.

The view lasted nearly two thousand years because it matched ordinary observation. Feathers fall slower than stones. A thrown stone eventually stops. The heavens move in circles while earthly things fall straight.

Galileo tested the claim about falling. He used inclined planes to slow the motion enough to measure with the tools he had. Balls of different weight rolled down the same plane in the same time. The distance covered increased with the square of the time. The acceleration was constant. In a vacuum, a feather and a metal ball fall together. Air resistance, not weight, explains the everyday difference.

Newton put the results into three laws. An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues in a straight line at constant speed, unless a force acts on it. Force equals mass times acceleration. For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Mass is the measure of inertia, the resistance to change in motion. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass. The two are proportional on Earth, but they are not the same thing. On the Moon the mass is unchanged and the weight is less.

Momentum is mass times velocity. In an isolated system it is conserved. When two objects collide, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after. Angular momentum is conserved in rotation. A spinning skater who pulls in her arms spins faster. The product of moment of inertia and angular speed stays constant.

Work is force times distance in the direction of the force. Energy is the capacity to do work. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Potential energy is the energy of position. In the absence of friction and other losses, mechanical energy is conserved. A pendulum converts kinetic to potential and back. Friction converts mechanical energy into heat. The first law of thermodynamics says that energy is never created or destroyed, only converted.

These laws are the foundation of classical mechanics. They describe the motion of planets, the flight of a baseball, and the structure of a bridge. They fail only at very high speeds, very strong gravity, or very small scales. In those regimes, relativity and quantum mechanics take over. For everything in between, Newton’s laws remain the working tools.

### The Principle of Stationary Action

Classical mechanics can be written in more than one way. Newton’s laws describe how forces change momentum from moment to moment. An equivalent description uses the principle of stationary action.

The action of a path is a quantity calculated from the kinetic energy and the potential energy along that path. For a particle moving from one point to another in a given time, the actual path is the one for which the action is stationary—usually a minimum. Nearby paths have nearly the same action. The path nature takes is the one that does not change the action to first order when the path is varied slightly.

This is not a statement that nature calculates. It is a mathematical fact about the equations. The path that satisfies Newton’s second law is the same path that makes the action stationary. The two descriptions are equivalent. One is local: the force at each point determines the acceleration at that point. The other is global: the entire path is the one that satisfies the stationary condition.

The principle extends to fields and to more complicated systems. In Lagrangian mechanics the action is the integral of the Lagrangian. The Euler-Lagrange equations that follow from the stationary condition are the equations of motion. In quantum mechanics the path-integral formulation assigns a phase to every path and sums them. The classical path is the one where the phases reinforce. The stationary-action principle is the classical limit of that sum.

The formulation is useful because it makes symmetries transparent. If the Lagrangian does not depend on a coordinate, the corresponding momentum is conserved. Time translation symmetry gives energy conservation. Spatial translation symmetry gives momentum conservation. Rotational symmetry gives angular-momentum conservation. Noether’s theorem connects continuous symmetries to conservation laws. The connection is clearer in the action formulation than in the force formulation.

### The Principle of Least Action

The principle of least action states that the actual path taken by a system between two configurations is the path that makes the action stationary. In symbols:

S = ∫ L  dt,    L = T − V.

For a particle the Lagrangian is kinetic energy minus potential energy. The condition δ S = 0 yields the Euler–Lagrange equations, which are equivalent to Newton’s laws. The same variational statement works for fields. The action for the electromagnetic field or for the metric of general relativity produces Maxwell’s equations or the Einstein equation when it is required to be stationary.

Feynman regarded the principle as the most fundamental formulation of classical mechanics. It makes no reference to forces. It refers only to the comparison of entire paths.

The principle does not require the action to be a minimum. It requires it to be stationary. In some cases the stationary path is a maximum or a saddle. The terminology “least action” is traditional and slightly inaccurate. The content is the stationarity condition. That condition is sufficient to generate the equations of motion for every fundamental theory now in use.

### Least Action in Light and Everyday Motion

The same idea governs light. In a medium whose refractive index varies, light takes the path of stationary travel time. That is Fermat’s principle, the optical form of the action principle. The parabola of a thrown stone, the bending of light at an interface and the minimal surface of a soap film are all cases in which the observed shape makes a simple integral stationary. No separate force law is needed: the force law follows from the variational statement.

### Worked Examples: Least Action and Optics

Example 1. Light travels from air into glass (n = 1.5). The angle of incidence is 30°. What is the angle of refraction?

Snell’s law: n<sub>1</sub>sin θ<sub>1</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>sin θ<sub>2</sub>. sin θ<sub>2</sub> = sin 30<sup>°</sup> / 1.5 = 1/3. θ<sub>2</sub> ≈ 19.5<sup>°</sup>.

Example 2. Show that the optical path length is stationary for the actual ray in a plane mirror.

The geometric path that reflects with equal angles is the shortest path that touches the mirror (image method). Any other path is longer. The action (travel time) is therefore stationary.

Example 3. A soap film adjusts its shape. Why is the surface a minimal surface?

The surface energy is proportional to area. The equilibrium shape minimizes area subject to the boundary conditions—the definition of a minimal surface. The same variational principle governs the film and the light ray.

### Conservation Laws

Energy, momentum, and angular momentum are conserved in every isolated system. The conservation laws follow from symmetries of the underlying action, as Noether’s theorem shows.

In mechanics the statements are elementary. The total energy of a collection of particles interacting through forces that derive from a potential is constant. The total momentum is constant when no external force acts. The total angular momentum about any fixed point is constant when no external torque acts. The same statements hold, with the appropriate field expressions, for the electromagnetic field and for the gravitational field.

Apparent violations are always the result of an incomplete accounting. Heat is disordered kinetic energy. Radiation carries both energy and momentum. When those contributions are included, the balances close. No experiment has shown a violation of any of the three laws in an isolated system.

The laws define the quantities they conserve. Energy is the quantity that is constant because the laws do not depend on the absolute time. Momentum is conserved for the parallel reason that the laws do not care where in space they are applied. The definitions are operational and have been confirmed from the scale of elementary particles to the scale of galaxy clusters.

### Energy Is Only a Number

Richard Feynman introduced the conservation of energy with a parable. A child owns a number of indestructible blocks, and a watchful parent counts them each evening. One evening a block is missing. It turns out to be in a toy chest. Another evening the count is off again, and the missing block is found under the bath water, whose level has risen by a measurable amount. The parent invents rules for the hiding places and keeps the books balanced.

Energy is like that. Nothing in nature is labeled energy. It is a quantity we calculate from other things, such as speeds, heights, temperatures and fields, and it has the remarkable property that the total, correctly calculated, never changes. When the sum seems to fail, physicists look for a hiding place: a new form of energy. Sometimes they find one. The neutrino was proposed in just this way, to account for energy that seemed to vanish in beta decay.

The parable is also honest about a limit. It tells us how to keep the accounts and not what is being accounted. That the number is constant is a fact, tied by Noether’s theorem to the sameness of the laws from one moment to the next.

### Conservation of Energy from Time-Translation Invariance

Noether’s theorem associates a conservation law with every continuous symmetry. Invariance of the action under time translation implies conservation of energy. If the Lagrangian does not depend explicitly on time, the quantity E = ∑<sub>i</sub> q̇<sub>i</sub>(∂ L)/(∂q̇<sub>i</sub>) − L is constant along the motion. For the standard mechanical Lagrangian this quantity is T + V.

The same reasoning applies to fields. Invariance under time translation yields a conserved energy-momentum tensor. The integral of its time-time component over a spatial volume is the total energy. Apparent non-conservation always signals that the system under consideration is not isolated or that the Lagrangian has an explicit time dependence.

The link between time-translation symmetry and energy conservation is exact within the domain of the variational principle. It supplies the deepest reason that energy is conserved.

### The Motions of the Earth

The Earth rotates on its axis once every sidereal day (86 164 s). It revolves about the Sun once every sidereal year (365.256 days). The axis is tilted 23.4° to the orbital plane; the tilt varies between 22.1° and 24.5° with a 41 000-year period. The axis itself precesses with a 25 800-year period and nutates with an 18.6-year period of 19 arc-seconds. These three astronomical cycles—obliquity, precession, and eccentricity—modulate the seasonal distribution of sunlight and have produced the succession of ice ages recorded in ice cores and marine sediments.

The Earth’s orbit is an ellipse of eccentricity 0.017. The semi-major axis is one astronomical unit, 149.6 million kilometers. The orbital speed is 29.8 km/s. The Sun itself orbits the galactic center at 220 km/s, completing one revolution in about 225 million years. The Solar System oscillates above and below the galactic plane with a period of roughly 62 million years.

Relative to the cosmic microwave background the Solar System moves at 370 km/s. All of these motions are unfelt. Uniform velocity produces no local effect; only accelerations are detectable, and most of the accelerations associated with the larger motions lie below the threshold of human sensation. The principle that uniform motion is equivalent to rest was stated by Galileo and remains the foundation of both Newtonian and relativistic mechanics.

### The Rotation of Rigid Bodies

A rigid body has six degrees of freedom: three of translation and three of rotation. The rotational motion is governed by the angular-momentum equation. The moment of inertia tensor relates angular velocity to angular momentum. For a principal-axis rotation the relation is scalar. For a general rotation the angular-velocity vector and the angular-momentum vector are not parallel.

Euler’s equations describe the free rotation of a rigid body. They predict that rotation about the axis of intermediate moment of inertia is unstable. A book tossed into the air rotates stably about its longest or shortest axis and tumbles about the intermediate axis. The instability is geometric. It follows from the conservation of energy and angular momentum alone.

Precession occurs when a torque acts on a spinning body. The angular-momentum vector moves perpendicular to the torque. The result is the slow conical motion of a spinning top or of the Earth’s axis under the gravitational torque of the Sun and Moon. The same mathematics describes the motion of a gyroscope and the stabilization of a bicycle wheel.

The kinetic energy of rotation is 1/2 Iω<sup>2</sup>. It is independent of the translational kinetic energy. Both are conserved separately when no external torque or force acts. The separation is a consequence of the rigidity constraint.

### Oscillations

An oscillation is a periodic motion about an equilibrium. For small amplitudes the restoring force is proportional to the displacement. The motion is then simple harmonic. The period is independent of amplitude and is given by 2π√(m/k) for a mass on a spring and by 2π√(l/g) for a simple pendulum.

When friction is present the oscillation is damped. The amplitude decays exponentially. When the damping is light the frequency is nearly unchanged. When the damping is critical the system returns to equilibrium as quickly as possible without oscillating. When the damping is heavier the return is slower and monotonic.

A driven oscillator responds most strongly when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency. The response is resonance. The amplitude at resonance is limited by the damping. The phase of the response shifts from in-phase below resonance to out-of-phase above resonance. The same behavior appears in electrical circuits, in atoms driven by light, and in mechanical structures driven by wind or earthquakes.

Coupled oscillators exchange energy. Two pendulums connected by a weak spring exhibit beats. The energy flows back and forth at a frequency set by the coupling strength. The normal modes of the system are the patterns in which every part oscillates at the same frequency. Any motion can be written as a superposition of normal modes.

### The Flow of Fluids

A fluid is a substance that cannot support a static shear stress. It flows. The motion is described by the Navier–Stokes equation, which expresses the conservation of momentum for a continuous medium. The equation contains a term for pressure gradients, a term for viscous stresses, and a term for external forces such as gravity.

At low speeds and high viscosities the flow is laminar. Layers slide past one another with little mixing. At high speeds or low viscosities the flow becomes turbulent. Turbulence is characterized by eddies on many scales and by an enhanced rate of mixing and dissipation. The transition is governed by the Reynolds number, the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces. Above a critical value the laminar solution is unstable.

Bernoulli’s principle follows from the steady, inviscid limit of the momentum equation. Along a streamline the sum of pressure and kinetic-energy density is constant when gravity is neglected. The principle explains the lift of an airfoil, the curve of a spinning ball, and the operation of a carburetor. It is an energy statement for an idealized fluid. Real fluids always dissipate some energy through viscosity.

The same equations describe the flow of air, of water, of blood, and of the molten rock in the Earth’s mantle. The mathematics is universal. The observed patterns differ only because the Reynolds numbers and the boundary conditions differ.

### Worked Examples: Fluid Flow and Bernoulli

Example 1. Water flows through a pipe that narrows from 10 cm to 5 cm diameter. The speed in the wide section is 2 m s<sup>−1</sup>. What is the speed in the narrow section?

Continuity: A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub>. Area ratio = 4. v<sub>2</sub> = 8 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Example 2. Use Bernoulli’s equation to find the pressure drop.

P<sub>1</sub> + 1/2ρ v<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> = P<sub>2</sub> + 1/2ρ v<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>. Δ P = 1/2ρ(v<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> − v<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>) = 30 kPa (taking ρ = 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>).

Example 3. An airfoil has flow speed 50 m s<sup>−1</sup> over the upper surface and 40 m s<sup>−1</sup> over the lower surface. Estimate the pressure difference.

Δ P ≈ 1/2ρ(v<sub>u</sub><sup>2</sup> − v<sub>l</sub><sup>2</sup>) ≈ 550 Pa. For a wing of area 20 m<sup>2</sup> the lift is about 11 kN—sufficient to support a light aircraft.

The calculations assume incompressible, inviscid flow. They nevertheless give the correct order of magnitude for many practical devices.

### Worked Examples: Orders of Magnitude

**Verbal** A ball thrown upward slows, stops, and falls. The same acceleration that slows it is the acceleration that speeds it on the way down. The direction of the acceleration never changes. Only the direction of the velocity changes.

**Calculation** A 2 kg mass falls 5 m. Potential energy lost = mgh = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98 J. If the energy appears as kinetic energy, v = √(2 × 98/2) = 9.9 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

**Verbal** Two slits produce a pattern of bright and dark bands. Closing one slit removes the bands. The bands require both paths. The requirement is not classical.

**Calculation** Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through slits 0.1 mm apart. On a screen 2 m away the fringe spacing is λ D/d = 5 × 10<sup>−7</sup> × 2 / 10<sup>−4</sup> = 10 mm.

**Verbal** A star more massive than about eight solar masses ends as a neutron star or a black hole. The choice depends on the mass of the core that remains after mass loss. The dependence is observed in the remnant masses.

**Calculation** The Schwarzschild radius of the Sun is 2GM/c<sup>2</sup> ≈ 3 km. A solar-mass black hole is therefore smaller than a city. A billion-solar-mass black hole has a radius of order 3 × 10<sup>9</sup> km—roughly the size of the Solar System.

**Verbal** Across the whole sky the microwave background varies by only about one part in 10<sup>5</sup>. The small non-uniformities are the seeds of galaxies. The seeds are visible. The galaxies are the grown plants.

**Calculation** A temperature fluctuation of 100 µK on a 2.7 K background is a fractional perturbation of 100 × 10<sup>−6</sup>/2.7 ≈ 3.7 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. The same fraction appears in the density perturbations that later collapse.

The first pair uses this chapter; the others draw on light and interference ([Chapter 3](#ch_3)), black holes ([Chapter 22](#ch_22)) and the microwave background ([Chapter 32](#ch_32)). They recover the orders of magnitude that appear in nature.

## <a id="ch_2"></a>2. Heat and Disorder

### Heat and Thermodynamics

Heat is the transfer of energy that raises the temperature of a body or changes its state. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules. The two are related but distinct. A large cold object can contain more thermal energy than a small hot one.

The kinetic theory of gases treats a gas as a collection of molecules in random motion. Pressure is the force from molecules striking the walls. Boyle’s law (pressure times volume is constant at fixed temperature) and Charles’s law (volume is proportional to absolute temperature at fixed pressure) follow from the model. Absolute zero, about −273 degrees Celsius, is the temperature at which molecular motion would reach its minimum. It cannot be reached, but it can be approached.

Specific heat is the energy needed to raise the temperature of a given mass by one degree. Latent heat is the energy needed to change state without changing temperature—melting ice or boiling water. Water has a high specific heat and high latent heats. That is why it moderates climate and why sweating cools the body.

The first law of thermodynamics is the conservation of energy. Heat and work are both forms of energy transfer. The second law says that heat does not spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter one. Equivalently, an isolated system never loses entropy. Entropy is often called disorder; more precisely it counts the microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state. A gas expands into a vacuum because there are more ways for the molecules to be spread out than confined. The reverse is not impossible in principle, but it is so improbable that it is never observed.

Heat engines convert heat into work. They require a temperature difference. The efficiency is limited by the temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs. No engine can convert all the heat into work. That limit is not a matter of engineering. It is a consequence of the second law.

The same laws govern the cooling of a cup of coffee, the operation of a refrigerator, and the evolution of the universe. In an expanding universe, the total entropy increases. Local decreases are possible when energy is supplied from elsewhere. Life is such a local decrease. It maintains order by exporting disorder to its surroundings.

### Temperature, Gas Laws and Phases

Temperature is the quantity that is equal when two systems are in thermal equilibrium. It is proportional to the average kinetic energy per degree of freedom in an ideal gas. The proportionality constant is Boltzmann’s constant. Heat is energy transferred by virtue of a temperature difference.

In quantitative form the first law says that the change in internal energy of a system equals the heat added minus the work done by the system. Taken together with the second law, it forbids perpetual-motion machines of both the first and the second kind.

The ideal-gas law, PV = NkT, follows from the kinetic theory once the temperature is identified with the average kinetic energy. Real gases deviate from the law at high densities or low temperatures because of intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume. The deviations are described by the van der Waals equation and by more elaborate equations of state.

Phase transitions occur when the free energy of two different arrangements of the same molecules becomes equal. Melting, boiling, and sublimation are first-order transitions marked by latent heat and by a discontinuous change in density. The critical point is the end of the boiling curve, where the distinction between liquid and gas disappears.

### Worked Examples: Thermodynamics

Example 1. An ideal gas expands isothermally from 2 L to 4 L at 300 K. How much work is done by one mole?

W = RTln (V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>) = 1 730 J.

Example 2. A Carnot engine operates between 600 K and 300 K. What is its maximum efficiency?

η = 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> = 0.5 (50 percent).

Example 3. 1 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 100 °C. How much heat is required? (Specific heat 4 180 J kg<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>.)

Q = mcΔ T = 334 kJ. The same quantity of heat is released when the water cools.

These results follow directly from the first and second laws and from the definition of the ideal-gas temperature scale.

Example. One mole of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant volume from 300 K to 400 K. How much heat is absorbed, and how much work is done?

No work is done at constant volume, so Q = Δ U = 3/2R Δ T = 1.5 × 8.314 × 100 ≈ 1 250 J.

Example. A Carnot engine operates between 400 K and 300 K. Find its efficiency and the work produced per kilojoule of heat absorbed from the hot reservoir.

η = 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> = 0.25. Work = 250 J per kilojoule absorbed.

The results follow directly from the first law and from the definition of the Carnot efficiency. They are the upper bounds realized by no real engine.

Example. A heat engine absorbs 500 J from a hot reservoir and rejects 300 J to a cold reservoir. What is its efficiency? What is the maximum possible efficiency if the reservoirs are at 600 K and 300 K?

Efficiency = W/Q<sub>H</sub> = 200/500 = 0.4. Carnot efficiency = 1 − 300/600 = 0.5. The engine is irreversible.

Example. One mole of ideal gas is compressed adiabatically from 300 K and 10 L to 5 L. γ = 1.4. Find the final temperature.

T<sub>2</sub> = T<sub>1</sub>(V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>)<sup>γ−1</sup> = 300 × 2<sup>0.4</sup> ≈ 396 K.

The results follow from the definition of efficiency and from the adiabatic condition for an ideal gas.

### Chaos

A system can be deterministic and still be unpredictable in practice. Deterministic means that the future state is fixed by the present state and the laws. Unpredictable means that a small uncertainty in the present state grows so rapidly that the future cannot be calculated usefully beyond a limited time.

The classic example is the logistic map, x<sub>n+1</sub> = r x<sub>n</sub> (1 − x<sub>n</sub>). For some values of the parameter r the sequence is periodic. For others it is chaotic. Nearby starting points diverge exponentially. The rate of divergence is measured by the Lyapunov exponent. When the exponent is positive, the system is chaotic.

The same behavior appears in continuous systems. Edward Lorenz studied a simplified model of atmospheric convection. The equations are deterministic. The solutions are sensitive to initial conditions. Two trajectories that begin close together separate until they bear no useful relation. The atmosphere is such a system. Weather forecasts lose skill after about two weeks because the initial uncertainties, however small, grow to the size of the weather itself. Climate, which is the statistics of the weather, remains predictable on longer scales.

Chaos is not randomness. The trajectory is unique. It is confined to a strange attractor of lower dimension than the full phase space. The attractor has structure. The structure is fractal. The motion on the attractor is aperiodic. Small changes in parameters can move the system from periodic to chaotic behavior through a sequence of period doublings. The ratios of the parameter intervals approach a universal constant.

Most real systems are neither purely regular nor purely chaotic. The solar system is stable on human timescales and chaotic on timescales of tens of millions of years for the inner planets. Turbulence in fluids is chaotic. The heart and the brain show both regular and chaotic dynamics. The existence of chaos shows that exact laws do not guarantee practical predictability. The distinction is quantitative. It depends on the Lyapunov time and on the precision of the initial data.

### Lyapunov Exponents and Predictability

A chaotic system has at least one positive Lyapunov exponent, and the exponents obey a bookkeeping rule: their sum equals the average rate at which phase-space volume contracts. In a dissipative system that sum is negative, so the attractor has zero volume and a non-integer dimension.

Chaos needs nonlinearity and, for continuous-time systems, at least three dynamical degrees of freedom. It appears in low-dimensional systems such as the logistic map at parameter value 4, the Lorenz equations, double pendulums and driven oscillators, and also in high-dimensional ones such as turbulence, climate and neural networks. The limit on prediction is practical, not fundamental. Statistical properties such as invariant measures and correlation functions remain well defined, and forecasts succeed inside the predictability horizon.

### Solitons

A soliton is a localized wave that propagates without changing shape and that survives collisions with other solitons intact. The classic example is the solitary wave observed by John Scott Russell in a canal in 1834: a single elevation of water that traveled for miles without dispersing. The mathematical model is the Korteweg–de Vries equation

∂<sub>t</sub> A + A∂<sub>x</sub> A + b∂<sub>x</sub><sup>3</sup> A = 0.

Its solutions interpenetrate and emerge unchanged. The same behavior appears in optical fibres, in plasmas, and in certain magnetic materials.

A soliton is intermediate between a particle and a wave. It is localized like a particle and extended like a wave. It carries energy, momentum, and, in some cases, topological charge. Because the shape is preserved by a balance between nonlinearity and dispersion, the soliton is stable against small perturbations.

Solitons have been used to transmit data over long optical links and to model domain walls, dislocations, and certain elementary excitations in condensed matter. They remain classical solutions of nonlinear wave equations. Their quantum counterparts appear as stable particles or as topological defects in quantum field theory. No fundamental soliton has been observed that is not already accounted for by the Standard Model or by general relativity.

## <a id="ch_3"></a>3. Waves, Sound and Light

### Waves and Their Distinguishing Properties

A wave is a traveling disturbance that carries energy and momentum without a net transport of matter. Sound, water waves, light, and gravitational waves all satisfy the definition. Six properties distinguish wave motion from the motion of rigid bodies.

Superposition: linear waves add and can cancel. The result is interference. Diffraction is the consequence of interference that allows waves to spread around obstacles. Refraction is the change of direction at an interface where the propagation speed changes. Dispersion is the dependence of speed on frequency; it separates colors in a rainbow and stretches distant thunder. Damping is the progressive loss of amplitude. Polarization is the restriction of the oscillation direction for transverse waves.

None of these six effects occurs for the center-of-mass motion of ordinary rigid bodies. Their presence is therefore diagnostic of wave motion. Light exhibits all six. Gravitational waves have shown superposition, damping, and polarization; the remaining three are still unobserved.

Every sinusoidal wave obeys λ f = c, where λ is the wavelength, f the frequency, and c the phase speed. When c depends on λ, the wave is dispersive. Sound in air is nearly non-dispersive, which is why speech remains intelligible at a distance. Water waves are strongly dispersive.

The energy density of a harmonic wave is proportional to the square of the time and space derivatives of the displacement. The momentum density is proportional to the product of those derivatives. Reflection from a fixed obstacle reverses the component of momentum normal to the surface, producing equal angles of incidence and reflection.

### Huygens’ Principle and the Dimensionality of Space

In three spatial dimensions a wave front may be reconstructed by treating every point on the front as the source of a secondary spherical wavelet. The envelope of the wavelets gives the position of the front at a later time. The construction, due to Huygens, correctly describes reflection, refraction, and, with Fresnel’s addition of interference, diffraction. It is a direct consequence of the wave equation in an odd number of dimensions greater than or equal to three.

The principle fails in two dimensions. A circular pulse leaves a wake; the interior never returns to rest. A stone dropped into a still pond continues to radiate after the stone has vanished. The mathematical reason is that the delta-function solution of the wave equation that propagates outward and leaves no residual amplitude exists only when the dimension is odd and at least three. In even dimensions every frequency travels at a different speed, so a sharp pulse cannot be maintained.

The practical consequence is that a room becomes dark when the light is switched off, and that speech ends when the speaker stops. Both facts depend on our living in a three-dimensional space. In a two-dimensional world the same signals would continue indefinitely.

### Worked Examples: Waves and Superposition

Example 1. Two sound waves of equal amplitude and frequencies 440 Hz and 442 Hz interfere. What is the beat frequency?

Beat frequency = |f<sub>1</sub> − f<sub>2</sub>| = 2 Hz. The intensity rises and falls twice per second.

Example 2. A wave on a string has wavelength 0.5 m and frequency 200 Hz. What is its speed?

v = fλ = 100 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Example 3. In a double-slit experiment the slits are 0.2 mm apart and the screen is 2 m away. Light of wavelength 600 nm is used. What is the fringe spacing?

Δ y = λ L/d = 6 mm.

The same relations govern interference in water waves, sound, light and electron diffraction.

Example. A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic. The length is 1.2 m and the wave speed is 240 m s<sup>−1</sup>. Find the frequency.

Wavelength of the third harmonic = 2L/3 = 0.8 m. Frequency = v/λ = 300 Hz.

Example. Two loudspeakers 2 m apart emit the same 340 Hz tone. An observer walks along the line joining them. At what distances from the midpoint is the sound loudest?

Path difference must be an integer number of wavelengths. λ = v/f = 1 m. Loudest at path differences 0, 1 m, 2 m, … The midpoint (path difference 0) is a maximum.

These calculations use only the relations v = fλ and the interference condition. They recover the standing-wave and two-source patterns observed in ordinary acoustics.

Example. A standing wave on a string has nodes 0.25 m apart. The wave speed is 200 m s<sup>−1</sup>. What is the frequency of the fifth harmonic?

Distance between nodes = λ/2 = 0.25 m, so λ = 0.5 m. Fundamental wavelength for a string of length L = nλ/2 with n = 5 gives L = 1.25 m. Frequency of fifth harmonic = 5v/(2L) = 400 Hz.

Example. Two coherent sources 3 m apart emit 600 Hz sound in air (v = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>). How many interference maxima lie along the line joining the sources?

λ = 340/600 ≈ 0.567 m. Maximum path difference = 3 m. Number of maxima = 2 × (3/0.567) + 1 ≈ 11.

The calculations use only wavelength, path difference and the standing-wave condition.

### Sound and the Human Voice

Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure wave. Its speed is √(γ P/ρ), approximately 340 m/s at room temperature. The speed is nearly independent of frequency, so speech remains intelligible over distance. Dispersion is weak; an echo reproduces the original waveform with only minor distortion.

The human voice is produced by the vibration of the vocal folds. Air from the lungs passes through the glottis. The Bernoulli effect lowers the pressure when the folds approach, drawing them together; the pressure then rises and the folds separate. The cycle repeats at the fundamental frequency of the note. The vocal tract acts as a resonator that filters the harmonic spectrum, producing the formants that distinguish vowels.

The intensity range of the voice exceeds 80 dB. The frequency range of a trained singer can span more than five octaves. The same physical elements—energy source, oscillator, resonator, and radiator—appear in every musical instrument. The voice is distinguished by the continuous control the singer exerts over tension, airflow, and cavity shape.

Otoacoustic emissions confirm that the ear itself generates sound. The hair cells of the cochlea oscillate spontaneously. The emissions can be measured with sensitive microphones and are used to diagnose hearing without invasive procedures.

### Light

Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium. It reflects from a smooth surface so that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. It refracts when it passes from one medium to another. The change in direction is described by Snell’s law. Lenses use refraction to focus light. Convex lenses converge rays. Concave lenses diverge them. The eye, the camera, the microscope, and the telescope are all applications of these rules.

White light is a mixture of wavelengths. A prism separates them into a spectrum. Each element produces a characteristic set of spectral lines when heated or when light passes through its vapor. Those lines are the fingerprints used to identify elements in the laboratory and in stars. The Doppler shift of the lines measures motion toward or away from the observer.

Light turns out to be an electromagnetic wave, and it does not need a medium. The speed in vacuum is a constant, about 299,792 kilometers per second. Experiments designed to detect motion through a supposed ether, most famously the Michelson-Morley experiment, found no such effect. Special relativity took the constant speed of light as a postulate. Time and length are relative. Mass and energy are equivalent. The relation is E = mc<sup>2</sup>.

Light also behaves as particles, called photons. Each photon carries energy in proportion to its frequency. The photoelectric effect, in which light ejects electrons from a metal, is explained by that particle nature. The wave and particle pictures live together in the single framework of quantum mechanics.

Polarization, interference, and diffraction are wave effects. They are used in sunglasses, in holography, and in the measurement of molecular structure. The same light that carries information from distant galaxies also carries the signals in optical fibers. The physics is the same. The applications differ.

### Optics and Quantum Mechanics

Classical optics treats light as a wave. Interference, diffraction, and polarization follow from the wave equation. The speed in vacuum is c. In a medium it is c/n, where n is the refractive index. Lenses and mirrors redirect rays according to the law of reflection and Snell’s law of refraction. These rules are exact in the geometric-optics limit and are recovered as the short-wavelength limit of the wave theory.

Quantum mechanics assigns an amplitude to each path a photon can take. The probability is the square of the sum of the amplitudes. The same rule produces the interference pattern in a double-slit experiment when single photons are sent one at a time. The photon is detected at one place. The pattern builds from many detections. No trajectory is observed between source and detector. The calculation uses every path.

The photoelectric effect and Compton scattering show that light delivers energy and momentum in discrete quanta. The energy of a photon is E = hν. The momentum is E/c. These relations are confirmed by the threshold frequencies of photoemission and by the wavelength shift in Compton scattering. The wave and particle descriptions are complementary. Each is exact in its domain. Neither is complete alone.

Quantum electrodynamics unifies the two. The electromagnetic field is quantized. Photons are its quanta. Electrons interact by exchanging virtual photons. The theory reproduces classical optics in the appropriate limit and adds the quantum corrections measured in the Lamb shift and the anomalous magnetic moment. Optics is the classical limit of quantum electrodynamics. The underlying rules are quantum.

## <a id="ch_4"></a>4. Electricity, Magnetism and Fields

### Electricity and Magnetism

Electric charge comes in two kinds, called positive and negative. Like charges repel. Opposite charges attract. The force follows an inverse-square law, Coulomb’s law. Charge is conserved. It is quantized. The elementary unit is the charge of the electron or the proton.

A current is a flow of charge. In a metal wire the carriers are electrons. Resistance converts electrical energy into heat. Ohm’s law relates voltage, current, and resistance. Power is the product of voltage and current. Batteries convert chemical energy into electrical energy. Generators convert mechanical energy into electrical energy by moving conductors in magnetic fields.

Magnetism and electricity are two aspects of the same interaction. A moving charge produces a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field drives an electric one. Oersted showed that a current deflects a compass needle. Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field induces a current. Maxwell unified the two in a set of equations. Those equations predict that a changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field, and vice versa, and that the disturbance propagates as a wave at the speed of light. Light is that wave.

The Earth is a magnet. Its field is generated by motions in the liquid outer core. Over geological time it flips polarity at irregular intervals. It deflects much of the solar wind away from the surface. Compasses align with it. Birds and other animals use it for navigation.

Transformers change voltage by electromagnetic induction. Motors convert electrical energy into mechanical energy. The entire electrical grid rests on these principles. Alternating current is used for transmission because transformers can step the voltage up for long distances and down for use. Direct current is used in electronics and in some long-distance lines. The underlying physics is the same.

Semiconductors control the flow of charge with small signals. Transistors, diodes, and integrated circuits are built from them. The electronics of a computer and the power system of a city are different scales of the same electromagnetic interaction.

### Maxwell’s Equations

James Clerk Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism in 1865. He did this without the aid of a committee, which may explain why it worked. The four equations that bear his name describe all classical electromagnetic phenomena. They also predict that light is an electromagnetic wave, a result that was considered rather sporting of them.

The first equation is Gauss’s law for electricity. The flux of the electric field through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by the permittivity of free space. In differential form it states that the divergence of the electric field is proportional to the charge density. Charge is the source of the electric field. There are no magnetic monopoles. The corresponding equation for the magnetic field states that the flux of the magnetic field through any closed surface is zero. The divergence of the magnetic field is zero. Magnetic field lines form closed loops.

Faraday’s law states that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an electromotive force. In differential form the curl of the electric field equals the negative of the rate of change of the magnetic field. A changing magnetic field produces an electric field. The direction is given by Lenz’s law: the induced field opposes the change that produces it.

Ampère’s law, as corrected by Maxwell, states that the curl of the magnetic field is proportional to the total current density plus the displacement current. The displacement current is the term Maxwell added: the rate of change of the electric field. The reverse also holds: a changing electric field produces a magnetic field. The two fields can sustain each other.

In free space, with no charges or currents, the equations combine to give wave equations for both fields. The waves travel at the speed c = 1/√(μ<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>0</sub>). That speed matches the measured speed of light. Light is an electromagnetic wave. The same equations describe radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. They differ from one another only in frequency.

The equations are linear. Solutions can be superposed. They are also Lorentz invariant. The same equations hold in every inertial frame when the fields are transformed correctly. That invariance was one of the clues that led to special relativity. The classical theory is complete within its domain. It fails at the quantum level, where the field is quantized and the photon appears, and it fails at the Planck scale, where gravity cannot be ignored. Within the domain of classical electromagnetism the equations remain exact.

### The Electromagnetic Field

In the field picture the electromagnetic interaction is carried by two vector fields, the electric field E and the magnetic field B, defined at every point of space and time. Charges are their sources, and Maxwell’s equations tie the fields to the charges and to each other.

The energy density of the field is proportional to E<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup> B<sup>2</sup>. The momentum density is proportional to the Poynting vector E × B. Both quantities are conserved when the field interacts with charges, provided the mechanical energy and momentum of the charges are included. The field therefore carries energy and momentum exactly as a wave must.

The Lorentz force law gives the force on a charge moving in the field. Together with Maxwell’s equations it constitutes the classical theory of electromagnetism. The theory is accurate from the scale of atoms to the scale of galaxies whenever quantum effects and gravitational curvature can be neglected.

### Collective Electrodynamics

Carver Mead has argued that the electromagnetic field can be understood as a consequence of the quantum phase of charged particles rather than as an independent entity. In this view the vector potential is the fundamental object. It sets the phase standard for the electrons. The electric and magnetic fields are derived quantities.

The starting point is the phase of the electron wave function. A charged particle moving in a potential acquires a phase proportional to the line integral of the vector potential. When many electrons share a common phase, as they do in a superconductor, the collective phase is a macroscopic observable. The supercurrent is proportional to the gradient of that phase. The magnetic field is related to the curl of the potential, and the quantization of flux follows from the requirement that the phase be single-valued around a closed loop.

From the collective behavior one can recover Maxwell’s equations. The electric field appears as the force that changes the momentum, and the magnetic field appears as the quantity whose flux is quantized. The energy and momentum stored in the fields can be expressed in terms of the potentials and the charges. The classical fields are the large-scale description of the underlying phase relationships.

The approach does not replace quantum electrodynamics. It offers a different route to the same classical limit, beginning from the quantum mechanics of the charges rather than from the fields. It makes the Aharonov–Bohm effect and the Josephson effect natural rather than surprising, because both are direct statements about phase. It also clarifies why the potentials, which are gauge-dependent, can still have physical consequences: the gauge-invariant phase differences are what the charges measure.

The account is consistent with experiment. It does not alter any tested prediction of classical electromagnetism or of QED. It changes the order of explanation. The fields are what the charges do, collectively, when their phases are taken into account. Whether this order is more fundamental is a question of interpretation. The mathematics and the measurements remain the same.

### The Aharonov–Bohm Effect

A magnetic field can affect an electron that never enters the region where the field is nonzero. In the Aharonov–Bohm effect an electron beam is split, passed on either side of a long solenoid, and recombined. The magnetic field is confined inside the solenoid. Outside, the field is zero. The vector potential is not zero. The relative phase between the two paths depends on the magnetic flux through the solenoid. The interference pattern shifts when the flux is changed. The shift has been measured with the field completely shielded from the electrons.

The effect shows that the vector potential has physical consequences in quantum mechanics even where the field vanishes. In classical mechanics only the fields appear in the force law. In quantum mechanics the phase of the wave function depends on the line integral of the potential. The phase is gauge-dependent, but the phase difference around a closed loop is gauge-invariant and equal to the enclosed flux in appropriate units. The effect is topological. It depends on the flux, not on the local field along the path.

The same principle appears in superconducting rings. A superconducting loop encloses flux in discrete quanta. The quantization follows from the requirement that the macroscopic wave function be single-valued. The Aharonov–Bohm phase is the underlying mechanism. The effect has been observed with electrons, with neutrons, and in solid-state devices. It is a direct demonstration that the electromagnetic potentials are not merely a mathematical convenience.

### The Vacuum

Empty space is not empty. Quantum field theory assigns a zero-point energy to every mode of every field. The energy of a harmonic oscillator in its ground state is 1/2 ħ ω. Summing over all modes gives a formally infinite vacuum energy. A cutoff at the Planck scale produces a density many orders of magnitude larger than the observed cosmological constant.

The Casimir effect, taken up below, shows that vacuum energy has measurable consequences. What it measures is a difference in vacuum energy between two arrangements, not the absolute value, which no experiment of this kind can reach.

Measured from the acceleration of the cosmic expansion, the vacuum energy density is about 10<sup>−9</sup> joules per cubic meter. The naive quantum-field estimate exceeds it by up to 120 orders of magnitude. That mismatch is the cosmological-constant problem of [Chapter 33](#ch_33).

The vacuum also fluctuates. Virtual particle pairs appear and disappear. They contribute to the Lamb shift, to the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron, and to the running of coupling constants. Those effects are calculated and measured to high precision. The vacuum is therefore both the source of the most precise predictions in physics and the source of the largest discrepancy between theory and observation. The two facts coexist. The resolution is not yet known.

### The Casimir Effect

The Casimir effect is a force between uncharged conducting plates that arises from the modification of the vacuum modes of the electromagnetic field. Between the plates the boundary conditions exclude modes whose wavelengths do not fit. The resulting difference in zero-point energy produces an attractive force per unit area F/A = -(π<sup>2</sup>ħ c)/(240 d<sup>4</sup>) for perfect conductors separated by distance d.

The effect is a macroscopic manifestation of vacuum fluctuations. The same mode-modification principle appears in other geometries and for other fields. The Casimir effect confirms that boundary conditions alter the vacuum energy of quantum fields.

The Casimir force has been measured between a sphere and a plate and between two plates. The force is attractive for perfect conductors. For real metals it is reduced by finite conductivity and by surface roughness. Temperature corrections become important at separations greater than a micrometer. The measurements agree with theory once these corrections are included.

The effect can be repulsive for certain combinations of materials and intervening fluids. The repulsion has been observed. It does not permit extraction of energy from the vacuum. The plates must still be separated by external work. The force is a consequence of the change in vacuum mode density. It is not a source of free energy.

# <a id="part_2"></a>Part II: The Quantum World

*The rules of the very small, and what they let us build*

## <a id="ch_5"></a>5. Quantum Rules and Quantum Matter

Quantum mechanics is the rule book for atoms, light and everything built from them. Its rules are few, strange, and better tested than any others in science. This chapter states them, then shows them at work in matter that is cold enough, or clean enough, for quantum behavior to become visible on a large scale.

Energy comes in lumps. In 1900 Max Planck explained the spectrum of glowing bodies by assuming that light is emitted in packets of energy E = hν, where ν is the frequency and h is Planck’s constant, about 6.6 × 10<sup>−34</sup> joule-seconds. In 1905 Einstein showed that light also arrives in such packets, photons, which is why the photoelectric effect has a sharp frequency threshold.

Matter has waves too. In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed that a particle of momentum p has a wavelength h/p, and electron beams were soon seen to diffract from crystals. In a double-slit experiment, electrons or photons sent one at a time each arrive at a single spot, yet the spots build up an interference pattern. Neither “particle” nor “wave” alone describes that behavior.

The theory describes a system by a wave function: a set of complex numbers, called amplitudes, one for each possible outcome. The Schrödinger equation fixes how the wave function changes in time, smoothly and deterministically. When a measurement is made, the probability of an outcome is the squared magnitude of its amplitude (the Born rule). Amplitudes add before they are squared, and that is where interference comes from.

A system can be in a superposition of states that would exclude each other in classical physics, and two or more systems can share a joint state that cannot be split into separate descriptions. That is entanglement, the subject of [Chapter 7](#ch_7). Some pairs of quantities cannot both be sharp at once. For position and momentum the limit is Heisenberg’s uncertainty relation, Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2, with ħ = h/2π. It is a property of waves, not a defect of instruments, and it sets the size of atoms ([Chapter 15](#ch_15)).

Particles also carry spin, an intrinsic angular momentum that comes in whole or half multiples of ħ. Fermions, with half-integer spin, obey the Pauli exclusion principle: no two can share a state, which gives atoms their shells and makes matter solid. Bosons, with integer spin, crowd into the same state. The sections below follow that crowding into Bose–Einstein condensates, superconductors and lasers, and then into newer quantum phases. What a measurement actually is, and how the classical world emerges, is left to [Chapter 6](#ch_6).

### Bose–Einstein Condensates

A Bose–Einstein condensate is a state of matter in which a macroscopic number of bosons occupy the same quantum state. It forms when a dilute gas of bosonic atoms is cooled below a critical temperature, typically a few hundred nanokelvin. The transition is marked by the appearance of a macroscopic wave function and by a peak in the momentum distribution at zero momentum.

The condensate is described by the Gross–Pitaevskii equation, a nonlinear Schrödinger equation that includes the mean-field interaction. Experiments have demonstrated matter-wave interference, quantized vortices, superfluidity and the suppression of inelastic collisions. Condensates of photons, polaritons and magnons have also been realized. The state provides a controllable macroscopic quantum system. It is used to simulate condensed-matter models, to perform precision interferometry and to study the crossover between quantum and classical behavior.

The critical temperature for Bose–Einstein condensation in a dilute gas scales as the density to the two-thirds power and as the inverse of the atomic mass. Evaporative cooling in magnetic or optical traps reaches that range. The condensate fraction grows as the temperature is lowered further.

Interactions are characterized by the s-wave scattering length. The scattering length can be tuned with magnetic Feshbach resonances. Attractive interactions produce collapse above a critical atom number. Repulsive interactions stabilize the condensate and permit the observation of sound waves, solitons and quantized vortices. The same systems realize analog models of black-hole horizons and of cosmological particle creation. The laboratory control is precise. The underlying quantum statistics are those of ideal bosons modified by weak interactions.

### Superconductivity

Below a critical temperature some materials conduct electricity with zero resistance. A current in a superconducting loop persists for years without measurable decay. The material also expels magnetic fields, the Meissner effect. The transition is sharp. It is a phase transition.

The microscopic theory is the BCS theory. Electrons near the Fermi surface form pairs, Cooper pairs, bound by an attractive interaction mediated by lattice vibrations. The pairs are bosons. They condense into a single macroscopic quantum state. The condensate has a well-defined phase. The phase is coherent across the sample. Scattering that would produce resistance in a normal metal cannot occur without breaking pairs, and the energy cost is finite. The resistance is zero.

A junction between two superconductors separated by a thin insulator allows a supercurrent to flow with no voltage, the Josephson effect. The current depends on the phase difference across the junction. An applied voltage produces an alternating current at a frequency proportional to the voltage. The constant of proportionality is 2e/h. The relation is exact and is used to define the volt. Magnetic flux through a superconducting ring is quantized in units of h/2e, the factor of 2 reflecting that the carriers are pairs. The quantization is observed.

High-temperature superconductors, discovered in 1986, become superconducting at temperatures above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen. Their mechanism is not fully understood. The conventional BCS theory does not account for them. They are used in magnets, in sensors, and in some power applications. The zero-resistance state and the flux quantization remain the defining experimental signatures. Both follow from the existence of a macroscopic coherent phase.

The Meissner effect is the expulsion of magnetic flux from the interior of a superconductor. It is distinct from perfect conductivity. A perfect conductor would freeze in the flux present when it became resistanceless. A superconductor actively expels flux. The expulsion is a thermodynamic equilibrium property.

Type-I superconductors expel flux completely below a critical field and then revert to the normal state. Type-II superconductors allow flux to penetrate in quantized vortices above a lower critical field. The vortices form a lattice. The mixed state persists until an upper critical field. High-temperature superconductors are extreme type-II materials. Their upper critical fields are high. The vortex lattice and its pinning determine the critical current. Both the Meissner effect and the vortex state are macroscopic quantum phenomena.

### Time Crystals

A time crystal is a quantum system that spontaneously breaks time-translation symmetry. In its simplest realization a periodically driven many-body system develops a response that oscillates at a subharmonic of the drive frequency. The subharmonic motion persists indefinitely in the idealized limit and is protected by many-body localization or by other mechanisms that prevent heating to infinite temperature.

Laboratory realizations have been achieved with trapped ions, nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, and superconducting qubits. The observed oscillations match the predicted subharmonic response and are robust against small perturbations. The systems are not perpetual-motion machines. They are driven. The novelty is the spontaneous breaking of the discrete time symmetry of the drive.

Time crystals enlarge the catalog of possible phases of matter. They demonstrate that quantum systems can exhibit order in the time domain analogous to spatial crystallinity. Their practical utility is still exploratory. Their existence shows that the symmetry principles governing phases of matter extend to the temporal domain.

### Topological Phases of Matter

Topological phases are quantum states of matter whose distinguishing properties are invariant under continuous deformations of the Hamiltonian. The integer quantum Hall effect is the classic example. The Hall conductance is quantized in units of e<sup>2</sup>/h and is determined by a topological invariant—the Chern number—rather than by material details.

Topological insulators possess conducting surface states that are protected by time-reversal symmetry. The surface states are helical: spin and momentum are locked. Backscattering is suppressed. Superconducting analogs—topological superconductors—can host Majorana zero modes at defects. The modes obey non-Abelian statistics and are candidates for fault-tolerant qubits.

The classification of topological phases uses symmetry and dimensionality. Interactions and disorder modify but do not erase the topological distinction in the simplest cases. Experimental realizations include quantum-Hall systems, topological insulators, and engineered superconducting structures. The phases enlarge the set of possible electronic states beyond the conventional band-insulator and metal dichotomy. Their protected boundary modes are robust against local perturbations.

The Chern number is an integer topological invariant of a filled band. The invariant is unchanged by continuous deformations of the Hamiltonian that do not close the gap. Disorder that preserves the gap does not destroy the quantization. The robustness is topological.

Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators are characterized by a Z<sub>2</sub> invariant. The invariant protects an odd number of helical surface states. Magnetic impurities that break time-reversal symmetry can gap the surface. Non-magnetic disorder cannot. The protection has been observed in transport and in photoemission. The same topological classification extends to superconductors and to interacting systems. The invariants organize the phases. They do not by themselves determine the material realization.

### Quantum Optics

Quantum optics studies the quantum properties of light and its interaction with matter at the level of individual photons and atoms. A single-photon source emits one photon at a time. A single-photon detector registers that photon with high efficiency. Interference of single photons in a Mach–Zehnder interferometer demonstrates that the photon takes both paths when no which-path information is available.

Cavity quantum electrodynamics couples an atom to a high-finesse optical cavity. The coupling strength can exceed the decay rates, producing reversible exchange of excitation—vacuum Rabi oscillations. The same regime allows deterministic generation of entangled atom–photon states and the realization of quantum gates between distant atoms mediated by photons.

Squeezed light has reduced noise in one quadrature at the expense of increased noise in the conjugate quadrature. It improves the sensitivity of interferometers beyond the standard quantum limit and is used in gravitational-wave detectors. Photon antibunching and Bell tests with photons are routine. Quantum optics supplies both the experimental foundation of quantum information and a precision tool for metrology.

The Hong–Ou–Mandel effect is the interference of two identical photons at a beam splitter. When the photons arrive simultaneously they exit together in the same output port. The coincidence rate drops to zero. The dip is a direct signature of bosonic exchange symmetry. It is used to characterize single-photon sources and to implement linear-optical quantum gates.

Light comes in kinds that differ in their photon statistics. A coherent state from a laser has Poissonian photon counts. A single-photon Fock state has exactly one photon. Squeezed vacuum emits photons in correlated pairs. Photon counting and homodyne detection tell them apart, and each kind has its use, from quantum cryptography to the quantum-noise reduction in gravitational-wave detectors mentioned above.

## <a id="ch_6"></a>6. Measurement, Decoherence and Interpretations

### The Measurement Problem

The measurement problem is the question of how a definite outcome emerges from a quantum superposition. The Schrödinger equation is linear and deterministic, so it never picks a single result on its own. The Born rule gives probabilities. It does not describe the occurrence of a single result. Collapse postulates add the selection by hand. They are not derived from the unitary dynamics.

Decoherence explains the suppression of interference. It does not explain the occurrence of one outcome rather than another. Many-worlds interpretations deny that a selection occurs. Bohmian mechanics adds particle positions. Objective-collapse models modify the equation. None is established. The problem is the gap between the unitary formalism and the definite events of experience. The gap remains open.

### Decoherence

A quantum system that interacts with its environment becomes entangled with the environment. The reduced state of the system, obtained by tracing over the environmental degrees of freedom, loses the off-diagonal terms that encode interference. The process is decoherence. It occurs rapidly for macroscopic objects. A dust grain in air decoheres in a time far shorter than any practical observation. Interference between macroscopically distinct positions becomes unobservable. The basis in which interference disappears, the pointer basis, is selected by the form of the interaction, and for macroscopic objects it is approximately the position basis. The resulting diagonal density matrix looks like ignorance about which outcome occurred, but it is an improper mixture, not a definite result.

Decoherence does not destroy the global superposition. The full state of system plus environment remains pure if it began pure. The local description of the system alone becomes mixed. Interference terms are still present in the global state. They are dispersed into correlations with the environment and cannot be recovered without measuring the environment in a precisely controlled way. For ordinary environments that control is impossible.

The process explains why macroscopic superpositions are not seen. It does not by itself select one outcome. The global state still contains every branch. Decoherence makes the branches effectively independent. It supplies the physical reason that the measurement problem is invisible in practice. It does not solve the problem of why one branch is experienced. That question remains interpretation-dependent.

Decoherence rates have been calculated and measured for systems ranging from single ions to superconducting circuits. The agreement is quantitative. The phenomenon is established. Its implications for the ontology of quantum mechanics are not.

### The Quantum-to-Classical Transition

The quantum-to-classical transition is the emergence of classical behavior from quantum mechanics. Treating the decohered state as a classical mixture is adequate for prediction and incomplete for ontology.

The transition is continuous. Mesoscopic systems display partial coherence. The degree of classicality increases with the separation of the components and with the strength of the environmental interaction. No sharp boundary exists. The transition is well-described by decoherence for all practical purposes. The residual conceptual questions are those of the measurement problem. They are not resolved by the practical success.

### Worked Examples: Quantum Measurement

Example 1. A spin-1/2 particle is prepared in the state (|↑⟩ + |↓⟩)/√2. What are the probabilities of measuring spin up or spin down along the z-axis?

Each probability is |1/√2|<sup>2</sup> = 1/2.

Example 2. The same particle is measured and found to be up. It is then measured again immediately along the same axis. What is the outcome?

The second measurement yields up with certainty. The state has collapsed to |↑⟩.

Example 3. An electron is confined to a one-dimensional box of width 0.1 nm. What is the minimum uncertainty in its momentum? What kinetic energy does that imply?

Δ x ≈ 0.1 nm. Δ p ≥ ħ/(2Δ x) ≈ 5 × 10<sup>−25</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup>. E ≥ (Δ p)<sup>2</sup>/(2m) ≈ 1 eV. The estimate matches the order of magnitude of atomic energy levels.

Example 4. A radioactive nucleus has a half-life of 1 hour. What is the probability that it decays in the next minute?

Decay constant λ = ln 2 / T<sub>1/2</sub>. Probability in time t ≪ T<sub>1/2</sub> is ≈ λ t = 0.0115.

The calculations illustrate the Born rule, state reduction, the uncertainty principle and exponential decay—the operational content of quantum measurement.

### Many-Worlds Interpretation

As an answer to the measurement problem, many-worlds says that nothing needs answering. The universal wave function never collapses; apparent collapse is the branching of the wave function into components that no longer interfere, and observers are branched along with everything else.

The full account, with its difficulty over the origin of probabilities, appears in the discussion of the multiverse. What matters here is the comparison with the other options.
