This interpretation adds no postulates and no new dynamics, it is not experimentally distinguishable from collapse models in which the collapse is irreversible and the branches do not interfere, and its price is ontological: the reality of every unobserved branch.

### Bohmian Mechanics

Bohmian mechanics supplements the wave function with particle positions. The positions evolve according to a guidance equation determined by the wave function. The wave function itself evolves by the Schrödinger equation. The particles have definite positions at all times. The apparent randomness arises from ignorance of the initial positions.

The theory reproduces the Born-rule statistics for a particular distribution of initial positions. The distribution is preserved by the dynamics. The theory is deterministic and non-local. The non-locality is required by Bell’s theorem. It does not permit signaling. The theory is empirically equivalent to standard quantum mechanics. Its advantage is ontological clarity. Its cost is the addition of unobservable trajectories and the explicit non-locality.

### Objective Collapse Models

Objective collapse models modify the Schrödinger equation so that superpositions of macroscopically distinct states decay spontaneously. The collapse is a physical process. It occurs with a rate that increases with the number of particles. Microscopic systems are essentially unaffected. Macroscopic superpositions collapse rapidly.

The models predict deviations from standard quantum mechanics. The deviations are small. They are constrained by matter-wave interferometry and by the absence of anomalous heating. No deviation has been observed. The models solve the measurement problem by altering the dynamics. They introduce new parameters. The parameters are bounded but not excluded. The models remain possible extensions.

### Quantum Darwinism

Quantum Darwinism proposes that the classical world emerges through the redundant encoding of information in the environment. Pointer states are those that survive decoherence and proliferate their information. Observers who access fragments of the environment obtain the same information. The redundancy defines objectivity.

The proposal accounts for the preferred basis and for the agreement among observers. It does not select a single outcome. All pointer states are encoded. The appearance of a single outcome still requires an interpretation of the branching or an additional postulate. The framework is consistent with decoherence. It extends it by emphasizing redundancy. It remains an account of classicality, not a solution to the measurement problem.

### Consistent Histories

The consistent-histories approach assigns probabilities to sets of histories that satisfy a consistency condition. The condition ensures that the probabilities obey the classical sum rules. Inconsistent sets do not receive probabilities. The approach avoids explicit collapse. It requires the selection of a consistent set. The selection is not given by the formalism.

Different consistent sets can be incompatible. The approach does not privilege one. It therefore does not explain why one set of events is experienced. It supplies a framework in which classical reasoning can be applied to quantum systems. The framework is mathematically precise. The physical interpretation of the multiplicity of sets remains open.

### Relational Quantum Mechanics

Relational quantum mechanics asserts that the quantum state of a system is relative to another system. There is no absolute state. Events are interactions. The state is the information that one system has about another. The approach dissolves the measurement problem by denying the existence of an observer-independent state.

The approach is consistent with the predictions of quantum mechanics. It requires care in the treatment of sequences of measurements. It does not add dynamical postulates. Its cost is the abandonment of an absolute quantum state. The cost is accepted by its proponents as the price of consistency. The approach remains a minority interpretation.

### Quantum Bayesianism

Quantum Bayesianism interprets the quantum state as an agent’s information or degrees of belief. The state is not a property of the system. It is a property of the agent. Measurement updates the agent’s beliefs. The approach avoids ontological questions about collapse. It relocates the state to the agent.

The approach reproduces the operational predictions. It must explain why agents who communicate agree. The explanation relies on the common information acquired through interaction. The approach is operationally clear. Its metaphysical claim—that the state is not ontic—is disputed. The dispute does not affect the calculations. It affects the interpretation of what the calculations describe.

## <a id="ch_7"></a>7. Entanglement and Bell’s Theorem

### The Inequality That Cannot Be Satisfied

In 1964 John Bell wrote an inequality that any local hidden-variable theory must obey. Quantum mechanics predicts that the inequality can be violated. The prediction was tested. It was violated. The violation has been confirmed with photons, atoms, ions and superconducting circuits. The loopholes have been closed. The inequality is not satisfied.

The result does not permit faster-than-light signaling, but it does rule out outcomes fixed in advance by local variables. The correlations are stronger than any local mechanism can produce. The first tests were delicate; the latest are conclusive, and versions of them are now teaching-laboratory demonstrations. Local realism, the joint assumption that outcomes are predetermined and that no influence travels faster than light, is false, and the falsity is measured.

### Bell’s Theorem and the Experiments

In 1935 Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen argued that quantum mechanics is incomplete. They considered two particles that have interacted and then separated. A measurement on one instantly determines the result of a corresponding measurement on the other. If the particles have definite properties all along, the correlation is ordinary. If they do not, the theory appears to require a nonlocal influence. Einstein called the second possibility spooky.

Experiments beginning in the 1970s and culminating in the work of Aspect, Dalibard, and Roger in 1982 measured the correlations with polarizers whose settings were changed while the particles were in flight. The results matched the quantum prediction and violated the Bell inequality. Later experiments closed the main loopholes: the detection loophole, the locality loophole, and the freedom-of-choice loophole. Three loophole-free tests in 2015 settled the matter, and Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics for the experiments.

The experiments rule out local hidden-variable theories but do not select among the remaining interpretations ([Chapter 6](#ch_6)). Each side’s outcomes stay random; only the joint statistics show the violation, which is why no signal can be sent. The same resource drives quantum teleportation ([Chapter 8](#ch_8)).

The theorem and the experiments fix one boundary. Any complete account of the correlations must abandon either locality or the assumption that the outcomes are determined by preexisting local variables, or both. The boundary is experimental.

### How the Inequality Works

Two particles are prepared in an entangled state and sent to distant observers. Each observer chooses a measurement setting and records a binary outcome. A local hidden-variable theory assumes that the outcomes are predetermined by variables carried with the particles and that each observer’s result depends only on the local setting and on those shared variables. Under this assumption the correlations obey an inequality. One standard form (CHSH) states that a certain combination of four correlation functions cannot exceed 2 in absolute value.

Quantum mechanics predicts a larger value. For the spin singlet the correlation is minus the cosine of the angle between the analysers. Suitable choices of angle yield 2√2 ≈ 2.828. The quantum prediction therefore lies outside the bound required by local hidden variables.

### Entanglement as a Resource

Quantum entanglement is a correlation between subsystems that no assignment of pre-existing local properties can reproduce. For two spin-1/2 particles in the singlet state, spin measurements along the same axis are perfectly anti-correlated; along axes at an angle θ the correlation is −cos θ. The same resource powers quantum teleportation, super-dense coding and device-independent cryptography, so entanglement is both a foundational feature of quantum mechanics and a practical tool.

Entanglement is monogamous. A system maximally entangled with one partner cannot be entangled with a third. The monogamy relation is quantitative. It bounds the sum of the squared concurrences. The bound is saturated by the singlet and by GHZ states in appropriate limits.

Entanglement can be distilled. From many weakly entangled pairs one can extract a smaller number of nearly maximally entangled pairs by local operations and classical communication. The reverse process—entanglement dilution—converts maximally entangled pairs into a larger number of weakly entangled pairs. The two processes define the entanglement of formation and the distillable entanglement. For pure bipartite states the two measures coincide. For mixed states they may differ. The difference is a signature of bound entanglement that cannot be distilled.

### Worked Examples: Quantum Entanglement

Example 1. The singlet state of two spin-1/2 particles is |ψ⟩ = 1/(√2)(|↑↓⟩ − |↓↑⟩). What is the probability that both particles give the same result when measured along the same axis?

The probability is zero. The outcomes are perfectly anti-correlated.

Example 2. The same state is measured with the two analysers at a relative angle θ. What is the probability that the outcomes differ?

The probability is cos <sup>2</sup>(θ/2). For θ = 0 the probability is 1 (always different). For θ = 120<sup>°</sup> the probability is 1/4. Combined at suitable angles, correlations of this form violate the Bell inequality that any local hidden-variable theory must satisfy.

Example 3. An entangled photon pair is produced in the state 1/(√2)(|HH⟩ + |VV⟩). One photon is measured in the diagonal basis and found to be D. What is the state of the other photon?

The other photon is immediately in the state D. The measurement has projected the joint state.

Example 4. Two parties share a singlet. Alice measures her spin along z and obtains ↑. She tells Bob the result by ordinary communication. What can Bob conclude about his own spin?

Bob knows his spin is ↓ along z. He cannot use the information to send a signal faster than light, because Alice’s outcome is random. The correlations appear only after the results are compared.

These examples recover the perfect anti-correlations, the angular dependence that violates Bell inequalities, the instantaneous update of the joint state, and the no-communication theorem—the operational content of entanglement.

### The Free Will Theorem

The free will theorem of Conway and Kochen states that if experimenters have freedom in the choice of measurement settings, then the responses of entangled particles are not determined by prior information. The theorem assumes the quantum predictions and a locality condition. It concludes that the particles’ responses are not functions of the past.

The theorem is a variant of Bell’s theorem. It emphasizes the freedom of the experimenter. The freedom is the assumption that the settings are not correlated with the hidden variables. The assumption is necessary for the derivation. It is not proven. The theorem sharpens the conflict between determinism, locality and the quantum predictions. It does not resolve it.

### Leggett–Garg Inequalities

Leggett–Garg inequalities bound the correlations of measurements performed on a single system at different times. They assume macroscopic realism and non-invasive measurability. Quantum mechanics violates the inequalities. The violations have been observed in superconducting qubits, photons and other systems.

The inequalities test the applicability of classical realism to macroscopic objects. Their violation shows that the systems do not possess pre-existing values that are merely revealed by measurement. The tests are complementary to Bell tests. They probe temporal rather than spatial correlations. The violations confirm the quantum predictions for the systems examined. They do not yet extend to everyday macroscopic objects.

### Contextuality

Contextuality is the dependence of measurement outcomes on the set of compatible measurements performed together. The Kochen–Specker theorem shows that no non-contextual hidden-variable theory can reproduce the predictions of quantum mechanics in Hilbert spaces of dimension greater than two. The theorem is state-independent.

Contextuality is a feature of the quantum formalism. It has been demonstrated in experiments with photons, neutrons and ions. It is a resource for quantum computation. Certain computational advantages require contextuality. The phenomenon is distinct from non-locality. It appears in single systems. It is a fundamental obstruction to classical simulations of quantum mechanics.

### Quantum Steering

Quantum steering is the ability of one party to influence the state of a distant party by choice of measurement. It is intermediate between entanglement and Bell non-locality. Not all entangled states are steerable. All Bell-nonlocal states are steerable. Steering can be verified with one trusted and one untrusted party.

The phenomenon has been demonstrated experimentally. It is a resource for one-sided device-independent cryptography. The hierarchy—entanglement, steering, Bell non-locality—organizes the strengths of quantum correlation. Each level excludes a larger set of classical models. Steering is the intermediate level. It is both theoretically sharp and experimentally accessible.

### Device-Independent Quantum Information

Device-independent protocols rely only on the observed correlations. They do not require characterization of the devices. Security is certified by the violation of a Bell inequality. The certification is independent of the internal workings of the apparatus. Quantum key distribution and random-number generation have been implemented in the device-independent setting.

The implementations require high-efficiency detection and space-like separation. Both have been achieved. The rates are low. The principle is established. Practical deployment awaits higher rates and longer distances. The approach eliminates side-channel attacks that exploit imperfect device characterization. It replaces them with the requirement of a loophole-free Bell violation.

## <a id="ch_8"></a>8. Quantum Information and Computation

A classical computer stores bits, each a zero or a one. A quantum computer stores qubits, which can be placed in combinations of zero and one, and entangled with one another. The point is not that a qubit holds both values in a way you can read out. A measurement still yields a zero or a one. The point is that the computation can explore amplitudes, and amplitudes can cancel.

The advantage of a quantum computer is interference. Amplitudes for wrong answers cancel. Amplitudes for right answers add. For this to help, the problem must have a structure that an algorithm can exploit. Factoring has such a structure, which is why Shor’s algorithm matters to cryptography. Searching an unstructured list has less, which is why Grover’s algorithm offers only a square-root speedup. Simulating a quantum system has the structure by definition, which is why chemistry and materials are the applications scientists emphasize.

### No-Cloning and Quantum Information

An unknown quantum state cannot be copied. Suppose a machine takes a system in an arbitrary state and produces two systems in that same state, while leaving the original unchanged. The linearity of quantum mechanics forbids it. If the machine works for two orthogonal states, it fails for their superposition. The proof is short, and the result is called the no-cloning theorem.

The theorem has practical consequences. It prevents the use of quantum states as ordinary classical bits that can be duplicated and checked. It is the reason quantum key distribution can detect eavesdropping. Any attempt to measure or copy the quantum signals disturbs them in a way that the legitimate parties can observe. It also limits what a quantum computer can do with an unknown state. The state can be teleported if the original is destroyed, but it cannot be cloned.

The theorem does not forbid copying known states or classical information; it forbids only the perfect copying of unknown quantum states. Approximate cloning is possible, with a fidelity that is bounded and too low to evade the security proofs of key distribution. The restriction is both a limitation and a resource.

Quantum information is carried by qubits. A qubit can be in a superposition of two states. Two qubits can be entangled. The joint state cannot be written as a product of individual states. Measurement of one qubit instantly correlates with the measurement of the other, regardless of distance. The correlation does not allow faster-than-light signaling. The outcomes are random. Only when the results are compared does the correlation appear. Entanglement is a resource for computation and for communication. It is also the feature that makes the measurement problem sharp. The linear evolution produces superpositions. The observed world contains definite outcomes. How the transition occurs is not settled by the formalism.

The no-cloning theorem, entanglement, and the limits on signaling are established. They follow from the linearity and the tensor-product structure of quantum mechanics. They constrain every interpretation and every proposed application.

### Quantum Key Distribution

Quantum key distribution allows two parties to generate a shared secret key. Security rests on the no-cloning theorem and on the disturbance caused by measurement. The BB84 protocol uses four polarization states. The E91 protocol uses entangled pairs and Bell violation. Both have been implemented over optical fibre and free space.

The secret-key rate decreases with distance because of loss and noise. Quantum repeaters are required for global distances. Prototype repeaters exist. They are not yet practical. The security proofs assume ideal devices or are device-independent. Real devices introduce side channels. Countermeasures exist. The protocols are information-theoretically secure under the stated assumptions. The assumptions must be enforced in practice.

### Quantum Teleportation

Quantum teleportation transfers an unknown quantum state from one system to another using a shared entangled pair and classical communication. The sender performs a joint measurement. The receiver applies a correction conditioned on the classical result. The state is destroyed at the sender and recreated at the receiver. No information is transmitted faster than light.

Teleportation has been demonstrated with photons, atoms, ions and superconducting circuits. It is a primitive for quantum networks and for measurement-based computation. The fidelity is limited by the quality of the entanglement and by the accuracy of the operations. High-fidelity teleportation over laboratory distances is routine. Extension to long distances requires quantum repeaters. The protocol is both a fundamental demonstration and a practical tool.

### Quantum Networks

A quantum network distributes entanglement and transmits quantum states among multiple nodes. The nodes are quantum processors or memories. The links are photonic channels. Quantum repeaters extend the range by entanglement swapping and purification. The network enables distributed quantum computation, blind quantum computation and long-distance key distribution.

Prototype networks with a few nodes exist. They demonstrate entanglement distribution and teleportation. Scaling to many nodes requires memories with long coherence times, high-efficiency interfaces, and error correction. The requirements are engineering challenges. The architectural principles are established. The network is the quantum analog of the classical internet. It does not yet exist at comparable scale.

### Quantum Computing

A quantum computer stores information in qubits. A qubit is a two-level quantum system that can exist in a superposition of its basis states. An n-qubit register can therefore occupy a superposition of all 2<sup>n</sup> classical bit strings simultaneously.

Entanglement and interference allow certain algorithms to extract global properties of a function with fewer queries than any classical algorithm. Shor’s algorithm factors large integers in polynomial time by finding the period of a modular exponential function. Grover’s algorithm searches an unstructured database of N items in roughly √N steps. Both rely on the coherent evolution of superpositions and on a final measurement that yields the desired result with high probability.

The practical obstacles are decoherence and gate errors. Interaction with the environment destroys the relative phases that encode the computation. Quantum error-correcting codes spread the logical information across many physical qubits so that local errors can be detected and reversed without measuring the logical state. Fault-tolerant thresholds exist: if the physical error rate lies below a few parts in 10<sup>3</sup> to 10<sup>4</sup>, arbitrarily long computations are possible in principle.

Present devices contain tens to a few hundred qubits and execute circuits of limited depth. They have demonstrated small instances of quantum advantage on specially chosen sampling tasks. They have not yet run Shor’s algorithm on integers large enough to threaten cryptographic systems. The gap between the theoretical algorithms and large-scale, error-corrected machines remains the central engineering problem.

The computational model does not violate the Church–Turing thesis in its modern form. It supplies a different complexity scaling for particular problems. The scaling originates in the same interference of amplitudes that appears in every other quantum experiment.

### Quantum Error Correction

Quantum error correction protects quantum information against decoherence and gate errors. A logical qubit is encoded in a subspace of several physical qubits. The code detects errors by measuring stabilizer operators that commute with the logical operators. The measurement reveals the error without revealing the logical state. A recovery operation then restores the state.

The surface code is a leading candidate. It requires only nearest-neighbor interactions on a two-dimensional lattice. Its threshold is approximately 1 percent. Below the threshold, increasing the code distance suppresses the logical error rate exponentially. Above the threshold, adding qubits makes the error worse. Present devices operate near or below the threshold for small distances. Scaling to the distances required for useful algorithms remains an engineering challenge. The existence of the threshold shows that fault-tolerant quantum computation is possible in principle.

The threshold theorem states that if the physical error rate lies below a constant threshold, then arbitrarily long quantum computations can be performed with only polylogarithmic overhead. The theorem requires that errors are local and that fresh ancilla qubits can be supplied. It does not require that the errors are independent, only that their correlations decay sufficiently fast.

Magic-state distillation converts noisy non-Clifford states into purer ones. It is the leading method for implementing the non-Clifford gates required for universality. The overhead in qubits is steep, and reducing it is an active research area. Concatenated codes and topological codes both achieve thresholds. Topological codes are preferred for their higher thresholds and for their compatibility with two-dimensional architectures. The theorem guarantees that fault tolerance is possible. It does not guarantee that it is easy.

### Topological Quantum Computation

Topological quantum computation encodes information in non-Abelian anyons. The information is stored in the fusion space. Gates are implemented by braiding. The braiding is topological. It is insensitive to local perturbations. The protection is passive. Error correction is still required for non-topological operations and for leakage.

Ising anyons are realized in the fractional quantum Hall state at filling factor 5/2 and in certain superconducting systems. They are not universal. Additional non-topological gates are needed. Fibonacci anyons are universal. They have not been realized. The approach offers high thresholds in principle. The experimental realization of non-Abelian anyons with the required properties remains incomplete. The theoretical framework is mature.

### Measurement-Based Quantum Computation

Measurement-based quantum computation performs the computation by a sequence of single-qubit measurements on a pre-entangled resource state. The resource is a cluster state or a graph state. The measurements are adaptive. The basis of each measurement depends on previous outcomes.

The approach separates the creation of entanglement from the computation. The entanglement can be prepared offline. The computation itself consists of measurements. The separation is advantageous for photonic implementations. Photon loss remains the principal error. Error correction is possible. Its computing power equals that of the circuit model. It has been demonstrated on small scales. Scaling requires high-fidelity resource states and feed-forward.

### Adiabatic Quantum Computation

Adiabatic quantum computation encodes the solution of a problem in the ground state of a final Hamiltonian. The system is prepared in the ground state of an initial Hamiltonian and evolved slowly to the final Hamiltonian. The adiabatic theorem guarantees that the system remains in the ground state if the evolution is slow enough. The runtime scales with the inverse square of the minimum gap.

The model is universal. It is equivalent to the circuit model. Practical implementations are limited by the gap and by thermal excitations. Quantum annealing is a related heuristic. It does not guarantee the ground state. Both approaches are studied for optimization problems. Speed-ups over classical algorithms are not guaranteed for all instances. They are possible for some.

### Quantum Annealing

Quantum annealing is a heuristic method for finding the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian. A transverse field is applied and slowly reduced. Tunneling allows the system to escape local minima. The method does not guarantee the optimal solution. It can outperform simulated annealing on some instances. It can underperform on others.

Commercial devices implement quantum annealing with thousands of qubits. The qubits are noisy. The connectivity is limited. Benchmarking against classical algorithms is ongoing. Advantages have been claimed for specific problem classes. The claims are contested. The devices are useful for studying quantum dynamics. Their advantage for practical optimization remains unproven.

### Variational Quantum Algorithms

Variational quantum algorithms use a parameterized quantum circuit and a classical optimizer. The circuit prepares a trial state. The classical optimizer adjusts the parameters to minimize a cost function. The approach is hybrid. It is suitable for noisy intermediate-scale devices. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm and the variational quantum eigensolver are examples.

The algorithms do not require fault tolerance. Their performance is limited by noise and by the difficulty of the classical optimization. Barren plateaus—regions of exponentially small gradients—impede training for some circuits. Mitigation strategies exist. The algorithms are a practical approach for present hardware. Their asymptotic advantage is not established.

### Blind Quantum Computation

Blind quantum computation allows a client to delegate a computation to a server without revealing the input, the output or the algorithm. The client prepares single qubits and sends them to the server. The server entangles them and measures according to instructions. The instructions are chosen so that the server learns nothing about the computation. The client obtains the result.

A photonic demonstration has been carried out. Security rests on the no-signaling principle and on the client’s ability to prepare states from a restricted set. The protocol enables private computation on a remote quantum computer. It does not require the client to possess a universal quantum computer. The client needs only to prepare and measure single qubits. The capability is a distinctive feature of quantum networks.

### Building One, and What It Is For

Building the machine is a fight with noise. A qubit is a physical system, and physical systems interact with their surroundings. The interaction leaks information and destroys the amplitudes. Error correction encodes one logical qubit in many physical qubits so that errors can be detected and fixed faster than they occur. The overhead is large. A useful error-corrected machine requires many physical qubits per logical qubit, with error rates below a threshold. Recent experiments have demonstrated error correction that improves as the code grows, which is the necessary direction. They have not yet produced a machine that runs Shor’s algorithm on cryptographically relevant numbers.

Cryptography has not waited. Public-key systems based on factoring or on related problems are vulnerable in principle to a large quantum computer. New systems, based on problems believed to resist quantum attack, have been standardized and are being adopted. The migration is slow because it touches everything that authenticates and encrypts. It is underway because data recorded today can be stored and decrypted later. The correct engineering response precedes the machine.

The phrase “quantum supremacy” or “quantum advantage” has been used for demonstrations in which a quantum device performed a particular task faster than a classical computer. The tasks were chosen to suit the device. They were real comparisons and not, by themselves, useful computations. The useful threshold is a calculation that someone wanted for an independent reason, done better than by any classical method. That threshold has not been clearly passed for a commercially relevant problem. It is the threshold that matters.

Quantum computing is therefore best understood as a new kind of instrument, powerful where interference helps and irrelevant where it does not. If the engineering succeeds, the first deep scientific returns are likely to be in the simulation of molecules, materials, and perhaps nuclear physics. Those are returns worth having. They are not a general replacement of classical computing. Most of what computers do will remain classical, because most of what computers do does not need amplitudes.

The classical competition should not be underestimated. Algorithms and hardware for classical simulation of quantum systems improve. A claimed quantum advantage has to beat the best classical method, not a naive one. Several early claims were later matched or approached classically. The race is real. It is a reason to be precise about what has been shown. It is also a reason the useful applications, when they come, will be in problems where the quantum structure is essential and the classical simulation is genuinely hard, not in problems where a cleverer classical programmer had not yet looked.

The qubit zoo is a sign of an early technology. Superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons, and spins in solids are all in use. Each has advantages in speed, in connectivity, or in stability. None has won. A mature technology usually settles on one or two platforms. Quantum computing has not settled. The unsettled state is a reason for parallel investment and a reason not to treat any one company’s roadmap as the field’s. Roadmaps are plans. The platforms are the evidence. The evidence is still a competition.

Education and workforce are part of the timeline. A technology that requires specialists in physics, in engineering, and in the algorithms will be limited by how many such people exist. Programs to train them are part of the investment. The timeline for useful machines is set by error rates and by scale, and also by whether the people who can build and use the machines are available. Neither factor should be omitted. Hardware roadmaps that ignore the workforce describe a laboratory success. A field is a laboratory plus a community that can reproduce and extend it.

## <a id="ch_9"></a>9. Quantum Field Theory and Electrodynamics

### Quantum Field Theory

Quantum field theory is the framework that combines quantum mechanics with special relativity. The fundamental objects are fields defined at every point of spacetime. Particles appear as quanta of those fields. The theory is formulated so that the laws take the same form in every inertial frame and so that no signal propagates faster than light. It predicts the existence of antiparticles, the spin-statistics connection and the CPT theorem.

Interactions are local. The Lagrangian density at each point depends only on the fields and their derivatives at that point. The resulting S-matrix elements are computed by Feynman diagrams. Each diagram corresponds to a possible sequence of emissions and absorptions. The sum of diagrams yields the probability amplitude for a given process. Renormalization absorbs the infinite contributions of high-energy virtual particles into a finite number of measured parameters. After renormalization the predictions are finite and accurate.

The Standard Model is a quantum field theory. Its gauge symmetries dictate the interactions of quarks, leptons and the Higgs field. Quantum electrodynamics, the oldest and simplest part, predicts the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron to more than ten significant figures. Quantum chromodynamics accounts for the spectrum and scattering of hadrons once confinement is accepted. The electroweak theory unifies the electromagnetic and weak interactions and predicted the W, Z and Higgs bosons before they were observed.

The framework fails when gravity becomes strong: attempts to quantize gravity perturbatively fail because the theory is non-renormalizable, and no consistent quantum field theory of the metric itself is known. At accessible energies, however, quantum field theory is the most precise description of nature that exists. Every confirmed particle-physics experiment is a test of it.

### Quantum Electrodynamics

Quantum electrodynamics is the quantum field theory of the electromagnetic interaction. It describes electrons, positrons and photons. The interaction is local and gauge-invariant. The coupling constant is the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137.

Feynman diagrams organize the perturbative expansion, and renormalization absorbs the divergences into the measured values of the electron mass and charge. The sections that follow describe both in detail.

The theory is the most precise in physics. The anomalous magnetic moment of the electron agrees with experiment to more than ten significant figures. The Lamb shift, the hyperfine structure of hydrogen and the scattering of electrons and positrons are likewise predicted to high accuracy. Quantum electrodynamics is the unbroken U(1) sector of the Standard Model. It is the prototype of a successful quantum field theory.

### The Precision of Quantum Electrodynamics

Quantum electrodynamics is the theory of electrons, positrons, and photons. It is the most precisely tested theory in physics. The magnetic moment of the electron is predicted and measured to more than ten significant figures. The agreement holds.

The Dirac equation gives the electron a g-factor of exactly 2. Quantum corrections change it. The leading correction, calculated by Schwinger in 1948, is a = (g-2)/2 = α/(2π), where α is the fine-structure constant. Higher-order terms in powers of α have been calculated. The experimental value of the anomaly is a<sub>e</sub> = 0.00115965218059(13). The theoretical value, limited by the precision of α itself, matches within the uncertainties.

The Lamb shift is the splitting between the 2s<sub>1/2</sub> and 2p<sub>1/2</sub> levels of hydrogen. In the Dirac theory they are degenerate. The measured interval is about 1057 MHz. The dominant contribution comes from the electron’s interaction with the fluctuating electromagnetic field. A smaller contribution, about −27 MHz, comes from vacuum polarization, the Uehling effect. The full calculation, including higher orders, matches the measurement.

The fine-structure constant is not constant. It runs with the energy scale. Vacuum polarization screens the charge at long distances. At shorter distances the effective charge is larger. The running is logarithmic. At the mass of the Z boson, 1/α is about 128.9 rather than 137.0. The running is measured in scattering experiments and is consistent with the calculation.

Renormalization is the procedure that makes these predictions finite, as the technical section below explains. It is not an arbitrary subtraction. It is required by the structure of the theory and constrained by gauge invariance, and the Ward identity ensures that the renormalization of the vertex and of the electron field are related, so that the charge remains universal.

The precision is possible because the expansion parameter α is small. Each additional loop is suppressed by another factor of α/π. The same methods applied to the strong force do not converge in the same way at low energy. QED is both a working computational tool and a demonstration that a quantum field theory can be defined, renormalized, and tested to extraordinary accuracy. Its success fixes the standard against which other theories are judged.

### Feynman’s Account of Quantum Electrodynamics

Richard Feynman presented quantum electrodynamics in a form that begins with amplitudes rather than with fields. Every photon carries a complex amplitude, which can be drawn as an arrow. The arrow has a length and a direction. The probability that an event occurs is the square of the length of the final arrow. When an event can happen in more than one way, the arrows for the different ways are added before the square is taken. Interference is the result of that addition. Nature, it seems, prefers to do the arithmetic first and the squaring later, which is the opposite of the order most of us learned in school and have been regretting ever since.

Light is partially reflected from a surface of glass. The probability depends on the thickness of the glass. The calculation sums the amplitudes for reflection from the front surface and from the back surface. The relative phase depends on the extra distance traveled. The same rule accounts for the reflection from a mirror, the focusing of a lens, and the diffraction by a grating. In each case every possible path contributes an amplitude. Paths near the classical path have nearly the same phase and add constructively. Paths far from the classical path cancel.

An electron also carries an amplitude for going from one point to another. The amplitude depends on the proper time along the path. An electron can emit or absorb a photon. Those three processes—the photon going from place to place, the electron going from place to place, and the electron emitting or absorbing a photon—are the only ingredients. Every electromagnetic process is a combination of them. The combinations are drawn as diagrams. Each diagram corresponds to a term in the calculation. The terms are added, and the square of the sum is the probability.

The theory is approximate. Higher-order diagrams contain loops and produce large intermediate numbers. Those numbers are absorbed into the measured mass and charge of the electron. Once that is done, the remaining predictions are finite. The magnetic moment of the electron, the Lamb shift, and the scattering of light by light have all been calculated and checked against experiment. The agreement is the strongest quantitative success in physics.

The account does not eliminate the mathematics. It shows what the mathematics is doing. Amplitudes are added for every way an event can happen. The classical path is the path that survives the addition. The photon is the quantum of the electromagnetic field. The same rules govern the emission of light by an atom, the reflection of light by a mirror, and the forces between charges. The strangeness is not removed. It is located in the rule that the arrows must be added before they are squared.

### The Technical Structure of Quantum Electrodynamics

Feynman’s formulation of quantum electrodynamics supplies a set of rules for calculating any electromagnetic process. The amplitude for a particle to go from one point to another is given by a propagator. For the electron the propagator is the Green function of the Dirac equation. For the photon it is the Green function of the wave equation. Both are known in closed form.

An interaction occurs when an electron emits or absorbs a photon. The vertex contributes a factor proportional to the charge and to the Dirac matrix γ<sup>μ</sup>. Momentum is conserved at every vertex. The full amplitude for a process is the sum of the amplitudes for every diagram that connects the initial state to the final state. Each internal line is a propagator. Each closed loop is integrated over the momentum that circulates in it.

The path-integral version of the same theory states that the amplitude is the sum over all field histories of e<sup>iS/ħ</sup>, where S is the classical action. The Feynman rules are the perturbative expansion of that sum. The two formulations are equivalent. The diagrams are a bookkeeping device for the expansion. They are not pictures of trajectories.

Ultraviolet divergences appear in the loop integrals. They are handled by renormalization. The bare mass and charge in the Lagrangian are not the measured mass and charge. The difference absorbs the divergent parts. After renormalization every physical prediction is finite. Infrared divergences appear when massless photons are emitted with vanishing energy. They cancel in any observable that sums over all soft photons that cannot be resolved. The cancellation is guaranteed by the theory’s structure.

The same rules give the anomalous magnetic moment, the Lamb shift, the running of the charge, and the cross sections for scattering and pair production. Each additional loop is suppressed by a power of the fine-structure constant. The expansion is therefore practical. The theory remains the prototype of a renormalizable quantum field theory. Its rules are specific to electrons and photons. The same diagrammatic method, with different vertices and propagators, is used for the other forces.

### Path Integrals

The path-integral formulation expresses the quantum amplitude for a process as a sum over all possible histories. Each history contributes a phase e<sup>iS/ħ</sup>, where S is the classical action of that history. The dominant contributions come from paths near the classical path, where the phase is stationary. Quantum corrections arise from the fluctuations around it.

The formulation is equivalent to the operator formalism. It makes Lorentz invariance and the connection to classical mechanics manifest. It is the natural language for gauge theories and for the quantization of constrained systems. In statistical mechanics the same integral, continued to imaginary time, yields the partition function.

Feynman introduced the path integral for non-relativistic quantum mechanics and later extended it to quantum electrodynamics. It remains the standard starting point for perturbative calculations in the Standard Model and for many non-perturbative approaches. The classical limit ħ → 0 recovers the principle of least action. The path integral therefore unifies the classical and quantum descriptions within a single expression.

### Feynman Diagrams

Feynman diagrams are graphical representations of the terms in the perturbative expansion of a quantum field theory. External lines denote incoming and outgoing particles. Internal lines denote virtual particles. Vertices denote interactions. Each diagram corresponds to an integral over the momenta of the virtual particles. The integral is weighted by the coupling constants and by the propagators of the internal lines.

The diagrams automatically incorporate particle creation and annihilation, crossing symmetry and the correct combinatorial factors. They make the order of a calculation visible. Loop diagrams represent quantum corrections. Tree diagrams are classical. Renormalization subtracts the divergent parts of the loop integrals and replaces them with measured parameters.

The same diagrams are used in condensed-matter theory and in statistical mechanics. Their utility is practical. They convert an abstract expansion into a set of concrete integrals that can be evaluated. Every precision test of quantum electrodynamics and of the electroweak theory has been performed with Feynman diagrams. They are the computational language of perturbative quantum field theory.

### Renormalization

Renormalization absorbs the divergences of loop integrals into a finite number of measured parameters. In a renormalizable theory the number of such parameters does not increase with the order of perturbation theory. Quantum electrodynamics and the Standard Model are renormalizable. Gravity is not. Higher-dimension operators in an effective theory are suppressed by powers of a high scale. They become important only near that scale.

The renormalization group describes how the parameters change with scale. Couplings that grow in the ultraviolet indicate new physics or a Landau pole. Couplings that grow in the infrared indicate confinement or the generation of a mass gap. The group organizes the relation between physics at different energies. It does not remove the need for experimental input. It determines how that input is extrapolated.

### Anomalies in Quantum Field Theory

Anomalies are symmetries of the classical action that are broken by quantum effects. The chiral anomaly is the non-conservation of the axial current in the presence of gauge fields. It is required for the decay of the neutral pion and for the resolution of the U(1) problem in QCD. Gauge anomalies must cancel for consistency. In the Standard Model they cancel between quarks and leptons.

The cancellation is a constraint on the particle content. It is satisfied by the observed fermions. Gravitational anomalies impose further constraints. Anomalies are not defects. They are calculable quantum effects that have observable consequences. Their cancellation or non-cancellation determines which theories are consistent.

### Instantons

Instantons are classical solutions of the Euclidean field equations. They describe tunneling between topologically distinct vacua. In QCD they contribute to the mass of the eta-prime and to the violation of U(1) axial symmetry. Their density is suppressed at high temperature. The suppression is observed in the restoration of the symmetry above the deconfinement transition.

In the electroweak theory instantons violate baryon and lepton number. The rate is negligible at zero temperature. It becomes unsuppressed above the electroweak scale. The process is the basis of electroweak baryogenesis and of leptogenesis scenarios that rely on sphalerons. Instantons are non-perturbative. They are not captured by Feynman diagrams. They are required for a complete description of the vacuum structure.

### Symmetry Breaking

Spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs when the ground state of a system does not share the symmetry of the Lagrangian. The symmetry is not absent. It is realized non-linearly. Goldstone’s theorem states that each broken continuous generator produces a massless boson. In a gauge theory the Goldstone bosons are absorbed by the gauge fields, which become massive. The Higgs mechanism is the relativistic realization of this process.

Explicit breaking by a small term in the Lagrangian gives the would-be Goldstone bosons a small mass. Pions are the approximate Goldstone bosons of chiral symmetry. Their mass is small compared with the scale of chiral symmetry breaking. The same pattern appears in condensed-matter systems. Superconductors, magnets and liquid crystals all break symmetries spontaneously. The resulting collective modes are the analogs of Goldstone bosons. The phenomenon is general.

# <a id="part_3"></a>Part III: Particles, Nuclei and Atoms

*From quarks and the Standard Model up through nuclei and atoms to chemistry and materials*

## <a id="ch_10"></a>10. The Standard Model of Particle Physics

### The Particle That Should Not Have Been Found

In 2012 two experiments at the Large Hadron Collider announced the discovery of a particle with a mass of 125 GeV. The particle decayed in the ways predicted for the Higgs boson. The decays were rare. The background was large. The signal emerged only after years of data and after the application of every available discrimination technique. The emergence was gradual. It was also unambiguous.

The particle completes the Standard Model. It does not explain the Standard Model. Its mass is not predicted. Its couplings are measured, not derived. The measurements agree with the theory. The agreement is a triumph. It is also a reminder that the triumph is incomplete. The theory that predicted the particle does not predict why the particle has the mass it has. The mass is an input. The input is now known. The reason for the input is not.

### The Standard Model in Brief

The Standard Model is a renormalizable quantum field theory based on SU(3)<sub>c</sub> × SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub>. It contains three generations of quarks and leptons and a single Higgs doublet. Nineteen parameters, most of them Yukawa couplings that set the fermion masses, remain free. They are measured, not predicted; grand unification and supersymmetry would reduce the count under assumptions not yet confirmed.

Precision tests confirm the model to high accuracy. The electron magnetic moment, the W and Z masses and the Higgs couplings agree with the predictions after radiative corrections. Neutrino masses require an extension. Dark matter and the baryon asymmetry lie outside the model.

The theory is the most successful description of the non-gravitational interactions. Its incompleteness is quantitative. No contradiction with existing data has been established. No complete ultraviolet completion is known.

### Particles and Forces

The Standard Model describes the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions. It contains twelve fermions—six quarks and six leptons—and the gauge bosons that mediate the forces. The Higgs boson generates the masses of the W and Z bosons and of the fermions through the Yukawa couplings.

![Quarks, generation I to III: up 2.2 MeV, charm 1.27 GeV, top 173 GeV; down 4.7 MeV, strange 93 MeV, bottom 4.18 GeV. Leptons: electron 0.511 MeV, muon 106 MeV, tau 1.78 GeV; electron, muon and tau neutrinos, each below 0.45 eV. Force carriers: gluon 0, photon 0, Z boson 91.2 GeV, W boson 80.4 GeV. Higgs boson 125 GeV.](scripts/rev16/figures/fig3_standard_model.png)

*Figure 2. The particles of the Standard Model, with rounded masses.*

The electromagnetic and weak interactions are unified in the electroweak theory. At energies above the electroweak scale the distinction disappears. The strong interaction is described by quantum chromodynamics. Quarks carry color charge and are confined. Free quarks are never observed. The observed hadrons are color-neutral combinations of quarks.

Every particle the model predicts has been found, and the measured masses and couplings agree with it to high precision. It still leaves out gravity and says nothing about why its parameters have the values they do.

### Symmetries of the Standard Model

The Standard Model is defined by its gauge symmetry group SU(3)<sub>c</sub> × SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub>. The factor SU(3)<sub>c</sub> is the color group of the strong interaction. Quarks transform as triplets; gluons as an octet. The group remains unbroken. Its coupling grows at low energy and confines quarks and gluons into color-singlet hadrons.

The factor SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub> is the electroweak group. Left-handed fermions transform as doublets under SU(2)<sub>L</sub>; right-handed fermions are singlets. The Higgs field is a doublet. Its vacuum expectation value breaks SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub> to the electromagnetic U(1)<sub>em</sub>. Three of the four gauge bosons acquire mass and become the W<sup>±</sup> and Z. The unbroken generator is the photon. The same vacuum expectation value generates fermion masses through Yukawa couplings.

The gauge symmetries dictate the form of every interaction vertex. They forbid proton decay at the renormalizable level and guarantee the cancellation of anomalies once the observed fermion content is included. Global symmetries are fewer. Baryon number and lepton number are accidental consequences of the gauge structure and the particle content. They are conserved by all renormalizable terms. Neutrino masses, if Majorana, violate lepton number by two units and lie outside the minimal Standard Model.

Discrete symmetries (charge conjugation, parity, time reversal) are violated by the weak interaction. Their observed pattern is reproduced by the complex phases in the Yukawa matrices. The gauge symmetry group, together with the representation content of the fermions and the Higgs, constitutes the entire defining structure of the Standard Model.

### The Higgs Mechanism

The Higgs mechanism generates masses for the W and Z bosons and for the fermions. A complex scalar doublet acquires a vacuum expectation value. Three of its four degrees of freedom become the longitudinal polarizations of the W and Z. The fourth remains as the Higgs boson. The vacuum expectation value is fixed by the Fermi constant. The Higgs mass is fixed by the self-coupling. Both are measured.

Fermion masses arise from Yukawa couplings to the same vacuum expectation value. The couplings are free parameters spanning about six orders of magnitude, from the electron to the top quark, and nothing in the model fixes them. Why the Higgs mass sits so far below the Planck scale is the hierarchy problem of [Chapter 11](#ch_11). The mechanism works; its deeper origin is unknown.

### The Higgs Boson Since 2012

The Higgs boson was discovered in 2012 at a mass of approximately 125 GeV. Its couplings to the W, Z and to the heavy fermions agree with Standard Model predictions within present uncertainties. The self-coupling has not yet been measured. The width is narrow, consistent with the expected decay channels. No deviation that requires new physics has been established.

The vacuum is metastable in the Standard Model. The Higgs self-coupling runs negative at high scales. The lifetime of the vacuum exceeds the age of the universe for the measured masses. New physics below the instability scale can stabilize the vacuum. Its absence so far leaves the metastability intact. The observation confirms the mechanism. It does not reveal the origin of the potential or the reason for the particular mass.

### The Core Theory and Everyday Life

The physicist Sean Carroll has given the name Core Theory to the combination of the Standard Model of particle physics with general relativity, treated as a quantum field theory at ordinary energies. The claim made for it is bold and well founded. Everything in daily experience, from chemistry and the shapes of molecules to living cells, brains and the weather, is governed by the fields and forces already in the Core Theory.

The argument is that any new particle or force strong enough to affect atoms and molecules at ordinary energies would long ago have shown itself in accelerators and precision experiments. The room for new physics at these scales is almost gone. The exceptions are on cosmic scales, dark matter and dark energy among them, and they do not touch daily life.

This is not a claim that everything is predictable or that the Core Theory explains everything. It cannot predict the weather a month ahead, and it says nothing about why the fields are what they are. The claim is narrower: what remains unknown lies at extreme energies, tiny distances or huge scales, and the laws that run ordinary life are known.

## <a id="ch_11"></a>11. Beyond the Standard Model

### Grand Unified Theories

Grand unified theories embed the Standard Model gauge group in a single simple group. The smallest example is SU(5). Larger groups such as SO(10) and E<sub>6</sub> are also studied. At energies far above the electroweak scale the unified symmetry is unbroken. Quarks and leptons occupy common multiplets. The strong, weak and electromagnetic couplings are different low-energy manifestations of a single coupling.

Unification predicts that the three Standard Model couplings meet at a single high scale when evolved with the renormalization-group equations. In the minimal non-supersymmetric SU(5) model they miss. In the minimal supersymmetric extension they meet near 10<sup>16</sup> GeV. The same scale suppresses the rate of proton decay. Present experimental limits on the proton lifetime already exclude the simplest non-supersymmetric models and constrain the supersymmetric ones.

The theories also relate quark and lepton masses and, in SO(10), naturally accommodate a right-handed neutrino, supplying a seesaw mechanism for the observed neutrino masses. They do not explain the number of generations or the hierarchy of Yukawa couplings. Supersymmetric versions introduce new particles that have not been observed. Non-supersymmetric versions are already ruled out by coupling unification and proton decay.

No direct evidence for grand unification exists. The ideas remain the most economical framework that links the three non-gravitational forces and that relates the matter content of the Standard Model. Their confirmation or exclusion will require either the discovery of proton decay, the observation of supersymmetric partners, or a decisive mismatch in the high-scale extrapolation of the couplings.

### The Seesaw Mechanism

The seesaw mechanism accounts for the extreme smallness of neutrino masses. In the Standard Model the left-handed neutrinos are massless. The introduction of a right-handed neutrino that is a singlet under the Standard Model gauge group permits two additional mass terms: a Dirac mass m<sub>D</sub> that couples the left-handed neutrino to the right-handed neutrino, and a Majorana mass M for the right-handed neutrino alone.

Because no gauge symmetry forbids the Majorana term, M may lie near the grand-unification or Planck scale. Diagonalization of the resulting mass matrix yields a light eigenvalue m<sub>ν</sub> ≈ m<sub>D</sub><sup>2</sup>/M and a heavy eigenvalue approximately equal to M. A large M therefore forces m<sub>ν</sub> to be tiny. The ordinary neutrino mass is suppressed by the ratio of the electroweak scale to the high scale.

The construction also breaks lepton number, by two units. It thereby permits neutrinoless double-beta decay. In SO(10) grand unified theories the right-handed neutrino is required to complete the spinor representation that contains one generation; the seesaw appears automatically. The mechanism remains the most economical explanation of the observed neutrino masses within a grand-unified framework. Direct evidence for the heavy right-handed states is absent.

### The Hierarchy Problem

The hierarchy problem is the sensitivity of the Higgs mass to ultraviolet physics. Quadratic divergences require fine-tuning if the cutoff lies far above the electroweak scale. The fine-tuning is of order (v/Λ)<sup>2</sup>. For a Planck-scale cutoff it is one part in 10<sup>32</sup>. No symmetry of the Standard Model protects the mass.

Supersymmetry cancels the quadratic divergences. Composite Higgs models replace the elementary scalar with a bound state. Extra dimensions lower the cutoff. None of these solutions has been confirmed. The absence of superpartners below a TeV increases the residual tuning. The problem is conceptual. It is not a contradiction with data. It is a reason to expect new physics near the electroweak scale. That expectation has not yet been fulfilled.

### Naturalness

Naturalness is the expectation that dimensionless parameters of order one are typical and that large hierarchies require explanation. The expectation is aesthetic and historical. It has been successful in some cases—the charm quark was predicted by the absence of flavor-changing neutral currents. It has failed in others—the cosmological constant is unnaturally small.

The failure does not invalidate the criterion. It shows that the criterion is not infallible. Anthropic selection or environmental scanning can produce apparently unnatural values. The criterion remains a guide for model building. It is not a theorem. Its continued use is justified by its past successes and tempered by its known failures.

### Supersymmetry

Supersymmetry relates bosons and fermions. Each particle has a superpartner whose spin differs by one-half. The symmetry cancels quadratic divergences and unifies the gauge couplings at a high scale. It supplies a dark-matter candidate if R-parity is conserved. The lightest superpartner is stable.

No superpartners have been observed. Limits from colliders exceed a TeV for many colored states. The limits increase the residual fine-tuning. The symmetry may be broken at a higher scale. It may be absent. The motivations—hierarchy, unification, dark matter—remain. The experimental support is absent. The theory is a well-motivated extension that has not been confirmed.

### The Theta Term and the Strong CP Problem

The QCD Lagrangian admits a term proportional to the topological charge. The coefficient is an angle θ. The term violates CP. Experimental limits on the neutron electric dipole moment require θ to be smaller than 10<sup>−10</sup>. No symmetry of the Standard Model sets θ to zero. The smallness is the strong CP problem.

The Peccei–Quinn mechanism promotes θ to a dynamical field. The field relaxes to zero. Its excitation is the axion. The axion is a candidate for dark matter. Laboratory and astrophysical searches constrain its mass and coupling. No detection has been confirmed. The mechanism solves the strong CP problem if the axion exists. The existence is not yet established.

### Axions

Axions are hypothetical particles that solve the strong CP problem. They are light, weakly interacting, and can constitute the dark matter. The mass is inversely proportional to the decay constant. Astrophysical bounds require the decay constant to be large, so the mass is small—microelectronvolts or below for the dark-matter window.

Searches use resonant cavities in magnetic fields, nuclear magnetic resonance, and broadband techniques. The cavity experiments scan the mass range by tuning the frequency. No signal has been found in the ranges examined. The remaining parameter space is large. A detection would solve both the strong CP problem and the dark-matter problem. The absence of a detection so far constrains but does not exclude the particle.

### Sterile Neutrinos

Sterile neutrinos are singlets under the Standard Model gauge group. They interact only through mixing with the active neutrinos or through gravity. They are required in the seesaw mechanism. Their masses can range from sub-electronvolt to the grand-unification scale. Light sterile neutrinos have been invoked to explain anomalies in short-baseline oscillation experiments. The anomalies are not confirmed by all experiments.

Cosmological bounds limit the contribution of light sterile neutrinos to the energy density in the early universe. The bounds are in tension with the parameter space preferred by some anomalies. Heavy sterile neutrinos are constrained by the non-observation of their decay products and by the success of Big Bang nucleosynthesis. The particles remain hypothetical. They are a minimal extension that can generate neutrino masses.

### Leptogenesis

Leptogenesis generates the baryon asymmetry from a lepton asymmetry. Heavy right-handed neutrinos decay out of equilibrium. The decays violate CP. The resulting lepton asymmetry is partially converted into a baryon asymmetry by electroweak sphalerons. The mechanism operates naturally within the seesaw framework.

The required right-handed neutrino masses lie above 10<sup>9</sup> GeV in the simplest versions. Lower scales are possible with resonant enhancement or with additional fields. The mechanism links the baryon asymmetry to the origin of neutrino masses. It has not been experimentally confirmed. It remains the most economical explanation that connects two otherwise separate facts—the smallness of neutrino masses and the existence of the baryon asymmetry.

### Electroweak Baryogenesis

Electroweak baryogenesis generates the baryon asymmetry during the electroweak phase transition. A strongly first-order transition provides the departure from equilibrium. CP violation in the bubble walls generates a chiral asymmetry. Sphalerons convert it into a baryon asymmetry outside the bubbles. Inside the bubbles the sphalerons are suppressed and the asymmetry is frozen.

The Standard Model transition is a crossover. It is not first-order. Extensions that strengthen the transition—additional scalars, supersymmetry—are required. Those extensions are constrained by the Higgs mass and by the non-observation of new particles. The mechanism is testable. It predicts electric dipole moments and modifications of the Higgs potential. Neither has been observed at the required level. The scenario remains possible in limited regions of parameter space.

## <a id="ch_12"></a>12. Dense Matter and the Strong Force

### The Equation of State of Dense Matter

The equation of state of matter at supranuclear density is unknown. It is constrained by nuclear theory at low density, by the maximum mass of neutron stars, and by the tidal deformability measured in gravitational-wave events. A maximum mass above two solar masses requires a relatively stiff equation of state. The tidal deformability of GW170817 requires that the equation of state not be too stiff at 1–2 times nuclear density.

Hyperons, deconfined quarks or Bose condensates may appear at high density. Each softens the equation of state. Their presence is limited by the maximum-mass constraint. Laboratory heavy-ion collisions probe the equation of state at high temperature and moderate density. They do not reach the cold, high-density conditions of neutron-star cores. The core composition remains an open question. The constraints from astrophysics are now quantitative.

### Inside a Neutron Star

A neutron star is about twelve kilometers across and heavier than the Sun, and it has layers. A thin atmosphere and an ocean of ordinary plasma cover a crust, where atomic nuclei form a rigid crystal lattice permeated by free neutrons. Deeper, where the density approaches that of an atomic nucleus, nuclei are predicted to merge into strange shapes called nuclear pasta, in rods and sheets. Beneath lies a core of neutron-rich matter, probably superfluid and, in the case of the protons, superconducting.

What lies at the center is not known. It may be neutrons alone, or neutrons with heavier particles, or quark matter, and the answer fixes the maximum mass a neutron star can have. Observations constrain it from three directions: the heaviest known stars have about two solar masses, the gravitational waves of colliding stars show how readily they deform, and X-ray timing from the NICER telescope has measured the radii of nearby pulsars at about 11 to 13 kilometers.

Because no laboratory can make matter so dense and cold, neutron stars are the only way to test what nuclear forces do under such pressures. Each new measurement rules out a family of models.

### Little Bangs: Heavy-Ion Collisions

To make quark matter in the laboratory, physicists collide heavy nuclei at nearly the speed of light, gold at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider in New York and lead at the Large Hadron Collider in Geneva. For an instant, a region the size of a nucleus reaches a temperature of several trillion kelvin, hotter than the early universe a microsecond after the Big Bang. Protons and neutrons melt, and quarks and gluons move freely.

The surprise of the first results was that the new state did not behave like a gas. It flowed like a nearly perfect liquid, with almost no internal friction. The ratio of its viscosity to its entropy is close to a value that string-theory calculations had suggested as a lower bound, a link between particle collisions and the black-hole holography of [Chapter 24](#ch_24).

The collisions last far less than a trillionth of a trillionth of a second, and the quark-gluon plasma cannot be observed directly. Its properties are inferred from the pattern of particles that fly out, and the fireball’s expansion is modeled with relativistic fluid dynamics. These experiments probe matter at high temperature and low density. The cold, dense matter inside neutron stars remains out of reach.

### Quark Matter

Quark matter is the phase in which quarks are deconfined. It is expected at densities several times nuclear density or at temperatures above approximately 150 MeV. Lattice QCD calculations show a crossover at zero chemical potential. At high chemical potential the transition may be first-order. The critical point, if it exists, has not been located.

Neutron-star cores may contain deconfined quarks. The possibility is constrained by the maximum mass and by the tidal deformability. Hybrid stars with quark cores are compatible with present data for some equations of state. Pure quark stars are disfavoured. Heavy-ion collisions create a quark-gluon plasma at high temperature and low density. The plasma behaves as a nearly perfect fluid. Its properties are measured. The cold, dense phase remains inaccessible to experiment.

### Color Superconductivity

Color superconductivity is the pairing of quarks at high density and low temperature. The pairing is analogous to ordinary superconductivity. It gaps the quark spectrum and breaks color symmetry. Several phases are possible. The color-flavor-locked phase pairs all three colors and flavors. It is electrically neutral and may form the ground state of cold quark matter.

The gap is estimated to be tens of MeV. It affects the cooling and the transport properties of a quark core. No observational signature has been confirmed. The phase is a prediction of QCD at high density. Its realization in neutron stars depends on the density reached in the core and on the strange-quark mass. Both are uncertain. The phase remains a theoretical possibility whose astrophysical consequences are under study.

### The Chiral Magnetic Effect

The chiral magnetic effect is the generation of an electric current along a magnetic field in a medium with chiral imbalance. It is a macroscopic manifestation of the chiral anomaly. In heavy-ion collisions the effect may produce a charge separation across the reaction plane. Experimental searches have reported signals consistent with the effect. Backgrounds from ordinary physics have not been fully excluded.

The effect is also predicted in Weyl and Dirac semimetals. It has been observed in those materials. The condensed-matter realization confirms the theoretical mechanism. The heavy-ion realization remains under debate. The effect illustrates how a quantum anomaly can produce a macroscopic transport phenomenon. Its cosmological consequences, if any, are speculative.

## <a id="ch_13"></a>13. Nuclei, Fission and Fusion

### Nuclear Binding Energy

The mass of a nucleus is less than the mass of its separated protons and neutrons. The difference is the binding energy. For helium-4 the difference is about 0.75 percent of the mass. That corresponds to about 28 MeV. A chemical bond is a few electron-volts. Nuclear binding is millions of times stronger.

When the binding energy per nucleon is plotted against mass number, the curve rises from hydrogen, peaks near iron and nickel at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, and then declines slowly toward uranium. Light nuclei release energy by fusing toward the peak. Heavy nuclei release energy by fission toward the peak. Iron sits at the top. A star that has built an iron core has no further nuclear source of energy.

The shape of the curve follows from the competition between the strong force and the electromagnetic force. The strong force is short-range. A nucleon in the interior of a large nucleus is bound to all its neighbors. A nucleon on the surface is bound to fewer. Small nuclei are mostly surface. Adding nucleons helps. The electromagnetic repulsion between protons is long-range. It grows faster with the number of protons. In large nuclei the repulsion begins to win. Extra neutrons add strong-force binding without adding charge. Beyond lead and bismuth no stable combination exists.

Fusion in the Sun requires protons to approach within the range of the strong force. At the temperature of the solar core the typical kinetic energy is far below the Coulomb barrier. Fusion occurs by quantum tunneling. The probability is low. A given proton in the core waits billions of years before it fuses. The Sun’s power density is only a few hundred watts per cubic meter. It shines because it is large and well insulated, not because the reactions are rapid.

Fission of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235, triggered by a neutron, releases about 200 MeV and two or three additional neutrons. If, on average, one of those neutrons causes another fission, the reaction is sustained. A small fraction of the neutrons are delayed by the decay of fission products. That delay allows a reactor to be controlled. In a bomb the multiplication is rapid and uncontrolled. Natural reactors operated at Oklo in Gabon about two billion years ago, when the uranium-235 abundance was higher and groundwater moderated the neutrons.

Radioactive decay follows an exponential law. After one half-life half the nuclei remain. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years and is used to date organic material up to about 50,000 years. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years and is used to date the solar system. The range of half-lives is explained by tunneling through the nuclear barrier. A small change in the barrier height or width changes the lifetime by many orders of magnitude.

### Nuclear Stability and the Valley of Stability

Stable nuclei lie in a narrow band on the plot of proton number versus neutron number. For light nuclei the band follows N ≈ Z. For heavier nuclei the band bends toward neutron excess because of the increasing Coulomb repulsion among protons. The band is the valley of stability.

Nuclei outside the valley decay toward it. Neutron-rich nuclei decay by beta emission. Proton-rich nuclei decay by positron emission or electron capture. The most stable nuclei near iron have the highest binding energy per nucleon. Fusion below iron and fission above it therefore both release energy.

Magic numbers—2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126—mark closed nuclear shells. Nuclei with magic proton or neutron numbers are especially stable. The shell model of the nucleus accounts for the magic numbers in the same way that the atomic shell model accounts for the noble gases. The existence of superheavy islands of stability beyond the known elements is a prediction of the same model. No such island has yet been reached by experiment.

The valley of stability and the shell closures together determine which isotopes exist long enough to be studied and which can be used as fuels, tracers, or chronological markers. The nuclear landscape is as structured as the electronic periodic table.

### Worked Examples: Binding Energy and Fission

Example 1. Calculate the energy released in the fission of one <sup>235</sup>U nucleus into typical fragments of mass 95 and 138, plus two neutrons.

Mass of <sup>235</sup>U = 235.044 u. Mass of fragments + neutrons ≈ 234.846 u. Defect = 0.198 u. Energy = 0.198 × 931.5 MeV ≈ 184 MeV. (The accepted average is ~200 MeV when all products are included.)

Example 2. How many fissions per second are required to produce 3 GW of thermal power?

Energy per fission ≈ 200 MeV = 3.2 × 10<sup>−11</sup> J. Rate = 3 × 10<sup>9</sup> / 3.2 × 10<sup>−11</sup> ≈ 9.4 × 10<sup>19</sup> fissions s<sup>−1</sup>.

Example 3. A reactor operates for one year at that power. What mass of <sup>235</sup>U is consumed?

Number of fissions = 9.4 × 10<sup>19</sup> × 3.16 × 10<sup>7</sup> ≈ 3.0 × 10<sup>27</sup>. Mass = 3.0 × 10<sup>27</sup> × 235 u ≈ 1 200 kg. (Actual fuel loading is larger because of incomplete burn-up.)

The same arithmetic fixes the fuel requirements and the waste inventory of every power reactor.

### Nuclear Fission

Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter fragments. The fragments lie closer to the iron peak and therefore possess higher binding energy per nucleon. The difference appears as kinetic energy of the fragments, neutrons, and gamma rays. Each fission of uranium-235 or plutonium-239 releases roughly 200 MeV, tens of millions of times the energy of a chemical bond.

A chain reaction occurs when the neutrons emitted by one fission induce further fissions. In a reactor the reaction is controlled by moderators and control rods so that exactly one neutron per fission continues the chain. In a weapon the reaction is uncontrolled and multiplies rapidly. Both devices rely on the same nuclear process.

The fuel is limited to a few fissile or fertile isotopes. Uranium-235 is the only naturally occurring fissile nuclide. Plutonium-239 and uranium-233 are produced by neutron capture in reactors. Spent fuel contains a mixture of fission products, many of them radioactive with half-lives from seconds to millions of years. The long-lived components dominate the waste-management problem.

Fission supplies about 10 percent of the world’s electricity. The energy density is roughly a million times higher than that of chemical fuels. The engineering constraints are heat removal, neutron economy, and containment of radioactive material.

### Nuclear Fusion

Fusion is the joining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus closer to the iron peak. The energy release per nucleon is larger than in fission for the lightest fuels. The most accessible reaction on Earth is the fusion of deuterium and tritium:

<sup>2</sup>H + <sup>3</sup>H → <sup>4</sup>He + n + 17.6 MeV.

The Coulomb barrier must be overcome. In stars the barrier is penetrated by quantum tunneling at temperatures of tens of millions of kelvin. On Earth the same temperatures must be reached and the plasma confined long enough for the reaction rate to exceed the energy losses. Magnetic confinement and inertial confinement are the two principal approaches.
