No terrestrial device has yet produced sustained net electrical power. Experimental reactors have achieved brief periods in which the fusion energy exceeded the energy delivered to the plasma. The engineering requirements—materials that withstand intense neutron fluxes, tritium breeding, and continuous heat extraction—remain unsolved at industrial scale.

Fusion fuels are abundant. Deuterium is extracted from water. Tritium can be bred from lithium. The reaction products are not long-lived radioactive wastes. The practical obstacles are technical, not fundamental.

### Cold Fusion

Cold fusion is the claim that nuclear fusion can occur at ordinary temperatures in condensed matter. The original reports involved electrolysis of heavy water with palladium electrodes. Excess heat and occasional nuclear signatures were announced. Subsequent attempts to reproduce the results under controlled conditions have failed.

The Coulomb barrier between two deuterons at room temperature is many orders of magnitude too high for an appreciable tunneling rate. No known solid-state effect lowers the barrier sufficiently. Claims of anomalous heat have not been accompanied by the neutron or gamma-ray fluxes required by the proposed fusion reactions. When nuclear products are reported they appear at levels inconsistent with the claimed energy release.

The scientific consensus is that cold fusion, as originally described, does not occur. Research into low-energy nuclear reactions continues in a few laboratories. No verified, reproducible demonstration of net energy gain from such reactions has been published in the peer-reviewed literature. The energy-release mechanisms that are known to work remain the high-temperature processes of stellar fusion and of thermonuclear weapons, and the neutron-induced fission of heavy nuclei.

### Nuclear Power

A nuclear power reactor maintains a controlled fission chain reaction. The heat is transferred to a working fluid that drives turbines. Light-water reactors use ordinary water as both moderator and coolant. Heavy-water, graphite-moderated, and fast-neutron reactors employ different combinations of fuel, moderator, and coolant.

The thermal efficiency is limited by the Carnot factor and by the temperature the fuel cladding and coolant can tolerate. Typical efficiencies are 30–35 percent. The remainder of the fission energy appears as waste heat. Capacity factors of operating reactors commonly exceed 90 percent. The fuel lasts years before it must be replaced.

Safety systems are designed to shut the reactor down and remove decay heat even if external power is lost. Accidents have occurred when those systems failed or were overwhelmed. The radiological consequences depend on the inventory of fission products released and on the effectiveness of containment. Waste remains radioactive for times that range from decades to hundreds of thousands of years. Geological disposal is the method adopted or planned by every country that operates reactors.

Nuclear power produces no carbon dioxide during operation. The life-cycle emissions are comparable to those of wind and lower than those of solar photovoltaics when construction and fuel-cycle energy are included. The constraints are cost, waste, proliferation risk, and public acceptance.

### Nuclear Weapons

A fission weapon assembles a supercritical mass of uranium-235 or plutonium-239 so rapidly that the chain reaction multiplies before the device disassembles. The yield is measured in kilotons of TNT equivalent. The first weapons produced yields of tens of kilotons. Later designs reached hundreds of kilotons.

A thermonuclear weapon uses the energy of a fission primary to compress and heat a secondary containing lithium deuteride. The high temperature and density ignite fusion. Additional fission of a uranium tamper can increase the yield further. Yields of tested devices have exceeded 50 megatons. The design is limited by engineering practicality rather than by nuclear physics.

The effects are blast, thermal radiation, prompt ionizing radiation, and residual fallout. The relative importance of each depends on the yield, the altitude of detonation, and the environment. No shielding short of massive earth or concrete protects against a close burst. The long-term radiological hazard is dominated by a few fission products, notably strontium-90 and caesium-137, and by any unfissioned plutonium.

The existence of the weapons follows directly from the energy release of fission and fusion. Their non-use in war since 1945 is a political fact, not a physical one. The physics that makes them possible is the same physics that powers the stars and that can power reactors.

### The Origin of the Elements

Hydrogen and most of the helium were produced in the first three minutes. The remaining elements were produced in stars. Helium burning yields carbon and oxygen. Carbon burning and oxygen burning yield neon, magnesium, silicon, and sulfur. Silicon burning yields iron-group nuclei. Beyond iron, neutron-capture processes produce the heavier elements.

The slow neutron-capture process operates in asymptotic-giant-branch stars. The rapid process operates in neutron-star mergers and possibly in some supernovae. The observed abundance patterns of the heavy elements match the predictions of these two processes once the neutron fluxes and the seed nuclei are specified.

Supernovae and stellar winds return the newly synthesized nuclei to the interstellar medium. Subsequent generations of stars form from the enriched gas. The Sun formed from gas already enriched by earlier generations of stars. The Earth and its inhabitants are made of nuclei that were forged in earlier stars and ejected in their deaths.

The abundances measured in the solar system, in other stars, and in the interstellar medium are consistent with this history. Nuclear astrophysics therefore accounts for the chemical composition of ordinary matter.

### The Reaction That Should Not Have Been Possible

In 1938 Bethe calculated the carbon-nitrogen-oxygen cycle. The cycle allows stars more massive than the Sun to fuse hydrogen into helium. The calculation solved the problem of how stars shine. It also predicted that the Sun’s energy source is the proton-proton chain, not the CNO cycle. The prediction was confirmed decades later by the detection of solar neutrinos.

The neutrinos arrived in fewer numbers than expected. The deficit lasted thirty years. The resolution was neutrino oscillation. The neutrinos changed flavor on the way from the Sun to the Earth. The change required that neutrinos have mass. The mass is small but real. The non-zero mass is the first confirmed physics beyond the original Standard Model.

The chain of inference runs from a calculation of stellar energy to a modification of particle physics. The chain is unbroken. It began with the question of why the Sun is hot. It ended with the discovery that the lightest known particles have mass. The ending was not anticipated. It was required by the data.

## <a id="ch_14"></a>14. Neutrinos

In beta decay the energy of the emitted electron is not fixed. It forms a continuous spectrum. If the nucleus simply emitted an electron, energy and momentum would not be conserved. Wolfgang Pauli proposed in 1930 that a light, neutral particle carries away the missing energy and momentum. Enrico Fermi named it the neutrino and built a theory of beta decay around it. The particle was detected in 1956 by Cowan and Reines using a reactor as the source.

Neutrinos interact only through the weak force and gravity. A typical solar neutrino can pass through a light-year of lead with a substantial probability of no interaction. About 65 billion solar neutrinos pass through each square centimeter of the Earth every second. Over a human lifetime only a few interact with atoms in the body.

There are three flavors: electron, muon, and tau. They have small but nonzero masses. The mass eigenstates are mixtures of the flavor eigenstates. A neutrino produced as one flavor can be detected as another after traveling a distance. This is neutrino oscillation. It was confirmed by experiments with solar neutrinos, atmospheric neutrinos, and reactor neutrinos. The oscillation data determine the mass-squared differences and the mixing angles. The absolute mass scale is not yet known. It is below about 0.1 eV.

Neutrinos are produced in the Sun by the fusion reactions, in supernovae, in the atmosphere by cosmic-ray interactions, in reactors, and in the early universe. They carry information from regions that light cannot leave. The detection of neutrinos from supernova 1987A confirmed that the core collapse releases most of its energy in neutrinos. Neutrino telescopes now observe high-energy neutrinos from distant sources.

The existence of three light neutrino species was established by the width of the Z boson. The Standard Model accommodates the oscillations by giving the neutrinos small masses, either as Dirac particles or as Majorana particles. Which possibility is realized is not yet known. The neutrinos are the lightest known massive particles. They are also the most numerous, after the photons of the cosmic microwave background.

### Neutrino Mass and Mixing

Neutrino oscillation experiments measure two mass-squared differences and three mixing angles. The atmospheric difference is approximately 2.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> eV<sup>2</sup>. The solar difference is approximately 7.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> eV<sup>2</sup>. The mixing angles are large. One is near maximal. The CP-violating phase is only weakly constrained. The mass ordering—normal or inverted—remains unknown.

The absolute mass scale is bounded by the endpoint of tritium beta decay, by the rate of neutrinoless double-beta decay if neutrinos are Majorana, and by the effect of neutrino mass on the cosmic microwave background and on large-scale structure. Cosmology bounds the sum of the masses below about 0.07 to 0.12 eV, depending on which data sets are combined. The bounds are consistent. They do not yet determine the individual masses. The seesaw mechanism remains the most economical explanation of the smallness of the masses.

The Majorana or Dirac nature of the neutrino is undecided. Neutrinoless double-beta decay is possible only if neutrinos are Majorana. The decay violates lepton number by two units. Current experiments set lower limits on the half-life of order 10<sup>26</sup> years. The limits translate into upper bounds on the effective Majorana mass. The bounds do not yet exclude the inverted ordering. They constrain the normal ordering only in part of the parameter space.

Cosmological bounds on the sum of neutrino masses come from the suppression of small-scale structure. Free-streaming neutrinos erase perturbations below their free-streaming length. The effect is measured in the cosmic microwave background and in galaxy surveys. The bounds are model-dependent. They assume the standard thermal history. Non-standard cosmologies can relax them. Laboratory bounds from beta decay are model-independent. Both sets of bounds continue to improve. Neither has yet reached the lower limit set by the oscillation data.

### Catching the Ghost Particle

A neutrino interacts so rarely that detecting one needs a huge detector, a very low background and a great deal of patience. The Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan holds 50 000 tonnes of ultrapure water in a mine, surrounded by thousands of light sensors that catch the faint flash when a neutrino strikes a nucleus. Its observation that atmospheric neutrinos change flavor, and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory’s demonstration that solar neutrinos do the same, earned the 2015 Nobel Prize for Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald.

The IceCube observatory instruments a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice with sensors. In 2013 it detected neutrinos with energies of a thousand trillion electronvolts, and in 2018 it traced one to a blazar, a first identification of a source of high-energy neutrinos. The burst from supernova 1987A, about two dozen neutrinos in all, showed that a collapsing star releases most of its energy this way.

Their mass is measured by the energy spectrum in tritium decay, where the KATRIN experiment in Germany has set an upper limit below one electronvolt, and by cosmology. The relic neutrinos left from the Big Bang, about a hundred per cubic centimeter for each type, have been predicted but never detected. The future experiments DUNE in the United States and Hyper-Kamiokande in Japan aim to measure the mass ordering and any difference between neutrinos and antineutrinos.

## <a id="ch_15"></a>15. Atoms and the Periodic Table

### The Afternoon the Atom Became Real

In 1905 Einstein published a paper on Brownian motion. He calculated how far a pollen grain should wander if it were being struck by invisible molecules. The calculation matched the observations. The match was quantitative. Atoms were no longer a useful fiction. They were real, and they had a size.

The paper was short. It did not require a new apparatus. It required only the recognition that the random walk of a visible particle is the visible signature of invisible collisions. Once the signature was calculated, the invisible became measurable. Perrin confirmed the numbers a few years later. The confirmation ended a debate that had lasted a century.

The same paper also gave a value for Avogadro’s number. The value was close to the modern one. The closeness was not an accident. It was the result of treating the molecular hypothesis as a quantitative claim rather than a philosophical preference. The preference had been optional. The claim was not.

### The Atomic Hypothesis

Richard Feynman once asked what single sentence would carry the most scientific knowledge to a civilization that had lost everything else. His answer was the atomic hypothesis: all things are made of atoms, small particles in perpetual motion that attract one another a little way apart and repel when pressed together. In that sentence, he said, there is an enormous amount of information about the world, if only a little imagination and thinking are applied.

The sizes are the first surprise. An atom is to an apple as an apple is to the Earth. A glass of water holds more molecules than a glass could hold grains of sand if the sand filled the oceans many times over. The picture also explains the everyday behavior of water. At the surface, molecules leave the liquid and return to it. When the departures and returns balance, the water is in equilibrium with its vapor, and the glass stops getting emptier. Warm it and the departures win.

The hypothesis was a respectable idea for two thousand years and a settled fact for little more than a century. Einstein’s analysis of Brownian motion, described above, and Perrin’s measurements made it hard to doubt.

### The Development of Chemistry

Chemistry began as practical craft. Fire, metals, dyes, and medicines were used long before they were understood. The Greeks proposed that matter was made of four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—or of atoms. Neither account was tested by measurement.

Alchemy mixed the practical with the mystical. It sought the transformation of metals and the elixir of life. It developed laboratory techniques—distillation, sublimation, crystallization—that later chemistry kept. It did not develop a quantitative theory.

The transition came with measurement. Robert Boyle defined an element as a substance that could not be broken down further by chemical means. He studied the behavior of gases. The phlogiston theory explained combustion as the release of a substance called phlogiston. The theory was useful until the weights were measured carefully. When a metal burns, it gains weight. If it loses phlogiston, it should lose weight. The contradiction was fatal.

Antoine Lavoisier established the modern account. Combustion is combination with oxygen. Mass is conserved. He introduced a systematic nomenclature. Chemistry became quantitative. The gases were isolated: carbon dioxide, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen. The composition of air and of water was established.

John Dalton’s atomic theory explained the fixed proportions in which elements combine. Each element has atoms of a characteristic weight. Compounds are combinations of atoms in simple ratios. Avogadro’s hypothesis—that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles—resolved the confusion over atomic weights. Berzelius determined accurate atomic weights and introduced the modern symbols.

Organic chemistry was long thought to require a vital force. Friedrich Wöhler’s synthesis of urea from inorganic materials in 1828 undermined the claim. Organic compounds are carbon compounds. They follow the same rules as inorganic compounds. Structural formulas, valence, and the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms followed. Isomers have the same composition and different structures. Optical isomers differ in the arrangement of atoms in space.

The periodic table organized the elements by atomic weight and by property. Mendeleev left gaps and predicted the properties of the missing elements. The predictions were confirmed. The modern table, ordered by atomic number, is described below.

Physical chemistry applied thermodynamics and kinetics to reactions. Catalysis speeds reactions without being consumed. Ionic dissociation explained the behavior of acids, bases, and salts in solution. Synthetic organic chemistry produced dyes, drugs, and polymers. The same principles that explain a laboratory reaction explain the chemistry of a cell and the chemistry of an industry. The history is the progressive replacement of qualitative ideas by quantitative ones.

### The Atom and the Nucleus

Matter is made of atoms. The idea is ancient. The modern form began with chemistry. Elements combine in fixed proportions. Dalton’s atomic theory explained the proportions.

Atoms are mostly empty space. The nucleus, containing protons and neutrons, is tiny and dense. The electrons occupy the outer regions. Rutherford’s scattering experiments showed the nuclear structure. Bohr’s model placed electrons in discrete energy levels. Quantum mechanics replaced the orbits with orbitals, regions of probability. The spectra of atoms are the transitions between those levels.

Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei. Alpha particles are helium nuclei. Beta particles are electrons or positrons. Gamma rays are high-energy photons. The half-life is the time for half of a sample to decay. It is characteristic of the isotope and independent of temperature or chemical form. Radioactive dating uses those clocks. Carbon-14 serves for organic material younger than about 50,000 years. Uranium-lead dates rocks billions of years old.

Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons. Some are stable. Some are radioactive. Artificial isotopes are produced in reactors and accelerators. They are used as tracers in medicine and in research.

Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus into lighter ones, releasing energy. It powers reactors and was used in the first nuclear weapons. Nuclear fusion joins light nuclei into heavier ones. It powers the Sun and the stars. Controlled fusion for power remains an engineering challenge. The physics is understood. The sustained, net-energy reaction on Earth is not yet routine.

The binding energy of the nucleus comes from the strong force. A nucleus weighs less than its protons and neutrons weigh apart. The difference appears as energy, by E = mc<sup>2</sup>. That is the source of nuclear energy. It is also the source of the energy released in the Sun. The same relation that appears in relativity governs the power of a star and the energy of a reactor.

### The Size of Atoms and the Binding of Nuclei

The sizes of atoms are set by the balance between the electrostatic attraction of the nucleus and the kinetic energy required by the uncertainty principle. Typical atomic radii are a few tenths of a nanometer. Typical nuclear radii are a few femtometers, so the emptiness of the atom is extreme: if a nucleus were the size of a pea, its atom would fill a large concert hall.

The nucleus contains protons and neutrons bound by the strong interaction. The binding energy per nucleon reaches a maximum near iron. Lighter nuclei can release energy by fusion; heavier nuclei can release energy by fission. Both processes are observed in nature and in technology.

### The Periodic Table

The periodic table arranges the elements by atomic number. The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus and the number of electrons in the neutral atom. The arrangement reveals the periodic recurrence of chemical properties. Elements in the same column share the same number of valence electrons and therefore similar chemistry.

The modern table is the consequence of the quantum structure of the atom. Electrons occupy orbitals labeled by the principal quantum number n, the angular-momentum quantum number l, and the magnetic and spin quantum numbers. The Pauli principle limits each orbital to two electrons. The order of filling—1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, and so on—produces the observed periods and the transition metals, lanthanides, and actinides.

The table is predictive. The existence and properties of missing elements were forecast before their discovery. The same quantum rules that generate the table also generate the spectra, the ionization energies, and the ionic radii. The periodic table is therefore not an empirical chart. It is the display of the allowed electronic configurations of the elements.

### Electron Shells

The principal quantum number n defines the shell. Shells are labeled K, L, M, … or simply by n = 1, 2, 3, …. The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n<sup>2</sup>. Within a shell the orbitals are s, p, d, f, corresponding to l = 0, 1, 2, 3.

The energy of an orbital depends primarily on n and secondarily on l. In multi-electron atoms the dependence on l produces the familiar order of filling. The 4s orbital lies below the 3d orbital, so potassium and calcium fill 4s before the transition metals fill 3d. The same inversion occurs for 5s–4d and 6s–5d–4f.

Closed shells are chemically inert. The noble gases have filled shells and high ionization energies. Atoms with one electron outside a closed shell are alkali metals. Atoms with one vacancy in a shell are halogens. The shell structure therefore accounts for the principal chemical families and for the stability of the octet.

The radial probability density of an s orbital has maxima whose number equals n. Higher shells are larger. The increase in size down a group and the decrease across a period follow from the changing effective nuclear charge and from the successive filling of shells. The shells are the spatial expression of the quantum numbers.

### Isotopes

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that differ in neutron number. They have the same atomic number and therefore the same electron configuration and the same chemistry. They differ in mass and in nuclear stability.

Most elements have more than one stable isotope. Tin has ten. The mass number A is the sum of protons and neutrons. The atomic mass of an element is the weighted average of the masses of its naturally occurring isotopes. High-resolution mass spectrometry separates the isotopes and measures their abundances.

Unstable isotopes decay by emission of alpha particles, beta particles, or gamma rays, or by electron capture or spontaneous fission. The half-life is characteristic of each nuclide. Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years. The decay chains of the heavy elements and the production of cosmogenic isotopes supply clocks for geology and archaeology.

Isotopic fractionation occurs in physical and chemical processes because of the mass difference. Light isotopes diffuse and react slightly faster. The resulting variations in isotope ratios record temperature, diet, and provenance. The same mass difference is negligible for the chemistry of the outer electrons. Isotopes are therefore chemically almost identical and nuclearly distinct.

### Worked Examples: Electron Shells and Isotopes

Example 1. How many electrons can occupy the n = 3 shell?

Maximum = 2n<sup>2</sup> = 18. (The shell contains 3s, 3p and 3d orbitals.)

Example 2. Natural chlorine is 75.8 percent <sup>35</sup>Cl and 24.2 percent <sup>37</sup>Cl. What is its atomic mass?

0.758 × 35 + 0.242 × 37 = 35.48 u. (The accepted value is 35.45 u; the difference is experimental rounding.)

Example 3. The half-life of <sup>14</sup>C is 5 730 years. What fraction remains after 10 000 years?

N/N<sub>0</sub> = 2<sup>−10000/5730</sup> ≈ 0.30. About 30 percent remains. The same calculation dates organic samples.

These exercises recover the structure of the periodic table and the practical use of isotopic clocks from the underlying quantum and nuclear rules.

Example. Write the ground-state electron configuration of iron (Z = 26).

1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>6</sup>. (The 4s orbitals fill before 3d; the configuration is the observed ground state.)

Example. How many unpaired electrons does the Fe<sup>3+</sup> ion possess in a high-spin octahedral complex?

Fe<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>5</sup>. High-spin places one electron in each of the five d orbitals. Five unpaired electrons.

The configurations follow from the Pauli principle and from the relative energies of the orbitals. They organize the chemistry of the transition metals.

### Quantum Mechanics of the Atom

The electrons in an atom are described by the Schrödinger equation. The solutions are stationary states labeled by quantum numbers. The energy levels of hydrogen are E<sub>n</sub> = -13.6 eV/n<sup>2</sup>. Transitions between levels emit or absorb photons whose frequencies match the observed spectral lines.

The Pauli exclusion principle requires that no two electrons occupy the same state. The principle, together with the Coulomb interaction, produces the shell structure of the periodic table. Chemical bonding arises when atoms share or transfer electrons so as to fill or empty outer shells.

The uncertainty principle limits the simultaneous knowledge of position and momentum. An electron confined to an atomic volume must possess a minimum kinetic energy. That kinetic energy balances the electrostatic attraction and sets the size of the atom. The same balance determines the sizes of molecules and the lattice spacings of solids.

Measurement collapses the wave function onto an eigenstate of the measured observable. The probability of each outcome is the squared modulus of the corresponding amplitude. The rule has been confirmed in every tested system. The interpretation of the collapse remains open. The predictive content does not.

### Worked Examples: Atomic Spectra and the Bohr Model

Example 1. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted when a hydrogen atom falls from n = 3 to n = 2.

1/λ = R(1/2<sup>2</sup> − 1/3<sup>2</sup>). R = 1.097 × 10<sup>7</sup> m<sup>−1</sup>. λ = 656 nm (the red Balmer line).

Example 2. What is the ionization energy of hydrogen from the ground state?

E = 13.6 eV.

Example 3. A muon (mass 207 m<sub>e</sub>) replaces the electron in hydrogen. By what factor does the Bohr radius shrink?

The radius scales inversely with the reduced mass, which for a muon bound to a proton is about 186 m<sub>e</sub>. The muonic atom is therefore roughly 190 times smaller. Its X-ray transitions are correspondingly higher in energy and are used to measure nuclear charge radii.

The formulae recover the observed hydrogen spectrum and the scaling that appears in exotic atoms.

## <a id="ch_16"></a>16. The Chemistry of Bonds and Reactions

### Electronegativity and the Periodic Table

Electronegativity increases from left to right across a period and decreases down a group. Fluorine is the most electronegative element. The alkali metals are the least. The trend follows from the effective nuclear charge felt by the valence electrons and from the distance of those electrons from the nucleus.

The difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms estimates the percentage of ionic character. A difference of 1.7 corresponds roughly to a bond that is 50 percent ionic. The estimate is approximate. It nevertheless correctly predicts that sodium chloride is ionic, that hydrogen chloride is polar covalent, and that the carbon–hydrogen bond is nearly non-polar.

The same scale explains the acid–base behavior of the oxides and the hydrides. Elements of high electronegativity form acidic oxides. Elements of low electronegativity form basic oxides. The amphoteric oxides lie in between. The pattern is a direct consequence of the electron-attracting power of the central atom.

Electronegativity is not a quantum-mechanical observable. It is a useful parameter derived from thermochemical data. More rigorous calculations replace it with computed charge distributions. The qualitative ordering it provides remains intact.

### The Chemical Bond

The chemical bond is the attractive interaction that holds atoms together in molecules and solids. Pauling showed that the bond can be understood as a resonance hybrid of ionic and covalent contributions. The covalent contribution arises when electrons are shared between atoms. The ionic contribution arises when electrons are transferred. The actual bond is a quantum-mechanical mixture of the two.

The strength of the bond is measured by the energy required to separate the atoms. Typical covalent bond energies range from about 1 eV for weak bonds to several eV for strong bonds. The length of the bond is the average distance between the nuclei. Both quantities are determined by the balance between the electrostatic attraction of the electrons to the nuclei and the kinetic energy and mutual repulsion of the electrons.

Electronegativity, described in the preceding section, supplies the bookkeeping. It organizes the periodic table and predicts the polarity of molecules, and it remains a useful semi-empirical tool even though more precise quantum calculations are now routine.

The same framework accounts for the tetrahedral carbon atom, the structure of the peptide bond, and the hydrogen bond that stabilizes water and biological macromolecules. The chemical bond is therefore the link between atomic physics and the structures of ordinary matter.

### Resonance and Molecular Structure

Many molecules cannot be represented by a single Lewis structure. Benzene is the classic example. The two Kekulé structures differ only in the placement of the double bonds. The actual molecule is a resonance hybrid in which the electrons are delocalized around the ring. The hybrid has a lower energy than either classical structure. The difference is the resonance energy.

The same description applies to the carbonate ion, the nitrate ion, and the peptide bond. In each case the observed bond lengths are intermediate between single and double bonds, and the molecule is more stable than any single Lewis structure would predict. Resonance is the classical language for what molecular-orbital theory describes as delocalized electrons occupying bonding orbitals that extend over several atoms.

The concept does not imply that the molecule oscillates between structures. It implies that the true wave function is a superposition. The superposition is stationary. The measured properties are those of the hybrid. The language of resonance remains useful for qualitative reasoning even when full quantum calculations are available.

### The Hydrogen Bond

A hydrogen bond is the attractive interaction between a hydrogen atom bonded to an electronegative atom and another electronegative atom. The typical strength is 0.1–0.4 eV, weaker than a covalent bond and stronger than a van der Waals interaction. The bond is directional. The hydrogen atom lies approximately on the line joining the two electronegative atoms.

Water is liquid at room temperature because of hydrogen bonds. Each molecule can form up to four. The resulting network gives ice its open structure and its lower density than liquid water. The same bonds stabilize the secondary structure of proteins and the base pairing of nucleic acids. The double helix of DNA is held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.

The bond is largely electrostatic, with a smaller covalent contribution arising from charge transfer. Its strength and directionality make it the principal organizing force in aqueous chemistry and in molecular biology. Without it, the structures of liquid water, of proteins, and of DNA would not exist in their observed forms.

### Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is the loss of electrons. Reduction is the gain of electrons. The two processes occur together. The substance that loses electrons is oxidized. The substance that gains electrons is reduced. The pair constitutes a redox reaction.

The tendency of a half-reaction to occur is measured by its standard reduction potential. The potential is the voltage of a cell in which the half-reaction is coupled to the standard hydrogen electrode. A positive potential means the half-reaction proceeds spontaneously as a reduction under standard conditions. The difference in potential between two half-reactions gives the voltage of the corresponding galvanic cell and, through the relation Δ G = -nFE, the free-energy change.

The same scale organizes the chemistry of the elements. Metals with negative reduction potentials dissolve in acid. Metals with positive potentials do not. The potentials also determine the products of electrolysis and the feasibility of industrial redox processes. They remain the practical measure of electron-transfer tendency.

### Acids and Bases

An acid is a proton donor. A base is a proton acceptor. The definition, due to Brønsted and Lowry, covers aqueous and non-aqueous chemistry. The strength of an acid is measured by the equilibrium constant of its dissociation. The negative logarithm of that constant is the pKa. Strong acids have negative pKa values. Weak acids have positive values.

The pH of a solution is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen-ion activity. In pure water at 25 °C the pH is 7. The product of the hydrogen-ion and hydroxide-ion concentrations is the ion-product constant K<sub>w</sub> = 10<sup>−14</sup>. The relation fixes the pH once either concentration is known.

Buffer solutions resist changes in pH. They contain a weak acid and its conjugate base in comparable amounts. Addition of strong acid or base shifts the ratio but leaves the pH nearly constant until one component is exhausted. The same principle operates in blood, where the carbonic-acid–bicarbonate system maintains the pH near 7.4.

The concepts of acidity and basicity extend to Lewis acids and bases, in which the acid accepts an electron pair and the base donates one. The extension includes coordination chemistry and many catalytic processes. The proton definition remains the most useful for aqueous solution chemistry.

### Chemical Kinetics

Chemical kinetics is the study of reaction rates. The rate of an elementary reaction is proportional to the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient in the rate-determining step. The proportionality constant is the rate constant k.

The temperature dependence of k is given by the Arrhenius equation k = A e<sup>−E</sup><sub>a</sub><sup>/RT</sup>, where E<sub>a</sub> is the activation energy. Only collisions that supply at least E<sub>a</sub> produce products. Catalysts lower E<sub>a</sub> by providing an alternative path. They do not change the equilibrium constant.

Integrated rate laws give the concentration as a function of time. First-order reactions decay exponentially. Second-order reactions follow a different algebraic form. The half-life is independent of concentration only for first-order processes. Radioactive decay is the classic example.

The same formalism describes enzyme kinetics once the Michaelis–Menten mechanism is adopted. At low substrate concentration the rate is first-order in substrate. At high concentration the enzyme is saturated and the rate is zero-order. The framework therefore covers both ordinary chemical reactions and the catalytic steps of biochemistry.

### Chemical Equilibrium

Chemical equilibrium is the state in which the forward and reverse rates of a reaction are equal. The equilibrium constant K is the ratio of the rate constants and is related to the standard free-energy change by Δ G<sup>°</sup> = -RTln K. When Δ G<sup>°</sup> is negative, K > 1 and products are favored. When Δ G<sup>°</sup> is positive, reactants are favored.

Le Chatelier’s principle states that a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting in the direction that reduces the disturbance. Addition of a reactant, increase of pressure for a reaction that reduces the number of gas molecules, or removal of a product all drive the reaction forward. Temperature changes shift the equilibrium according to the sign of Δ H.

The equilibrium constant is independent of the path and of the presence of a catalyst. It depends only on temperature. The approach to equilibrium, by contrast, is accelerated by catalysts. The distinction between thermodynamics and kinetics is therefore sharp. Equilibrium fixes the final composition. Kinetics fixes the time required to reach it.

### Electrochemistry

Electrochemistry is the coupling of chemical reactions to the flow of electric charge. In a galvanic cell a spontaneous redox reaction generates a potential difference. The cell potential under standard conditions is the difference of the standard reduction potentials of the two half-reactions. The relation to free energy is Δ G = -nFE, where n is the number of moles of electrons transferred and F is Faraday’s constant.

The Nernst equation corrects the potential for non-standard concentrations: E = E<sup>°</sup> − RT/nFln Q. At equilibrium E = 0 and the equation reduces to the expression for K.

Electrolytic cells reverse the process. An external voltage drives a non-spontaneous reaction. The same half-reactions occur, but in the opposite direction. Industrial production of aluminum, chlorine and many organic compounds relies on electrolysis. Corrosion is an uncontrolled galvanic process in which a metal is oxidized by atmospheric oxygen. All of these phenomena are governed by the same thermodynamic and kinetic relations.

### Organic Chemistry and Functional Groups

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon forms stable chains and rings because the C–C bond is strong and because carbon can form four covalent bonds. The resulting molecular diversity is organized by functional groups—local arrangements of atoms that confer characteristic reactivity.

Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated. Alkenes and alkynes contain multiple bonds and undergo addition. Aromatic rings exhibit special stability due to delocalization. Substitution of heteroatoms produces alcohols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amines and amides. Each class displays a limited set of typical reactions.

The same functional-group logic governs biochemistry. Proteins are polyamides. Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Lipids are largely hydrocarbon chains with polar head groups. Nucleic acids are phosphate-linked sugars bearing heterocyclic bases. The reactions of metabolism are the reactions of these functional groups, catalyzed by enzymes and regulated by the cell.

Stereochemistry adds a further layer. Carbon atoms bearing four different substituents are chiral. Biological systems almost invariably use one enantiomer. The preference is a historical fact of terrestrial evolution, not a chemical necessity. The functional-group classification nevertheless remains the organizing principle of both laboratory and biological organic chemistry.

### Polymers and Macromolecules

A polymer is a large molecule built by the repetition of smaller units. Synthetic polymers are produced by chain-growth or step-growth polymerization. The degree of polymerization, the architecture (linear, branched, cross-linked) and the tacticity determine the mechanical properties. Thermoplastics soften on heating. Thermosets do not. Elastomers return to their original shape after large deformations.

Biological macromolecules are polymers of defined sequence. Proteins are linear polypeptides that fold into specific three-dimensional structures. Nucleic acids are linear polynucleotides that store and transmit information. Polysaccharides serve structural and storage roles. In each case the covalent backbone is formed by condensation reactions. Non-covalent interactions—hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, ionic pairs—stabilize the higher-order structure.

The physical chemistry of polymer solutions and melts is described by scaling laws. The radius of a flexible chain grows as a power of its length. Entanglements dominate the viscoelasticity of concentrated solutions and melts. The same concepts apply, with modifications, to the crowded interior of a cell. Polymer science therefore links synthetic materials to the macromolecules of life.

### Surface Chemistry and Catalysis

Surface chemistry studies reactions that occur at interfaces. Adsorption may be physical (van der Waals) or chemical (covalent or ionic). The Langmuir isotherm describes monolayer adsorption when sites are equivalent and non-interacting. Real surfaces are heterogeneous. Coverage depends on temperature and on the partial pressure or concentration of the adsorbate.

Heterogeneous catalysis occurs when a reactant adsorbs, reacts on the surface, and the product desorbs. Metals, metal oxides and zeolites are common catalysts. The surface lowers the activation energy by stabilizing the transition state. Industrial processes—ammonia synthesis, petroleum cracking, catalytic converters—rely on such surfaces. Homogeneous catalysis uses soluble complexes. The distinction is practical rather than fundamental. Both accelerate attainment of equilibrium without shifting its position.

Enzyme catalysis is the biological counterpart. The active site binds the substrate, stabilizes the transition state, and releases the product. Rate enhancements of 10<sup>6</sup> to 10<sup>17</sup> are common. The underlying physical chemistry—adsorption, activation-energy reduction, and product release—is the same as in industrial catalysis. Surfaces and active sites are therefore central to both technology and metabolism.

## <a id="ch_17"></a>17. Solids, Soft Matter and Plasma

### Semiconductors

A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator and can be controlled. Silicon is the most common. In a pure crystal the valence band is full and the conduction band is empty. The energy gap between them is about 1.1 electron-volts. At room temperature a few electrons have enough thermal energy to cross the gap. The conductivity is low but not zero.

Doping changes the conductivity by many orders of magnitude. Adding a small fraction of phosphorus or arsenic introduces extra electrons. The material is n-type. Adding boron introduces holes—missing electrons that behave as positive carriers. The material is p-type. A junction between p-type and n-type material forms a diode. Current flows easily in one direction and is blocked in the other. The junction also separates charge and produces a voltage when light falls on it. That is the basis of a solar cell.

A transistor uses a small current or voltage to control a larger current. In a bipolar transistor a small base current controls a larger collector current. In a field-effect transistor a voltage on the gate controls the current between source and drain. Both act as switches and as amplifiers. A modern integrated circuit contains billions of transistors on a single chip. The transistors are formed by doping selected regions of a silicon wafer and depositing insulating and conducting layers. The minimum feature size is now a few nanometers.

The same quantum mechanics that explains the band gap explains the operation of the devices. Electrons in the crystal occupy energy bands. The exclusion principle prevents them from all occupying the lowest states. The gap, the doping, and the junctions are applications of those rules. The technology that processes information is built from the same physics that describes the atom.

### The Structure of Solids

In a crystalline solid the atoms occupy the sites of a regular lattice. The lattice may be simple cubic, face-centered cubic, body-centered cubic, hexagonal, or one of the less symmetric Bravais types. The repeating unit is the unit cell. X-ray diffraction measures the spacing and the symmetry of the cell.

Electrons in a solid form energy bands. When a band is partially filled the solid is a metal and conducts electricity. When a band is full and separated by a gap from the next empty band the solid is an insulator or a semiconductor. The size of the gap determines the electrical behavior. Silicon and germanium are semiconductors because their gaps are a fraction of an electron-volt. Diamond is an insulator because its gap is several electron-volts.

Defects control many properties. Vacancies, interstitials, and dislocations allow plastic deformation. Impurity atoms donate or accept electrons and thereby dope a semiconductor. Grain boundaries in a polycrystalline material scatter electrons and phonons and raise the electrical and thermal resistance.

The same band structure that determines conductivity also determines optical absorption, magnetism, and superconductivity. The macroscopic properties of a solid are therefore the collective consequence of the quantum states of its electrons and of the geometry of its lattice.

### Materials Science

Materials science studies the relationship between the structure of a material and its properties. Structure is examined at successive scales: electronic, atomic, crystalline, microstructural and macroscopic. Properties include mechanical strength, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, optical response and chemical reactivity. The link between structure and property is the central organizing principle.

Crystalline metals conduct electricity because their valence electrons are delocalized. Semiconductors conduct only when electrons are excited across a band gap; the gap can be engineered by doping. Ceramics are hard and brittle because their bonding is ionic or covalent and dislocation motion is difficult. Polymers range from rigid thermosets to elastomers according to chain architecture and cross-linking. Composite materials combine phases to obtain properties unavailable in any single constituent.

Processing determines microstructure. Casting, deformation, heat treatment, thin-film deposition and additive manufacturing each produce characteristic defect populations and grain sizes. Those features control strength, toughness and functional performance. The same principles govern both traditional alloys and modern nanomaterials. Materials science is the discipline that turns the periodic table and the laws of solid-state physics into objects that can be manufactured and used.

The mechanical behavior of materials is governed by defects. Dislocations allow plastic deformation in metals at stresses far below the theoretical strength of a perfect crystal. Grain boundaries impede dislocation motion; smaller grains therefore raise the yield strength (Hall–Petch relation). Alloying, work hardening and precipitation hardening are practical methods of increasing dislocation density or of placing obstacles in their path.

Optical properties follow from the same band structure. Photons with energy greater than the gap are absorbed, doping introduces carriers and shifts the Fermi level, and the framework describes LEDs, photovoltaic cells and transistors.

Soft matter—polymers, colloids, liquid crystals—responds strongly to small forces, a subject taken up below. Biological materials are soft matter under genetic control, with the extra constraint that the structure must be grown, not merely fabricated.

### Soft Matter

Soft matter comprises materials whose mechanical response is dominated by energies comparable to thermal energy. Polymers, colloids, liquid crystals, foams and biological tissues belong to the class. Entropic forces, self-assembly and large fluctuations are characteristic. A polymer chain in solution adopts a random-walk configuration. The free energy cost of stretching is entropic. Colloidal particles interact through van der Waals, electrostatic and depletion forces. The interactions can be tuned to produce crystals, glasses or gels.

Liquid crystals possess orientational order without full positional order. They flow like liquids and respond to electric fields like crystals. The combination is the basis of display technology. Biological soft matter—cytoskeletal networks, membranes, extracellular matrix—is under active, energy-consuming control. The same physical principles operate. The additional feature is continuous energy input that maintains the system far from equilibrium. Soft matter therefore links polymer physics, colloid science and cell biology.

Polymer solutions exhibit scaling regimes. In a good solvent the chain is swollen. In a poor solvent it collapses. At the theta point the excluded-volume interaction vanishes and the chain is ideal. The osmotic pressure and the viscosity follow power laws of concentration whose exponents are predicted by scaling and confirmed by experiment.

Colloidal glasses form when the volume fraction is high enough that particles are caged by their neighbors. The glass transition is kinetic. Crystallization is thermodynamically preferred but may be suppressed by polydispersity or by rapid concentration increase. Active colloids consume energy and display collective motion absent in equilibrium systems. The same crowding and activity govern the cytoplasm. Soft-matter concepts therefore describe both synthetic materials and the interior of the cell.

### Plasma Physics

A plasma is an ionized gas in which the charged particles exhibit collective behavior. The Debye length is the distance over which electric fields are screened. When the system size greatly exceeds the Debye length the plasma description applies. Magnetic fields confine plasmas because charged particles gyrate around field lines. The gyro-radius decreases with field strength and increases with particle energy.

Fusion plasmas are confined in tokamaks and stellarators. The goal is to maintain temperatures and densities at which the fusion power exceeds the power required for heating and confinement. Instabilities—kink, ballooning, turbulence—limit the achievable parameters. In December 2022 the laser-driven National Ignition Facility released more fusion energy than its lasers delivered to the target, but no device has yet produced net electrical power. The same plasma physics governs the solar corona, the interstellar medium and laboratory discharges. The equations are those of magnetohydrodynamics supplemented by kinetic theory where collisions are rare.

Magnetohydrodynamics treats the plasma as a conducting fluid. The magnetic field is frozen into the fluid in the limit of perfect conductivity. Field lines are advected with the flow. Magnetic reconnection violates the frozen-in condition in localized regions where resistivity or kinetic effects become important. Reconnection converts magnetic energy into kinetic and thermal energy. It powers solar flares and permits changes in magnetic topology.

In fusion devices turbulence driven by temperature and density gradients transports heat and particles outward. The transport exceeds collisional predictions by orders of magnitude. Suppression of the turbulence by sheared flows or by magnetic shear is an active research goal. The same turbulent transport operates in accretion disks and in the interstellar medium. The equations are shared. The boundary conditions differ.

# <a id="part_4"></a>Part IV: Space, Time and Gravity

*Relativity, gravitational waves and black holes*

## <a id="ch_18"></a>18. The Speed of Light and Special Relativity

### The Moment the Rules Changed

In 1905 a patent clerk in Bern published a remarkable run of papers within a single year. One showed that light comes in packets. One showed that atoms are real. One showed that time and space are not what they seem. None of the papers was long. None required a large laboratory. Together they dismantled the classical picture of the world.

The clerk was not trying to be revolutionary. He was trying to remove inconsistencies. The inconsistencies would not go. Maxwell’s equations refused to tolerate a preferred frame. The photoelectric effect refused to tolerate continuous energy. Brownian motion refused to tolerate a continuum without atoms. The resolutions were simple once stated. They were not simple to accept. Acceptance took years. The years did not restore the old rules. The old rules were gone.

The episode is the clearest modern example of a quiet calculation overturning an entire ontology. It has not been the last. It remains the standard against which later revolutions are measured. Most of them have been louder. None has been cleaner.

### The Speed of Light as a Conversion Factor

The speed of light in vacuum is defined to be exactly 299 792 458 m/s. The meter is the distance light travels in 1/299 792 458 of a second. The definition makes c a conversion factor between the units of length and time rather than a quantity to be measured.

The invariance of c is a physical fact. The numerical value is a convention. Once the value is fixed, measurements of length become measurements of time and vice versa. The same convention appears in the natural units used in particle physics, where c = 1 and energies are quoted in electron-volts.

The definition does not alter any prediction of relativity. It merely chooses the units in which the invariant speed has the value 1. All measurable ratios remain unchanged. The practical advantage is that length standards can be realized by time standards, which are more stable.

### The Speed of Light and the Structure of Spacetime

The invariance of the speed of light forces the replacement of Galilean spacetime by Minkowski spacetime. The interval ds<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup>dt<sup>2</sup> − dx<sup>2</sup> − dy<sup>2</sup> − dz<sup>2</sup> is the same for every inertial observer. Surfaces of constant interval are hyperboloids. The light cone, ds = 0, bounds the causal future and past of every event.

Coordinates of different inertial frames are related by Lorentz transformations. These transformations mix space and time and leave the interval unchanged. The classical notions of absolute simultaneity and absolute time are thereby eliminated. All observable relativistic effects—time dilation, length contraction, the relativistic velocity addition law—follow from the geometry of the light cone and from the invariance of ds.

The same geometry persists locally in the presence of gravity. Global curvature modifies the relation between neighboring light cones but does not alter the local limiting speed. The invariance of c remains the structural foundation of both special and general relativity.

### The Doppler Effect

The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency caused by relative motion between source and observer. For sound the shift depends on whether the source or the observer is moving, because sound propagates in a medium. For light in vacuum the shift depends only on the relative velocity.

In the low-speed limit the fractional frequency change is v/c for both cases. At relativistic speeds the formula becomes

f = f<sub>0</sub>√((1-β)/(1+β)),

where β = v/c and the velocity is the component along the line of sight. Recession lowers the frequency; approach raises it.

The effect is measured in the spectra of stars and galaxies, in radar speed guns, and in the precise timing of pulsars. It also appears in the transverse Doppler shift, a purely relativistic time-dilation effect that has been confirmed with fast ions. The same principle underlies the cosmological redshift once the expansion of space is taken into account.

No experiment has shown a dependence of the vacuum speed of light on the speed of the source. The Doppler formula for light is therefore a direct consequence of the invariance of c.

### Aberration of Light

Aberration is the apparent displacement of a star’s position caused by the motion of the observer. The Earth moves at 30 km/s around the Sun. A telescope must therefore be tilted by an angle θ ≈ v/c in the direction of motion in order to keep the star centered. The annual change in the required tilt is the aberration ellipse.

Bradley measured the effect in 1728 and thereby determined the speed of light to within a few percent of the modern value. The same measurement demonstrated that the Earth moves. The classical formula is sufficient for the Earth’s orbital speed. At higher speeds the relativistic expression

tan θ = (sin θ′)/(γ(cos θ′+β))

must be used. The formula has been confirmed with particle beams and with precise astrometry.

Aberration is distinct from parallax. Parallax is a change in direction caused by a change in the observer’s position. Aberration is a change caused by the observer’s velocity. Both effects are present in stellar observations and must be separated.

### The Michelson–Morley Experiment

The Michelson–Morley experiment compared the speed of light in two perpendicular directions. An interferometer was floated on mercury and rotated. No shift of the interference fringes was observed at the level of sensitivity corresponding to the Earth’s orbital speed.

The null result is explained by the invariance of c. Every inertial observer measures the same speed. There is no preferred frame in which light travels at a different speed. Subsequent experiments with lasers, cryogenic resonators, and particle beams have confirmed the isotropy to better than one part in 10<sup>17</sup>.

The experiment did not disprove the existence of a medium. It showed that if a medium exists, it does not define a rest frame that can be detected by measuring the two-way speed of light. The one-way speed is fixed by convention once the two-way speed is known to be isotropic. The result remains one of the foundations of special relativity.

### The Experiment That Should Not Have Worked

In 1887 Michelson and Morley measured the speed of light in two perpendicular directions. They expected a difference. The Earth is moving. Light should take longer in the direction of motion. The difference was not there. The experiment was repeated. The difference was still not there.

The null result eliminated the luminiferous aether. It did not immediately suggest the correct replacement. Lorentz and Fitzgerald proposed length contraction as a patch. Einstein proposed that the speed of light is the same in every inertial frame and that simultaneity is relative. The proposal was not a patch. It was a replacement. The replacement survived every subsequent test.

The experiment is still cited because it is simple, decisive, and historically pivotal. Modern versions are many orders of magnitude more sensitive than the original, and the null result remains. The aether has not returned. The lesson is that a sufficiently clean null result can remove an entire theoretical structure. The structure does not always notice at once.

### Length Contraction and Time Dilation

A rod moving lengthwise relative to an observer is measured to be shorter than its proper length by the factor √(1-v<sup>2</sup>/c<sup>2</sup>). A clock moving relative to an observer is measured to run slow by the same factor. Both effects follow from the invariance of the speed of light and from the definition of simultaneity.

The proper length is the length measured in the frame in which the rod is at rest. The proper time is the time measured by a clock that travels with the object. Coordinate length and coordinate time differ from these invariants once relative motion is present. The differences have been confirmed by the extended lifetimes of fast muons, by the operation of particle accelerators, and by the frequency shifts of clocks flown in aircraft.

The effects are reciprocal. Each observer finds the other’s rods contracted and the other’s clocks slow. There is no contradiction because the observers disagree on which events are simultaneous. The invariant is the spacetime interval. All measured contractions and dilations are projections of that interval onto different axes.

### The Twin Paradox

Two twins separate. One remains on Earth. The other travels at high speed to a distant point and returns. The traveling twin ages less. The difference is the difference in proper time along the two world-lines. The stay-at-home twin follows a straight path in spacetime. The traveler follows a bent path. Along the bent path less proper time passes.

The acceleration that reverses the traveler’s velocity is not the source of the asymmetry. The asymmetry exists between any two paths that begin and end at the same events. Acceleration is needed only to make the paths meet again. Once the paths are fixed, the proper-time difference is fixed by the geometry.

The effect has been measured with atomic clocks flown around the world and with unstable particles circulating in storage rings. In every case the moving clock records less proper time. The result is a direct consequence of the invariance of the spacetime interval. It does not require general relativity.

### Mass, Energy and Momentum in Relativity

The energy and momentum of a particle form a four-vector. Its magnitude is the rest energy mc<sup>2</sup>. The relations are

E = γ mc<sup>2</sup>,    p = γ mv,    E<sup>2</sup> = p<sup>2</sup>c<sup>2</sup> + m<sup>2</sup>c<sup>4</sup>.

At low speeds the expressions reduce to the Newtonian kinetic energy and momentum plus the constant rest energy. At high speeds the energy grows without bound as v approaches c. No finite energy can accelerate a massive particle to the speed of light.

The same relations hold for systems of particles and for fields once the appropriate total four-momentum is used. Mass can be converted into other forms of energy and vice versa. The conversion is observed in particle–antiparticle annihilation, in nuclear reactions, and in the mass defect of bound systems. The factor c<sup>2</sup> is large, so macroscopic mass changes are minute except in nuclear and particle processes.

The invariant mass of a system is not the sum of the rest masses of its parts. Binding energy and relative kinetic energy contribute. The invariant mass is the magnitude of the total four-momentum. It is the quantity that is conserved in every inertial frame.

### Worked Examples: Time Dilation and Length Contraction

Example 1. A muon is created 10 km above the Earth’s surface with speed 0.998c. Its proper lifetime is 2.2 µs. Does it reach the ground?

Proper lifetime τ = 2.2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s. Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1-0.998<sup>2</sup>) ≈ 15.8. Lifetime in the Earth frame t = γτ ≈ 35 µs. Distance traveled = 0.998c × 35 × 10<sup>−6</sup> ≈ 10.4 km. The muon reaches the ground.

Example 2. A rod of proper length 1 m moves at 0.6c relative to an observer. What length does the observer measure?

γ = 1.25. Contracted length L = L<sub>0</sub>/γ = 0.8 m.

Example 3. Two events occur 3 m apart and 10 ns apart in the laboratory. Is the interval time-like or space-like?

cΔ t = 3 m. Δ x = 3 m. c<sup>2</sup>Δ t<sup>2</sup> − Δ x<sup>2</sup> = 0. The interval is null (light-like).

These calculations use only the definitions of γ and of the invariant interval. They reproduce the results measured in cosmic-ray and accelerator experiments.

### Faster than Light

Special relativity requires that no signal or causal influence travel faster than light in vacuum. The requirement follows from the invariance of the speed of light and from the demand that cause precede effect in every inertial frame. A signal that outruns light in one frame arrives before it is sent in another frame. The reversal permits closed causal loops. No consistent physics of such loops is known.

Quantum mechanics does not evade the limit. Entanglement correlates measurement outcomes. It does not transmit controllable information. The no-communication theorem shows that local operations on one subsystem cannot alter the reduced state of the other. Any protocol that appears to signal faster than light either fails when the statistics are computed correctly or relies on a classical channel that itself respects the light-speed limit.

Tachyonic fields—fields whose quanta have imaginary mass—appear in some unstable theories. They signal an instability, not a usable faster-than-light particle. The instability is removed by shifting to the true vacuum. No stable tachyon has been observed.

Group velocities greater than c occur in regions of anomalous dispersion. The signal velocity, defined by the front of a sharp pulse, remains at or below c. The apparent superluminal group velocity does not carry information outside the light cone. Experiments confirm the distinction.

No confirmed observation has shown a causal influence propagating faster than light. The light-cone structure of spacetime and the no-communication theorem remain intact. Claims to the contrary have not survived scrutiny.

### Everything Moves at the Speed of Light in Spacetime

In special relativity the four-velocity of any massive particle has constant magnitude c. The particle’s path through spacetime is parameterized by proper time. The components of the four-velocity satisfy

u<sup>μ</sup> u<sub>μ</sub> = -c<sup>2</sup>.

When the particle is at rest in a given frame, the entire four-velocity points in the time direction. When the particle moves, part of the four-velocity is spatial. The spatial speed can never reach c because the time component would then vanish and the magnitude condition would fail. The trade-off is exact. Motion through space reduces the rate at which the particle advances through coordinate time, which is the observed time dilation.

Massless particles travel on null geodesics. Their four-velocity is undefined in the same sense, but their world-lines satisfy ds = 0. They move at c through space and do not advance in proper time. The same geometric fact covers both cases: every causal trajectory is limited by the light cone, and every massive trajectory maintains a four-velocity of fixed magnitude c.

The statement is therefore not that every object races through space at light speed. It is that every object moves through spacetime at light speed. The division between the time part and the space part depends on the frame. The magnitude does not. The geometry enforces the division. Nothing massive can convert its entire motion into spatial motion. The conversion would require the time component to disappear, which the invariant interval forbids.

### Relativity Visualized

Lewis Carroll Epstein presented special relativity through diagrams in which every object moves at the speed of light through spacetime. A vertical axis is proper time. A horizontal axis is space. A particle at rest traces a vertical line. A moving particle traces a diagonal line. The length of the spacetime path between two events is the same for every traveler. Tilting a path toward the horizontal trades vertical progress for horizontal progress. The diagrams make time dilation and length contraction geometric facts rather than algebraic surprises.

In the diagram a light ray runs at 45 degrees. Any massive particle’s world-line lies inside that angle. The faster the particle moves through space, the less proper time it accumulates between two coordinate-time slices. The slowing of clocks is the reduced vertical progress. Length contraction appears when one asks for the simultaneous positions of the two ends of a moving rod. Simultaneity is a horizontal slice in the rod’s rest frame and a tilted slice in the laboratory frame. The tilted slice intersects a shorter segment of the rod’s world-tube. The contraction is the difference in the slices.

In these pictures the traveling twin’s bent path accumulates less vertical length than the straight path of the stay-at-home twin. The difference is visible as a shorter vertical projection. No acceleration is required for the comparison once both twins are reunited; the acceleration merely allows the paths to meet again. The diagram shows the result without coordinates.

Epstein’s construction does not alter the predictions of special relativity. It supplies a geometric reading in which the invariance of the spacetime interval is primary and the familiar effects are projections. The reading is pedagogically effective. It is fully equivalent to the standard algebraic treatment.

### Einstein’s Contributions

In 1905 Einstein published four papers that altered physics. The first explained the photoelectric effect by treating light as quanta of energy hν. The second gave the theory of Brownian motion and thereby a direct estimate of atomic size. The third presented the special theory of relativity. The fourth showed that mass and energy are related by E = mc<sup>2</sup>.

Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same in every inertial frame. The consequences are the relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, length contraction, and the invariance of the spacetime interval. The theory has been confirmed by particle lifetimes, by the operation of the Global Positioning System, and by every high-energy experiment.

In 1915 Einstein completed the general theory. Gravity became the curvature of spacetime itself. The Einstein field equation relates that curvature to the distribution of energy and momentum. The theory predicts the deflection of light by the Sun, the precession of Mercury’s perihelion, gravitational redshift, and gravitational waves. All have been observed. The same equation, applied to the cosmos, yields the expanding universe and the existence of black holes.

Einstein also introduced the cosmological constant, later set to zero, then restored by observation as the simplest model of dark energy. He contributed to the foundations of quantum statistics (Bose–Einstein condensation) and, with Podolsky and Rosen, formulated the argument that quantum mechanics appears incomplete. The argument led to Bell’s theorem and to experiments that confirmed the quantum predictions.

The body of work therefore spans the photoelectric effect, the atomic hypothesis, special and general relativity, the mass–energy relation, and the early critique of quantum completeness. Each part has been tested. Each remains in use.

### The Maximum Force

General relativity implies a maximum force. The value is c<sup>4</sup> / 4G, about 3 × 10<sup>43</sup> newtons. No larger force can be exerted. The same limit appears as a maximum power c<sup>5</sup> / 4G. Both follow from the requirement that the horizon of a black hole cannot be crossed by a signal and from the definition of the horizon itself.

The limit is local. It applies to the flow of energy or momentum through a surface. Distant objects can recede faster than light because the intervening space expands. The force limit does not constrain that recession. It constrains what can be done at a single place.

The limit is not an extra postulate. It is a rewriting of the content of the Einstein equation in the language of force and power. Experimental tests are indirect. They consist of the confirmed predictions of general relativity itself. No violation has been observed.

The bound is easiest to read through the hoop conjecture: a system whose energy is squeezed inside its own Schwarzschild radius forms a horizon. Try to deliver more than c<sup>4</sup>/4G through a surface and the stress-energy gathered there would already have formed one. The limit is, in effect, saturated during the last moments of black-hole mergers.

The matching bound on power is the force limit multiplied by c, about 10<sup>52</sup> W. Both limits are classical statements. Quantum corrections are expected near the Planck scale, but nothing suggests that they would remove the existence of an upper bound.

### A Table of Limits

Several of the great constants of physics can be read as limits. The speed of light is the greatest speed at which any signal or influence can travel. Planck’s constant is the smallest quantum of action, so that no process can involve less than a fixed amount of it. Boltzmann’s constant sets a smallest unit of entropy. The maximum force and maximum power of general relativity, met in the preceding sections, are limits of the same kind. Christoph Schiller’s free textbook [*Motion Mountain*](#bib_42) organizes a whole course in physics around this idea.

The limits come from different theories, and they are claims about what can be measured, not necessarily about the grain of nature itself. Together they give the Planck units, the natural scales of length, time and mass at which quantum theory and gravity must be combined. Every limit on the table has so far survived every test. A confirmed violation of any one of them would be among the most important results in the history of physics.

## <a id="ch_19"></a>19. Gravity and Curved Spacetime

### Gravitation

Newton’s law of universal gravitation states that every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The same law that makes an apple fall keeps the Moon in orbit.

The Moon falls toward the Earth continuously. Its sideways velocity is high enough that it keeps missing. The orbit is the path of continuous free fall. The same description applies to every planet around the Sun and every satellite around its planet.

The gravitational constant was measured in the laboratory by Cavendish in 1798. With it, the mass of the Earth can be calculated from the acceleration of gravity at the surface. The Earth is not a perfect sphere. It bulges at the equator because it rotates. The equatorial radius is about 21 kilometers larger than the polar radius. The difference is small but measurable.

Escape velocity is the speed needed to leave a body’s gravitational field without further propulsion. From Earth’s surface it is about 11.2 kilometers per second. From the Moon it is lower. From a black hole it exceeds the speed of light, which is why nothing can leave.

Orbits can be circles, ellipses, parabolas, or hyperbolas, depending on the energy. Closed orbits are ellipses with the central body at one focus. This was Kepler’s first law, deduced from Tycho Brahe’s observations before Newton explained why. The period of an orbit depends on the size of the orbit and the mass of the central body. That relation is used today to weigh stars, planets, and black holes.

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces, yet it dominates at large scales because it is always attractive and has infinite range. The other forces cancel or are short-ranged. General relativity refined the picture. Gravity is the curvature of spacetime. The predictions differ from Newton’s at high precision or near strong masses. For the Solar System and for most engineering, Newton’s inverse-square law is still accurate enough.

### The Equivalence of Inertial and Gravitational Mass

Galileo argued that all bodies fall with the same acceleration in the absence of air resistance. The argument is that a heavy body and a light body tied together must fall at the same rate as either alone; otherwise the combination would be inconsistent. Newton later distinguished inertial mass (the quantity that appears in F = ma) from gravitational mass (the quantity that appears in the inverse-square law). Their equality is required by the observation that all bodies fall alike.

The equality has been tested to a few parts in 10<sup>15</sup> with torsion balances, lunar laser ranging and the MICROSCOPE satellite. General relativity promotes it to a principle, described in the next section.

No composition dependence has been found. Bodies of different materials, different nuclear binding energies, and different gravitational self-energies fall at the same rate within experimental limits. The result constrains theories that attempt to modify general relativity or to introduce new long-range forces.

### The Equivalence Principle

The local effects of a gravitational field are indistinguishable from the effects of acceleration. An observer in a freely falling elevator finds that objects float. An observer in a uniformly accelerating rocket in free space finds that objects fall. No local experiment can tell the two situations apart.

The principle implies that light bends in a gravitational field and that clocks run at different rates at different heights. Both effects have been measured. The bending of light by the Sun is 1.75 arc-seconds. The fractional frequency shift between two clocks separated by height h is gh/c<sup>2</sup>.

General relativity elevates the principle to the statement that spacetime is curved. Freely falling world-lines are geodesics. The curvature is related to the distribution of energy and momentum by the Einstein equation. The equivalence principle is the local limit of that equation. It remains the conceptual foundation of the geometric theory of gravity, and it demands that every form of energy gravitate, binding energy included.

### Gravitational Redshift

A clock deeper in a gravitational potential runs slow relative to a clock higher up. The fractional shift is ΔΦ/c<sup>2</sup>, where Φ is the Newtonian potential. The effect is independent of the mechanism of the clock. It has been measured with gamma rays over a height of 22 meters, with atomic clocks over centimeters, and with the frequency standards of the Global Positioning System.

The same shift appears in the light emitted by the surface of a white dwarf or by the accretion disk of a black hole. In the Schwarzschild geometry the exact formula is √(1-2GM/rc<sup>2</sup>). At the horizon the redshift becomes infinite. No signal from the horizon itself can reach a distant observer.

The redshift is a direct consequence of the equivalence principle. It does not require the full apparatus of general relativity, only the local indistinguishability of gravity and acceleration. Its confirmation is therefore a confirmation of that principle.

### Geodesics and Free Fall

In general relativity a freely falling particle follows a geodesic—the straightest possible path in curved spacetime, and the path of extremal proper time between two events. The geodesic equation is

d<sup>2</sup>x<sup>μ</sup>/dτ<sup>2</sup> + Γ<sup>μ</sup><sub>αβ</sub>dx<sup>α</sup>/dτdx<sup>β</sup>/dτ = 0.

The Christoffel symbols Γ are determined by the metric. In the Newtonian limit the equation reduces to the ordinary acceleration g.
