Light follows null geodesics. The condition ds = 0 replaces the proper-time parameterization. The same equation therefore governs both massive particles and photons. The observed bending of light and the Shapiro delay are the integrated effects of the Christoffel symbols along the path.

No force appears in the geodesic equation. The curvature of spacetime does all the work. The Newtonian force is the low-speed, weak-field approximation to that curvature. The geometric description is exact within classical general relativity.

### Gravity as Spacetime Geometry

Newton’s law of gravity works well for most purposes. It treats gravity as a force between masses. Einstein’s general relativity replaces the force with geometry. Mass and energy curve spacetime. Objects in free fall follow the straightest available paths in that curved geometry. Those paths are called geodesics.

The equivalence principle is the starting point. In a small enough region, the effects of a uniform gravitational field cannot be distinguished from the effects of acceleration. A person standing in a closed elevator that is accelerating upward feels the same as a person standing at rest in a gravitational field. A person in free fall feels weightless, even near a massive body. The International Space Station is in free fall around Earth. Its occupants are weightless because they and the station are following the same geodesic.

What cannot be eliminated by free fall is the difference in the field across a finite distance. That difference is tidal gravity. Two apples dropped side by side fall along slightly converging paths because they are aimed at the center of the Earth. Two apples dropped one above the other separate because the lower one is deeper in the field and accelerates more. The relative acceleration of nearby free-falling objects is the operational signature of spacetime curvature. It is called geodesic deviation. On a flat geometry, parallel paths remain parallel. On a curved geometry, they converge or diverge. The same geometry that produces the tides produces the orbits of planets.

The full field equation of general relativity relates the curvature of spacetime to the distribution of energy and momentum. Pressure also contributes. For ordinary matter the pressure term is negligible. Inside a neutron star it is not. The pressure that supports the star against collapse also adds to its gravity. That feedback limits the maximum mass of a neutron star.

Light follows the geometry as well. During a solar eclipse the apparent positions of stars near the Sun’s limb are shifted by the amount predicted by the theory. The orbit of Mercury advances by an extra 43 arcseconds per century beyond the Newtonian prediction from the other planets. Clocks run slower deeper in a gravitational field. The effect is measured with atomic clocks on the ground and in orbit. GPS satellites require corrections from both special and general relativity. Without them the system would accumulate errors of kilometers per day.

The theory reduces to Newton’s law in the weak-field, low-speed limit. It departs from Newton where fields are strong or speeds are high. The departures have been measured. They match the predictions.

### The Fabric of Spacetime

Spacetime is a four-dimensional manifold, and the Einstein field equation ties its curvature to the stress-energy tensor, the bookkeeping of energy, momentum and pressure. With no energy present the geometry is flat.

The geometry is dynamic. It changes when matter moves, and its ripples, gravitational waves, travel at the speed of light and carry energy and momentum ([Chapter 21](#ch_21)). Their detection from merging black holes and neutron stars shows that spacetime is not a fixed background but a physical field.

At ordinary scales the geometry is smooth. At the Planck scale, about 10<sup>−35</sup> meters, quantum effects are expected to dominate and the classical description to fail. Candidate theories replace the smooth manifold with discrete structures, strings or other entities ([Chapter 34](#ch_34)); none has been confirmed by experiment. From the laboratory to the cosmos, the description that works is the smooth geometry of general relativity coupled to the Standard Model.

### The Einstein Equation

In compact form the field equation reads:

G<sub>μν</sub> = (8π G)/c<sup>4</sup>T<sub>μν</sub>.

The Einstein tensor G<sub>μν</sub> is built from the Ricci tensor and the scalar curvature. It is divergenceless. The energy-momentum tensor T<sub>μν</sub> is likewise divergenceless by local conservation of energy and momentum. The equation is therefore consistent.

In vacuum T<sub>μν</sub> = 0 and the equation reduces to R<sub>μν</sub> = 0. The Schwarzschild and Kerr solutions are vacuum solutions. When matter is present the equation determines the metric once an equation of state is supplied. For a perfect fluid the energy-momentum tensor is fixed by the density, the pressure, and the four-velocity.

The equation is nonlinear. The gravitational field carries energy and therefore acts as its own source. The nonlinearity is negligible in the Solar System and essential near black holes and in the early universe. No exact general solution is known. Numerical methods and perturbative expansions are used for all but the simplest cases.

### The Schwarzschild Solution

The Schwarzschild metric describes the spacetime outside a spherical, non-rotating mass. In standard coordinates it reads

ds<sup>2</sup> = -(1-2GM/rc<sup>2</sup>)c<sup>2</sup>dt<sup>2</sup> + (1-2GM/rc<sup>2</sup>)<sup>−1</sup>dr<sup>2</sup> + r<sup>2</sup>dΩ<sup>2</sup>.

The coefficient of dt<sup>2</sup> vanishes at r = 2GM/c<sup>2</sup>. That surface is the event horizon. Inside the horizon the roles of t and r interchange. Every future-directed path ends at the central singularity.

The solution predicts the correct perihelion precession of Mercury, the correct deflection of light, and the correct Shapiro time delay. It is the unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution of the Einstein equation. Any departure from spherical symmetry or from vacuum requires a different metric. For slowly rotating bodies the Kerr metric supplies the first corrections.

The horizon is a global feature. A local observer falling through it notices nothing special. The curvature invariants remain finite. Only the inability to send a signal to infinity distinguishes the interior.

### Gravitational Lensing

Mass curves spacetime and therefore deflects light. The deflection angle for a ray that passes a mass M at impact parameter b is 4GM/bc<sup>2</sup> in the weak-field limit. When the alignment is precise the deflection produces multiple images, arcs, or a complete Einstein ring.

Galaxy clusters act as lenses for background galaxies. The shapes and positions of the lensed images reconstruct the projected mass distribution of the cluster. The reconstruction includes both luminous and dark matter. The method has mapped dark-matter halos on scales from galaxies to clusters and has measured the masses of individual galaxies.

Microlensing by stars or planets produces a temporary brightening of a background source. The technique has detected exoplanets and has constrained the abundance of compact dark-matter objects. All observed lensing is consistent with general relativity. No deviation that would require a modified theory of gravity has been established.

### The Record of General Relativity

Because gravity carries energy of its own, the Einstein equation is nonlinear: the field acts as its own source. Its exact solutions include the Schwarzschild and Kerr black holes, the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker cosmologies of [Chapter 31](#ch_31), and gravitational waves.

The equivalence principle, gravitational redshift, light deflection, the Shapiro delay, frame-dragging and the decay of the binary pulsar all agree with the predictions, and gravitational-wave signals match the waveforms computed by numerical relativity. The theory fails at singularities and, in its present form, cannot be combined with quantum mechanics. No observational trace of quantum corrections has been found. Wherever curvature is not extreme, the classical theory is the standard description of gravity.

## <a id="ch_20"></a>20. Relativity at Work: GPS and Beyond

### GPS and Relativity

The Global Positioning System determines position by measuring the travel time of radio signals from satellites whose locations are known. The required timing accuracy is a few nanoseconds. At that precision both special-relativistic and general-relativistic effects are large enough to matter.

The net effect is that satellite clocks advance by roughly 38 microseconds per day relative to ground clocks. Left alone, the drift would ruin navigation within minutes. The correction is applied by offsetting the satellite clock frequency before launch and by continuous relativistic modeling in the receiver software.

The 38-microsecond daily advance of the satellite clocks is the sum of two opposing effects. The special-relativistic slowing is 1/2 v<sup>2</sup>/c<sup>2</sup>. With v = 3.9 km/s the fractional shift is -8.3 × 10<sup>−11</sup>, or −7.2 µs per day. The general-relativistic speeding is ΔΦ/c<sup>2</sup>. The gravitational potential difference between the Earth’s surface and the GPS orbital radius (26 600 km) produces +5.3 × 10<sup>−10</sup>, or +45.6 µs per day. The algebraic sum is +38.4 µs per day.

A constant frequency offset of −4.465 parts in 10<sup>10</sup> is applied to the satellite clocks before launch. The offset cancels the average relativistic rate difference. Residual variations caused by orbital eccentricity are calculated in the receiver from the broadcast ephemeris and removed in real time. The eccentricity term can reach several tens of nanoseconds and must be included if meter-level accuracy is required.

Without any relativistic correction the range error would accumulate at 11 km per day. After one minute the error would already exceed 7 m—larger than the nominal accuracy of the civil signal. The corrections are therefore not optional refinements. They are part of the basic operation of the system.

The same satellites provide a continuous test. The clock rates measured by the ground segment match the predicted combination of special- and general-relativistic shifts to within the stability of the clocks themselves (parts in 10<sup>13</sup> or better). Independent experiments with hydrogen masers flown on aircraft and with optical clocks compared over height differences of a few tens of centimeters have confirmed the same formulae at still higher precision. GPS is simply the most widely used realization of those formulae.

### Worked Examples: GPS Clock Corrections

Example 1. If the relativistic offset were left uncorrected, how large a ranging error would accumulate in one hour?

38.4 µs per day is 1.6 µs per hour. Light travels 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup> × 1.6 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s ≈ 480 m in that time, so the position error would grow by nearly half a kilometer every hour.

Example 2. A satellite orbits with eccentricity 0.02. What is the maximum additional relativistic clock correction?

The eccentricity term has amplitude 2√(GMa) e/c<sup>2</sup> ≈ 2.3 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s × e. For e = 0.02 that is about 46 ns, which corresponds to a range error of roughly 14 m if it is not applied.

Example 3. After 10 years of continuous operation, by how much would an uncorrected satellite clock have drifted relative to ground time?

38.4 µs day<sup>−1</sup> × 365.25 × 10 ≈ 0.140 s. Corresponding range error ≈ 42 000 km, larger than the GPS constellation itself.

The numerical values are those used in the actual GPS interface specifications. The system would be unusable without them.

### Other Practical Consequences of Relativity

Particle accelerators must include relativistic mass increase and time dilation in their design. The Large Hadron Collider accelerates protons to 0.999999991 c. The relativistic energy is 7 TeV while the rest energy is only 0.938 GeV. Magnets, radio-frequency cavities and beam-lifetime calculations all use the relativistic relations. Without them the machine would not function.

Muon storage rings measure the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. The muons are born polarized and decay preferentially along their spin direction. Because of time dilation they live long enough to circle the ring thousands of times. The observed precession frequency matches the prediction of quantum electrodynamics only when the relativistic kinematics are correctly included.

Commercial airline crews accumulate measurable extra proper time relative to ground personnel because of the combined velocity and gravitational shifts. The difference is a few microseconds per intercontinental flight—detectable with modern atomic clocks but irrelevant to human aging. The same calculation applied to a hypothetical high-speed interplanetary craft shows that the travelers would return younger than their stay-at-home twins by amounts that grow rapidly once v exceeds a few tenths of c.

In every case the corrections are quantitative, confirmed, and indispensable once the relevant precision or energy is reached. Relativity is not confined to exotic regimes. It is embedded in the everyday infrastructure of navigation, high-energy physics and precision time-keeping.

## <a id="ch_21"></a>21. Gravitational Waves

A gravitational wave is a ripple in the curvature of spacetime that propagates at the speed of light. It is produced by any accelerating mass quadrupole. The strongest sources are the mergers of black holes and neutron stars.

The waves stretch and compress space transversely. A ring of free particles is deformed into an ellipse that oscillates at the wave frequency. The strain is minute. For a stellar-mass merger at cosmological distance the fractional change in length is of order 10<sup>−21</sup>.

Laser interferometers have detected dozens of such events. The waveforms match the predictions of general relativity. The arrival of gravitational waves from a neutron-star merger coincided with a gamma-ray burst and with an optical transient, confirming that the waves travel at c to high precision.

The detections open a new observational window. They measure the masses and spins of black holes, the equation of state of neutron-star matter, and the expansion rate of the universe. Future detectors will extend the reach to the entire observable volume and to lower frequencies.

The strain amplitude of a gravitational wave from a binary merger scales as the chirp mass to the five-thirds power and inversely as the luminosity distance. Matched filtering against theoretical templates extracts the signal from detector noise. The templates are computed from the post-Newtonian expansion and from numerical relativity.

The first detection, GW150914, was a binary black-hole merger roughly 400 megaparsecs away, in which about three solar masses were radiated away as gravitational waves in a fraction of a second. Later events include black-hole pairs far heavier than expected and binary neutron stars. The catalog now holds well over two hundred events, and the masses, spins and local expansion rate are measured from them. The gravitational-wave window is independent of electromagnetic radiation.

### The Signal That Traveled for a Billion Years

In 2015 a gravitational-wave detector in Louisiana twitched. A second detector in Washington twitched 7 milliseconds later. The twitches matched the waveform of two black holes spiraling together and merging. The black holes were 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal had been traveling since before animals existed. It arrived on a September morning.

The detectors had been built to measure a change in length of one part in 10<sup>21</sup>. That is a fraction of the diameter of a proton across a 4-kilometer arm. The change was detected. The waveform matched the prediction of general relativity to high precision. No other known process produces that waveform. The black holes merged. The waves crossed the universe. The mirrors moved. The movement was recorded.

The event was the first direct detection of gravitational waves and the first observation of a binary black-hole merger. It was also a demonstration that a prediction made a century earlier, about a distortion of spacetime too small to imagine, could be turned into a recorded trace. The trace is now routine. It was not routine that morning.

### The Stochastic Gravitational-Wave Background

A stochastic gravitational-wave background is the superposition of unresolved sources. Astrophysical backgrounds arise from binary mergers across cosmic history. Cosmological backgrounds can arise from inflation, from phase transitions or from cosmic strings. The two classes are distinguished by their spectra and by their anisotropy.

Pulsar timing arrays are sensitive to the nanohertz band. Ground-based detectors are sensitive to the audio band. Space-based detectors will cover the millihertz band. A detection in any band constrains the source population. A detection of a cosmological background would probe physics at energies far above those accessible to colliders. No such cosmological background has been confirmed. The astrophysical background from binaries is expected and may already have been seen.

### How a Gravitational-Wave Detector Works

The LIGO detectors in Hanford, Washington, and Livingston, Louisiana, are L-shaped, with arms four kilometers long. A laser beam is split, sent down both arms and reflected back from mirrors, and the two beams are recombined. If the arms have the same length, the light waves cancel at the detector. A passing gravitational wave stretches one arm while squeezing the other, and a trace of light gets through. The change in length to be detected is about a thousandth of the width of a proton.

Reaching that sensitivity took decades. The mirrors, each weighing 40 kilograms, hang from multi-stage suspensions to isolate them from ground vibration. The laser light is bounced back and forth hundreds of times to lengthen the effective arm. The whole apparatus sits in one of the largest ultra-high vacuums ever built, and the instrument is now so quiet that quantum noise in the light itself limits it, which is partly reduced with squeezed light.

Detectors in Italy (Virgo) and Japan (KAGRA) work with LIGO, so that signals can be located on the sky by their arrival times. The 2017 Nobel Prize went to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne for the founding of LIGO. A space-based detector, LISA, is planned for the 2030s to detect waves of much lower frequency.

### The Binary Pulsar: Waves Before Detection

Direct detection came in 2015, but the case for gravitational waves was already strong. In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a pulsar orbiting another neutron star, and the timing of its pulses allowed the orbit to be measured with extraordinary precision. General relativity predicted that such a system should lose energy as gravitational waves and that the stars should spiral together, shortening the orbital period by a small, calculable amount.

Decades of observation showed that the orbit shrinks exactly as predicted, to better than one percent. It was an indirect proof that the waves carry off energy, and Hulse and Taylor received the Nobel Prize in 1993. The two stars will merge in about 300 million years, and the merger will resemble, at far higher frequencies, the events LIGO now detects in other systems.

The story shows how a prediction can be confirmed long before it can be observed directly. It also shows why the direct detection mattered. It opened a new window, allowing the strongest events in the universe, mergers of black holes, to be heard as well as inferred.

## <a id="ch_22"></a>22. Black Holes

### What a Black Hole Is

A black hole is a region of spacetime from which no signal can reach distant observers. The boundary of the region is the event horizon. In the Schwarzschild solution the horizon lies at the radius r<sub>s</sub> = 2GM/c<sup>2</sup>, which is about 3 km for a solar-mass object. Once inside the horizon, every path forward leads to the central singularity.

The sections that follow take up how such objects form and shine, what their horizons are like, how they can be described with temperature and entropy, and the unresolved question of what becomes of information that falls in.

No observation contradicts the general-relativistic description of the exterior. The interior, the singularity, and the ultimate fate of the information remain outside present experimental reach.

### Horizons, Tides and the Singularity

The event horizon is not a material surface. It is the set of points beyond which all future-directed paths remain inside. Nothing of ordinary density is compressed to the Schwarzschild radius: for the Sun it is about three kilometers, for the Earth about nine millimeters. Only stellar cores above the maximum mass of a neutron star can collapse past that point.

Once an object crosses the horizon, the geometry prevents escape. Tidal forces become extreme near a small black hole. They stretch an object along the radial direction and compress it transversely. For a supermassive black hole the horizon is so large that the tidal forces at the horizon itself are mild. The singularity, where curvature becomes infinite according to classical general relativity, lies in the future of any observer who crosses the horizon.

### Black-Hole Thermodynamics

A black hole has a temperature and an entropy. The temperature is the Hawking temperature

T = (ħ c<sup>3</sup>)/(8π GMk<sub>B</sub>).

The entropy is the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy

S = k<sub>B</sub>c<sup>3</sup>A/4Għ,

where A is the area of the horizon. Both quantities follow from the combination of general relativity, quantum field theory, and thermodynamics.

The temperature is inversely proportional to the mass. A solar-mass hole has a temperature of about 60 nanokelvin, colder than the microwave background, so it absorbs more than it emits. Only a hole lighter than roughly 4.5 × 10<sup>22</sup> kg, about the mass of the Moon, is hotter than the background and loses mass; one lighter than a few times 10<sup>11</sup> kg would already have evaporated. The emission is thermal, following a black-body curve at the Hawking temperature.

The entropy is proportional to the horizon area, not to the volume. The proportionality suggests that the fundamental degrees of freedom of a black hole reside on its surface. The same area law appears in the holographic principle. No complete microscopic accounting of the entropy is known for a generic black hole. For certain extremal holes in string theory the counting of microstates reproduces the area law.

The four laws of black-hole mechanics are formally identical to the laws of thermodynamics. The zeroth law states that surface gravity is constant over the horizon of a stationary black hole. The first law relates changes in mass, area, angular momentum and charge. The second law states that the horizon area never decreases in classical processes. The third law states that surface gravity cannot be reduced to zero in a finite number of operations.

Hawking radiation supplies the missing identification. Surface gravity is proportional to temperature. Area is proportional to entropy. With those identifications the laws become the ordinary laws of thermodynamics applied to black holes. The generalized second law asserts that the sum of black-hole entropy and the entropy of matter outside the hole never decreases. The law has been verified in a variety of thought experiments and is required for consistency.

For a solar-mass hole the entropy is enormous, about 10<sup>77</sup> k<sub>B</sub>. The thermodynamic description is robust even though the microscopic accounting is not.

### Black Holes in Astrophysics

Stellar-mass black holes form in the collapse of massive stars and grow by accretion and by mergers. Supermassive black holes, millions to billions of solar masses, occupy the centers of most large galaxies.

Gravitational-wave detectors have recorded the mergers of stellar-mass black holes. The waveforms match the numerical solutions of the Einstein equation.

Matter falling toward a black hole forms an accretion disk. Viscosity transports angular momentum outward and allows the gas to spiral inward. The released gravitational energy heats the disk and can power quasars and X-ray binaries. The efficiency of conversion of rest mass to radiation can exceed 10 percent, higher than nuclear fusion.

No information about the interior can reach an external observer, and the classical theory ends at the singularity, where a quantum description will be needed. The exterior geometry is nevertheless accurately described by the Kerr or Schwarzschild solution.

### Black-Hole Imaging

The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of the supermassive black hole in M87 and later the shadow in Sgr A*. The shadow diameter is approximately five times the Schwarzschild radius for a non-spinning hole. The measured diameter agrees with the prediction of general relativity given the independently measured mass and distance. The image is formed by strong gravitational lensing of emission from the accretion flow.

The observations constrain deviations from the Kerr metric. They do not yet measure the spin with high precision. Polarization maps the magnetic field near the horizon. The field is ordered. The observations confirm that the object is consistent with a black hole. They do not prove the existence of an event horizon. They are the highest-resolution test of strong-field gravity yet performed.

### Primordial Black Holes

Primordial black holes could have formed from large density perturbations in the early universe. Their masses can range from the Planck mass to many solar masses. They are constrained by the absence of evaporation signals, by microlensing, by dynamical effects and by the gravitational-wave background. In most mass windows they can constitute only a fraction of the dark matter.

The window near asteroid masses remains less constrained. A detection would constitute both a dark-matter candidate and a probe of the primordial power spectrum on small scales. No confirmed detection exists. The possibility is not excluded. It is tightly bounded.

### The Black-Hole Interior

The interior of a black hole is the region behind the event horizon. In classical general relativity it is causally disconnected from the exterior. In the quantum theory the disconnection is not absolute. The island calculations assign part of the interior to the entanglement wedge of the exterior radiation after the Page time. The assignment is state-dependent.

An infalling observer encounters a smooth geometry in the semi-classical approximation. The approximation fails near the singularity and, possibly, at the horizon of an old black hole. The failure at the horizon is the firewall question. No consensus exists. The interior is both a region of classical spacetime and a quantum system whose degrees of freedom are shared with the exterior. The sharing is the content of the island formula. Its implications for the experience of the infalling observer remain under debate.

### Singularities and Chronology Protection

The Penrose–Hawking singularity theorems show that, under general conditions, gravitational collapse and cosmological expansion produce incomplete geodesics. Classical general relativity predicts its own breakdown. The theorems assume the null energy condition and the existence of a trapped surface or a cosmological focusing condition. Both are satisfied in realistic collapse and in the hot early universe. The classical theory therefore cannot be the final description.

Hawking also examined the possibility of closed timelike curves. A closed timelike curve would let a traveler come back to the very event of departure. He conjectured that the laws of physics prevent their formation. The conjecture is called chronology protection. Quantum effects near a would-be chronology horizon produce a divergent stress-energy tensor. The back-reaction is expected to destroy the horizon before closed timelike curves appear. The argument is plausible but unproven. No confirmed example of a chronology-violating spacetime is known. The protection, if it holds, keeps the causal structure of the observed universe intact.

### Wormholes

A wormhole is a hypothetical tunnel connecting two distant regions of spacetime. In the simplest mathematical models the tunnel is held open by matter that violates the null energy condition. Ordinary matter does not. Quantum fields can violate the condition locally and briefly. Whether they can do so on the scale and for the duration needed to keep a macroscopic wormhole open is unknown.

No wormhole has been observed. General relativity permits the solutions. It does not require them. Traversable wormholes would allow shortcuts between distant points and, in some arrangements, closed timelike curves. Closed timelike curves permit paths that return to the same event. They raise consistency problems. Proposals that prevent their formation or that render them unstable exist. None is confirmed.

The existence of wormholes is therefore an open question in classical and quantum gravity. They are not required by any confirmed observation. They are not forbidden by the present form of the field equations when exotic matter is allowed. Until a quantum theory of gravity is established, or until an observation demands them, they remain mathematical possibilities without empirical support.

### Wormholes and Entanglement

Not every wormhole needs exotic matter to exist on paper. Non-traversable ones appear in the maximally extended Schwarzschild geometry, joining two asymptotic regions through a throat that pinches off faster than any signal could cross it.

Quantum versions—entanglement wormholes or ER=EPR—identify certain entangled states with non-traversable wormholes. The identification is precise in anti-de Sitter space. It supplies a geometric picture of entanglement. It does not yield a shortcut for signaling. The wormhole remains non-traversable.

Their theoretical interest lies less in travel than in the connection they suggest between geometry and entanglement, and in the constraints they place on energy conditions. Both topics remain active, and neither has produced a confirmed macroscopic wormhole.

## <a id="ch_23"></a>23. Hawking Radiation and the Vacuum

### Hawking Radiation

Hawking radiation is the thermal flux emitted by a black hole. It arises when quantum fields propagate on the curved spacetime of a collapsing body. The spectrum seen by a distant observer is thermal at the temperature

T = (ħ c<sup>3</sup>)/(8π G M k<sub>B</sub>).

Heavier holes are colder. A solar-mass hole radiates at about 60 nanokelvin, far below the cosmic microwave background. A hole of about 5 × 10<sup>11</sup> kg has a temperature near 2 × 10<sup>11</sup> K and a lifetime close to the present age of the universe.

The radiation carries energy, angular momentum and charge. It reduces the mass of the hole. The final stage of evaporation is unknown. It has not been observed directly. Without it, black-hole thermodynamics would contradict the ordinary second law.

### How Hawking Found the Radiation

Hawking announced the result in 1974. Bekenstein had argued that a black hole should carry entropy proportional to its horizon area, and Hawking at first resisted, because an object with entropy must have a temperature and therefore must radiate. His own calculation, which joins quantum field theory to the geometry of a collapsing star, showed that the radiation is real.

The popular picture of virtual pairs split by the horizon, with one partner escaping, is a heuristic for the mismatch between vacuum modes described elsewhere, not a literal account of the calculation.

The result implies that black holes have a temperature and, by the first law, an entropy equal to one quarter of the horizon area in Planck units. The derivation links gravity, quantum mechanics and thermodynamics, which is why it is treated as a landmark although the radiation from an astrophysical hole has never been observed.

### Derivation and Thermodynamics of Hawking Radiation

Hawking radiation follows from the mismatch between the vacuum defined at past null infinity and the vacuum defined at future null infinity when a horizon is present. Modes that cross the horizon during collapse become entangled. Tracing over the interior partner leaves the exterior mode in a thermal state. The temperature measured at infinity is T = ħκ/(2π k<sub>B</sub> c), where κ is the surface gravity. For a Schwarzschild hole κ = c<sup>4</sup>/(4GM) and the familiar expression T = ħ c<sup>3</sup>/(8π GMk<sub>B</sub>) is recovered.

The same temperature appears in the Euclidean path integral. The metric continued to imaginary time is regular at the horizon only when the period is 2π/κ. That period is precisely the inverse temperature of a thermal state. The agreement of the Lorentzian mode analysis and the Euclidean periodicity confirms that the radiation is thermal.

Energy conservation requires that the hole lose mass as it radiates. The luminosity scales as 1/M<sup>2</sup>. The heat capacity is negative: as the hole loses mass its temperature rises and the evaporation accelerates. The process continues until the semi-classical approximation fails near the Planck mass. The flux satisfies the thermodynamic laws of black holes: area increase, constant surface gravity on the horizon, and the first law relating mass, area and angular momentum.

### The Unruh Effect

The Unruh effect is the prediction that a uniformly accelerating observer in the Minkowski vacuum will detect a thermal bath of particles. The temperature is T = (ħ a)/(2π k<sub>B</sub> c), where a is the proper acceleration. The effect is a consequence of the mismatch between the Minkowski vacuum and the Rindler vacuum associated with the accelerating observer’s horizon.

The Unruh effect is conceptually important because it shows that the particle content of a quantum field is observer-dependent and because it is formally related to Hawking radiation.

Reaching a temperature of 1 K would take an acceleration of order 10<sup>20</sup> m s<sup>−2</sup>, far beyond anything macroscopic objects experience. Electrons in the focus of the most intense lasers approach the regime, which is why proposed tests look for a faint thermal signature in their response. No conclusive detection has been reported.

The analogy with Hawking radiation is exact in the semiclassical limit. Both come from comparing the vacuum defined by inertial modes with the vacuum defined by modes tied to a horizon, here the Rindler horizon of the accelerating observer. Both also rest on entanglement between modes on either side of that horizon.

### Quantum Foam

Wheeler suggested that spacetime at the Planck scale is not smooth. Geometry fluctuates, and the uncertainty principle applied to the metric makes the fluctuations of order one at lengths near 10<sup>−35</sup> m. The fluctuations are large enough that the classical manifold description fails. He called the fluctuating geometry quantum foam. Virtual black holes, wormholes, and changes of topology appear and disappear on timescales of the Planck time. The average geometry over larger scales remains the smooth spacetime of general relativity.

No direct observation of the foam exists. Particle accelerators reach energies many orders of magnitude below the Planck energy. Indirect limits come from the absence of certain effects that large fluctuations would produce: dispersion of light from distant sources, or violations of Lorentz invariance. The limits constrain the size of the fluctuations but do not rule out a foamy structure at the Planck length.

The idea is a qualitative expectation from combining general relativity and quantum mechanics. A full quantum theory of gravity would replace the expectation with a definite spectrum of fluctuations or with a different microstructure. Until that theory exists, quantum foam remains a plausible picture of the short-distance regime and an untested one.

## <a id="ch_24"></a>24. The Black-Hole Information Question

### The Information Question

Hawking radiation is thermal, and a thermal spectrum is determined by temperature alone. It contains no information about the matter that formed the black hole. If the hole evaporates completely, the information appears to be lost. Quantum mechanics requires unitary evolution. Information should be preserved. The conflict is the information question.

Hawking initially concluded that information is destroyed. Later calculations and the AdS/CFT correspondence suggested that it is preserved. The radiation is not exactly thermal. Subtle correlations among successive quanta can, in principle, encode the initial state. The correlations are exponentially small until the final stages of evaporation. Recovering them is impractical. Their existence would restore unitarity.

No consensus exists on the detailed mechanism. Proposals include remnants, information return in the late radiation, and modifications of the horizon itself. The question remains open. It is a precise conflict between the semiclassical calculation and the requirement of unitary quantum evolution. Its resolution is expected to constrain any quantum theory of gravity.

### The Page Curve and the Paradox

A black hole that forms from a pure quantum state and evaporates completely into thermal radiation appears to leave behind a mixed state. The map from pure to mixed states is non-unitary. Unitarity is a fundamental requirement of quantum mechanics. The conflict is the information paradox.

The paradox becomes acute for an old black hole. Once more than half the initial entropy has been radiated, the remaining black hole has less entropy than the radiation already emitted. If the evaporation continues to be thermal, the total state cannot purify. The Page curve—the entanglement entropy of the radiation—must therefore rise and then fall if unitarity is to be preserved. A purely thermal spectrum produces a curve that rises indefinitely.

Recent calculations that include quantum extremal surfaces reproduce a Page curve that turns over. The island formula assigns part of the black-hole interior to the entanglement wedge of the radiation after the Page time. The result suggests that information is released in subtle correlations and that the final state is pure. The calculations have been performed in simplified models and in low-dimensional gravity. Their extension to realistic, asymptotically flat black holes is incomplete.

Alternative proposals include remnants that store the information, modifications of the radiation at late times, and non-unitary evolution. None is free of difficulties. The island calculations are the first to recover the Page curve from a semi-classical gravitational path integral. They indicate that the paradox may be resolved without abandoning unitarity or introducing new degrees of freedom beyond those already present in quantum gravity. A fully controlled demonstration for an evaporating four-dimensional black hole does not yet exist.

### Black-Hole Complementarity

Black-hole complementarity is the proposal that the descriptions of physics given by an observer who remains outside a black hole and by an observer who falls in are both valid, yet cannot be compared by any single observer. The external observer sees infalling matter approach the horizon asymptotically, thermalize, and eventually return as Hawking radiation. The infalling observer crosses the horizon without drama and encounters the matter in a perfectly regular spacetime region. No experiment accessible to either observer reveals a contradiction.

The principle was introduced to reconcile unitarity of the exterior evolution with the equivalence principle at the horizon. It asserts that the two accounts are complementary in the same sense that position and momentum are complementary: both are correct, but they cannot be simultaneously sharp for the same observer. Information that has crossed the horizon is, for the external observer, encoded in the radiation; for the infalling observer it remains in the interior. Because the observers cannot communicate after the horizon is crossed, no direct conflict arises.

Complementarity faces difficulties once the black hole is old. An external observer who collects the early radiation and then jumps in can, in principle, meet the same quantum information both outside and inside, violating the no-cloning theorem. The firewall argument sharpens the tension: preservation of exterior unitarity appears to require a high-energy barrier at the horizon that would destroy an infalling observer. Complementarity alone does not resolve the conflict.

Later developments—entanglement wedges, islands, and the Page curve—modify the original picture. They suggest that the interior degrees of freedom are not independent of the exterior radiation after the Page time. The complementarity of the two descriptions survives in a weakened form, but the precise location of the information and the experience of the infalling observer remain model-dependent. Complementarity is therefore a useful organizing idea whose detailed implementation is still incomplete.

### Firewalls

The firewall argument states that unitarity, the equivalence principle and effective field theory outside the horizon cannot all be maintained for an old black hole. If the late radiation is entangled with the early radiation, as unitarity requires, and the horizon is a smooth vacuum, as the equivalence principle requires, then each late mode would have to be entangled both with the early radiation and with its interior partner. Monogamy of entanglement forbids that. One of the three assumptions must fail, and a firewall, a high-energy barrier at the horizon, is what preserves unitarity at the cost of the equivalence principle.

The argument has not been resolved. Island calculations suggest that the interior is not independent of the exterior radiation after the Page time. The suggestion softens the conflict. It does not eliminate it for all observers. The firewall remains a possible outcome. It is not required by present calculations. The tension between unitarity and smoothness is real. Its resolution is model-dependent.

### Replica Wormholes

Replica wormholes are saddle points of the gravitational path integral that compute the entanglement entropy. They connect the replicas of the radiation through the black-hole interior. Their contribution dominates after the Page time. The dominance produces the turnover of the Page curve. The wormholes are not traversable. They are a calculational device.

The same saddles appear in the calculation of the purity and of higher Rényi entropies. They are required for consistency with unitarity. Their existence in the path integral is a consequence of the Euclidean gravitational action. It does not imply that an observer can travel through them. The wormholes resolve the entropy calculation. They do not by themselves resolve the experience of the infalling observer.

### The Island Formula

The island formula computes the entanglement entropy of the radiation as the minimum of the generalized entropy of a region that includes an island inside the black hole. The formula is S = min ( (Area(∂ I))/4G<sub>N</sub> + S<sub>matter</sub>(R ∪ I) ). The minimum is taken over islands I. After the Page time the minimum includes a non-empty island. The formula reproduces the Page curve.

It has been derived from the replica trick in gravitational path integrals. It applies to evaporating black holes in anti-de Sitter space and in certain flat-space models. Its validity for realistic astrophysical black holes is assumed but not proven. The formula is the sharpest present statement of how information escapes. It remains a semi-classical expression.

### Quantum Extremal Surfaces

A quantum extremal surface is a surface that extremizes the generalized entropy. It reduces to the ordinary Ryu–Takayanagi surface when the bulk entropy is negligible. When the bulk entropy is large the surface moves. In the island calculation the quantum extremal surface lies inside the horizon after the Page time. Its area plus the bulk entropy of the island and the radiation gives the Page curve.

The surface is a generalization of the classical extremal surface. It incorporates the leading quantum correction. Higher-order corrections exist. They are small in the semi-classical limit. The concept unifies the classical area term with the bulk entanglement. It is the geometric object that appears in the island formula and in the derivation of the Page curve.

### The Information Paradox in AdS/CFT

In AdS/CFT the formation and evaporation of a black hole is dual to the unitary evolution of a thermal state in the boundary theory. Unitarity is therefore guaranteed. The paradox becomes the question of how the bulk calculation reproduces the unitary result. The island formula and the replica wormhole provide the bulk mechanism. They modify the entropy calculation after the Page time.

The resolution is explicit in low-dimensional models and in certain supersymmetric theories. Its extension to higher-dimensional, asymptotically flat black holes is not complete. The AdS/CFT example demonstrates that a unitary resolution is possible within a consistent theory of quantum gravity. It does not yet supply the resolution for the black holes that form in our universe.

### The Holographic Principle

The holographic principle states that the information content of a spatial region is bounded by the area of its boundary, not by its volume. The bound is saturated by a black hole: the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy is proportional to the horizon area measured in Planck units. The principle therefore asserts that a black hole is the maximum-entropy object of a given size.

Its strongest realization is the AdS/CFT correspondence, described next.

In asymptotically flat space or in de Sitter space no equally precise duality is known. The principle is nevertheless used as a guide. It suggests that the degrees of freedom of quantum gravity are nonlocal and that locality itself is an approximate, emergent notion. It also supplies an upper limit on the entropy that can be stored in any region, a limit already respected by all known physical systems.

No direct experimental test exists. The principle remains a theoretical constraint inferred from black-hole thermodynamics and from the structure of gauge/gravity duality. Its ultimate scope—whether it governs every consistent quantum theory of gravity—is still open.

### The AdS/CFT Correspondence

The AdS/CFT correspondence is an exact duality between a theory of quantum gravity in (d+1)-dimensional anti-de Sitter space and a conformal field theory in d dimensions that lives on the boundary of that space. The best-studied example equates type-IIB string theory on AdS<sub>5</sub> × S<sup>5</sup> with N=4 super-Yang–Mills theory in four dimensions.

Bulk fields are dual to boundary operators. The mass of a bulk field fixes the conformal dimension of the dual operator. Correlation functions computed by Witten diagrams in the bulk equal correlation functions computed by Feynman diagrams in the boundary theory. The dictionary extends to finite temperature: a black hole in AdS is dual to a thermal state in the CFT. The Bekenstein–Hawking entropy equals the thermal entropy of the boundary theory.

Real-time dynamics, transport coefficients and far-from-equilibrium evolution can likewise be mapped between the two sides.

The duality is a conjecture supported by a large number of matching calculations. It has not been proved in full generality. It applies strictly to anti-de Sitter asymptotics. Its conceptual importance lies in the demonstration that a higher-dimensional gravitational theory can be exactly equivalent to a lower-dimensional quantum field theory without gravity, and that spacetime geometry can emerge from quantum entanglement.

### Holography and Entanglement

The Ryu–Takayanagi formula equates the entanglement entropy of a boundary region with the area of a bulk minimal surface. The formula has been verified in many examples. It suggests that spacetime geometry is encoded in the entanglement structure of the boundary theory. In anti-de Sitter space the statement is exact. Its extension to other asymptotics is incomplete.

Entanglement wedge reconstruction shows that bulk operators inside the wedge can be represented as boundary operators. The reconstruction is state-dependent for operators behind horizons. The dependence is consistent with the island calculations of black-hole evaporation. Holography therefore supplies both a definition of quantum gravity in certain spacetimes and a concrete realization of the idea that geometry emerges from entanglement.

# <a id="part_5"></a>Part V: Planets, Stars and Galaxies

*From our own Solar System out to other stars and the galaxies that hold them*

## <a id="ch_25"></a>25. The Solar System

The Sun is an ordinary star, a ball of hot gas about 1.4 million kilometers across, held together by its own gravity and powered by the fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core. It contains more than 99 percent of the mass of the Solar System. Everything else—planets, moons, asteroids, comets—is debris left from the cloud that formed it about 4.6 billion years ago.

The planets fall into two groups. The inner four are small and rocky: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. The outer four are large and gaseous or icy: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Pluto, once counted as a planet, is now classified as a dwarf planet, one of many icy bodies beyond Neptune.

Mercury is the smallest and closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere, a heavily cratered surface, and extreme temperature swings. Venus is similar to Earth in size but utterly different in condition. A thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide produces a runaway greenhouse effect. Surface temperatures exceed 460 degrees Celsius, and the pressure is about ninety times that at Earth’s surface. Probes that landed there survived only briefly.

Earth is the one planet known to have liquid water on its surface and life. Its Moon is unusually large relative to the planet. The leading account of the Moon’s origin is a giant impact early in the Solar System’s history, which threw debris into orbit that then gathered into the Moon. The Moon’s distance is about 384,000 kilometers, a figure first estimated reasonably by Greek astronomers and refined ever since.

Mars is smaller than Earth, cold, and thin-aired. Orbiters and rovers have mapped ancient river valleys, lakebeds, and minerals that form in water. Liquid water is not stable on the surface today. Ice exists at the poles and underground. Whether Mars ever had life remains open. No confirmed evidence has been found.

Jupiter is the largest planet, more massive than all the others combined. It is mostly hydrogen and helium, with a small rocky core. Its Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has persisted for centuries. Jupiter has dozens of moons. The four largest—Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto—were seen by Galileo in 1610. Io is volcanically active. Europa has a subsurface ocean under ice.

Saturn is known for its rings, which are made of ice and rock particles, mostly close to the planet. It too is a gas giant with many moons. Titan, the largest, has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane. Enceladus vents water from a subsurface ocean.

Uranus and Neptune are ice giants, smaller than Jupiter and Saturn, rich in water, ammonia, and methane ices as well as hydrogen and helium. Uranus rotates on its side. Neptune has the strongest winds in the Solar System. Both have ring systems and moons. Triton, Neptune’s largest moon, orbits backward and is geologically active.

Asteroids are rocky bodies, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy bodies from farther out. When a comet approaches the Sun, ice vaporizes and forms a tail. Meteorites that reach Earth are samples of these smaller bodies. Some are primitive material from the early Solar System. Their ages, measured by radioactive dating, confirm that the system formed about 4.56 billion years ago.

The planets were visited by robotic probes beginning in the 1960s. Every planet has now been studied at close range. Samples have been returned from the Moon, from asteroids, and from a comet. The picture that emerged is more varied than the one available in the 1980s, and still incomplete in its details. The formation process—a disk of gas and dust around a young star, grains sticking together, cores growing, gas giants capturing envelopes before the gas dispersed—is the working account. It fits the evidence from our system and from the disks now seen around other young stars.

### The Collision That Made the Moon

Four and a half billion years ago a body the size of Mars struck the Earth. The impact melted both. Debris was thrown into orbit. Most of the iron had already sunk into the Earth’s core, so the debris was rocky. It gathered into the Moon. The whole event lasted hours. The consequences are still here.

The Moon stabilizes the Earth’s obliquity. Without it the tilt would wander chaotically. Seasons would be unpredictable. The impact also set the length of the day and the distance to the Moon. Both have changed since. The day has lengthened. The Moon has receded. The recession is measured. It is 3.8 centimeters per year. The measurement is a laser beam bounced off a mirror left by astronauts. The mirror is still there. The beam still returns.

The collision is the reason there is a large moon, a stable climate, and a mirror on the lunar surface. It is also the reason the Earth–Moon system carries a particular angular momentum. The angular momentum is a fossil of the impact. It has not been erased.

### The Origin of the Moon

The Moon formed in a giant impact. A Mars-sized body struck the proto-Earth late in the accretion of the terrestrial planets. The collision ejected a disk of silicate vapor and melt into Earth orbit. The disk cooled and condensed. The Moon accreted from that disk within a few thousand years.

The hypothesis accounts for the Moon’s low density, its depletion in iron relative to Earth, and the identical oxygen-isotope ratios of lunar and terrestrial rocks. It also accounts for the angular momentum of the Earth–Moon system. Alternative models—capture, co-accretion, or fission of a rapidly spinning Earth—fail to satisfy the same constraints simultaneously.

High-resolution simulations show that the impactor’s core merged with Earth’s core while the mantle material formed the disk. Subsequent equilibration between the disk and the Earth’s atmosphere and magma ocean produced the observed isotopic match. The same event left Earth with a molten surface and an atmosphere of rock vapor. Both cooled within a few thousand years.

The impact occurred after the Earth had already differentiated. The Moon is therefore younger than the oldest terrestrial minerals. Radiometric ages of lunar samples place the event between 4.5 and 4.4 billion years ago. The hypothesis remains the only scenario consistent with the dynamical, chemical and chronological evidence.

### Late Heavy Bombardment

The Late Heavy Bombardment is a hypothesized spike in the impact rate approximately 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago. It was inferred from the ages of lunar basins. Dynamical models of planetary migration can produce such a spike if the giant planets crossed resonances. The spike would have sterilized the surface of the Earth and may have delivered volatiles.

Recent re-analysis of lunar samples suggests that the basin ages are spread over a longer interval. The evidence for a sharp spike is weaker than once thought. A declining but still elevated impact rate is sufficient to explain the data. The bombardment, whether spiked or declining, was the final stage of planetary accretion. It ended before the earliest evidence of life. The temporal relation is consistent with either a causal or a coincidental connection.

### The Nice Model

The Nice model is a dynamical scenario in which the giant planets formed in a compact configuration and later migrated. The migration was driven by interaction with a massive planetesimal disk. A resonance crossing between Jupiter and Saturn triggered an instability. The instability scattered the ice giants, depleted the disk, and produced the Late Heavy Bombardment.

The model reproduces the present orbits of the giant planets, the structure of the Kuiper belt, and the capture of the Trojan asteroids. Variants differ in the timing and in the initial conditions. The broad picture—an early compact configuration followed by an instability—is widely accepted. The precise timing and the mass of the disk remain adjustable. The model links the architecture of the outer Solar System to a single dynamical event.

### The Grand Tack

The Grand Tack is a model in which Jupiter migrated inward to approximately 1.5 AU and then outward. The reversal was caused by the capture of Saturn into resonance. The inward migration truncated the inner planetesimal disk. The truncation limited the mass available to form Mars and scattered water-rich planetesimals into the terrestrial region.

The model accounts for the small mass of Mars and for the delivery of water to Earth. It requires a specific sequence of migration and resonance capture. Alternative explanations for the mass of Mars exist. The Grand Tack is one consistent scenario. It is not uniquely required by the data. It illustrates how the early migration of the giant planets can shape the terrestrial planets.

### Planetary Atmospheres

A planetary atmosphere is a gaseous envelope retained by gravity. Retention depends on the planet’s mass, radius and temperature and on the mass of the gas molecules. Light gases escape more readily. Earth retains nitrogen and oxygen but has lost most of its primordial hydrogen and helium. The giant planets retain hydrogen and helium because of their deeper gravitational wells and lower temperatures.

Composition is set by formation and by subsequent processing. Primary atmospheres are captured from the nebula. Secondary atmospheres are released by outgassing and by impacts. Photochemistry, condensation and escape then modify the mixture. Earth’s oxygen is almost entirely biological. Venus and Mars have carbon-dioxide atmospheres produced by outgassing and by the failure to sequester carbon in surface reservoirs.

Circulation is driven by differential heating. Hadley cells, jets and vortices redistribute heat. The Coriolis force organizes the flow into bands on rapidly rotating planets. Greenhouse gases raise the surface temperature above the effective radiating temperature. The same radiative and dynamical principles operate on every planet that possesses an atmosphere. The outcomes differ because mass, rotation rate, distance from the star and composition differ.

### Planetary Interiors

Planetary interiors are layered by density. Differentiation occurs early, while the body is molten or partially molten. Metals sink to form a core. Silicates form a mantle. Lighter materials form a crust. The process releases gravitational energy and establishes the radial structure observed today.

Heat sources are accretion, differentiation, radioactivity and, in some cases, tidal dissipation. Heat is transported by conduction, convection and, near the surface, by volcanism and hydrothermal circulation. Convection in a liquid iron core, organized by rotation, generates a magnetic dynamo. Earth, Mercury, Ganymede and the giant planets possess dynamos. Mars and Venus do not at present.

The equation of state of the constituent materials under high pressure determines the radius for a given mass. Laboratory and theoretical equations of state, combined with gravity and magnetic data, constrain the size of cores and the presence of light elements. The same methods applied to exoplanets yield bulk compositions once mass and radius are measured. Interior structure is the outcome of formation, differentiation and thermal evolution.

### Moons and Ring Systems

Most planets possess moons. Regular moons orbit in the equatorial plane and in the same sense as the planet’s rotation. They condensed from circumplanetary disks or were captured and subsequently circularized. Irregular moons have inclined, eccentric or retrograde orbits and are captured objects.

Tidal interaction transfers angular momentum. It drives moons outward or inward according to whether they orbit beyond or inside the synchronous radius. Io is heated by tidal flexing and is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System. Europa, Ganymede and Enceladus maintain subsurface oceans by the same mechanism. The Earth’s Moon is receding and lengthening the day.

Ring systems are composed of ice and rock particles orbiting inside the Roche limit. Planetary rings are continually resupplied by the fragmentation of small moons and are sculpted by resonances and by shepherd satellites. Saturn’s rings are the most massive and are probably young on geological timescales. The same dynamical processes—tides, resonances and collisions—govern both moons and rings throughout the Solar System and are expected around exoplanets.

### Europa

Europa is a moon of Jupiter. Its surface is water ice. Beneath the ice lies a global ocean of liquid water, maintained by tidal heating. The ocean is in contact with a rocky seafloor. Hydrothermal activity at that interface is expected. The ice shell is estimated to be kilometers to tens of kilometers thick. Chaos terrains and possible plumes suggest that material from the ocean reaches the surface.

The combination of liquid water, rock and chemical energy makes Europa one of the most plausible sites for extant life beyond Earth. Any life would be independent of sunlight and would rely on chemical gradients. No direct sample of the ocean has been obtained. Surface radiation from Jupiter’s magnetosphere processes the ice and may destroy organic molecules near the surface. Future missions that fly through plumes or land and drill will test the habitability of the ocean more directly. Until then Europa remains a high-priority target whose subsurface environment satisfies the principal requirements for life as known on Earth.

### Enceladus

Enceladus is a small moon of Saturn. It is geologically active. Plumes of water vapor and ice grains erupt from fractures at the south pole. The plumes are fed by a subsurface ocean. Cassini flew through the plumes and detected water, salts, silica nanoparticles, molecular hydrogen and organic molecules. The hydrogen and silica indicate ongoing hydrothermal reactions between the ocean and a rocky core. The ocean is alkaline, and in laboratory tests some Earth methanogens grow under similar conditions.

The energy source is tidal heating. The ocean is global or nearly global and is in contact with rock. The same chemical disequilibria that support ecosystems at Earth’s hydrothermal vents are therefore present. The plumes provide a natural sample-return mechanism. No unambiguous biosignature has been identified. The detected organics are consistent with both abiotic and biological origins. Enceladus is accessible. Its ocean can be sampled without landing or drilling. It remains one of the most favorable places in the Solar System to search for extant life.

### Titan

Titan is the largest moon of Saturn. It possesses a thick nitrogen atmosphere and surface lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane. The surface temperature is 94 K. Water ice forms the bedrock. A subsurface water ocean may exist beneath the ice crust, decoupled from the hydrocarbon surface.

The atmosphere is rich in organic compounds produced by photochemistry. Methane is continuously destroyed and must be replenished. The surface liquids are solvents in which a non-aqueous biochemistry could, in principle, operate. No such biochemistry is known. Reaction rates at 94 K are extremely slow. Any life in the hydrocarbon lakes would have to use a chemistry very different from terrestrial life. The subsurface ocean, if it exchanges material with the rocky interior, would offer a more conventional aqueous habitat. Titan therefore presents two distinct environments. Neither has yielded evidence of life. Both remain targets for future exploration.

### Ganymede and Other Icy Moons

Ganymede, larger than the planet Mercury, is the largest moon in the Solar System. It possesses an intrinsic magnetic field and a subsurface ocean sandwiched between ice layers. The ocean is probably not in direct contact with the rocky mantle. Tidal heating is weaker than on Europa. Callisto may also harbor a subsurface ocean. Both moons are less energetically active than Europa. Io, the innermost of Jupiter’s large moons, is the opposite case: its tidal heat drives the most intense volcanism known.

Triton, a captured moon of Neptune, shows geysers of nitrogen and a young surface. It may retain internal heat. Smaller icy moons throughout the outer Solar System display varying degrees of geological activity. In each case the availability of liquid water, chemical energy and contact with rock determines the habitability potential. Moons that combine all three are rare. Europa and Enceladus are the clearest examples. The others remain possible but less favorable. Comparative study of these worlds constrains the range of conditions under which subsurface oceans can persist and under which life, if it arises, could be sustained.

## <a id="ch_26"></a>26. Small Bodies and Visitors

### Asteroids

Asteroids are rocky and metallic bodies that orbit the Sun, predominantly in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter. Sizes range from meters to hundreds of kilometers. The largest, Ceres, is a dwarf planet. Most are irregular fragments. Collisions continually grind them down and produce dust.

Composition varies. C-type asteroids are carbon-rich and primitive. S-type are stony. M-type are metallic. The differences record the radial temperature gradient in the original disk and subsequent dynamical mixing. Some asteroids are rubble piles held together by gravity. Others are monolithic. Spacecraft have visited several and returned samples. The samples confirm that many meteorites are asteroid fragments.

Asteroids are the parent bodies of most meteorites. They also supply a fraction of Earth’s water and organic material. Near-Earth asteroids are those whose orbits approach Earth’s. Their impact hazard is quantified by size-frequency distributions. Deflection concepts exist. The same population records the collisional and dynamical history of the inner Solar System.

### Comets

Comets are icy bodies that originate in the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud. When perturbed onto orbits that bring them close to the Sun they develop comae and tails. The coma is a temporary atmosphere of sublimated ices and entrained dust. The tails are pushed by radiation pressure and by the solar wind.

Short-period comets come from the Kuiper belt and are confined near the ecliptic. Long-period comets come from the Oort cloud and arrive from all directions. Both reservoirs are surviving planetesimals from the outer disk. Spacecraft encounters have shown that comet nuclei are porous, low-density aggregates of ice and dust. Jets of gas and dust are localized. The surfaces are darker than expected.

Comets delivered volatiles and organic compounds to the inner planets. Their deuterium-to-hydrogen ratios vary. Some match Earth’s oceans. Others do not. The contribution of cometary water remains quantitatively uncertain. Comets are also time capsules of the outer Solar System’s composition at the epoch of planet formation.

### Meteoroids, Meteors and Meteorites

A meteoroid is a solid object smaller than an asteroid moving in interplanetary space. When it enters an atmosphere it produces a meteor—the luminous trail of ablated material. If a fragment reaches the ground it is a meteorite.

Meteorites are classified by composition and texture. Chondrites are primitive and contain chondrules. Achondrites, irons and stony-irons are differentiated. The classes correspond to different parent-body histories. Isotopic measurements date the formation of the parent bodies to within a few million years of the Solar System’s origin. Some meteorites contain pre-solar grains older than the Sun. Others contain amino acids and other organic molecules formed in space.

The flux of meteoroids is continuous. Micrometeorites dominate the mass influx to Earth. Larger impacts are rarer and are recorded in the cratering history of the Moon and planets. The same objects link laboratory samples to the asteroids and comets observed remotely. They are the principal source of hands-on material from beyond Earth.

### Interstellar Objects

Interstellar objects are bodies that are not gravitationally bound to the Sun. Two have been identified: 1I/‘Oumuamua and 2I/Borisov. ‘Oumuamua showed no coma and an unusual light curve. Borisov was an active comet. Both entered the Solar System on hyperbolic trajectories and are now leaving.

Their existence demonstrates that planetesimals are ejected from other planetary systems. The ejection mechanisms are the same scattering processes that operate in the Solar System. The number density of such objects in interstellar space is estimated from the detection rate and from the survey volume. The estimate is consistent with the expected yield of planet formation and dynamical clearing.

Composition and physical properties can be measured during the brief interval when an object is near the Sun. Spectroscopy of Borisov revealed familiar cometary molecules. ‘Oumuamua’s nature remains less clear. Future surveys will detect more. Each detection supplies a sample of another system’s planetesimal population. Interstellar objects are therefore messengers from elsewhere in the Galaxy.

### Planetary Defense

An asteroid impact is the one natural disaster that people can in principle prevent. A rock about 20 meters across exploded over Chelyabinsk in Russia in 2013, releasing the energy of several hundred kilotonnes of explosives and injuring about 1,500 people, mostly by glass from broken windows. In 1908 a larger body devastated about 2,000 square kilometers of Siberian forest at Tunguska. Impacts large enough to threaten a civilization are far rarer, and the great majority of the biggest near-Earth asteroids have already been found.

Surveys by ground telescopes and space missions track near-Earth objects, so that an impact can be predicted decades ahead. The asteroid Apophis, once thought to have a small chance of hitting Earth, will pass within about 32,000 kilometers on 13 April 2029, closer than some satellites, and is now known not to be an impact threat.

In September 2022 the DART spacecraft crashed into Dimorphos, a small moon of the asteroid Didymos, and shortened its orbit by about 32 minutes. It showed that a spacecraft can alter an asteroid’s path. The method works only with enough warning, which is why finding the objects early matters. Sample-return missions, such as Japan’s Hayabusa2 from Ryugu and NASA’s OSIRIS-REx from Bennu, also let us study the composition of the bodies we might have to move.

### The Kuiper Belt and the Oort Cloud

Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy bodies left from the formation of the planets. Pluto, discovered in 1930, is its best-known member. The New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015 and found mountains of water ice, nitrogen glaciers and a thin atmosphere, a far more active world than expected. In 2019 it passed Arrokoth, a small object made of two lobes joined gently, which looks like a relic of the slow gathering of the earliest planetesimals.

Much farther out, between a few thousand and perhaps a hundred thousand times the Earth–Sun distance, is the Oort cloud, a roughly spherical halo of comets. It has never been observed directly. Its existence is inferred from the orbits of long-period comets, which arrive from every direction. Passing stars or the tidal pull of the Galaxy occasionally nudge one inward.

These distant regions hold material that has hardly changed since the Solar System formed. They are the most distant part of the Sun’s domain, and the most poorly mapped.

## <a id="ch_27"></a>27. Planets Around Other Stars

### Exoplanets

Exoplanets are planets that orbit stars other than the Sun. More than five thousand have been confirmed. Detection methods include the radial-velocity reflex of the star, the photometric transit of the planet across the stellar disk, gravitational microlensing, and direct imaging. Each method is biased toward different masses and orbital distances.

Atmospheric characterization is possible for transiting planets. The diversity of architectures found shows that planet formation is robust and that the Solar System is not an inevitable template.

### Exoplanet Detection, Demographics and Atmospheres

The radial-velocity method measures the star’s reflex motion. Precision of 1 m s<sup>−1</sup> detects Jupiter-mass planets at a few astronomical units and super-Earths on close orbits. The transit method measures the periodic dimming when a planet crosses the stellar disk. The depth gives the planet-to-star radius ratio. Combined with a mass from radial velocity or from transit-timing variations, the bulk density follows.

Occurrence studies show that planets are abundant. The average number of planets per star is of order unity. Super-Earths and mini-Neptunes are the most common size class. A radius gap near 1.5–2 Earth radii separates predominantly rocky planets from those that retained substantial envelopes. Hot Jupiters exist but are rare. Rocky planets inside the habitable zones of their stars occur at rates of tens of percent around Sun-like and smaller stars.

Transmission spectroscopy during transit reveals atmospheric composition. Starlight filtered through the planetary limb carries absorption features of atoms and molecules. Water, sodium, potassium, carbon monoxide and methane are among the species seen. Clouds and hazes mute features on many worlds. Emission spectroscopy and phase curves measure dayside temperatures and heat redistribution. Strongly irradiated hot Jupiters can develop temperature inversions. The data demonstrate that exoplanet atmospheres span a wide range of metallicities, carbon-to-oxygen ratios, temperature structures and aerosol properties, and that they are not scaled versions of Solar-System atmospheres. Biosignature searches are limited by stellar activity, cloud cover and the present precision of the observations.

### Exomoons

Exomoons are moons orbiting planets that themselves orbit stars other than the Sun. None has been confirmed. Detection is more difficult than planet detection because the moon’s signal is weaker and is superimposed on the planetary signal.

Transit-timing variations and transit-duration variations can reveal a moon. The planet’s transit times and durations oscillate as the planet and moon orbit their common center of mass. The amplitude scales with the moon-to-planet mass ratio and with the moon’s orbital distance. Photometric dips caused by the moon itself are possible but require high precision and favorable geometry. Direct imaging of a moon is beyond present capability except for the most massive, widely separated cases.

Habitability considerations differ from those for planets. A moon can be tidally heated even when it lies far outside the stellar habitable zone. The same mechanism that maintains oceans on Europa and Enceladus could operate around giant exoplanets. An atmosphere and a magnetic field, if present, would further improve prospects. Formation pathways include accretion in a circumplanetary disk, capture, and giant impacts. All are expected to occur. The absence of confirmed detections is a consequence of observational limits, not of physical rarity. Future transit missions and extremely large telescopes will enlarge the searchable parameter space.

### How the First Exoplanets Were Found

The first planet orbiting an ordinary star was announced in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, who earned a share of the 2019 Nobel Prize. The star was 51 Pegasi, and the planet was a surprise, a world with about half the mass of Jupiter orbiting in just over four days, closer to its star than Mercury is to the Sun. Such hot Jupiters had no place in theories based on our Solar System, and showed that planets can migrate after they form.

The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, stared at one patch of sky for years and measured the tiny dimming as planets crossed their stars. It found thousands of candidates and showed that planets are the rule. The most common sizes, between Earth and Neptune, have no counterpart in the Solar System. TESS, launched in 2018, surveys the whole sky for nearby stars.

Among the discoveries are Proxima b, a planet of roughly Earth’s mass in the habitable zone of the nearest star, and TRAPPIST-1, a small, cool star about 40 light-years away with seven planets of roughly Earth’s size. The James Webb Space Telescope now measures their atmospheres, so far with results that show the difficulty of keeping an atmosphere around planets of such stars.

### Strange New Worlds

The census of exoplanets has turned up types that nobody predicted. Hot Jupiters orbit so close that their upper atmospheres are heated to thousands of degrees. Lava worlds, rocky planets with a day side hot enough to melt rock, orbit even closer. Planets with extremely low density, called super-puffs, are larger than Neptune but far lighter. Some planets orbit two stars, like the fictional Tatooine, and at least one has been found orbiting a pulsar.

Free-floating planets also exist, ejected from their systems and wandering the Galaxy without a star. They are found when their gravity briefly brightens the light of a background star, a technique that suggests they may be common. Some may have been thrown out when planets scattered each other in young systems.

These discoveries show how limited our Solar System is as a template. Planet formation produces an enormous variety, and the arrangement of the Solar System, with small rocky planets in the inside and giants outside, is only one outcome among many. Whether it is a typical one is a question that the surveys have only begun to answer.

### Planetary Habitability

Planetary habitability is the capacity of a world to support liquid water on or beneath its surface for geological periods. The first filter is the habitable zone, the range of distances from a star at which a rocky planet can keep liquid water on its surface, examined in [Chapter 46](#ch_46).

Additional factors matter. Plate tectonics recycles carbon and stabilizes climate on billion-year timescales. A magnetic field may limit atmospheric escape. The presence of a large moon stabilizes obliquity. None of these is strictly necessary.

The only known inhabited planet is Earth. The conditions that permitted the origin and persistence of life here are partly understood. Which of those conditions are essential, and which are contingent, is not. Whether any rocky planet in a habitable zone is inhabited remains an open observational question.
