Habitability is a physical prerequisite, not a guarantee.

## <a id="ch_28"></a>28. Stars and Stellar Remnants

### Stars and Nuclear Burning

A star is a self-gravitating ball of plasma in which nuclear fusion supplies the energy that balances radiative loss. On the main sequence the fusion reaction is the conversion of hydrogen to helium. The proton–proton chain dominates in stars of solar mass and below. The CNO cycle dominates in more massive stars. Both release about 0.7 percent of the rest mass as energy.

The structure of a star is fixed by four equations: hydrostatic equilibrium, mass continuity, energy transport, and energy generation. The solutions form a one-parameter family labeled by mass. Low-mass stars are cool and long-lived. High-mass stars are hot, luminous, and short-lived. The Sun will remain on the main sequence for about ten billion years.

When hydrogen is exhausted in the core the star contracts, heats, and ignites helium, swelling into a red giant. Stars below about eight solar masses stop at carbon and oxygen, shed their envelopes, and leave white dwarfs. In more massive stars later stages build neon, oxygen, silicon and finally iron. Beyond iron fusion absorbs energy, the core collapses, and the result is a supernova that leaves a neutron star or a black hole. The ejected material enriches the interstellar medium with the heavy elements from which later planets and life are made.

The observed Hertzsprung–Russell diagram matches the predicted tracks and lifetimes. Mass is the primary determinant of a star’s fate; composition and rotation add secondary effects. Stellar evolution is therefore one of the best-tested applications of nuclear physics and of hydrostatics.

### The Initial Mass Function

The initial mass function is the distribution of stellar masses at birth. It rises from the brown-dwarf regime, peaks near 0.2–0.3 solar masses, and declines as a power law above one solar mass. The slope of the power law is approximately -2.3. The function is observed to be similar in different environments. Variations exist. They are smaller than the uncertainties.

The origin is the turbulent fragmentation of molecular clouds combined with the physics of accretion and feedback. Simulations reproduce the broad shape. They do not yet predict the peak and the slope from first principles. The function determines the luminosity, the chemical yield and the remnant population of a stellar generation. It is an empirical input to models of galaxies and of chemical evolution.

### Brown Dwarfs

Brown dwarfs are objects below the hydrogen-burning limit of approximately 0.08 solar masses. They are supported by electron degeneracy. They cool continuously. Their spectra show methane, water and, in the coolest objects, ammonia. Masses range from the deuterium-burning limit of 13 Jupiter masses up to the hydrogen-burning limit.

They are abundant. Their space density is comparable to that of stars. They form by the same turbulent fragmentation that produces stars. Some may form by disk fragmentation or by ejection from multiple systems. Their atmospheres are laboratories for cloud physics and for non-equilibrium chemistry. They bridge the gap between stars and planets. The distinction is one of formation and of mass, not of a sharp physical boundary.

### Worked Examples: Stellar Structure and Lifetimes

Example 1. The Sun’s luminosity is 3.8 × 10<sup>26</sup> W. How much mass is converted to energy each second?

Δ m = L/c<sup>2</sup> = 4.2 × 10<sup>9</sup> kg s<sup>−1</sup>.

Example 2. A star has twice the Sun’s mass. Roughly how does its main-sequence lifetime compare?

Luminosity scales approximately as M<sup>3.5</sup>. Lifetime scales as M/L ≈ M<sup>−2.5</sup>. The star lives about 0.18 times as long as the Sun.

Example 3. Why does the core of a massive star eventually collapse?

When the core is iron, fusion no longer releases energy. Electron degeneracy pressure supports the core only up to the Chandrasekhar mass. Beyond that limit the core collapses on a dynamical time-scale of seconds.

The estimates reproduce the observed mass–luminosity relation and the fate of massive stars.

Example. Estimate how long the Sun can shine on core hydrogen, given that fusion releases 0.7 percent of the rest mass and that only the innermost tenth of the Sun’s mass ever reaches fusion temperature.

Energy available: 0.007 × 0.1 × 2 × 10<sup>30</sup> kg × (3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>)<sup>2</sup> ≈ 1.3 × 10<sup>44</sup> J. At 3.8 × 10<sup>26</sup> W this lasts 3.4 × 10<sup>17</sup> s, about eleven billion years, in good agreement with the accepted main-sequence lifetime.

Example. A star of 10 solar masses has a luminosity roughly 10<sup>3.5</sup> times solar. Estimate its main-sequence lifetime relative to the Sun.

Lifetime scales as M/L ≈ 10/10<sup>3.5</sup> ≈ 0.003 solar lifetimes, or a few tens of millions of years.

The estimates recover the observed mass–luminosity–lifetime relation.

### Stellar Nucleosynthesis

Hydrogen burns by the proton–proton chains in stars like the Sun and by the CNO cycle in hotter, heavier stars. The later stages, from helium burning to the iron peak and the neutron-capture processes beyond it, are traced element by element in [Chapter 13](#ch_13). The yields depend on a star’s mass, metallicity and rotation. Stellar-evolution codes calculate them, and the results match the observed abundances of the major species, with discrepancies left for some rare isotopes. Stars made the elements from carbon to uranium; the Big Bang supplied the hydrogen, the helium and a trace of lithium.

### Supernovae

Core-collapse supernovae end the lives of stars more massive than about eight solar masses. The iron core collapses to nuclear density. A shock is launched. Neutrino heating revives the shock. The explosion ejects the envelope and leaves a neutron star or a black hole. Type Ia supernovae are thermonuclear explosions of white dwarfs that reach the Chandrasekhar mass. They are standardisable candles.

Both classes enrich the interstellar medium. Core-collapse events produce oxygen, neon and magnesium. Type Ia events produce iron. The light curves and spectra are modeled in three-dimensional simulations. The simulations reproduce the gross features. The details of the explosion mechanism and of the progenitor channels remain under study. The events are both the endpoints of stellar evolution and the principal sources of heavy elements.

### The Pair-Instability Supernova

Stars with helium cores between approximately 64 and 133 solar masses encounter the pair-instability. Electron–positron pair production softens the equation of state. The core contracts, ignites oxygen explosively, and is completely disrupted. No remnant remains. The explosion produces a characteristic yield rich in silicon and deficient in elements heavier than zinc.

The predicted mass gap in the black-hole mass function has been searched for in gravitational-wave catalogs. Events inside the gap have been reported. Their interpretation is debated. They may indicate that the instability is less absolute than calculated, or that the progenitors retained less mass than expected. The gap, if real, is a direct signature of the pair instability. Its absence or partial filling constrains mass loss and binary evolution.

### The Star That Should Have Been Invisible

In 1967 a graduate student noticed a repeating radio signal. The signal was precise. It repeated every 1.3 seconds. The first explanation considered was an artificial beacon. The explanation was discarded when a second source was found. The sources were pulsars—rotating neutron stars.

A neutron star is what remains when a massive star’s core gives way. Its density is that of an atomic nucleus. Its magnetic field is a trillion times stronger than Earth’s. The rotation sweeps a beam of radiation across the sky. When the beam crosses the Earth, a pulse is recorded. The pulse is the lighthouse effect of an object the size of a city spinning at hundreds of revolutions per second.

The discovery was accidental. The explanation was not. The existence of neutron stars had been predicted decades earlier. The prediction had been regarded as exotic. The pulses made it ordinary. The ordinary object is still one of the most extreme in the universe. Its surface gravity is a hundred billion times Earth’s. Its existence is now routine. It was not routine in 1967.

### Neutron Stars and Pulsars

A neutron star is the collapsed core of a massive star. Its mass is typically 1.4 solar masses compressed into a radius of about 12 km. The mean density exceeds nuclear density. The object is supported against gravity by neutron degeneracy pressure and by nuclear repulsive forces.

Many neutron stars are observed as pulsars. A pulsar is a rapidly rotating, highly magnetized neutron star whose radio or X-ray beams sweep across the observer. Periods range from milliseconds to seconds. The fastest pulsars are spun up by accretion in binary systems. Timing precision can reach nanoseconds and is used to test general relativity and to search for gravitational waves.

How matter behaves at several times nuclear density is still not known. Mass and radius measurements of pulsars constrain it. The heaviest precisely measured neutron stars exceed two solar masses, ruling out the softest equations of state. Mergers of neutron-star binaries produce short gamma-ray bursts, kilonovae and gravitational waves, and are a principal site of rapid neutron-capture nucleosynthesis. Neutron stars are therefore both laboratories for dense matter and agents of chemical enrichment.

### Neutron-Star Mergers

Neutron-star mergers produce gravitational waves, short gamma-ray bursts and kilonovae. The gravitational-wave signal encodes the masses and the tidal deformability. The electromagnetic counterparts confirm the production of heavy elements by the rapid neutron-capture process. The 2017 event GW170817 supplied the first multi-messenger observation. The inferred ejecta mass and composition match the requirements for the r-process.

The merger rate is consistent with the rate needed to account for the observed abundances of the heaviest elements. The equation of state of dense matter is constrained by the tidal deformability and by the maximum mass. Both constraints favor a relatively stiff equation of state. Future events will tighten the constraints. The mergers are a laboratory for dense matter, for nucleosynthesis and for strong-field gravity.

### Magnetars

Magnetars are neutron stars with surface magnetic fields of 10<sup>14</sup> to 10<sup>15</sup> G. The fields are inferred from the spin-down rate and from the energetics of X-ray bursts. The energy reservoir is the magnetic field. Decay and reconnection power the persistent emission and the bursts. Giant flares release up to 10<sup>46</sup> erg.

A Galactic magnetar produced a fast radio burst in 2020. The association demonstrates that at least some fast radio bursts originate from magnetars. Whether all do is unknown. The birth rate of magnetars is sufficient to account for the volumetric rate of bursts if each magnetar produces many bursts. The objects are the strongest magnets in the universe. Their activity links neutron-star physics to the transient radio sky.

### Pulsar Timing Arrays

Pulsar timing arrays monitor the arrival times of pulses from millisecond pulsars. A gravitational-wave background produces a correlated timing residual. The correlation has a characteristic angular dependence. A signal consistent with that dependence was reported by several arrays in 2023, at about three to four standard deviations. The amplitude is higher than the simplest predictions from supermassive black-hole binaries. The discrepancy may indicate additional sources or a different binary evolution.

The arrays work at nanohertz frequencies, far below the bands of ground- and space-based interferometers; [Chapter 21](#ch_21) places them in the full gravitational-wave spectrum. If the signal is confirmed as a background, it measures the population of supermassive black-hole binaries and limits any cosmological sources in the same band.

### Gamma-Ray Bursts

Gamma-ray bursts are the most luminous electromagnetic events in the universe. Long bursts are associated with the core collapse of massive stars. Short bursts are associated with neutron-star mergers. Both launch relativistic jets. The prompt emission lasts from milliseconds to minutes. The afterglow lasts for days to months.

The isotropic-equivalent energy can exceed 10<sup>54</sup> erg. Beaming reduces the true energy by two orders of magnitude. The bursts are observed to redshift 9 and beyond. They probe the early universe and the properties of relativistic shocks. The association of short bursts with gravitational waves has been confirmed. The association of long bursts with supernovae is established. Both classes are now multi-messenger sources.

### Tidal Disruption Events

A tidal disruption event occurs when a star passes within the tidal radius of a supermassive black hole. The star is torn apart. Roughly half the debris is ejected. Half remains bound and accretes. The accretion produces a luminous flare that declines as a power law. The peak luminosity can exceed that of a supernova.

Dozens of events have been observed in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray surveys. Some launch relativistic jets. The events probe the stellar population in galactic nuclei and the spin of the black hole. The fallback rate and the circularization efficiency remain uncertain. The observations confirm that stars are disrupted. They do not yet yield precision measurements of black-hole spin.

## <a id="ch_29"></a>29. Fast Radio Bursts and High-Energy Messengers

### Fast Radio Bursts

Fast radio bursts are radio pulses lasting milliseconds. Thousands have been detected since the first was found in 2007. Each burst arrives spread out in frequency, the low frequencies later than the high, and the size of that delay, the dispersion measure, counts the free electrons along the line of sight. For every confirmed burst it exceeds what our own Galaxy can supply, which places the sources at cosmological distances. That makes the bursts probes as well as puzzles: their dispersion and scattering weigh the ionized gas between the galaxies.

The energy problem is severe. The brightest bursts release 10<sup>31</sup> to 10<sup>33</sup> joules in milliseconds, comparable to or more than the Sun emits in a day, from a region at most a few hundred kilometers across, since a larger source would smear the pulse in time. Only coherent emission, in which charges radiate in step, can do that.

A minority of sources repeat, and repeaters can be traced to their host galaxies. In 2020 a magnetar in our own Galaxy, SGR 1935+2154, produced a burst, which secures magnetars as at least one source. Non-repeating bursts may share that origin or come from cataclysmic events such as neutron-star mergers or the collapse of supramassive neutron stars. Most bursts have no detectable counterpart at other wavelengths.

The rotation measure of a fast radio burst constrains the magnetic field along the line of sight. Several bursts show large rotation measures, indicating that they originate in dense, magnetized plasma. The plasma may be local to the source or may lie in the host galaxy. Scattering and scintillation further probe the turbulent medium.

Repeating sources exhibit burst storms—clusters of hundreds of bursts within hours—followed by long quiescent intervals. The duty cycle is low. The energy distribution of bursts from a single repeater follows a power law similar to that of earthquake aftershocks or solar flares. The similarity suggests a self-organized critical process, possibly magnetic reconnection in a neutron-star magnetosphere. The hypothesis fits the data without being demanded by them.

### Fast Radio Burst Host Galaxies

Localized fast radio bursts reside in galaxies of various types. Some hosts are star-forming dwarfs. Others are massive ellipticals. The diversity indicates that the progenitors are not confined to a single galactic environment. Offsets from the centers of the hosts are consistent with the offsets of neutron-star populations. The association with magnetars is supported by the Galactic example and by the host properties of several repeating sources.

The dispersion measures, once the Galactic and host contributions are subtracted, measure the intergalactic electron column. Their values agree with the baryon density inferred from the microwave background. They confirm that the missing baryons reside in the warm-hot intergalactic medium. The bursts therefore serve both as probes of their hosts and as tracers of the ionized cosmic web.

### Cosmic Rays

Cosmic rays are high-energy charged particles that arrive at Earth from space. Their composition is roughly 90 percent protons, 9 percent helium nuclei and 1 percent heavier nuclei and electrons. Energies range from 10<sup>8</sup> eV to more than 10<sup>20</sup> eV. The flux falls steeply with energy.

Below about 10<sup>15</sup> eV the rays are predominantly Galactic. Supernova remnants are the leading candidate accelerators. Above that energy an extragalactic component dominates, though no one has yet pinned down where the most energetic particles originate. Magnetic fields deflect charged particles, erasing directional information except at the very highest energies. Neutral messengers—photons and neutrinos—preserve direction and are used to locate sources.

The rays interact in the atmosphere, producing extensive air showers. Ground arrays and fluorescence detectors reconstruct the primary energy and composition. The same particles contribute to the radiation dose at aircraft altitudes and have been proposed as a mutagenic factor over geological time. Their origin and acceleration mechanisms remain active research questions.

### Cosmic Rays Above the Knee

The cosmic-ray spectrum steepens at the knee, approximately 3 × 10<sup>15</sup> eV. A second steepening, the ankle, occurs near 10<sup>18</sup> eV. The knee is attributed to the maximum energy of Galactic accelerators or to a change in propagation. The ankle is attributed to the transition to extragalactic sources. The spectrum continues to 10<sup>20</sup> eV.

Above 10<sup>19</sup> eV the flux is suppressed. The suppression is consistent with the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin cutoff from interactions with the microwave background. It is also consistent with a maximum energy of the sources. The composition becomes heavier above the knee. Anisotropy limits and the absence of point sources already restrict what those accelerators can be. The particles are the highest-energy messengers that reach Earth.

### Ultra-High-Energy Neutrinos

Ultra-high-energy neutrinos are produced by the interaction of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays with the microwave background or by sources themselves. They propagate undeflected. Their detection would point back to the sources. IceCube has detected neutrinos up to a few PeV. No neutrinos above 10<sup>17</sup> eV have been confirmed.

Proposed detectors use radio emission from showers in ice or the atmosphere, or the fluorescence of horizontal air showers. The expected flux is low. The detection of even a few events would constrain the sources of the highest-energy cosmic rays and the composition of the cosmic-ray beam. The neutrinos are the only messengers that can travel cosmological distances at these energies without absorption or deflection.

### The Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin Cutoff

The Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin cutoff is the suppression of the cosmic-ray flux above approximately 5 × 10<sup>19</sup> eV. Protons above that energy lose energy by photopion production on the microwave background. The mean free path is tens of megaparsecs. Nuclei are limited by photodisintegration at similar energies. The cutoff is therefore a horizon.

The observed suppression is consistent with the cutoff. It is also consistent with a source maximum energy. The two interpretations are distinguished by composition and by anisotropy. Present data favor a mixed composition and show no strong anisotropy. The cutoff, if it is the GZK effect, implies that the sources of the highest-energy particles lie within a few hundred megaparsecs. Their identity remains unknown.

### The Solar Wind

The solar wind is a continuous outflow of plasma from the Sun’s corona. It consists mainly of protons and electrons with a few percent helium nuclei and trace heavier ions. At Earth’s orbit the typical speed is 400 km s<sup>−1</sup> and the density is a few particles per cubic centimeter. Fast streams originate in coronal holes. Slow streams originate near the equatorial streamer belt.

The wind is accelerated by thermal pressure gradients and by wave-particle interactions in the corona. It becomes supersonic within a few solar radii. The interplanetary magnetic field is frozen into the plasma and is drawn into a Parker spiral by the Sun’s rotation. Sector boundaries separate regions of opposite polarity.

The wind inflates the heliosphere, a bubble that extends far beyond the planets. It interacts with planetary magnetospheres and atmospheres. Earth’s magnetosphere deflects most of the wind. Unmagnetized bodies such as Venus and Mars lose atmosphere to stripping. Comet tails are shaped by the wind. Variations in wind speed and density, together with coronal mass ejections, produce geomagnetic storms. The same plasma outflow is expected from every star that possesses a hot corona. The solar wind is the local realization of a general stellar phenomenon.

## <a id="ch_30"></a>30. Galaxies and the Large-Scale Universe

### Large-Scale Structure

Large-scale structure is the pattern of galaxies, clusters, filaments and voids observed on scales from a few to several hundred megaparsecs. The pattern grew by gravitational instability from the primordial density fluctuations. Over-dense regions expanded more slowly, collapsed, and formed bound objects. Under-dense regions expanded faster and became voids.

Cold dark matter supplies the dominant gravitational potential. Baryons fall into the dark-matter wells after recombination. The resulting power spectrum of density fluctuations matches the spectrum measured in galaxy surveys and in the microwave background. Baryon acoustic oscillations ([Chapter 32](#ch_32)) appear in the galaxy distribution as a standard ruler.

N-body simulations that include cold dark matter, baryons and a cosmological constant reproduce the observed filamentary web, the abundance of clusters, and the internal structure of dark-matter halos. The same simulations show that structure formation is hierarchical: small objects form first and merge into larger ones. The process continues today. The large-scale distribution of matter is therefore the evolved imprint of inflationary initial conditions filtered by gravity and by the cosmic expansion.

### Galaxy Formation

Galaxies form by the gravitational collapse of dark-matter halos and the subsequent cooling of baryons. Small halos collapse first. They merge hierarchically into larger ones. Gas cools, forms stars, and is regulated by feedback from supernovae and from active galactic nuclei. The feedback prevents over-cooling and matches the observed stellar masses.

The morphology—disk, bulge, elliptical—depends on the merger history and on the angular momentum of the gas. Major mergers destroy disks and build ellipticals. Quiet accretion preserves disks. The observed mix of morphologies is reproduced in simulations that include both processes. The simulations require sub-grid recipes for star formation and feedback. The recipes are calibrated. They are not derived from first principles. The overall hierarchical picture is robust.

### Galaxies

Galaxies are gravitationally bound systems of stars, gas, dust and dark matter. The Milky Way is a barred spiral containing a few hundred billion stars. Elliptical galaxies are smooth and gas-poor. Irregular galaxies lack ordered structure. Most large galaxies host a supermassive black hole at the center.

Galaxies grow by accretion of gas and by mergers. Hierarchical merging is visible in both simulations and in the disturbed morphologies of many observed systems. Star formation occurs in the cold, dense phases of the interstellar medium. Supernova explosions and black-hole outflows heat and expel gas, which throttles the pace of star formation. The result is the observed range of stellar masses and morphologies.

Galaxies are not uniformly distributed. They form filaments, sheets and clusters surrounding voids—the cosmic web. The web is the evolved imprint of primordial density fluctuations. Galaxy surveys map the web to redshifts of order unity and beyond. The same large-scale structure that appears in the galaxy distribution is predicted by the cold-dark-matter model once the initial conditions are taken from the microwave background.

### Andromeda and Alpha Centauri

The Andromeda galaxy is the nearest large spiral to the Milky Way. It lies about 2.5 million light-years away. It contains roughly a trillion stars and is approaching the Milky Way at about 110 kilometers per second. The two galaxies are expected to merge in roughly four billion years. Andromeda has its own satellite galaxies and a supermassive black hole at its center. No individual planets have been resolved there. The distance precludes detailed spectroscopy of Earth-sized worlds with present instruments.

Alpha Centauri is the nearest star system to the Sun, 4.37 light-years away. It is a triple system. Alpha Centauri A and B are Sun-like stars that orbit each other. Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf that orbits the pair at a greater distance. Proxima has at least one confirmed planet, Proxima b, with a minimum mass near that of Earth and an orbital period of about 11 days. The planet lies in the star’s habitable zone, where liquid water could exist on the surface if the atmosphere is suitable. The star is active. Flares and high-energy radiation may erode atmospheres. No atmosphere has been detected. The system is the closest place where an Earth-sized planet in a temperate orbit is known to exist. Whether that planet retains water or supports life is unknown.

### Cosmic Voids

Cosmic voids are under-dense regions tens of megaparsecs across. They occupy most of the volume of the universe. Galaxies inside voids are bluer and more star-forming than average. The voids are the complementary structure to the filaments and clusters. Their size and emptiness are predicted by the cold-dark-matter model once the initial conditions are fixed by the microwave background.

Void statistics—abundance, density profiles, shapes—test gravity and dark energy. Modified-gravity models alter the growth rate inside voids. The observations are consistent with general relativity. They do not yet distinguish among dark-energy models. The voids are the largest structures in the universe. They are also the simplest. Their dynamics are dominated by expansion and by the absence of matter.

### The Lyman-Alpha Forest

The Lyman-alpha forest is the set of absorption lines in the spectra of distant quasars. Each line is produced by a cloud of neutral hydrogen along the line of sight. The forest traces the distribution of gas in the intergalactic medium at redshifts between 2 and 5. The absorption is sensitive to the density, temperature and ionization state.

The forest measures the matter power spectrum on small scales. It constrains the mass of warm dark matter and the amplitude of primordial fluctuations. It also measures the evolution of the ultraviolet background. The observations are consistent with cold dark matter and with a photoionized intergalactic medium. They supply an independent check on the parameters derived from the microwave background and from galaxy surveys.

### The Sunyaev–Zel’dovich Effect

The Sunyaev–Zel’dovich effect is the distortion of the microwave background by inverse-Compton scattering on hot electrons in galaxy clusters. The thermal effect shifts photons to higher frequencies. The kinetic effect is a Doppler shift caused by the cluster’s bulk motion. Both are independent of redshift. They therefore detect clusters at any distance.

Cluster counts as a function of redshift constrain the growth of structure and the dark-energy equation of state. The effect has been measured by ground-based and satellite experiments. The measurements agree with X-ray and weak-lensing masses once selection effects are included. The effect is a clean probe. It does not require the cluster to be bright in any other band.

### Weak Gravitational Lensing

Weak lensing is the small distortion of galaxy shapes by the intervening mass distribution. The distortion is statistical. It is measured by averaging the ellipticities of many galaxies. The signal constrains the projected mass. Tomography—division into redshift bins—constrains the growth of structure as a function of time.

Surveys measure the amplitude of matter fluctuations and the dark-energy equation of state. The measurements are consistent with the microwave-background results. They are independent. Systematic errors arise from intrinsic alignments and from photometric-redshift uncertainties. Both are controlled by calibration. Weak lensing is one of the principal probes of the late-time universe.

### Strong Gravitational Lensing

Strong lensing produces multiple images, arcs and Einstein rings when the alignment of source, lens and observer is close. The image positions and magnifications determine the mass distribution of the lens. Time delays between images of a variable source measure the Hubble constant. The measurement is independent of the distance ladder.

Lensing by galaxies and by clusters has been observed in large numbers. The mass profiles are consistent with cold dark matter. Substructure is detected through flux-ratio anomalies and through gravitational imaging. The substructure abundance tests the small-scale predictions of cold dark matter. The observations agree within present uncertainties. They do not yet reveal a discrepancy that requires warm dark matter or modified gravity.

### Magnetic Fields in the Universe

Magnetic fields are observed in planets, stars, galaxies and clusters. Galactic fields have strengths of a few microgauss and are ordered on kiloparsec scales. Cluster fields are of similar strength and are tangled. Intergalactic fields are constrained by the absence of certain cascade emission and by Faraday rotation. Lower limits of 10<sup>−17</sup> G have been claimed. Upper limits are 10<sup>−9</sup> G.

The origin is unknown. Primordial fields from the early universe, or fields generated by battery mechanisms and amplified by dynamos, are both possible. Dynamo action in galaxies is efficient. It can amplify seed fields to the observed strengths in a few rotation periods. The seed itself may be primordial or generated by early stars. The observations do not yet distinguish the scenarios.

### The Interstellar Medium

The interstellar medium is the gas and dust between the stars. It comprises cold molecular clouds, warm neutral and ionized gas, and hot coronal gas. The phases are in approximate pressure equilibrium. Molecular clouds are the sites of star formation. They are turbulent and magnetized. The turbulence is supersonic. It creates the density fluctuations that collapse under gravity.

Dust constitutes about one percent of the mass. It absorbs ultraviolet light and re-radiates in the infrared. It catalyzes the formation of molecular hydrogen. The medium is enriched by stellar winds and supernovae. It is depleted by star formation. The cycle regulates the metallicity and the star-formation rate of the galaxy. The same phases and processes operate in other star-forming galaxies.

### Molecular Clouds

Molecular clouds are the densest and coldest phase of the interstellar medium. Temperatures are 10–20 K. Densities exceed 10<sup>2</sup> cm<sup>−3</sup>. They are supported against gravity by turbulence and by magnetic fields. The support is temporary. Local regions collapse to form stars. The efficiency is low—a few percent—because feedback from the newly formed stars disperses the cloud.

The clouds are observed in molecular lines, principally CO, and in dust continuum. Their mass spectrum is a power law. The most massive clouds form the most massive stars. The relation between cloud properties and the resulting stellar population is the initial mass function problem. The leading explanation for the stellar population that results is the turbulent fragmentation of the clouds, and that explanation is not complete.

### Active Galactic Nuclei

Active galactic nuclei are powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes. The accretion disk radiates from the optical to the X-ray. A corona produces hard X-rays. Relativistic jets are launched in a subset of sources. The orientation of the observer relative to the disk and jet determines the observed class—quasar, Seyfert, radio galaxy, blazar.

The luminosity can reach 10<sup>47</sup> erg s<sup>−1</sup>. The radiative efficiency is approximately 10 percent for a non-spinning hole and higher for a spinning hole. Feedback from the radiation and the jets regulates star formation in the host galaxy. The same feedback is required in models of galaxy formation to match the observed stellar masses. Active nuclei are both luminous beacons and agents of galactic evolution.

### Quasars

Quasars are the most luminous active galactic nuclei. They are visible across the observable universe. Their spectra show broad emission lines from gas moving at thousands of kilometers per second. The lines are photoionized by the continuum. Absorption lines from intervening gas trace the intergalactic medium.

The quasar luminosity function peaks at redshift 2–3. The peak coincides with the peak of cosmic star formation. Both are regulated by the supply of cold gas. Quasars are used as backlights for absorption studies and as tracers of large-scale structure. Their clustering measures the bias of massive halos. The same objects that once seemed exotic are now standard tools of cosmology.

### Blazars

Blazars are active galactic nuclei whose jets point nearly toward the observer. Relativistic beaming amplifies the emission and shortens the variability timescale. The spectral energy distribution shows two peaks—one from synchrotron radiation, one from inverse-Compton scattering. The peaks can lie in the radio, optical, X-ray or gamma-ray bands.

Variability on timescales of minutes implies emitting regions smaller than the Schwarzschild radius of the central black hole. The implication requires Doppler boosting. Blazars are the dominant sources of the extragalactic gamma-ray background. They are also candidate sources of high-energy neutrinos. The association of one blazar with a high-energy neutrino has been reported. The association is not yet confirmed by additional events. The objects remain the brightest persistent sources in the gamma-ray sky.

# <a id="part_6"></a>Part VI: The Universe as a Whole

*The expanding cosmos, its hot beginning, its dark contents, and the nature of time*

## <a id="ch_31"></a>31. The Expanding Universe

The universe is expanding. This chapter covers how the expansion is measured, the equations that describe it, and the disputes that remain. [Chapter 32](#ch_32) follows the expansion back to its hot beginning, and [Chapter 33](#ch_33) turns to the dark components that now drive it.

### The Expansion of the Universe

Distant galaxies recede with a speed proportional to their distance. That is Hubble’s law, and its slope is the Hubble constant, about 70 kilometers per second per megaparsec (km s<sup>−1</sup> Mpc<sup>−1</sup>). The recession is seen in every direction. It is not an explosion from a center in space but a growth in the scale of space itself, described by a scale factor a(t). Light crossing expanding space is stretched with it, so the redshift z of a distant galaxy obeys 1 + z = 1/a, where a is the size of the universe at emission relative to today.

The same stretching has cooled the radiation left over from the hot early universe into the cosmic microwave background: a thermal spectrum at 2.725 kelvin whose small temperature ripples map the density fluctuations that later grew into galaxies.

The expansion rate has not been constant. Matter slowed it for most of cosmic history. About six billion years ago, when the universe was a little more than half its present age, it began to accelerate. Type Ia supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations and the microwave background all show this. The cause is called dark energy, a component with negative pressure whose density stays nearly constant while the density of matter falls. The name labels the effect; what dark energy is remains unknown.

Running the expansion backward with the measured contents gives an age of about 13.8 billion years, consistent with the ages of the oldest stars. The model behind that number combines general relativity, the Standard Model, cold dark matter and a cosmological constant (ΛCDM). Six parameters fit the microwave background, and the same six then predict the baryon acoustic scale, the light-element abundances and the growth of structure. It is the standard model of cosmology: wide in reach, not proven complete. Its two known strains, the Hubble tension and a milder mismatch in how strongly matter clumps, are described below.

### Why the Night Sky Is Dark

The darkness of the night sky is the first cosmological observation anyone can make, and it is not obvious. Suppose the universe were infinite, eternal and uniformly filled with stars. Then every line of sight would end on the surface of some star, and the whole sky would glow as brightly as the surface of the Sun. The puzzle is usually named for the astronomer Heinrich Olbers, who discussed it in 1823, though Kepler, Halley and others had met it earlier.

The way out is not that the distant stars are too faint or are hidden by dust, since dust would heat up and glow. The way out is that the universe has a finite age. Light from stars beyond about 13.8 billion light-years has not had time to arrive, so most lines of sight end in the dark. The expansion helps as well, by stretching the light that does arrive to longer wavelengths and lower energy. Edgar Allan Poe guessed something close to this in his prose poem *Eureka* in 1848, long before the evidence existed.

### Hubble and Webb

The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990 into low Earth orbit. Its primary mirror is 2.4 meters in diameter. It observes from the near-ultraviolet to the near-infrared. Servicing missions corrected its optics and replaced instruments. It has measured the expansion rate, imaged distant galaxies, and resolved disks around young stars.

The James Webb Space Telescope was launched in 2021 and operates at the Sun–Earth L2 point, 1.5 million kilometers from Earth. Its primary mirror is 6.5 meters across, composed of 18 gold-coated beryllium segments. A five-layer sunshield keeps the telescope near 40 kelvin. Webb observes from the red visible to the mid-infrared. The longer wavelengths penetrate dust and reach the redshifted light of the first galaxies.

Webb’s collecting area is more than five times Hubble’s. Its infrared sensitivity reveals galaxies that formed within a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, the atmospheres of exoplanets by transmission spectroscopy, and the interiors of star-forming clouds. Hubble continues to provide ultraviolet and optical coverage. The two telescopes are complementary. Together they span the electromagnetic spectrum from the ultraviolet to the mid-infrared and the cosmic timeline from the present to the first luminous objects.

### The Friedmann Equations

The Friedmann equations govern the expansion of a homogeneous and isotropic universe. The first equation reads

H<sup>2</sup> = (8π G)/3ρ − kc<sup>2</sup>/a<sup>2</sup> + (Λ c<sup>2</sup>)/3,

where H = ȧ/a is the Hubble parameter and k is the spatial curvature, zero for a flat universe. The second equation gives the acceleration:

(ä)/a = -(4π G)/3(ρ + 3p/c<sup>2</sup>) + (Λ c<sup>2</sup>)/3.

Matter and radiation decelerate the expansion. A cosmological constant or any component with w < -1/3 accelerates it. Present data require a positive acceleration and a density close to the critical density.

The equations are the Einstein equation applied to the Robertson–Walker metric. They assume homogeneity and isotropy on large scales. Both assumptions are supported by the isotropy of the microwave background and by the large-scale distribution of galaxies. Small-scale inhomogeneities are treated as perturbations on the Friedmann background.

### Radiation, Matter and Vacuum Eras

Solving the Friedmann equations for a single dominant component gives three simple histories. When radiation dominates, the scale factor grows as the square root of time. When matter dominates it grows as time to the power two-thirds. When a cosmological constant dominates, it grows exponentially, with a doubling time set by the Hubble parameter.

The real universe has passed through these regimes in that order. Radiation gave way to matter when the universe was some 50 000 years old, at a redshift near 3 400. Dark energy overtook matter in density roughly ten billion years after the Big Bang, at a redshift near 0.3; the acceleration itself had begun a few billion years earlier, once the repulsion of dark energy outweighed the pull of matter. We live early in the third era, and if the dark energy is a true constant, the exponential phase will last forever.

### Light-Travel Distance and the Size of the Observable Universe

The universe is 13.8 billion years old. Light emitted at the Big Bang has therefore been traveling for 13.8 billion years. That light-travel time corresponds to a distance of 13.8 billion light-years. The statement is correct and incomplete.

While the light traveled, space expanded. The regions that emitted the photons we now receive as the cosmic microwave background are no longer 13.8 billion light-years away. Their present-day (comoving) distance is approximately 46 billion light-years. The factor of roughly three is the stretching of space that went on while the light was in transit.

The particle horizon—the boundary of the observable universe—is therefore a sphere of comoving radius 46 billion light-years centered on the observer. Every observer, wherever located, is at the center of their own such sphere. The spheres overlap but are not identical. Nothing outside an observer’s particle horizon can yet have influenced them.

The numerical distinction is a direct consequence of expansion. It does not imply that anything travels faster than light. It implies only that the ruler used to measure distance today is longer than the ruler that would have been used when the light was emitted. Both the 13.8-billion-year age and the 46-billion-light-year radius are required for a consistent description.

### Worked Examples: Cosmology

Example 1. The Hubble constant is 70 km s<sup>−1</sup> Mpc<sup>−1</sup>. What is the approximate age of a matter-dominated flat universe?

t = 2/(3H). H = 70 km s<sup>−1</sup> Mpc<sup>−1</sup> = 2.27 × 10<sup>−18</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. t ≈ 9.3 Gyr. (The actual age is larger because of dark energy.)

Example 2. A galaxy has redshift z = 0.1. What is its approximate recession speed and distance?

For small z, v = cz ≈ 30 000 km s<sup>−1</sup>. Distance d = v/H ≈ 430 Mpc.

Example 3. The cosmic microwave background temperature today is 2.725 K. What was the temperature at redshift z = 1 100 (recombination)?

T = T<sub>0</sub>(1+z) = 3 000 K. The same scaling applies to the wavelength of every photon.

Example 4. Critical density today for H<sub>0</sub> = 70 km s<sup>−1</sup> Mpc<sup>−1</sup>.

ρ<sub>c</sub> = 3H<sup>2</sup>/(8π G) ≈ 9.2 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>, or about 5.5 hydrogen atoms per cubic meter.

These relations convert the observed Hubble constant, redshifts and background temperature into distances, ages and densities.

### The Hubble Tension

The Hubble constant measured from the local distance ladder is approximately 73 km s<sup>−1</sup> Mpc<sup>−1</sup>. The value inferred from the microwave background under the standard cosmological model is approximately 67 km s<sup>−1</sup> Mpc<sup>−1</sup>. The discrepancy is about five standard deviations. It is not an artifact of a single method. Multiple local probes give high values. Multiple early-universe probes give low values.

Proposed resolutions include new physics in the early universe that changes the sound horizon, or systematic errors in the distance ladder. Neither has been established. The tension remains. It is the most significant current discrepancy in cosmology. Its resolution will either reveal new physics or identify an unrecognized systematic. Both outcomes are informative.

### Gravitational-Wave Cosmology

Gravitational waves from binary mergers provide a standard siren. The waveform amplitude determines the luminosity distance. If an electromagnetic counterpart identifies the host galaxy, the redshift is obtained. The combination measures the expansion rate without a distance ladder. GW170817 yielded a measurement of the Hubble constant consistent with other methods. The uncertainty is large. Future events will reduce it.

The same events constrain the speed of gravity. The arrival of the gamma-ray burst within seconds of the waves bounds the difference from the speed of light at the level of parts in 10<sup>15</sup>. The bound eliminates large classes of modified-gravity models. The waves also probe the equation of state of dense matter through the tidal deformability. The cosmological and the strong-field uses are complementary.

## <a id="ch_32"></a>32. A Universe With a Birthday

### The Night the Universe Acquired a Temperature

In 1964 two radio engineers were measuring noise. They found a persistent hiss that came from every direction. The hiss was not the equipment. It was not the atmosphere. It was the universe itself. The temperature of the hiss was 2.7 kelvin. The temperature had been predicted by the Big Bang theory years earlier. The prediction had been forgotten. The measurement revived it.

The photons that produce the hiss left the universe when it was 380 000 years old. They have been traveling ever since. Their wavelength has stretched with the expansion. The stretch is the reason they are now microwaves. The spectrum follows the black-body curve with extraordinary fidelity. No other known process produces a perfect black-body spectrum across the entire sky.

The measurement ended the steady-state theory. It did not end debate. It relocated the debate to the details of the early universe. The details are now measured to parts in a hundred thousand. The hiss is still there. It is the oldest light that reaches us. It is also the most precisely measured thermal spectrum in nature.

### The Big Bang

The Big Bang is the hot, dense, expanding phase from which the observable universe emerged. It is not an explosion in pre-existing space. It is the expansion of space itself, and every comoving observer sees the same recession of distant galaxies and the same cooling of the radiation field.

Cosmologists divide the story into epochs, each tied to a temperature. Near 10<sup>15</sup> K, within a trillionth of a second, the electromagnetic and weak forces were still one electroweak force. Within about ten microseconds the universe had cooled enough for quarks to bind into protons and neutrons. Within the first few minutes the light nuclei formed. Some 380 000 years later the first atoms appeared and the universe became transparent. Each transition is calculated within the Standard Model and leaves no relic that contradicts it.

![First 50 000 years, seconds after the Big Bang: Planck time 10^-43 s, where known physics ends; inflation near 10^-34 s, if it happened; electroweak force splits near 10^-12 s; quarks bind into protons and neutrons near 10^-5 s; light nuclei form in the first minutes; matter outweighs radiation at about 50 000 years. Billions of years after the Big Bang: atoms form and the microwave background is released at 380 000 years; first stars about 0.2; reionization complete about 1; cosmic star formation peaks about 3.5; expansion starts to accelerate about 7.8; Sun and Earth form 9.2; today 13.8.](scripts/rev16/figures/fig2_cosmic_timeline.png)

*Figure 3. A timeline of the universe. Top: the first 50 000 years on a logarithmic scale of seconds. Bottom: the rest of cosmic history in billions of years.*

The very beginning is the frontier, taken up in the next section. What is secure is everything from nucleosynthesis onward, confirmed by several independent observations.

### The Origin of the Universe

To ask for the origin of the universe is to ask two different questions. One is how the hot, expanding phase began and what set its initial conditions. The other is whether anything came before it, or whether the question even has meaning. Observation reaches only the first, and only partly: the earliest direct evidence is the microwave background, and nothing earlier has been seen in light.

Before nucleosynthesis the energies exceeded those accessible to accelerators. The electroweak transition, the confinement of quarks into hadrons, and any preceding inflationary phase lie in that regime. Inflation, if it occurred, would have stretched a microscopic region to macroscopic size, diluted curvature, and generated the nearly scale-invariant fluctuations later seen in the microwave background. No direct relic of inflation has been detected. The hypothesis remains the simplest account of the initial conditions required by the later evolution.

The expansion itself has no center and no edge within the observable volume. Run the Friedmann equation backward under the assumptions of classical general relativity and ordinary matter, and it reaches a singularity in finite time. That result marks the limit of the theory more than a moment of creation, and no controlled calculation yet replaces it with an earlier state.

The origin of the low entropy that permits the thermodynamic arrow, the origin of the baryon asymmetry, and the nature of the dark-matter particles are likewise open. They are the questions a complete account of the beginning would have to answer.

### The First Three Minutes

The early universe was hot and dense. At temperatures above 10<sup>10</sup> K neutrons and protons were in equilibrium through weak interactions. As the universe expanded and cooled, the weak interactions froze out. The neutron-to-proton ratio was then fixed at about one to six. Below roughly 10<sup>9</sup> K deuterium became stable. Almost all the remaining neutrons were incorporated into helium-4. The process left roughly 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium by mass, plus trace amounts of deuterium, helium-3, and lithium-7.

The abundances match the observations of the oldest stars and of interstellar gas once the baryon density is set to the value measured by the microwave background. The agreement is one of the principal successes of the hot Big Bang. It fixes the conditions between about one second and three minutes after the initial singularity.

The clock mattered. Free neutrons decay with a mean life of about fifteen minutes, so the neutron fraction was already sinking as the universe cooled toward the temperature at which deuterium could survive. Had the nuclear fires lit much later, less helium would have formed; had the weak interactions frozen out earlier, more. The observed quarter by mass is therefore a direct readout of the expansion rate in the first seconds.

The first three minutes therefore determined the composition of ordinary matter. The subsequent three hundred thousand years determined the radiation we still detect. Both calculations rest on measured particle-physics cross-sections and on general relativity. Both match observation.

### Big Bang Nucleosynthesis

Between about one second and three minutes after the Big Bang the temperature fell from 10<sup>10</sup> K to 10<sup>9</sup> K. Neutrons and protons froze out of equilibrium. Nearly every neutron that survived ended up inside a helium-4 nucleus. Trace amounts of deuterium, helium-3, and lithium-7 were also produced.

The predicted mass fraction of helium-4 is approximately 0.25. The predicted abundances of the lighter isotopes depend sensitively on the baryon-to-photon ratio. That ratio is now measured independently from the microwave background. The abundances observed in the oldest stars and in interstellar gas match the predictions. The agreement fixes the conditions of the early universe and confirms that the expansion rate was close to the general-relativistic value.

No heavier elements were produced. The Coulomb barriers are too high and the densities fall too rapidly. All nuclei beyond lithium were synthesized later in stars. Big Bang nucleosynthesis therefore accounts for the light-element abundances and for nothing else.

### The Cosmic Microwave Background

The cosmic microwave background is thermal radiation that fills the universe. Its spectrum is that of a black body at 2.725 K. The radiation was released when the universe cooled to about 3000 K and electrons combined with nuclei to form neutral atoms. The photons have traveled freely ever since. The expansion has redshifted their temperature by a factor of approximately 1100.

The background is isotropic to one part in 10<sup>5</sup>. The small anisotropies are the imprint of density fluctuations that existed at recombination. Those fluctuations grew by gravitational instability into the galaxies and clusters observed today. The angular power spectrum of the anisotropies measures the baryon density, the dark-matter density, the curvature of space, and the spectral index of the primordial fluctuations.

Polarization of the background records the motion of the plasma at last scattering and, potentially, the presence of primordial gravitational waves. Current limits on the latter constrain the energy scale of inflation. The background therefore supplies the most precise cosmological data set available.

### Cosmic Inflation

Cosmic inflation is a brief epoch of accelerated expansion in the earliest universe. It is driven by the potential energy of a scalar field—the inflaton—that rolls slowly toward the minimum of its potential. While the field is slow-rolling the scale factor grows exponentially. A tiny, causally connected region is stretched to a size far larger than the present observable universe.

Both puzzles described in the previous section dissolve, because the whole observable universe descends from one small patch that was once in causal contact and was then stretched flat. Quantum fluctuations of the inflaton are stretched to cosmological wavelengths and become the nearly scale-invariant, adiabatic, Gaussian density perturbations observed in the microwave background.

The simplest models predict a tensor-to-scalar ratio r that measures the amplitude of primordial gravitational waves. Current upper limits are r < 0.03. Detection of a non-zero r would fix the energy scale of inflation. Non-detection continues to constrain the shape of the potential. Inflation ends when the inflaton reaches the bottom of its potential and oscillates, reheating the universe and initiating the hot Big Bang. The mechanism is theoretically attractive and consistent with all present data. It is not yet uniquely confirmed.

### The Horizon and Flatness Problems

The hot Big Bang accounts for the expansion, the microwave background, and the abundances of the light elements. It leaves two puzzles. The first is the horizon problem. The cosmic microwave background is uniform to one part in a hundred thousand in every direction. Regions that are now on opposite sides of the sky were never in causal contact in the standard expanding model. They had no time to exchange heat or information. Yet they have the same temperature. The second is the flatness problem. The density of the universe is close to the critical density that separates expansion forever from eventual recollapse. The critical density is unstable. A small departure early on grows rapidly. To be as close as it is today, the density at one second after the Big Bang had to match the critical value to one part in 10^15 or better. No mechanism in the standard model explains either fact.

Inflation supplies a mechanism. A brief period of accelerated expansion, driven by a scalar field in a false vacuum, stretches a small, causally connected region to a size larger than the present observable universe. The region is smoothed. Temperature differences are erased. The same expansion drives the density toward the critical value, so that the universe appears flat. The quantum fluctuations of the field are stretched to cosmic scales and become the seeds of later structure. The spectrum of those fluctuations is nearly scale-invariant. It matches the pattern measured in the microwave background and in the large-scale distribution of galaxies.

The idea was proposed in the early 1980s. It is not yet derived from a confirmed particle-physics model. The field that drove it has not been identified. The duration and the energy scale remain free parameters within broad limits. What the observations require is some process that produced a large, nearly uniform, nearly flat region with small density perturbations of the observed amplitude. Inflation is the leading candidate. Other proposals exist. None has yet replaced it. The problems it solves were already visible in the 1970s. The microwave data that confirmed the uniformity and the flatness arrived later. The sequence is the reverse of the usual one: the solution was offered before the precision measurements that made the problems sharp.

### Inflationary Predictions

Inflation predicts a nearly scale-invariant spectrum of scalar perturbations. The spectral index is slightly less than one. The observed value is n<sub>s</sub> ≈ 0.965. The amplitude is fixed by the height of the potential. Tensor modes are predicted with an amplitude set by the energy scale of inflation. The tensor-to-scalar ratio r is bounded above by 0.03. Non-detection continues to constrain the potential.

The perturbations are adiabatic and Gaussian to high precision. Isocurvature modes and non-Gaussianity are small. The predictions match the microwave-background data. They do not uniquely determine the inflaton potential. Many potentials remain compatible. The simplest monomial potentials are disfavoured. Plateau potentials are allowed. The data confirm the broad predictions. They do not yet identify the microphysical model, and rival scenarios that mimic the same spectrum can be told apart only by better measurements of non-Gaussianity or of primordial gravitational waves.

### Baryogenesis

Baryogenesis is the generation of the observed excess of matter over antimatter. The universe contains roughly 10<sup>9</sup> photons for every baryon, and essentially no antibaryons. Sakharov identified three necessary conditions: baryon-number violation, C and CP violation, and departure from thermal equilibrium.

The Standard Model contains all three ingredients. Electroweak sphalerons violate baryon number. The CKM matrix supplies CP violation. The electroweak phase transition can be out of equilibrium if it is strongly first-order. Quantitative calculation shows that the Standard Model CP violation and the strength of the transition are both insufficient to produce the observed asymmetry. Additional physics is required.

Two leading proposals, leptogenesis and electroweak baryogenesis, are described in [Chapter 11](#ch_11). A third, Affleck–Dine baryogenesis, uses scalar fields of supersymmetric theories. Each remains a hypothesis awaiting experimental support, and all of them tie the matter excess to physics beyond the Standard Model.

### Baryon Acoustic Oscillations

Baryon acoustic oscillations are the frozen sound waves of the pre-recombination plasma. The sound horizon at recombination is a standard ruler of approximately 150 Mpc. It appears as a peak in the galaxy correlation function and as a series of peaks in the microwave-background power spectrum. The angular scale of the peaks measures the angular-diameter distance to recombination. The same ruler measured in galaxy surveys at lower redshift measures the expansion history.

The measurements are consistent with a flat universe dominated by a cosmological constant. They constrain the dark-energy equation of state. They are independent of the supernova distance ladder. The agreement of the two methods strengthens the evidence for acceleration. The ruler is calibrated by the microwave background. Its use at late times is a direct geometric probe.

### Reionization

Reionization is the process by which the intergalactic medium was ionized by the first stars and galaxies. It occurred between redshifts of approximately 15 and 6. The optical depth to reionization is measured by the large-scale polarization of the microwave background. The measurement constrains the integrated ionizing output. Direct observations of high-redshift galaxies and of the Lyman-alpha forest constrain the timing.

The sources are predominantly galaxies. Quasars contribute at later times. The escape fraction of ionizing photons is uncertain. It is the principal free parameter in models. The process ended the cosmic dark ages. It is the last major phase transition in the history of the baryons. Its details are still being mapped by current and forthcoming telescopes.

### The Cosmic Infrared Background

The cosmic infrared background is the integrated emission from dust-obscured star formation across cosmic history. It peaks at wavelengths of 100–200 µm. The intensity is comparable to the optical background. Most of the energy was emitted at redshifts between 1 and 3. The sources are resolved by far-infrared and submillimeter telescopes. They are dusty star-forming galaxies.

The background constrains the total star-formation rate density. It is consistent with the rate inferred from ultraviolet and optical surveys once dust extinction is included. Fluctuations in the background probe the clustering of the unresolved sources. The fluctuations are detected. They match the expectations from known galaxy populations. The background is the bolometric record of cosmic star formation.

## <a id="ch_33"></a>33. Dark Matter and Dark Energy

### The Dark Sector at a Glance

Dark matter and dark energy are the two dominant components of the present universe. Neither emits, absorbs or scatters light, and both are detected solely through their gravitational effects.

Dark matter makes up roughly a quarter of the cosmic energy budget and dark energy roughly two-thirds to seven-tenths. Ordinary atoms, everything that shines or can be built into a star, a planet or a person, supply the remaining five percent. The expansion history and the growth of structure are described accurately once all three are included.

The two differ in character. Dark matter clumps: it gathers into halos, pulls galaxies together and shapes the cosmic web. Dark energy does not clump, and its density hardly changes as space expands. One slowed the expansion while structures formed; the other is speeding it up now. Neither has a known microphysical identity.

### Dark Matter

Galaxies rotate faster in their outer regions than the visible mass can explain. Clusters of galaxies bend light and bind hot gas more strongly than their luminous matter allows. The cosmic microwave background shows acoustic peaks whose positions require additional non-baryonic matter. These observations converge on a component that gravitates but does not emit, absorb, or scatter light at detectable levels. It is called dark matter.

The density of dark matter is about five times the density of ordinary matter. It is cold, meaning that its particles moved slowly when structures formed. Cold dark matter collapses into halos. Ordinary matter falls into the halos and forms galaxies. The halos are larger than the visible galaxies. Their presence is inferred from rotation curves, gravitational lensing, and the growth of structure.

No dark-matter particle has been detected in the laboratory. Candidates include weakly interacting massive particles, axions, and sterile neutrinos. Direct-detection experiments set limits on the scattering cross-section. Indirect searches look for annihilation products. Collider searches look for missing energy. None has produced a confirmed signal. The gravitational evidence remains. The identity of the matter does not.

Modified-gravity theories attempt to explain the observations without new particles. They reproduce some galactic rotation curves. They have greater difficulty with clusters, with the microwave background, and with the separation of mass and light in merging clusters. The dark-matter hypothesis accounts for all of these with one additional component. It is the working description. It is not yet a completed identification.

### Dark Energy

The expansion of the universe is accelerating. Type Ia supernovae at high redshift are fainter than they would be in a decelerating universe. The microwave-background acoustic peaks and the large-scale distribution of galaxies independently require a component that drives acceleration. The component has negative pressure. Its energy density is roughly constant as the universe expands. It is called dark energy.

The simplest model is a cosmological constant. Einstein introduced the term to permit a static universe. It was later set to zero. The observations revive it with a small positive value. The constant corresponds to an energy density of about 10<sup>−29</sup> grams per cubic centimeter. A naive quantum-field-theory estimate of the vacuum energy comes out many orders of magnitude too large, a mismatch examined below.

Other models allow the density to vary slowly. They are parameterized by an equation-of-state index w. Current data are consistent with w = -1, the value for a cosmological constant, to within a few percent. Future surveys of supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, and weak lensing will tighten the constraint. A clear departure from -1 would rule out the simplest model.

Dark energy dominates the present energy budget. It did not dominate in the past. Its presence sets the ultimate fate of the expansion. If it remains constant, the expansion continues forever and galaxies beyond the local group eventually leave the observable universe. The inference rests on the measured acceleration and on the assumption that the component persists. Both are supported by present data. Both remain open to revision.

### Beyond the Cosmological Constant

A true cosmological constant is only one way to make the universe accelerate. Quintessence replaces it with a slowly rolling scalar field whose energy density can change with time. Modified-gravity models alter the Einstein equation on large scales instead of adding a new substance. Each can be tuned to mimic a constant, which is why the choice is hard to make from the expansion history alone.

The tests are the expansion history and the growth rate of cosmic structure. A pure constant fixes both with no free parameters, so any measured drift in the equation-of-state parameter w, or any mismatch between how fast space expands and how fast structure grows, would point beyond it. Recent baryon-acoustic-oscillation maps, combined with supernova and microwave-background data, show a mild preference for dark energy that weakens with time. The significance depends on which supernova sample is used, and it has not been confirmed.

A constant also fixes when acceleration began. Because its density does not dilute, it overtook the falling matter density only recently, and the switch from deceleration to acceleration happened at a redshift near 0.7.

### The Cosmological-Constant Problem

The cosmological-constant problem is the discrepancy between the observed vacuum energy density and the value predicted by quantum field theory. Every quantum field possesses a zero-point energy. Summing the ground-state energies 1/2ħω of all modes up to the Planck scale yields a density of order 10<sup>113</sup> J m<sup>−3</sup>. Even a cutoff at the electroweak scale still produces ~ 10<sup>45</sup> J m<sup>−3</sup>.

The density inferred from the acceleration of the universe is approximately 6 × 10<sup>−10</sup> J m<sup>−3</sup>. The mismatch is between 50 and 120 orders of magnitude. No symmetry of the Standard Model cancels the vacuum energy. Unbroken supersymmetry would cancel the leading term, yet supersymmetry, if present, is broken at a scale that still leaves a residual many orders of magnitude too large.

Anthropic selection among many vacua can account for the fact that observers inhabit a region whose vacuum energy permits structure and life. It does not eliminate the fine-tuning inside any given vacuum. No dynamical mechanism is known that relaxes the vacuum energy to the observed value after the Standard Model parameters are fixed. The problem remains unsolved.

### A Number That Should Not Be Small

The cosmological constant is small, and it is not zero. Both halves of that sentence are measured. The explanation of either half is absent: no symmetry forces the value to vanish, and no mechanism is known that would relax it to the tiny number observed.

The smallness is not a detail. A much larger value would have driven matter apart before galaxies could form, and there would be no stars, no chemistry and no observers. That observation has led to anthropic arguments. They may be correct, yet they explain only in a thin sense: they derive what observers will find from the fact that observers exist, not from a dynamical principle.

The constant is therefore both the dominant component of the present universe and the least understood. Its smallness is the sharpest quantitative failure of present theory, and the failure is not hidden. It is written in the expansion rate of the universe and in the existence of the reader.

### Dark Matter Detection

Direct detection experiments search for the elastic scattering of dark-matter particles on nuclei or electrons. The expected rate is low. Detectors are placed underground to reduce cosmic-ray backgrounds. They use liquid xenon, liquid argon, or cryogenic crystals. No confirmed signal has been observed. The experiments exclude large regions of the parameter space for weakly interacting massive particles.

Indirect detection searches for annihilation or decay products—gamma rays, neutrinos, antimatter. Excesses have been reported and later attributed to astrophysical sources. Collider searches look for missing energy carried by particles that escape the detector. No significant excess has been confirmed. The absence of signals has pushed the favored mass range upward and the favored coupling strength downward. The particles, if they exist, have not yet been produced or detected in the laboratory.

Annual modulation is a predicted signature. The Earth’s orbital motion causes the dark-matter flux to vary by a few percent over the year. One experiment has reported a modulation. Others have not confirmed it. The discrepancy remains unresolved. Directional detectors aim to measure the arrival direction of the recoiling nucleus. The direction would point opposite the solar motion through the galactic halo. No directional detector has yet reached the required sensitivity.

Axion searches use resonant cavities in strong magnetic fields, where an axion would convert into a photon at a frequency set by its mass. The search is therefore a slow scan through frequencies, and nothing has turned up in the ranges covered so far. Much of the allowed mass range is still unexplored. Primordial black holes are constrained by microlensing, by dynamical effects on stars, and by the absence of evaporation signals. Across most mass ranges they can account for only a small share of it.

## <a id="ch_34"></a>34. Quantum Gravity, Strings and the Multiverse

### Quantum Gravity

Quantum gravity is the attempt to reconcile general relativity with quantum mechanics. General relativity describes spacetime as a dynamical geometry whose curvature is fixed by the distribution of energy and momentum. Quantum mechanics describes matter and fields by operators on a Hilbert space and by amplitudes that interfere. At ordinary energies the two frameworks are used in succession: quantum fields propagate on a fixed classical background. The approximation fails when curvature radii approach the Planck length, approximately 10<sup>−35</sup> m, or when energies approach the Planck energy, approximately 10<sup>19</sup> GeV.

No complete theory is known. The two best-developed research programs are string theory, which replaces point particles by extended objects, and loop quantum gravity, which quantizes geometry itself; both are described in the sections below. Other approaches—asymptotic safety, causal dynamical triangulations, and emergent-gravity scenarios—explore different quantization schemes or different ontological starting points. None has been experimentally confirmed.

The only present evidence that a quantum theory of gravity is required is the existence of singularities in the classical theory and the expectation that quantum effects cannot be neglected at the Planck scale.

The problem is therefore well-posed and unsolved. Its solution will determine whether spacetime is fundamental or emergent, whether information is preserved in black-hole evaporation, and whether the initial conditions of the universe can be derived rather than postulated.

### Loop Quantum Gravity

Loop quantum gravity is a non-perturbative, background-independent quantization of general relativity. The fundamental variables are holonomies of the Ashtekar connection along paths and fluxes of the densitised triad through surfaces. These variables are promoted to operators on a Hilbert space of spin-network states. A spin network is a graph whose edges carry SU(2) representations and whose nodes carry invariant tensors.

The area of a surface and the volume of a region become discrete operators. Their spectra are bounded below by multiples of the Planck area and the Planck volume. The classical continuum geometry is recovered only as an approximation when the spin network is finely grained and the expectation values of the geometric operators are large compared with the Planck scale.

The dynamics are encoded in a Hamiltonian constraint. Solutions of the constraint define the physical Hilbert space. In cosmological models the same techniques yield a difference equation for the scale factor. The equation replaces the big-bang singularity by a bounce at a critical density of order the Planck density. The bounce connects a contracting phase to an expanding phase. Whether the bounce is generic in the full theory is not yet established.

Matter can be coupled. Fermions and gauge fields are incorporated by extending the spin-network labels. The recovery of the Standard Model spectrum and of a realistic value of the cosmological constant has not been achieved. The theory also lacks a complete demonstration that its low-energy limit is classical general relativity plus quantum field theory on curved spacetime, although several calculations of graviton propagators and of black-hole entropy are consistent with that limit.

Loop quantum gravity therefore supplies a concrete realization of discrete quantum geometry and a possible resolution of cosmological singularities. It remains incomplete as a unified theory of all interactions and as a fully controlled continuum limit.

### String Theory and M-Theory

String theory replaces point particles by one-dimensional extended objects. The different vibrational modes of a string appear, at energies low compared with the string scale, as different particle species. One mode is a massless spin-2 state that couples precisely as a graviton. The theory therefore contains general relativity as a low-energy limit.

Consistent quantization requires additional spatial dimensions and, in the superstring versions, supersymmetry. The extra dimensions are compactified on a small manifold. The geometry and fluxes of the compact space determine the spectrum and couplings of the four-dimensional effective theory. A large number of distinct compactifications exist, forming what is called the landscape.

The theory is perturbatively finite order by order. Non-perturbative definitions are available in certain backgrounds via dualities, including the AdS/CFT correspondence. These dualities relate apparently different string theories and relate string theory to ordinary quantum field theories. They have not yet produced a unique, realistic vacuum.

Direct experimental tests are absent. The string scale is expected to lie near the Planck energy, far beyond accelerator reach. Indirect signatures—supersymmetric partners, extra dimensions, or modified gravitational laws at short distances—have not been observed. String theory remains the most developed framework that unifies gravity with the other interactions in a quantum-mechanically consistent manner. As a theory of nature it is still unfinished.

Five consistent superstring theories exist in ten dimensions. In the mid-1990s it was shown that they are related by dualities, and that a single eleven-dimensional framework, called M-theory, contains all five as different limits. Membranes and higher-dimensional objects appear in the eleven-dimensional description, and its low-energy limit is eleven-dimensional supergravity.

The framework also contains gauge fields and fermions and can accommodate chiral matter.

### Branes

A brane is an extended object on which open strings can end. A p-brane has p spatial dimensions. A 1-brane is a string. A 2-brane is a membrane. Higher-dimensional branes appear in string theory and in M-theory. The endpoints of open strings are confined to the brane. Closed strings propagate in the full spacetime, the bulk.

In some constructions the Standard Model fields are localized on a brane while gravity propagates in the extra dimensions. The weakness of gravity relative to the other forces can then be a consequence of the volume of the extra dimensions rather than of a high fundamental scale. The idea is called a brane-world. No experimental signature of large extra dimensions or of brane-localized matter has been confirmed.

Branes carry charges under antisymmetric tensor fields. They are stable when the charge is conserved. Parallel branes of the same charge repel. Branes and anti-branes attract and can annihilate. The annihilation can end an inflationary phase in some models. The process is calculable within the theory. It has not been observed.

Branes are therefore part of the extended-object spectrum of string theory and M-theory. They supply a geometric setting for gauge fields and a possible explanation for the hierarchy between gravity and the other forces. Both uses remain theoretical. No direct evidence for branes exists.

### Folded Dimensions

Extra spatial dimensions can be compactified. Their size is finite and small enough that they have not been detected. A circle of radius R is the simplest example.
