Momentum around the circle is quantized in units of 1/R. From the viewpoint of the large dimensions the quantized momentum appears as a tower of massive particles. The masses begin at 1/R and rise in steps of the same size. The tower is called a Kaluza–Klein tower.

If R is near the Planck length the tower begins at the Planck mass and is unobservable. If R is larger, the lightest modes could appear at accelerator energies. Searches for missing energy or for deviations from Newtonian gravity at short distances have set limits. No signal has been found. The radius of any flat extra dimension accessible to those searches must be smaller than roughly a tenth of a millimeter.

Compactification need not be a simple circle. The internal space can be a Calabi–Yau manifold or another curved geometry. The shape determines the spectrum of particles and the couplings that appear in the large dimensions. Different shapes produce different low-energy theories.

Folded dimensions therefore remain a consistent theoretical possibility. They supply a geometric origin for gauge symmetries in the original Kaluza–Klein construction and for the particle spectrum in string compactifications. They have not been observed. Their size, if they exist, lies below present experimental bounds.

### Everything, Everywhere, All at Once

The many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics asserts that the universal wave function evolves unitarily at all times. There is no collapse. Every outcome that has a non-zero amplitude is realized in some branch of the wave function. The branches do not interact once they have decohered. An observer who records one outcome is correlated with that branch and has no access to the others.

The interpretation was introduced by Everett in 1957. It reproduces the statistical predictions of ordinary quantum mechanics because the measure of branches in which a given relative frequency occurs matches the Born rule in the limit of many trials. The derivation of the Born rule from the unitary evolution alone is still debated. Decision-theoretic and envariance arguments have been offered. None is universally accepted.

The interpretation removes the measurement problem by denying that measurement is a special process. It multiplies the ontology. Every possible outcome occurs somewhere in the wave function. The multiplication is not observed. Decoherence explains why the branches do not interfere, but why one branch is the experienced world remains a question. The selection remains an open question within the interpretation.

No experiment distinguishes many-worlds from other interpretations that yield the same probabilities. The choice is metaphysical. The formalism is the same. The claim that all outcomes occur is an additional assertion about what the formalism describes. It is consistent. It is not required. It is not ruled out.

### Warped Extra Dimensions

Warped extra dimensions can generate hierarchies exponentially. The Randall–Sundrum model places the Higgs on a brane where the warp factor suppresses its mass, and it predicts Kaluza–Klein gravitons that have not been seen.

Such models remain a possible ultraviolet completion. They are constrained by precision tests and by the non-observation of new particles, but the constraints do not exclude all realizations.

### String Compactifications

String theory requires additional dimensions. Compactification on a Calabi–Yau manifold preserves supersymmetry in the low-energy theory. Fluxes and branes stabilize the moduli. The number of distinct compactifications is astronomically large. Each yields a different four-dimensional effective theory. The vast majority do not resemble the Standard Model.

No principle selects the compactification that reproduces the observed particle content and couplings. Anthropic selection among those that permit observers is one proposal. It is not predictive beyond the requirement of habitability. The compactifications demonstrate that string theory can produce four-dimensional physics. They do not yet demonstrate that it produces our physics. The gap is the absence of a selection mechanism.

### The Swampland

The swampland is the set of effective field theories that cannot be consistently coupled to quantum gravity. Swampland conjectures propose criteria that separate the landscape from the swampland. One conjecture states that the scalar potential must satisfy a lower bound on its gradient. Another states that towers of light states appear when a scalar field traverses a large distance in field space.

The conjectures are motivated by examples in string theory. They are not proven. If true, they constrain inflation and the cosmological constant. Some versions are in tension with the observed dark energy. The conjectures illustrate an attempt to extract general lessons from string theory without a complete non-perturbative definition. Their status is provisional.

### The Planck-Scale Cutoff

The Planck scale is the energy and length at which quantum field theory and general relativity are expected to cease being separately valid. The Planck length is LPl = √((ħ G)/c<sup>3</sup>) ≈ 1.6 × 10<sup>−35</sup> m. The Planck energy is EPl = √((ħ c<sup>5</sup>)/G) ≈ 1.2 × 10<sup>19</sup> GeV. At this scale the Schwarzschild radius of a quantum becomes comparable to its Compton wavelength. Gravity and quantum mechanics can no longer be treated independently.

In calculations of vacuum energy the Planck energy is therefore adopted as a natural ultraviolet cutoff. Modes of higher frequency are excluded because the present theory does not describe them. That choice gives the most extreme form of the cosmological-constant problem, discussed with the dark sector.

The cutoff is not an observed boundary. It is the point at which existing theories become unreliable. A complete theory of quantum gravity is expected to modify or cancel the vacuum contribution before the Planck scale is reached. No such mechanism is known. Lower cutoffs (electroweak, QCD) still leave a discrepancy of many orders of magnitude. The Planck scale merely marks the highest energy at which the problem can be posed within present frameworks.

### Unified Theories

Maxwell’s equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light. The electroweak theory unified the electromagnetic and weak forces. At energies above roughly 100 GeV the two forces are aspects of a single interaction. Below that scale the Higgs mechanism gives mass to the W and Z bosons and leaves the photon massless. The strong force is described by quantum chromodynamics. It has not been unified with the electroweak force in a confirmed theory.

Grand unified theories would embed the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces in a single gauge group; [Chapter 11](#ch_11) describes them. None is confirmed, and the proton decay they predict has not been seen.

Gravity is described by general relativity, a classical theory of curved spacetime. Gravity has no established quantum theory. String theory and loop quantum gravity are research programs. Neither has made a confirmed prediction that distinguishes it from the others or from general relativity plus the Standard Model. The Standard Model plus general relativity accounts for all confirmed particle-physics and gravitational phenomena. The unification of gravity with the other forces remains open.

The pattern of past unifications is clear. Phenomena once thought distinct were shown to be aspects of a single framework. The framework then made new predictions. The same pattern is sought for the remaining forces. It has not yet been completed.

### The Multiverse

The multiverse is the hypothesis that the observable universe is one of many domains that may differ in their physical parameters, initial conditions or even effective laws. Several distinct proposals exist.

Eternal inflation generates a multitude of bubble universes. Quantum fluctuations of the inflaton prevent inflation from ending everywhere at once. Each bubble thermalizes with potentially different vacuum energy and low-energy constants. The string-theory landscape supplies a large number of metastable vacua, making such variation conceivable. No observation has identified another bubble.

The many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, described in [Chapter 6](#ch_6), supplies a different kind of multiplicity: branches of one wave function rather than regions of one space. It adds no new dynamical law, and empirical distinction from other interpretations is lacking.

Other constructions include cyclic models, varying-speed-of-light scenarios, and mathematical ensembles in which every consistent structure is realized. None yields a unique, testable prediction that has been confirmed. Selection effects (anthropic reasoning) can explain why observers find themselves in a region compatible with life, but they do not predict the values of parameters that are already measured.

The multiverse therefore remains a set of theoretical possibilities. Some versions address the cosmological-constant problem or the initial conditions of inflation. All versions currently lack direct empirical support. The observable universe continues to be described, to high precision, by a single Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker geometry with a single set of low-energy constants.

### The Anthropic Principle

The values of the fundamental constants permit the existence of carbon-based life. Small changes in several of them would prevent it. The strong force, if slightly stronger, would bind the diproton and alter the path of stellar nucleosynthesis. If slightly weaker, deuterium would be unbound and the same path would close. The electromagnetic force and the electron-to-proton mass ratio set the sizes of atoms and the stability of molecules. The cosmological constant, if much larger, would have prevented the formation of galaxies. These relations are observed. They are not explained by a deeper theory that derives the constants.

The weak anthropic principle states that the observed values are restricted by the requirement that observers exist to measure them. Observers can exist only in regions or in universes where the constants allow the formation of stable nuclei, long-lived stars, planets, and chemistry complex enough for life. The principle is a selection effect. It does not explain why the constants have the values they have. It explains why we should not be surprised to find ourselves in a universe where those values permit our existence.

The strong anthropic principle asserts that the universe must have properties that allow life to develop at some stage. The final anthropic principle adds that information processing, once begun, will continue forever. Neither claim follows from the weak principle. Both go beyond the evidence. The weak principle is a reminder about sampling. The others are conjectures.

Hoyle predicted a resonance in carbon-12 that allows the triple-alpha process to proceed in stars. The resonance was found. The prediction is sometimes cited as an anthropic success. It was a nuclear-physics calculation guided by the requirement that carbon be produced. The requirement is empirical. Carbon exists. The calculation showed where the resonance had to lie. The episode illustrates how the existence of a known outcome can constrain an unknown parameter. It does not demonstrate that the parameter was chosen for that outcome.

The constants may be fixed by a more fundamental theory. They may vary across a multiverse, with observers appearing only in the compatible regions. Both possibilities are open. The anthropic observation records the compatibility. It does not decide the mechanism. The observation remains: the universe we inhabit is one in which the constants allow chemistry, stars, and observers. That fact is not in dispute. Its explanation is.

### Orders of Magnitude from the Constants

Many characteristic sizes and energies in physics follow from the fundamental constants by dimensional analysis. The Bohr radius is a<sub>0</sub> = ħ<sup>2</sup> / (m<sub>e</sub> e<sup>2</sup>). Atomic densities are then of order m<sub>N</sub> / a<sub>0</sub><sup>3</sup>, a few grams per cubic centimeter for light elements. The result matches the densities of ordinary solids and liquids.

Nuclear sizes follow from the range of the strong force. The pion Compton wavelength sets that range at about 1.4 femtometers. The binding energy per nucleon is a few MeV. The same constants that fix atomic sizes fix nuclear sizes once the strong coupling is given. The ratio of the two scales is large because the strong force is strong and short-range while electromagnetism is weaker and long-range.

Stellar masses and lifetimes are constrained by the same constants. A self-gravitating body of atomic density reaches a central temperature set by the balance of gravitational compression and electron degeneracy pressure. For the temperature to ignite hydrogen fusion the mass must lie in a range that produces main-sequence stars. The main-sequence lifetime is then fixed by the nuclear energy release and the luminosity. The Sun’s lifetime is long enough for planetary evolution and short enough that the universe is still young when the first such stars appear. Both facts follow from the constants once the requirement of stable nuclear burning is imposed.

Planetary atmospheres are retained only when the escape velocity exceeds the thermal speed of the gas at temperatures where liquid water or complex chemistry can exist. Bodies much smaller than Earth lose their atmospheres. Bodies much larger become gas giants. The window is set by gravity, temperature, and molecular mass. The existence of rocky planets with atmospheres is therefore a consequence of the same constants that permit stars and chemistry.

These relations do not require the anthropic principle. They are ordinary dimensional consequences of the measured constants. The anthropic observation is that the constants permit the relations to produce long-lived stars, rocky planets, and carbon chemistry at the same epoch. The dimensional results stand independently. They show how little freedom the constants leave once they are fixed.

## <a id="ch_35"></a>35. The Arrow of Time

The laws of mechanics are nearly symmetric under the reversal of time. If a set of particle trajectories is allowed, the reversed trajectories are also allowed. A film of two billiard balls colliding looks almost the same run backward. The exception is friction and other dissipative processes, which convert organized motion into heat.

Thermodynamics supplies the direction. The second law forbids the entropy of an isolated system from falling. Entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state. A gas that fills a room has far more arrangements than the same gas confined to one corner. The probability of the gas spontaneously returning to the corner is negligible. The direction of time in everyday experience is the direction of increasing entropy.

The universe began in a state of low entropy. The hot, dense early universe was smooth. Gravity later clumped matter into stars and galaxies, increasing the entropy. The low-entropy initial condition is what allows the second law to define a direction. Without it, there would be no preferred direction for the growth of entropy. Why the initial condition was low-entropy is an open question. It is not explained by the second law itself.

Memory and records point in the same direction. A memory is a correlation between a present state and a past state. The formation of that correlation increases the entropy of the surroundings. We remember the past and not the future because the past is the direction of lower entropy. The same asymmetry appears in the fact that causes precede effects in ordinary experience. The microscopic laws do not enforce the asymmetry. The boundary condition does.

The arrow is not absolute in every sense. In small systems fluctuations can temporarily decrease entropy. The decreases are rare and short-lived. On the scales of everyday objects and of the universe as a whole, the second law holds. The direction of time that we experience is the direction in which entropy increases. That is the content of the thermodynamic arrow. Other arrows—the psychological arrow, the causal arrow—align with it under the low-entropy initial condition. The alignment is observed. The ultimate reason for the initial condition is not yet known.

### Three Arrows of Time

The fundamental dynamical laws are time-reversal invariant. The observed world is not. Entropy increases. Memory points one way only. The asymmetry is the arrow of time.

The thermodynamic arrow is the increase of entropy. It originates in the low-entropy initial condition of the universe. The early universe was smooth. Smoothness is a low-entropy state for the gravitational field. Subsequent clumping into stars, galaxies and black holes raises the entropy. The psychological arrow—the fact that memory and records point toward the past—aligns with the thermodynamic arrow because records form only when entropy increases.

The cosmological arrow is the expansion itself. Expansion does not by itself define a direction of increasing entropy; the origin of the low initial entropy is taken up in the section on the arrow in cosmology.

### Time Reversal

The fundamental equations of classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and quantum mechanics are invariant under reversal of the time coordinate. If a sequence of events is allowed, the time-reversed sequence is also a solution. The equations do not prefer one direction.

The observed universe does. Entropy increases. Heat flows from hot to cold. Memory records the past, not the future. The asymmetry is statistical. Left alone, a system that starts in a low-entropy state will almost certainly move toward higher entropy. The early universe was in such a state. The microwave background and the smoothness of the large-scale geometry record that fact. Why the initial entropy was low is not explained by the time-symmetric equations.

Weak interactions violate time-reversal symmetry by a small amount. The violation has been measured in the decays of neutral kaons and B mesons. It is required by the observed excess of matter over antimatter. The effect is tiny. It does not account for the thermodynamic arrow. The thermodynamic arrow is explained by the initial condition, not by a fundamental asymmetry in the microscopic laws.

Time reversal is therefore a symmetry of the equations and a broken symmetry of the solutions we inhabit. The equations permit both directions. The universe we observe has a past boundary of low entropy and a future of higher entropy. The origin of that boundary remains an open question in cosmology.

### Entropy

Entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements that correspond to a given macroscopic state. A system with many accessible microstates has high entropy. A system with few has low entropy. The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. It stays the same in reversible processes and increases in irreversible ones.

The law is statistical. Every microstate is equally likely. There are vastly more microstates that look disordered than microstates that look ordered. A system that begins in a low-entropy state is therefore overwhelmingly likely to evolve toward higher entropy. The reverse evolution is not forbidden. It is improbable to a degree that makes it unobservable in ordinary systems.

Heat flows from hot to cold because the combined system has more microstates when the temperatures are equal. Gases expand to fill their containers because the expanded state has more arrangements. Living things, which keep their internal entropy low, are a special case taken up at the end of this chapter.

The early universe was in a state of remarkably low entropy. The microwave background is smooth to one part in a hundred thousand. That smoothness is a low-entropy condition for the gravitational field. The subsequent increase in entropy includes the formation of stars, galaxies, and black holes. Black holes have entropy proportional to the area of their event horizons. They dominate the entropy budget of the observable universe.

Entropy defines a direction in time. The microscopic equations are time-symmetric. The boundary condition of low entropy in the past is not. The second law is the macroscopic consequence of that boundary condition. Why the boundary condition was low remains unexplained.

### Maxwell’s Demon

Maxwell imagined a being that could sort molecules. A partition divides a box of gas. A small door in the partition is operated by the demon. When a fast molecule approaches from the left, the demon opens the door. When a slow molecule approaches, the demon leaves it closed. The right side grows hotter. The left side grows colder. Entropy appears to decrease without work being done. The second law seems violated.

The resolution is that the demon must acquire information. Measuring the speed of a molecule requires a physical interaction. The interaction increases the entropy of the measuring apparatus by at least as much as the entropy decrease in the gas. When the demon’s memory is erased to make room for the next measurement, the erasure dissipates heat. The total entropy of gas plus demon plus surroundings does not fall. The second law holds.

The argument was made precise by Szilard, Landauer, and Bennett. Landauer’s principle states that erasing one bit of information in a system at temperature T dissipates at least kT ln 2 of heat. The principle has been tested in small systems. The measured dissipation matches the bound. Information is physical. Its acquisition and erasure have thermodynamic costs.

The demon does not refute the second law. It illustrates that the law applies to the complete system, including whatever performs the measurement and the erasure. No known process sorts molecules in a way that reduces the entropy of an isolated system. The thought experiment remains useful because it forces the accounting to be complete.

### Feynman’s Ratchet

Richard Feynman asked a question about Maxwell’s demon that anyone can picture. Take a tiny wheel with vanes, immersed in a gas, and attach to its axle a ratchet with a pawl that lets the wheel turn only one way. Molecular impacts jostle the vanes at random. Surely the ratchet will turn the random jostling into steady rotation, and the wheel could lift a weight?

It cannot, if the whole device is at one temperature. The pawl is also a tiny object, and it too is knocked about by thermal motion. Every so often it bounces up and lets the wheel slip backward, and over time the forward and backward slips balance exactly. Only if the vanes are hotter than the pawl does the wheel turn, and then it is an ordinary heat engine moving heat from hot to cold, as the second law allows.

The lesson reaches into biology. Molecular motors in cells do move in one direction in a thermal bath, but they are never at a single temperature in this sense. They are driven by a continual supply of chemical free energy, usually from the splitting of ATP. Order in a cell is paid for, as the second law requires.

### The Arrow of Time in Cosmology

Cosmology adds the question of why the low-entropy boundary condition holds. Inflationary models push the condition to still earlier times without explaining why it was satisfied. If an explanation exists, it probably lies in quantum gravity or in a selection principle among possible initial states, and no such principle is established.

The expansion itself does not define the arrow. A contracting universe with the same low-entropy boundary condition would also have a thermodynamic arrow pointing away from that boundary. What the observations show is a particular solution, with a smooth beginning and an expansion that happens to run the same way as entropy. The alignment is a fact about the solution rather than a law.

### Friction and the Irreversibility of Everyday Motion

Friction converts ordered mechanical energy into disordered thermal energy. The conversion is irreversible. A sliding block comes to rest. The reverse process—a block spontaneously beginning to slide by absorbing heat from its surroundings—has never been observed. The second law of thermodynamics quantifies the irreversibility.

At the microscopic level every collision is reversible. The irreversibility appears only when the number of degrees of freedom is large. The ordered motion of the block is shared among an enormous number of molecular degrees of freedom. The probability of those degrees of freedom reorganizing so as to return the energy to the block is vanishingly small. Friction is therefore the macroscopic signature of the second law.

The same irreversibility appears in viscosity, in electrical resistance, and in the damping of sound. In each case a macroscopic current or oscillation decays while the entropy of the thermal bath increases. No exception is known. The arrow of everyday time is the arrow of increasing entropy.

### Static and Kinetic Friction

Friction is the force that opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact. Dry friction has a static coefficient that must be overcome before motion begins and a lower kinetic coefficient once motion is under way. Both coefficients are empirical. They depend on surface roughness, material and contamination. The microscopic origin is the formation and rupture of adhesive junctions and the interlocking of asperities.

The heat it generates is the everyday price of motion, and it is why no machine runs forever without a supply of energy. Lubrication reduces the coefficients by separating the surfaces with a fluid film. The same principles govern the design of bearings, brakes and joints. Biological joints are lubricated by synovial fluid. The engineering and the biology solve the same problem with different materials.

### Life and the Second Law

A living organism maintains a low internal entropy by exporting entropy to its surroundings. It takes in free energy—sunlight or chemical fuel—and returns heat and waste. The total entropy of organism plus surroundings increases. The second law is not violated.

The free energy is used to synthesize ordered macromolecules, to maintain concentration gradients, and to perform mechanical work. The efficiency of the conversion is limited by the Carnot factor and by the irreversibility of the chemical reactions. Typical biological efficiencies lie well below the theoretical maximum.

Evolution by natural selection increases the adaptedness of populations. It does not decrease the entropy of the biosphere. The information stored in genomes is paid for by the entropy exported during the metabolic processes that replicate and repair the DNA. The arrow of biological complexity points in the same direction as the thermodynamic arrow.

No known organism operates outside these constraints. Life is a far-from-equilibrium process that is fully consistent with the second law.

## <a id="ch_36"></a>36. What Is Time?

### The Measurement of Time

Time is measured by counting periodic processes. The rotation of the Earth, the orbit of the Moon, and the vibration of a quartz crystal have all served as clocks. The present definition of the second is 9 192 631 770 periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between two hyperfine levels of the caesium-133 atom.

Atomic clocks achieve stabilities better than one part in 10<sup>16</sup>. Optical clocks that use transitions in the visible or ultraviolet are expected to reach one part in 10<sup>18</sup>. At that level the gravitational redshift produced by a height difference of one centimeter becomes measurable. Clocks therefore function as gravimeters.

The same atomic transitions define the meter through the fixed value of the speed of light. Length and time are no longer independent. The practical realization of both units rests on the same quantum standard. The historical separation of the two quantities has been replaced by a single metrological foundation.

### The Block Universe

The block-universe view treats spacetime as a four-dimensional whole. Every event—past, present, and future—exists in the manifold. The passage of time is not an additional physical process. It is the relation between events ordered by the metric. An observer’s experience of “now” is the set of events on one spacelike surface. Different observers have different surfaces. None is privileged by the geometry.

The view is compatible with special and general relativity. The relativity of simultaneity already denies a universal present. The block description simply extends that denial to the entire history. Deterministic equations reinforce the picture: the solution on the whole manifold is fixed by data on any Cauchy surface. Stochastic equations replace a single block with a measure over blocks. In either case the fundamental object is the spacetime, not a moving present.

The view does not deny change. Change is the difference between events at different times. It denies that change requires a meta-time in which the present advances. The denial is metaphysical. Physics supplies the metric and the field equations. It does not supply an additional flowing now. Whether the block description is the correct ontology is not settled by experiment. It is a consistent reading of the existing formalism.

### Time as a Parameter

In ordinary quantum mechanics and in classical field theory, time is a parameter, not an operator. The state evolves with respect to an external time. Position is an operator. Momentum is an operator. Time is the variable that labels the evolution. There is no time operator conjugate to the Hamiltonian that satisfies the canonical commutation relation on the full Hilbert space. Pauli showed that a self-adjoint time operator bounded below by the spectrum of the Hamiltonian cannot exist.

The parameter status is unproblematic in non-gravitational physics. Clocks exist. They are physical systems whose readings correlate with the parameter. The correlations are reliable. The underlying equations remain parameterized by an external t.

In canonical quantum gravity the situation changes. The Hamiltonian constraint generates evolution. There is no external time. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation is timeless. Solutions are static wave functionals on the space of geometries. Time must be recovered, if at all, as a relation among the degrees of freedom. Different choices of internal clock yield different approximate Schrödinger equations. The recovery is approximate and contingent on the existence of suitable semiclassical degrees of freedom.

Time is therefore fundamental in the sense that the non-gravitational theories are written in terms of it, and emergent in the sense that a quantum theory of the gravitational field may not contain it as a basic variable. Both descriptions are in use. Neither has been shown to be the final one.

### Complex Time

The Schrödinger equation is first-order in time and contains the imaginary unit. The formal substitution t → -iτ converts it into a diffusion equation. The substitution is useful in calculations. Euclidean path integrals rotate the time contour to make the action positive and the integral convergent. Instanton methods and lattice gauge theory rely on the rotation. The rotation is a mathematical device. It does not imply that physical time is complex.

Some proposals in quantum gravity and in the study of the wave function of the universe treat the early universe as Euclidean and the later universe as Lorentzian. The signature of the metric changes. The change is a feature of particular minisuperspace models. It is not required by a general theory. No observation demands complex time coordinates.

Complex spacetime appears in twistor theory and in some string-theory constructions. The constructions are equivalent, in their physical predictions, to ordinary real spacetime plus additional structure. They do not alter the measured reality of real time intervals. Clocks still advance along real world-lines. The use of complex variables simplifies certain calculations. It does not replace the real parameter that orders events in the laboratory.

### Barbour and the End of Time

Julian Barbour argues that time is not a fundamental entity. What exists are configurations of the universe—complete specifications of the relative positions and velocities of all particles, or of the geometry of space. Each configuration is a point in a vast configuration space. There is no external time in which these configurations occur. Change is the difference between configurations. The experienced flow of time is the reading of records that correlate one configuration with another.

The proposal is motivated by the structure of general relativity and of quantum gravity. The Einstein equations can be cast in a form that contains no explicit time. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation is likewise timeless. Barbour interprets the absence of a time variable as evidence that time is absent from the fundamental description. Dynamics is replaced by a relation among configurations. A path through configuration space is a history. The path is selected by a principle of least action or by a quantum amplitude. No meta-time is required for the path to exist.

Records supply the arrow. A configuration that contains structures correlated with other configurations is a record of those configurations. The correlation is asymmetric because of the low-entropy boundary condition of the early universe. The asymmetry is not a property of time. It is a property of the distribution of configurations. Observers inside a configuration that contains records experience a direction. The direction is real as a relation. It is not an additional flowing substance.

The account does not deny the utility of time in laboratory physics. Clocks work. The Schrödinger equation with an external parameter is an excellent approximation when a suitable internal clock exists. The claim is that the parameter is emergent. It is constructed from correlations among the timeless configurations. Whether the construction can be carried through in a realistic quantum cosmology is an open technical question. The conceptual proposal is that the question has an affirmative answer and that time is therefore not fundamental.

### Time Prevents Everything from Happening at Once

The geometry of spacetime limits what can influence what. An event can affect another event only if a signal traveling at or below the speed of light can pass from the first to the second. The set of events that can be reached is the future light cone. The set that can reach the given event is the past light cone. Events outside both cones are spacelike separated. No causal influence passes between them.

The restriction is not an extra rule imposed on the laws. It is the causal structure already contained in the metric of special and general relativity. The same structure appears in quantum field theory. Operators at spacelike separation commute. Measurements in those regions do not disturb each other. The prohibition on faster-than-light signaling is therefore both geometric and quantum-mechanical.

Without the restriction every event could influence every other event. The notion of a localized experiment, of a record that is stable until it is read, and of a sequence of causes and effects would not exist. The existence of time as an ordering that prevents everything from occurring in one undifferentiated moment is the existence of this causal structure. The structure is observed. Signals do not outrun light. Records persist. The prevention is not metaphorical. It is the light-cone structure of the spacetime we inhabit.

### It from Bit

Wheeler proposed that every physical entity derives its significance from answers to yes-or-no questions. The slogan is “it from bit.” A particle, a field, or a region of spacetime acquires its properties through the registration of binary outcomes by measuring apparatus. The proposal does not claim that information replaces the field equations. It claims that the meaning of the physical quantities is fixed by the information those quantities yield under interrogation.

The idea draws on the structure of quantum mechanics. A measurement yields a definite result from a set of possible results. The result is recorded. Subsequent predictions use the updated state. Wheeler elevated the recording step from an epistemic convenience to an ontological primitive. Whether the elevation is required by the formalism is disputed. The formalism works with or without it. The proposal remains an interpretation.

Quantum information theory has since shown that information-theoretic constraints reproduce parts of quantum mechanics. No-cloning, no-deletion, and the existence of entanglement follow from simple axioms about information. These results are consistent with the spirit of the slogan. They do not demonstrate that spacetime or the metric emerges from bits. That demonstration is still absent.

### The Participatory Universe

Wheeler argued that the observer is a participator. The act of measurement is not a passive registration of a pre-existing value. It is an intervention that elicits one outcome from a set of possibilities. The universe, on this view, does not sit finished and independent of all acts of observation. Its definite properties are brought about, in part, by those acts.

The delayed-choice experiment illustrates the claim. A photon passes through a double slit. After it has passed, the experimenter chooses whether to measure which-path information or an interference pattern. The choice appears to determine whether the photon behaved as a particle or as a wave in the apparatus it has already traversed. The quantum calculation accounts for the statistics without assigning a trajectory. Wheeler read the result as evidence that the past is not fixed until the measurement is completed.

The reading is optional. The standard formalism predicts the same correlations whether or not one speaks of participation. No experiment has shown that a conscious observer is required. Apparatus alone suffices. The participatory language emphasizes that measurement outcomes are not revealed properties of a detached system. It does not alter the predictive rules. The rules remain those of quantum mechanics.

### The No-Boundary Proposal

Hawking and Hartle proposed that the wave function of the universe is given by a path integral over compact Euclidean geometries. There is no initial boundary. The universe does not begin at a singular edge. It is finite in the past yet without a boundary, in the same way that the surface of a sphere is finite yet has no edge.

The proposal selects a particular solution of the Wheeler–DeWitt equation. In simple minisuperspace models it yields a wave function that is large for geometries close to de Sitter space and small for highly irregular ones. The classical spacetime that emerges is an inflating universe. The arrow of time and the low initial entropy are related to the Euclidean section.

The proposal is a candidate boundary condition. It is not derived from a more fundamental theory. Different choices of contour and different operator orderings produce different wave functions. Observational tests are indirect. They constrain the duration and the spectrum of inflation. They do not uniquely confirm the no-boundary condition. The idea remains a well-defined and influential suggestion for the quantum origin of the classical universe.

### Conformal Cyclic Cosmology

Penrose has proposed that the universe consists of a sequence of aeons. Each aeon begins with a Big Bang and expands forever. In the remote future, after black holes have evaporated and massive particles have decayed or redshifted beyond relevance, only massless radiation remains. For massless particles the conformal geometry is all that matters; scale becomes meaningless. The infinite future of one aeon can be matched, by a conformal rescaling, to the Big Bang of the next. The low gravitational entropy of the new Big Bang is inherited from the smooth, empty state of the previous aeon.

The proposal requires no inflation and no multiverse. It uses only classical general relativity plus the assumption that rest mass eventually becomes irrelevant. It predicts concentric circles of anomalous temperature in the cosmic microwave background, produced by gravitational waves from black-hole encounters in the previous aeon. Claims of such circles have been published and disputed. The statistical significance remains contested.

The model is a possible extension of general relativity. It is not required by existing data. It offers one account of the low entropy of the Big Bang without invoking a special initial condition inside a single universe. Whether the predicted circles exist at the required amplitude is an observational question still under examination.

### The Omega Point

Frank Tipler has proposed that the universe will end in a final singularity, the Omega Point, in which infinite information processing becomes possible. In that state, he argues, every past event can be reconstructed and every possible mind can be emulated. The proposal is a cosmological conjecture joined to a claim about computation.

The conjecture requires that the universe recollapse and that the collapse be sufficiently chaotic for the available energy to be used for computation without limit. Current observations indicate that the expansion is accelerating. A recollapse is not expected. Even if the expansion later reversed, the conditions required for unbounded computation are not known to be satisfied. The second law still applies. The entropy of the universe increases. The energy available for computation is finite in any region that remains finite.

The further claim is that a sufficiently powerful computation could resurrect every person who has ever lived by simulating them. The claim assumes that a simulation of a person is the person. That assumption is contested. It also assumes that the required information about each person survives or can be reconstructed. Most information about individual lives is not preserved. The proposal does not supply a mechanism that recovers it.

The Omega Point is therefore a speculative extrapolation, not a prediction of established cosmology. Logic does not rule it out; the evidence does not support it; and the accelerating expansion, the second law and the absence of any known way to recover lost information stand in its way.

An older, non-mathematical version comes from Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, who pictured a future state of maximum complexity and consciousness toward which the universe evolves. Neither version follows from established physics. A closed universe recollapses and an accelerating one expands and cools, and neither trajectory contains an attractor that maximizes consciousness. Both ideas need assumptions from outside present theory.

### The Far Future of the Universe

The future can be forecast far further than the past can be recovered, because it is governed by laws we know. In about a billion years the Sun’s rising luminosity will end liquid water on Earth. In about five billion years it will swell into a red giant, and about then the Milky Way and Andromeda will merge. The merged galaxy will go on forming stars for some trillions of years, until the gas is used up.

The longest-lived stars, small red dwarfs, burn for ten trillion years or more. After the last of them fades, what remains are cold stellar remnants and black holes. If the proton is stable, as all experiments so far indicate, the remnants cool and persist. Black holes then evaporate by Hawking radiation, a stellar-mass hole in roughly 10<sup>67</sup> years and the largest supermassive holes in about 10<sup>100</sup>. What is left is a thin, cold gas of photons and light particles in an ever-expanding space.

That picture assumes that dark energy is a true constant. If it changes, the ending changes with it, from a stretching that tears apart structures to a reversal that brings everything back together. Present data favor the cold, empty ending. Nothing in the equations makes the far future matter to anyone, and the timescales are so long that the question is mostly one of understanding the laws rather than predicting events. Brian Greene’s [*Until the End of Time*](#bib_21) treats the same story at greater length, with the question of how mind and meaning fit into it.

# <a id="part_7"></a>Part VII: Life

*From the first chemistry that copied itself to chemistry we can write, and to ourselves*

## <a id="ch_37"></a>37. The Origin of Life

*Life is chemistry that persists, copies, and changes. How ordinary chemistry first managed that is unsolved.*

The Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. Within a few hundred million years, perhaps sooner, the planet had water and a crust. By about 3.5 billion years ago, and possibly earlier, life was present. The evidence is chemical and structural: traces in ancient rocks that look like the work of microbes, and isotopes sorted in ways life sorts them. The dates are argued. The conclusion is not. Life started early, and it started small.

No one has watched it start. The laboratory can show pieces. In 1953 Stanley Miller and Harold Urey sparked a mixture of gases then thought to resemble the early atmosphere and produced amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Later work showed that the early atmosphere was probably less helpful than they assumed, and that the blocks can form in other places: hydrothermal vents, drying ponds, impacts, the ices of space. Meteorites carry amino acids. The blocks are not the mystery. The organization is.

A living cell keeps a boundary, a metabolism, and a way to copy instructions. Which came first is the argument. Genes-first theories put copying at the center. RNA is the favorite molecule, because it can store information and catalyze reactions. An “RNA world” may have preceded DNA and proteins. Membrane-first theories put the compartment at the center. A bubble of lipid can grow and split, and chemistry inside can differ from chemistry outside. Metabolism-first theories put energy at the center. Vents on the seafloor offer natural proton gradients, the same kind of gradient cells still use. Each school has evidence. None has a cell.

The deeper requirement is a source of order that does not rely on a cell already being there. Energy flow can do that. A system that takes in energy and exports waste can maintain structure. Life, once started, is such a system. The origin problem is how the first structures became self-copying rather than merely persistent.

We should be honest about the gap. Origin-of-life research is a serious field with real constraints from geology, chemistry, and genetics. It does not have a standard model. When it does, the model will have to explain not only how the parts can form, but how they can assemble under conditions the early Earth actually offered, and why the genetic code has the form it has. Until then, the origin of life is the largest blank between cosmology and biology.

The geological constraints are tighter than the chemical possibilities. The early Earth was bombarded. It had oceans, at least intermittently, by about 4.4 billion years ago, judging from ancient mineral grains. It had land and water and mineral surfaces. It may have had an atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide and nitrogen, with less free oxygen than today. Oxygen came later, produced by life. Any origin scenario has to work under those conditions, or under conditions that local environments, such as vents or ponds, could have provided.

RNA is the leading candidate for an early genetic molecule because it can do two jobs. It can store a sequence, and it can fold into shapes that catalyze reactions. DNA stores sequence more stably and does not, by itself, catalyze. Proteins catalyze and do not, by themselves, store a replicable sequence in the same way. An RNA world, in which RNA did both jobs before DNA and proteins specialized, fits this division of labor. Laboratory RNA molecules have been evolved to copy other RNAs, though not yet to copy themselves with the reliability a living system would need. The gap is real and narrower than it was.

Membranes are the other early requirement that chemistry can supply. Fatty acids and related molecules form vesicles in water. The vesicles can grow by taking up more material and can divide. They can hold different chemistry inside than outside. A plausible origin does not need a modern cell membrane at the start. It needs some compartment that persists long enough for copying to matter. Mineral surfaces can also concentrate and organize molecules. They may have served as the first scaffolds.

Energy is the third requirement. A system that copies must be fed. Hydrothermal vents offer continuous chemical gradients. Alkaline vents, in particular, create natural proton gradients across mineral walls, and living cells still use proton gradients to make their energy currency. The resemblance may be a clue or a coincidence. Wet-dry cycles in ponds offer another energy regime, concentrating molecules and driving reactions that dilute water would not favor. Impact-delivered materials and atmospheric chemistry offer further inputs. More than one setting may have contributed. The origin need not have happened in a single kind of place.

What would count as a solution? A laboratory system that starts from plausible early-Earth materials, builds a compartment, a metabolism, and a copying molecule, and then evolves without further intelligent intervention, would be a powerful demonstration. No such system exists. Pieces exist. The distance from the pieces to the system is the current size of the problem. It is a scientific problem with constraints, not a mystery declared permanently closed to investigation. It is also not a solved problem wearing the costume of a solution.

The genetic code is part of the residue. Nearly all life uses the same mapping from DNA triplets to amino acids. The mapping is not random. Some features of it reduce the effect of errors. Whether the code was inevitable or a frozen accident is debated. Its near-universality is evidence that all known life shares an ancestry. It does not, by itself, say how the first copying began.

One more constraint is phylogenetic. The last universal common ancestor was already complex. It had a membrane, a genetic code, ribosomes, and a metabolism. The origin has to reach that complexity, or reach something that could evolve into it. Scenarios that stop at a self-copying molecule have done something important and have not yet done the whole job. Scenarios that start with a metabolic cycle have the same gap in reverse. The full path is the unsolved problem. Partial paths are the progress. Both should be reported, and neither should be sold as the complete crossing.

Time is available. Several hundred million years separate the formation of a habitable surface from the first widely accepted evidence of life. That is a long interval for chemistry. It is a short interval compared with the history that followed. The early appearance of life is sometimes taken to mean that life starts easily. It may mean that. It may mean that we have only one sample, and the sample happened to start early. One sample cannot calibrate a rate. The early start is a constraint on scenarios, not a measurement of how common life is on other worlds.

Laboratory systems that evolve are the closest current approach to a demonstration. RNA molecules have been evolved to perform new reactions. Protocells have been made to grow and divide. Neither has been closed into a system that starts from simple feedstocks and runs without intervention. Closing the loop is the goal. Partial closures are the published progress. A reader should treat a headline that says life has been created in the laboratory as a claim to check against the actual system. The actual systems are impressive and incomplete. Incomplete is the accurate word. It is also a word that describes a field in motion rather than a field that is stuck.

### The Definition of Life

No single definition of life is universally accepted. The working criteria used in exobiology are metabolism, reproduction, and evolution by natural selection. A system that maintains itself far from equilibrium, produces copies of itself, and can undergo heritable change that is subject to selection satisfies the criteria.

The criteria are operational. They do not require carbon chemistry or water. They do require a source of free energy and a mechanism of heredity. On Earth both requirements are met by chemistry based on carbon compounds in aqueous solution. Whether other chemistries can meet them is unknown. No example has been observed.

The same criteria distinguish life from non-life in laboratory experiments and in the search for biosignatures. A biosignature is a feature that is difficult to produce by abiotic processes. Atmospheric disequilibrium, chiral excesses, and complex organic polymers are candidates. None is conclusive by itself. The conjunction of several is more persuasive.

### The RNA World Hypothesis

The RNA world hypothesis proposes that early life used RNA both to store genetic information and to catalyze the reactions of metabolism. DNA later assumed the storage role and proteins assumed most catalytic roles. The hypothesis is motivated by the dual capacity of RNA and by the central position of RNA in modern translation and in many coenzymes.

Ribozymes demonstrate that RNA can catalyze specific reactions, including the formation of peptide bonds and the replication of short RNA strands. Laboratory evolution has produced ribozymes with improved polymerase activity. No ribozyme yet copies long RNA templates with the fidelity and speed required for an autonomous cell. The gap is quantitative, not qualitative.

Prebiotic synthesis of nucleotides under plausible early-Earth conditions has been demonstrated in several pathways. Polymerization on mineral surfaces or in wet–dry cycles yields chains of tens of nucleotides. The spontaneous appearance of a self-replicating ribozyme from such mixtures has not been shown. Once such a molecule exists, Darwinian evolution can in principle improve it.

The hypothesis does not claim that RNA was the first informational polymer. It claims that an RNA-based stage is sufficient to bridge geochemistry and the last universal common ancestor, and that the molecular fossils in modern cells are the expected remnants of that stage. Alternative scenarios that begin with proteins, with lipids, or with other nucleic acids remain possible. The RNA world is the most fully articulated and experimentally supported of the current proposals. It is not yet a demonstrated historical pathway.

### Prebiotic Chemistry

Prebiotic chemistry is the study of the reactions that could have produced the molecular components of life from inorganic and simple organic precursors under early-Earth conditions. The field began with the demonstration that electrical discharges in reducing gas mixtures yield amino acids. Subsequent work has produced sugars, nucleobases, nucleotides, lipids and short polymers by a variety of pathways.

Aqueous spark-discharge and photochemical reactions generate amino acids and some nucleobases. Formose-type chemistry produces sugars from formaldehyde. More recent pathways synthesize activated nucleotides from cyanosulfidic precursors under conditions that include ultraviolet irradiation and wet–dry cycling. Mineral surfaces catalyze polymerization. Lipid molecules spontaneously form vesicles that can grow and divide.

No single set of conditions has yet generated all required monomers and assembled them into replicating, compartmentalized systems. Concentrations, pH, temperature and the presence of interfering side reactions remain constraints. The chemical inventory of carbonaceous meteorites shows that many of the same compounds form in abiotic settings beyond Earth. The reactions are therefore cosmochemically plausible.

The experimental results establish that the building blocks of nucleic acids, proteins and membranes can arise without biological catalysts. They do not establish the sequence or the environment in which those building blocks first cooperated. That sequence is the unsolved core of the origin-of-life problem.

### Organic Molecules and Proteins

Life is built from organic molecules—molecules based on carbon. Carbon atoms form stable bonds with each other and with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and other elements. They can make chains, rings, and branches of almost any length. No other element does this as readily under the conditions of a planet’s surface.

The simplest organic molecules are hydrocarbons, chains of carbon and hydrogen. Adding oxygen, nitrogen, or other atoms produces alcohols, acids, amines, and the rest of the vocabulary of organic chemistry. The same rules of bonding that govern a laboratory reaction govern the chemistry inside a cell. There is no separate vital chemistry. There is ordinary chemistry in a special setting.

Proteins are the workhorse molecules of life. They are chains of amino acids. Twenty amino acids are standard in the proteins of Earth life. Each chain folds into a characteristic shape. The shape determines what the protein does. Some proteins are structural. Many are enzymes, catalysts that speed particular reactions by factors of millions or more. Without enzymes, the reactions of metabolism would be too slow to sustain life at ordinary temperatures.

The sequence of amino acids is specified by the gene. Change the gene, and in many cases you change the protein. The folding is determined by the sequence and by the cellular environment. Predicting the fold from the sequence was a long-standing problem. It is now largely solved for many proteins by computational methods trained on known structures. The experimental methods—X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy—still supply the reference structures.

Enzymes are specific. An enzyme that breaks down one sugar usually does not break down a different sugar. That specificity is why metabolism can be regulated. Pathways can be turned on or off by controlling the enzymes. Many drugs work by inhibiting a particular enzyme. The active site, the pocket where the reaction occurs, is the target.

Metabolism is the network of enzyme-catalyzed reactions that extract energy and build the molecules a cell needs. The central pathways—breaking down sugars, capturing energy in ATP, building amino acids and nucleotides—are shared across a wide range of life. The sharing is evidence of common ancestry. The variations are evidence of adaptation. A cell is a chemical system that maintains itself by running these pathways continuously, taking in fuel and exporting waste. Stop the flow, and the structure collapses.

### The Protein That Should Not Fold

A protein is a chain of amino acids. The chain folds into a specific three-dimensional structure in milliseconds to seconds. The number of possible conformations is astronomical. A random search would take longer than the age of the universe. The chain nevertheless finds the native structure reliably. The discrepancy is Levinthal’s paradox.

The resolution is that the search is not random. The energy landscape is funneled. Local interactions guide the chain toward the native state. Folding intermediates and chaperones assist. Misfolding occurs. It is the exception. The exception produces disease. The rule produces function.

The process is a demonstration that a high-dimensional search can be efficient when the landscape is structured. The structure is encoded in the sequence. The sequence is encoded in the genome. The genome is the product of selection. The selection has produced chains that fold. The chains that do not fold are not here. The reader is composed of those that do.

### Alternative Biochemistries

Carbon chemistry in water is the only known basis for life. Other possibilities have been examined. Silicon can form chains, but the bonds are weaker and the oxides are solid. The temperature range in which silicon chemistry remains fluid is narrow. Ammonia and methane can serve as solvents at lower temperatures. The reaction rates are slower. No self-replicating system based on either solvent has been demonstrated.

Energy sources other than chemical redox or sunlight are conceivable. Tidal heating, radiolysis, and geothermal gradients already power ecosystems on Earth that do not rely on photosynthesis. The same sources could operate elsewhere. The requirement is a sustained free-energy flux and a mechanism of heredity. The particular molecules that satisfy the requirement may vary.

Laboratory work has expanded the genetic alphabet with synthetic base pairs, which shows that other informational polymers are chemically possible. No living system built on them has been made, so alternative biochemistries remain possible but unsupported by observation.

## <a id="ch_38"></a>38. The Cell

The cell is the basic unit of life. Every organism is either a single cell or a collection of cells. The idea was established in the nineteenth century. It remains the foundation of biology.

Cells are of two broad kinds. Prokaryotic cells—bacteria and archaea—have no nucleus. Their DNA is in the cytoplasm. Eukaryotic cells—the cells of animals, plants, fungi, and protists—have a nucleus that holds the DNA, and they have other internal compartments. Mitochondria, which produce most of the cell’s usable energy, and chloroplasts, which carry out photosynthesis in plants and algae, were once free-living bacteria. They were taken in and became permanent. The evidence is their own DNA and the structure of their membranes.

A cell is bounded by a membrane made of lipids, with proteins embedded in it. The membrane controls what enters and leaves. Inside, the cytoplasm is crowded with molecules. It is not a bag of dilute solution. It is a dense, organized environment. In eukaryotic cells, an internal skeleton of protein filaments gives shape and moves cargo. Energy is obtained by oxidizing organic molecules or by photosynthesis, with ATP as the common currency, and information flows from DNA to RNA to protein.

Cells reproduce by dividing. In prokaryotes the process is relatively simple. In eukaryotes, mitosis parcels the chromosomes so that each daughter cell receives a full set. Meiosis, used in sexual reproduction, halves the chromosome number so that fertilization restores it. Errors in these processes cause many genetic diseases and contribute to cancer.

The cell cycle is regulated. Checkpoints ensure that DNA is copied accurately and that the cell is ready to divide. Failures of regulation are a hallmark of cancer. Many cancer drugs target the machinery of division or the signals that drive it.

Cells communicate. They release signals, and they carry receptors that detect signals from other cells or from the environment. Development—the building of a body from a fertilized egg—is a conversation among cells, guided by genes that are turned on and off in sequence. The same genes appear in different animals, used in different combinations. A gene involved in building an eye in a fly has a relative involved in building an eye in a mouse. The parts were reused. The arrangements diverged.

Every cell alive today is the product of an unbroken sequence of divisions stretching back to the origin of life. The sequence is the deepest continuity in biology. Understanding the cell is understanding the unit in which that continuity is maintained.

### Cell Theory and Germ Theory

The cell theory states that all living organisms are composed of cells and that cells arise only from pre-existing cells. The statement was assembled in the nineteenth century from observations by Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow. It replaced earlier views that living matter could arise spontaneously or that tissues were continuous substances. Every organism examined since has confirmed the rule. Viruses are not cells, but they replicate only inside cells.

The germ theory states that many diseases are caused by microorganisms. Pasteur’s experiments on fermentation and putrefaction, and Koch’s isolation of specific pathogens, established the link. The same organisms that cause disease can be cultured, identified, and, in many cases, killed or blocked. Antisepsis, antibiotics, and vaccines followed. The theory does not claim that every illness is infectious. It claims that infectious illnesses have microbial causes that can be demonstrated.

Both theories are now foundational. Cell theory organizes development, physiology, and evolution. Germ theory organizes public health and medicine. Neither required a new force. Both followed from the consistent application of microscopy, staining, and controlled experiment. The results are independent of the particular wording in which they were first announced. The observations remain.

### Spontaneous Generation and the Germ Theory

For most of history it seemed obvious that life could arise from non-life. Maggots appeared in meat. Mice appeared in grain. The process was called spontaneous generation. It was accepted by Aristotle and by most writers after him.

Experiments gradually closed the claim. In the seventeenth century Francesco Redi showed that maggots did not appear in meat if flies were kept away. In the eighteenth century Lazzaro Spallanzani showed that broth, boiled and sealed, did not spoil. Critics said the sealing excluded a vital principle in the air. In the nineteenth century Louis Pasteur settled the question with flasks that had curved necks. Air could enter. Dust and microbes could not. The broth stayed clear. When the neck was broken, it spoiled. Life comes from life.

The same work opened the germ theory of disease. Specific diseases are caused by specific microorganisms. Robert Koch set the criteria: the organism must be found in the diseased host, grown in pure culture, produce the disease when introduced into a healthy host, and be recovered again. Those postulates identified the agents of anthrax, tuberculosis, cholera, and many others.

Vaccination uses the immune system’s memory. Edward Jenner showed that cowpox protected against smallpox. Pasteur developed weakened strains that protected against other diseases. Antibiotics, beginning with penicillin, kill or stop bacteria without killing the host. Viruses are not affected by antibiotics. They are stopped by the immune system, by vaccines, or by antiviral drugs.

The disproof of spontaneous generation did not close the question of how life began. It closed the claim that life arises readily and continuously under ordinary conditions. The origin of life is a separate problem, pushed back to the early Earth, where conditions were different and time was long.

### Microbiology

Microbiology is the study of organisms too small to see without magnification. The group includes bacteria, archaea, many fungi, protists, and viruses. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. They lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their DNA is a circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, often accompanied by smaller plasmids. Eukaryotic microbes have nuclei and organelles.

Bacteria reproduce by binary fission. Under favorable conditions some species double in twenty minutes. They exchange genes by transformation, transduction, and conjugation. These processes move DNA between cells that are not parent and offspring. The result is rapid spread of traits, including antibiotic resistance.

Archaea resemble bacteria in size and simplicity but differ in membrane lipids, cell-wall chemistry, and the machinery of transcription and translation. Many live in extremes of temperature, salinity, or acidity. Some produce methane. Their ribosomal RNA sequences place them on a separate branch of the tree of life.

Fungi and protists are eukaryotes. Yeasts are unicellular fungi used in fermentation. Molds form filaments. Protists include algae that photosynthesize and protozoa that ingest food. Amoebae, described in their own section, are protists that move and feed by extending pseudopods.

Microbes drive the major chemical cycles of the planet. They fix nitrogen, produce oxygen, decompose organic matter, and generate methane. They also cause disease. The same tools—culture, microscopy, staining, and sequencing—identify both the beneficial and the pathogenic species. The distinction is ecological, not taxonomic.

### The Uncultured Majority

Culture-independent methods—16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomics—have revealed that the majority of microbial species have never been grown in the laboratory. The uncultured majority includes entire phyla. Their ecological roles are inferred from genomes and from environmental correlations. The inference is incomplete. It is already sufficient to show that microbial diversity and activity dominate the biosphere.

Prokaryotic metabolism is more diverse than that of all eukaryotes combined, and microbes cycle carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and metals from hydrothermal vents to the human gut. Viruses, the most abundant biological entities, regulate microbial populations and mediate horizontal gene transfer. The microbial world is therefore both the metabolic foundation of the biosphere and a continuous source of genetic innovation.

### Viruses

Viruses are particles that replicate only inside living cells. They consist of nucleic acid enclosed in a protein coat. Some have a lipid envelope derived from the host membrane. The nucleic acid is DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded, linear or circular. The coat protects the genome and, in many cases, attaches to a receptor on the host cell.

Outside a cell a virus is inert. It has no metabolism and no independent replication. Inside a susceptible cell it redirects the host machinery to copy its genome and synthesize its proteins. New particles assemble and leave, often destroying the cell. The host range is limited by the receptors the virus can bind. A virus that infects one species may be unable to infect another.

Bacteriophages infect bacteria. They were used to show that DNA, not protein, carries genetic information. Animal and plant viruses cause many diseases. Some insert their genome into the host chromosome and remain latent. Others kill the cell quickly. Retroviruses reverse-transcribe RNA into DNA that integrates into the host genome. The integrated form can be transmitted to daughter cells.

Viruses evolve. Mutation rates are high, especially in RNA viruses. Recombination and reassortment occur when multiple viruses infect the same cell. The result is rapid change in surface proteins and in host range. Vaccines and antiviral drugs select for resistant variants. The same processes that generate diversity in cellular organisms operate, at higher speed, in viruses.

Viruses are not classified as living by most definitions because they lack independent metabolism. They are biological entities that evolve and that affect every domain of life. They move genes between hosts, regulate microbial populations, and shape the evolution of immune systems. Their study is part of microbiology whether or not they are counted as organisms.

### Amoebae

Amoebae are unicellular eukaryotes that move by pseudopods. The pseudopod is a temporary extension of the cytoplasm. Actin filaments polymerize at the leading edge and push the membrane forward. Myosin and other motors contract at the rear. The cell advances. The same machinery is used for phagocytosis. The amoeba surrounds a particle of food, encloses it in a vesicle, and digests it with enzymes delivered from lysosomes.

Most amoebae are free-living. They inhabit soil, fresh water, and marine sediments. They feed on bacteria, algae, and detritus. A few species are parasitic. Entamoeba histolytica infects the human intestine and can invade the liver. Naegleria fowleri is free-living in warm water and can infect the brain if it enters through the nose. These cases are rare. Most amoebae never encounter a human host.

Amoebae were among the first microbes observed. Leeuwenhoek described them in the seventeenth century. Later workers used them to study cell movement, phagocytosis, and cytoplasmic streaming. The mechanisms proved to be general. The same actin–myosin system operates in the white blood cells of animals and in the crawling of many other cells. The amoeba is a convenient model because the entire organism is one cell and the behavior is visible under a light microscope.

The group is not a single evolutionary lineage. “Amoeba” describes a body plan that has evolved more than once. Some amoeboid organisms are closely related to animals and fungi. Others belong to distant branches of the eukaryotic tree. The shared appearance is convergent. The underlying cell biology is ancient.

### Endosymbiosis and Multicellularity

Eukaryotic cells contain mitochondria. Plant cells also contain chloroplasts. Both organelles have their own DNA, their own ribosomes, and double membranes. The DNA is circular, like bacterial DNA. The sequences show that mitochondria are related to alphaproteobacteria and chloroplasts to cyanobacteria. The organelles were once free-living bacteria that became permanent residents of host cells. The process is endosymbiosis.

The host gained the ability to produce ATP by oxidative phosphorylation or to fix carbon by photosynthesis. The endosymbiont gained a stable environment and a supply of nutrients. Over time most of the endosymbiont’s genes were transferred to the host nucleus. The organelles retained a reduced genome that encodes some of their own proteins. The arrangement is stable. It occurred once for mitochondria, early in eukaryotic history, and once for the primary chloroplast, in the ancestor of the Archaeplastida. Secondary endosymbioses, in which a eukaryotic cell engulfed another eukaryote that already had a chloroplast, occurred several times and produced the chloroplasts of other algal groups.

Multicellularity evolved independently many times. Animals, plants, fungi, and several groups of algae and bacteria all contain multicellular species. The transition requires cells to adhere, to communicate, and to differentiate. In animals the extracellular matrix and cell-adhesion molecules hold cells together. Signaling pathways control division and specialization. Programmed cell death removes cells that are no longer needed. The genetic toolkit for these functions existed in unicellular ancestors and was co-opted. The Cambrian radiation, about 540 million years ago, produced most of the major animal body plans in a geologically short interval. The causes are debated. They include rising oxygen, ecological interactions, and the evolution of developmental gene networks. The fossil record shows the outcome. The precise triggers remain under study.

### Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. In oxygenic photosynthesis water is the electron donor and oxygen is released. The overall reaction is 6 CO<sub>2</sub> + 6 H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6 O<sub>2</sub>. Light is absorbed by chlorophyll and accessory pigments in the thylakoid membranes. Two photosystems operate in series. Photosystem II splits water. Photosystem I reduces NADP<sup>+</sup>. The electron transport chain between them generates a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis.

The ATP and NADPH are consumed in the Calvin cycle. Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase fixes carbon dioxide into organic molecules. The cycle regenerates the acceptor and produces triose phosphates that are converted to sugars, starch or other compounds. The enzyme also reacts with oxygen, initiating photorespiration. The competition is an unavoidable consequence of the active-site chemistry.

Photosynthesis supplies the free energy and the reduced carbon that support almost all ecosystems. Its oxygen byproduct transformed the atmosphere. The same core reactions operate in cyanobacteria, algae and plants. Variations in carbon-concentrating mechanisms and in pigment composition adapt the process to different light and carbon regimes. The quantum efficiency of the light reactions is high. The overall energy efficiency of biomass production is far lower.

### Cellular Respiration

Cellular respiration extracts energy from organic molecules. Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytosol, yielding a net of two ATP and two NADH. In aerobic organisms pyruvate enters the mitochondria. The citric-acid cycle oxidizes the acetyl group to two molecules of carbon dioxide and produces additional reduced coenzymes. The electron-transport chain transfers electrons from NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> to oxygen. The free energy is used to pump protons. The return of protons through ATP synthase produces the majority of the ATP.

The overall yield from one glucose is approximately thirty ATP under cellular conditions. The theoretical maximum is higher. Proton leaks and the cost of transporting metabolites reduce the net gain. Anaerobic pathways regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> by reducing pyruvate to lactate or to ethanol and carbon dioxide. They yield only the two ATP from glycolysis.

The same respiratory chain operates in bacteria and in mitochondria. Mitochondria are the descendants of endosymbiotic bacteria. The chemiosmotic mechanism—proton gradient coupled to ATP synthesis—is universal among aerobic organisms. Respiration and photosynthesis are complementary. One stores energy in organic molecules and oxygen. The other releases it.

### Gene Expression and Regulation

Gene expression is the conversion of genetic information into functional products. Transcription produces an RNA copy of a DNA segment. In eukaryotes the primary transcript is processed: introns are removed, a cap and a poly-A tail are added. Translation on the ribosome converts the messenger-RNA sequence into a polypeptide. The genetic code is read in non-overlapping triplets.

Regulation occurs at every step. Transcription factors bind specific DNA sequences and recruit or block RNA polymerase. Chromatin structure modulates access. Alternative splicing generates multiple protein isoforms from one gene. Messenger-RNA stability and translational efficiency are controlled by proteins and small RNAs. Post-translational modifications activate, inhibit or target the finished protein.

The regulatory network of a cell is dense. A single transcription factor may control dozens of genes. Feedback loops, both positive and negative, produce switches, oscillators and homeostatic responses. The same basic machinery operates in bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes. The additional layers of chromatin, splicing and compartmentalization in eukaryotes allow more elaborate control. The outcome is that genetically identical cells can adopt different phenotypes according to their history and their environment.

### Development and Differentiation

Development is the progressive specialization of cells from a single zygote. Early cleavage produces a blastula. Gastrulation rearranges the cells into three germ layers. Subsequent inductive interactions between layers generate the organs. The process is controlled by gradients of signaling molecules and by sequential activation of transcription-factor networks.
