Cell differentiation is usually irreversible under normal conditions. The differentiated state is maintained by feedback loops in the gene-regulatory network and by chromatin modifications that are copied at mitosis. Stem cells retain the capacity to produce multiple cell types. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent. Adult stem cells are multipotent and replenish specific tissues.

Regeneration varies widely. Some animals replace entire limbs or organs. Mammals regenerate liver and blood but not limbs. The difference lies in the persistence of patterning information and in the ability of differentiated cells to re-enter the cell cycle or to be replaced by stem cells. The molecular toolkit—signaling pathways, transcription factors, and adhesive molecules—is ancient. The deployment of the toolkit differs. Development is therefore both conserved and plastic.

## <a id="ch_39"></a>39. Evolution and Genetics

*Once copying exists, evolution is difficult to avoid.*

Copies are not perfect. Changes appear. Some changes make the copy more likely to be copied again, in that environment. Those changes become common. The process requires no foresight. It requires inheritance, variation, and unequal success. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace stated the logic in 1858. The evidence since then has become overwhelming.

Evolution is not only selection. Drift, the luck of small populations, changes frequencies too. Genes move between lineages, especially in microbes. Development biases which variations appear. None of this repeals selection. It fills in the picture.

The theory’s power is that it connects. Antibiotic resistance, the fit of a moth to a tree, the useless hind limbs of a whale, and the shared code of all known life are one subject. A biology that rejected evolution would have to explain each of them again, separately, and worse.

Given enough time, and given the way development builds bodies, the changes that selection accumulates can be large. The logic does not require progress, purpose, or a direction toward complexity. Complexity has increased in some lineages and not in others, and bacteria have remained bacteria, with enormous biochemical sophistication, for billions of years. They are not failed animals. They are the most successful living things on Earth by number, by mass, and by tenure, and the history of life is mostly microbial.

The evidence is independent in kind and convergent in result. Fossils show a sequence. They do not show modern animals in the oldest rocks. They show earlier forms, then later forms, with transitional fossils in many lineages: fish with limb-like fins, dinosaurs with feathers, whales with hind limbs, hominins with intermediate brain sizes and bipedal skeletons. Biogeography shows that islands and continents carry the descendants of whoever could get there. Anatomy shows common structure under different uses. Embryology shows related species passing through related stages. Molecular biology shows the same code, shared genes, shared errors, and shared viral insertions. A single lineage explains all of these. Separate creation of each species would have to explain them again, one by one, as coincidences.

Genetics filled the gap Darwin noted. He did not know how traits were inherited or how variation was supplied. Mendel’s work, rediscovered at the start of the twentieth century, showed particulate inheritance. Later work identified the particles as stretches of DNA. Mutation, recombination, and gene flow supply variation. Selection, drift, and the biases of development filter it. The modern synthesis joined Mendel to Darwin. Later work has added regulatory genetics, developmental genetics, and the movement of genes between lineages, especially in microbes. The additions refine the mechanism. They do not replace the filter.

Speciation is the production of separate lineages that no longer freely intermix. It can happen when populations are divided by geography, and it can happen, less simply, without that division. Once separated, populations accumulate differences. Eventually they may be unable to produce fertile offspring together, or they may simply not meet. Species are real lineages. The boundaries can be messy, especially in plants and in microbes, where hybridization and gene transfer are common. Messy boundaries are what a branching process produces. They are not an objection to the process.

Human evolution is the same process applied to one lineage. The fossil and genetic evidence places the human lineage’s split from the chimpanzee lineage several million years ago. Bipedalism, larger brains, stone tools, and later language and culture accumulated. Other hominin species existed and are gone. Some of their genes remain in modern human populations, from episodes of interbreeding. The genetic difference between humans and chimpanzees is small in percentage and consequential in outcome, much of it in regulation rather than in the protein-coding sequence. Nothing in this requires a special biological mechanism for humans. It requires the ordinary mechanism acting on a particular lineage, plus the cultural inheritance that lineage eventually produced.

Evolution is as well supported as any theory in science. It is also, in its details, an active research field. The relative importance of selection and drift, the role of development in biasing variation, the frequency of gene transfer, and the genetic basis of particular adaptations are debated. Debate about details is not doubt about the framework. A reader can treat the framework as settled and the details as the place where new work happens. That is the accurate division.

Resistance is the evolution a person can watch. Bacteria exposed to an antibiotic evolve resistance, by mutation or by acquiring a gene from elsewhere. Viruses evolve as they spread. Tumors evolve under treatment. The process is not confined to the fossil record. It is a present mechanism. Medicine that ignores it produces resistant infections and resistant cancers. Agriculture that ignores it produces resistant pests. The practical importance of evolution is not only that it explains the history of life. It is that it is still running, on timescales that policy and medicine have to respect.

Sexual reproduction is a puzzle the theory has to solve, because it has a cost. An organism that reproduces sexually passes on only half its genes, relative to one that clones. The advantage that pays for the cost is probably the mixing of genes, which produces variety that helps in the presence of parasites and of changing conditions, and which clears harmful mutations. The debate about the exact advantage is ongoing. The existence of the cost is clear. The near-universality of sex among complex organisms suggests the advantage is large. The theory is strong enough to have puzzles of this kind. A weaker theory would not define them so sharply.

Convergence is the evidence that selection can reach similar solutions more than once. Eyes have evolved several times. Wings have evolved several times. Antifreeze proteins in cold-water fish have evolved separately in different lineages. Convergence shows that the space of possible forms is constrained by physics and by development, and that selection finds the workable regions of that space repeatedly. It is not evidence against common ancestry. It is evidence about the power of the filter once ancestry has supplied a lineage. The two together, shared descent and repeated solution, explain both the unity and the rhyming of life.

Evolution is the change in allele frequencies over time. Natural selection is the unequal reproductive success of variants. The process produces adaptation. Given reproductive isolation it produces speciation. The theory is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence.

The modern synthesis combined Mendelian genetics with natural selection. Later additions include neutral theory, kin selection and the recognition of horizontal gene transfer. None replaces the core. The core accounts for the fit between organisms and environments and for the hierarchical pattern of similarity.

The fossil record, comparative anatomy, biogeography and molecular sequences all corroborate the same branching history. The history is not complete. The major outlines are robust. Open questions concern rates, mechanisms of speciation and the relative importance of selection and drift in particular cases.

### Natural Selection

Natural selection is the differential reproductive success of individuals that differ in heritable traits. When the differences affect survival or fertility, the frequencies of the underlying alleles change. The change is evolution by natural selection.

The process requires three conditions: variation, heritability, and differential success. All three are observed. The response to selection is the product of the heritability and the selection differential. Artificial selection in domesticated plants and animals demonstrates the magnitude of the response when the conditions are met.

Selection can be directional, stabilizing, or disruptive. Directional selection shifts the mean of a trait. Stabilizing selection reduces variance. Disruptive selection favors the extremes. Sexual selection is the special case in which the differential success arises from competition for mates. All forms are documented in natural populations.

Selection acts on phenotypes. It therefore acts on genotypes only to the extent that they influence phenotypes. The mapping from genotype to phenotype is often complex. Epistasis, pleiotropy, and environmental effects modulate the response. The net result over geological time is the diversity of adapted organisms.

The appearance of design in living things is real. The eye focuses. The wing generates lift. The enzyme catalyzes a reaction at a rate that would otherwise take longer than the age of the universe. For centuries the inference was that such arrangements required a designer. The inference is unnecessary.

Natural selection is a process that produces cumulative adaptation without foresight. Variation exists. Some variants leave more offspring than others. The difference is heritable. Over generations the population changes. The change is not random. It is directed by the differential success of the variants in the environment they actually inhabit. The direction is local and retrospective. It does not aim at a distant goal. It does not require that any organism understand the process.

The cumulative character is essential. A single mutation rarely produces a complex organ. A sequence of mutations, each preserved because it conferred a small advantage in its own generation, can. The intermediates need not be useful for the final function. They need only be useful for something at the time they appear. The history is recoverable in the fossil record, in comparative anatomy, and in the sequences of genes. The same gene families appear in organisms that use them for different purposes. The pattern is the pattern of descent with modification, not the pattern of separate creation.

The process has no designer and no plan. It also has no guarantee of progress in any global sense. Lineages go extinct. Complexity can decrease. What it does guarantee is that, given variation, heritability, and differential reproduction, adaptation will accumulate where the conditions allow. The conditions have allowed it for more than three billion years. The result is the diversity of life. The mechanism is ordinary. The outcome is not.

### Genetics Before DNA

Darwin’s theory of natural selection required that offspring resemble their parents and that variation exist. It did not explain how the resemblance or the variation was transmitted. The mechanism was missing, and it arrived in stages: first Mendel’s factors and the chromosomes that carry them, described in the next sections, then mutation, and finally DNA itself.

Mutations are changes in genes. They arise spontaneously at low rates. Radiation and certain chemicals raise the rate. Most mutations are neutral or harmful. A rare few help in a particular environment. Natural selection acts on the variation that mutation supplies. The combination of mutation, selection, and the Mendelian transmission of genes is the modern synthesis. It is the working account of evolution.

The physical nature of the gene was unknown until the middle of the twentieth century. Experiments showed that DNA, not protein, carries the genetic information. The structure of DNA, a double helix with complementary bases, explained how it can be copied. A triplet code of bases specifies amino acids, and its near-universality is evidence of common ancestry.

The history from Mendel’s ratios to the structure of DNA took less than a century. The facts accumulated. The explanations followed. The same pattern continues.

### Mendel and the Chromosomes

Gregor Mendel crossed pea plants that differed in clear traits and counted the offspring. Tall crossed with dwarf gave all tall in the first generation. Self-pollination of those hybrids gave three tall to one dwarf in the next. The dwarf trait had not disappeared. It had been hidden. Mendel proposed that each plant carries two factors for each trait, that the factors separate when gametes form, and that one factor can mask the other. The ratios followed. The same pattern held for other traits he tested.

The factors are now called genes. They are segments of DNA. The separation Mendel inferred is the separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis. Each gamete receives one member of each pair. Fertilization restores the pair. The masking is dominance. The hidden factor is recessive. When both copies are recessive the trait appears. The arithmetic is the same whether the factors are abstract or molecular.

The work was published in 1866 and ignored. It was rediscovered in 1900 by investigators who had reached the same ratios. Within a few years the factors were located on chromosomes. Sutton and Boveri noted that chromosomes behave as Mendel’s factors must behave. Morgan’s group in fruit flies mapped genes to specific positions by measuring how often traits are inherited together. Linkage and recombination became measurable. The chromosome theory of inheritance was established.

The theory accounts for the transmission of traits. It does not by itself account for the origin of new traits. That required the later recognition of mutation. Together, Mendelian transmission and mutational variation supplied the genetic mechanism that Darwin’s theory had lacked. The mechanism is now molecular. The ratios Mendel counted remain.

Mendel established that inheritance is particulate. Each trait is controlled by factors that segregate and assort independently. In modern language the factors are genes. Diploid organisms carry two copies of each gene. The copies may be identical or different. The observable trait is the phenotype. The underlying combination is the genotype.

Segregation occurs in meiosis. The two copies of a gene separate so that each gamete receives one. Independent assortment occurs when genes lie on different chromosomes or are far apart on the same chromosome. Linked genes tend to be inherited together. The frequency of recombination measures the distance between them.

Dominance and recessiveness describe the relation between alleles. A dominant allele produces its phenotype when present in one copy. A recessive allele produces its phenotype only when present in two copies. Many traits are not simply dominant or recessive. They show incomplete dominance, codominance, or continuous variation produced by multiple loci and by the environment.

The Mendelian rules hold for the great majority of nuclear genes in sexual organisms. Exceptions—cytoplasmic inheritance, imprinting, and meiotic drive—are known and are themselves genetically controlled.

### The Double Helix

DNA is a double helix. Two strands of sugar and phosphate wind around each other. The bases point inward and pair. Adenine pairs with thymine. Guanine pairs with cytosine. The pairs are held by hydrogen bonds. The two strands run in opposite directions. The structure was proposed by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953.

The proposal rested on several lines of evidence. Erwin Chargaff had shown that in any sample of DNA the amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine, and the amount of guanine equals the amount of cytosine. The equality suggested pairing. X-ray diffraction images of DNA fibers, produced by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling at King’s College London, and by Maurice Wilkins, showed that the molecule is helical and supplied its dimensions. The best-known image, Photograph 51, is an X-shaped pattern characteristic of a helix. The pitch is about 3.4 nanometers. There are about ten base pairs per turn. The diameter is about 2 nanometers.

Franklin’s data reached Watson and Crick indirectly. Wilkins showed Watson Photograph 51. A report summarizing Franklin’s measurements was also seen. Watson and Crick used the constraints to build a physical model. Earlier attempts had failed because the chemistry was wrong. The successful model placed the sugar-phosphate backbones on the outside and the base pairs on the inside. The pairing of A with T and G with C made every rung the same width. The strands are antiparallel. The structure immediately suggested a copying mechanism. Each strand can serve as a template for a new complementary strand. Watson and Crick noted the implication in their paper.

Three papers appeared together in *Nature* in April 1953. One by Watson and Crick presented the model. One by Wilkins and colleagues presented diffraction data. One by Franklin and Gosling presented their X-ray results. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958 and was not eligible.

The structure explains how genetic information is stored and copied. The sequence of bases is the information. The complementary pairing is the copying rule. Mutations are changes in the sequence. The same double helix is found in bacteria, plants, animals, and humans. The differences are in the sequence, not in the architecture. The architecture is what makes inheritance possible.

### The Structure and Replication of DNA

The 1953 paper by Watson and Crick proposed a specific structure for the salt of deoxyribose nucleic acid. Two helical chains coil around the same axis. The chains are related by a dyad perpendicular to the fiber axis, so the sequences of atoms run in opposite directions. The bases are on the inside. The phosphates are on the outside. There is a residue every 3.4 angstroms along the axis. The angle between adjacent residues is 36 degrees, so the structure repeats after 10 residues, or 34 angstroms. The distance of a phosphorus atom from the axis is about 10 angstroms.

The chains are held together by hydrogen-bonded pairs of bases. One member of each pair is a purine and the other is a pyrimidine. The pairing rules are adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine, and they account for Chargaff’s ratios. It also makes every rung the same width, so the backbone is regular. The structure is open and contains a good deal of water. At lower water content the bases tilt and the structure becomes more compact. That matches the observation of two forms, A and B, depending on humidity.

A second paper by Watson and Crick, published weeks later, spelled out the genetical implications. The two chains are complementary. The sequence on one determines the sequence on the other. Before duplication the hydrogen bonds break and the chains unwind and separate. Each chain then serves as a template for a new complementary chain. The result is two pairs where there was one. The sequence is duplicated exactly. The genetic information is carried in the sequence of the bases. The paper did not explain how that sequence specifies proteins. That explanation came later.

The X-ray papers published with the model supplied the supporting measurements. Franklin and Gosling described the B form as a helix with the phosphate groups on the outside. Wilkins and colleagues reported similar dimensions from other samples and noted that the pattern is consistent with a helical structure. The model fit the data. Later crystallographic work confirmed the coordinates in detail.

The technical result is a molecule that can store a sequence and copy it. The sequence is the information. Complementarity is what makes the copying possible. Everything that followed in molecular biology rests on that architecture.

### DNA and the Genetic Code

Each strand of the double helix is a polymer of nucleotides, and the sequence of its four bases encodes information. The pairing allows each strand to serve as the template for the other.

The genetic code maps triplets of bases to amino acids. The code is nearly universal and is degenerate: most amino acids are specified by more than one codon. Translation occurs on the ribosome. Messenger RNA carries the transcript. Transfer RNA molecules bring the amino acids. The sequence of codons determines the sequence of the polypeptide.

Replication is semi-conservative. Each daughter molecule contains one parental strand and one new strand. The fidelity is high. Error rates are of order one in 10<sup>9</sup> to 10<sup>10</sup> bases after proofreading and mismatch repair. The residual errors, together with recombination and other rearrangements, supply the variation on which natural selection acts.

### Mutation and Variation

A mutation is a heritable change in the nucleotide sequence. Point mutations substitute one base for another. Insertions and deletions add or remove bases. Larger rearrangements include duplications, inversions, and translocations. The rate of point mutation in humans is approximately 10<sup>−8</sup> per base per generation.

Most mutations are neutral or deleterious. A minority are beneficial in a given environment. The supply of mutation is random with respect to need. Selection retains those changes that increase reproductive success and removes those that decrease it. The combination of mutation, selection, drift, and recombination generates the genetic variation observed within and between populations.

In large populations selection efficiently removes deleterious alleles, while in small populations drift lets them accumulate, and standing variation supplies the raw material for adaptation when the environment changes. Variation is measured by the heterozygosity of individuals and by the nucleotide diversity of populations. Typical values for humans are a few differences per thousand bases between any two genomes. The differences are the raw material of evolution and the basis of genetic individuality.

### The Gene That Was Not Supposed to Move

In 1948 Barbara McClintock reported that certain genes in maize changed position. The report was ignored. Genes were supposed to be fixed. Thirty years later the same phenomenon was found in bacteria. The genes were transposons. They move. They are now known to constitute a large fraction of many genomes, including the human genome.

The movement is not random. Some transposons are controlled. Others are silenced by the host. The silencing is imperfect. When it fails, the transposon can disrupt a gene or alter its regulation. The disruption is a mutation. The mutation is a source of variation. The variation is the raw material of evolution. The raw material includes sequences that were once regarded as junk.

The discovery did not overturn genetics. It enlarged it. The genome is not a static text. It is a text that contains instructions for editing itself. The editing is usually harmless. Occasionally it is consequential. The consequential edits are part of the history that produced the reader. The reader’s genome still contains the editors.

### Epigenetic Inheritance

Epigenetic inheritance is the transmission of information from one cell or organism to the next without a change in the DNA sequence. The principal molecular carriers are DNA methylation, histone modifications, and certain non-coding RNAs.

DNA methylation in vertebrates occurs mainly at cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides. Methylation patterns are copied by maintenance methyltransferases at replication. They typically repress transcription when present in promoters. Histone modifications—acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation and others—alter chromatin compaction and recruit regulatory proteins. Some modifications are re-established after replication by reader-writer complexes. Small RNAs can direct both DNA methylation and histone modification in a sequence-specific manner.

These marks are mitotically heritable and therefore maintain cell identity through development. Meiotic heritability is rarer. In mammals extensive reprogramming erases most methylation marks in the primordial germ cells and again in the early embryo. A few loci, including imprinted genes, escape erasure and produce parent-of-origin effects. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance beyond one or two generations has been documented in plants, nematodes and, under special conditions, in mammals. Its frequency and stability in humans remain limited.

Epigenetic mechanisms allow genetically identical cells to adopt stable, different phenotypes. They also provide a route by which environmental conditions can influence gene expression in the next generation without altering the nucleotide sequence. The nucleotide sequence itself remains the primary hereditary material. Epigenetic marks modulate its use.

### Genomic Imprinting

Genomic imprinting is the parent-of-origin-dependent expression of certain genes. An imprinted gene is expressed from only the maternal or only the paternal allele. The silent allele is marked by DNA methylation and histone modifications established in the respective germ line. The marks survive the genome-wide demethylation that occurs in the early embryo and are maintained through somatic cell divisions.

Approximately one hundred mammalian genes are imprinted. Many lie in clusters controlled by imprint control regions. The clusters frequently contain genes that regulate growth. Paternally expressed genes tend to promote growth. Maternally expressed genes tend to restrain it. The pattern matches the parental-conflict hypothesis: in species where offspring of one mother may have different fathers, paternal alleles favor greater maternal investment while maternal alleles favor conservation of resources for future offspring.

Imprinting is reset each generation. In the primordial germ cells the existing marks are erased. New marks are placed according to the sex of the developing individual. Failure to erase or reset an imprint produces disorders such as Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes, which result from opposite parental deletions or uniparental disomy of the same chromosomal region. Imprinting is known in mammals and in flowering plants. It is absent in birds and in most other vertebrates. It constitutes a regulated exception to the usual rule of biallelic expression.

### Parental-Conflict Theory of Imprinting

Parental-conflict theory accounts for the evolution of genomic imprinting. In species in which a female may produce offspring by different males, the genetic interests of maternal and paternal alleles diverge. Every offspring carries a full complement of the mother’s genes but, on average, only half of any given father’s genes relative to future half-siblings. A paternal allele therefore gains by increasing the resources extracted from the mother. A maternal allele gains by conserving those resources for later offspring.

Imprinting is the molecular consequence. Growth-promoting genes are expressed from the paternal chromosome and silenced on the maternal chromosome. Growth-restraining genes show the opposite pattern. The two sets of imprints reach an evolutionary equilibrium. Disruption of either imprint produces the over-growth or under-growth phenotypes observed in human imprinting disorders and in experimental deletions.

The theory predicts that imprinting will appear only where mothers provision offspring after fertilization and where multiple paternity is possible. It predicts the absence of imprinting where offspring are nutritionally independent at birth or where lifelong monogamy eliminates the conflict. The phylogenetic distribution of imprinting matches these predictions. The theory therefore supplies both a selective explanation for the existence of imprints and a set of comparative tests that the explanation has passed.

### Horizontal Gene Transfer

Horizontal gene transfer is the movement of genetic material between organisms other than by vertical descent. In bacteria it occurs by transformation, transduction and conjugation. Plasmids, transposons and bacteriophages are the principal vectors. The process allows rapid acquisition of new functions, including antibiotic resistance and metabolic pathways.

In eukaryotes horizontal transfer is rarer but documented. Endosymbiotic gene transfer moved thousands of genes from the mitochondrial and chloroplast ancestors into the nuclear genome. Other transfers from bacteria, fungi and plants into animals have been identified. The transfers complicate phylogenetic reconstruction. They do not erase the dominant vertical signal.

Horizontal transfer accelerates adaptation in prokaryotes and has contributed to eukaryotic genomes. It is a major reason that bacterial evolution cannot be represented by a simple tree. The same process spreads both useful genes and selfish elements. Its quantitative importance varies by domain. It is ubiquitous among bacteria and archaea and intermittent among eukaryotes.

### Population Genetics

Population genetics describes the change in allele frequencies under mutation, selection, migration, and drift. In an infinite population without those forces the frequencies remain constant. That is the Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. Real populations deviate from it.

Genetic drift is the random change in frequency caused by finite population size. Its strength is inversely proportional to the effective population size. Drift fixes neutral alleles and can override weak selection; selection dominates only when the selection coefficient exceeds the reciprocal of the effective population size. The molecular clock—the roughly constant rate of accumulation of neutral substitutions—is a consequence of drift.

Selection changes frequencies deterministically. The change per generation is proportional to the selection coefficient and to the variance in fitness. Migration homogenizes populations. Mutation introduces new alleles. The joint action of the four forces produces the patterns of variation observed in nature. The theory is quantitative and has been tested in laboratory populations and in the wild.

The framework accounts for the maintenance of polymorphism, the rate of molecular evolution and the genetic structure of subdivided populations, and it is the quantitative core of evolutionary genetics.

### Worked Examples: Population Genetics

Example 1. A recessive lethal allele has frequency 0.01. What fraction of the population dies from it each generation under random mating?

Frequency of homozygotes = q<sup>2</sup> = 10<sup>−4</sup>. One in ten thousand individuals is affected.

Example 2. A haploid allele with selective advantage s = 0.01 starts at frequency 0.001 in a large population. Approximately how many generations are required for it to reach frequency 0.5?

The odds p/(1-p) grow by a factor 1+s each generation. The odds must rise from about 0.001 to 1, so the time is ln (1000)/ln (1.01) ≈ 6.9/0.00995 ≈ 690 generations.

Example 3. In a population of effective size 10 000, what is the probability that a new neutral mutation eventually becomes fixed?

The fixation probability of a neutral allele is 1/(2N) = 5 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.

These elementary results are the starting point for every calculation of evolutionary rates and of the expected frequency of genetic disease.

### Speciation

Speciation is the process by which one population becomes two populations that no longer exchange genes. The most common route is allopatric. A geographic barrier divides the population. The separated groups diverge by selection and drift. When contact is restored, reproductive isolation may be complete.

Isolation can be prezygotic or postzygotic. Prezygotic barriers include differences in mating time, place, or behavior, and mechanical or gametic incompatibility. Postzygotic barriers include hybrid inviability and hybrid sterility. Both classes are observed. The genetic basis ranges from single loci to many loci of small effect.

Sympatric speciation, without geographic separation, is rarer but documented in plants through polyploidy and in some animals through habitat or host shifts. The essential requirement in every case is the cessation of gene flow. Once gene flow stops, independent evolution proceeds, and chromosomal rearrangements or cytoplasmic incompatibilities can speed the process. The result is the branching pattern of the tree of life.

### Classification and the Tree of Life

Aristotle listed hundreds of animals and grouped them. He noticed that the dolphin, though it looks like a fish and lives in the sea, breathes air and bears live young. He placed it with the mammals. The observation was correct. The principle was that structure and function matter more than habitat.

Carl Linnaeus, in the eighteenth century, gave the system its modern form. Every species receives a two-part name, genus and species. Species are grouped into genera, genera into families, families into orders, orders into classes, classes into phyla, phyla into kingdoms. The ranks are a filing system. They are useful for communication. They are not the deepest fact.

The deepest fact is descent. Darwin argued that the groups exist because of common ancestry. The tree of life is the diagram of that ancestry. Modern classification aims to make the groups reflect the branches of the tree. A group that includes an ancestor and all its descendants is monophyletic. Groups that do not are revised or abandoned.

The evidence is now molecular as well as anatomical. DNA sequences can be compared. The more similar the sequences, the more recent the common ancestor, in general. The comparisons have rearranged some branches. Birds are nested inside the dinosaurs. Fungi are closer to animals than to plants. The three domains—Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya—replace the older two-kingdom or five-kingdom schemes.

The number of described species is on the order of two million. The total number of species alive today is estimated in the millions more. Most are insects, microbes, and other small organisms. Extinction removes branches. Speciation adds them. The tree is not static. Classification is an attempt to describe it at a moment in time.

All cellular life shares a common ancestry. The evidence is the universal genetic code, the shared core of metabolic pathways, and the nested hierarchy of morphological and molecular similarities. Molecular sequences allow the hierarchy to be reconstructed as a phylogenetic tree.

The tree has three principal domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. Eukaryotes arose from a symbiotic association between an archaeal host and a bacterial endosymbiont that became the mitochondrion. Plants acquired a second endosymbiont, a cyanobacterium that became the chloroplast. Subsequent diversification produced the kingdoms and phyla recognized by traditional taxonomy.

Horizontal gene transfer is common among prokaryotes and has occurred between domains. It complicates but does not erase the vertical signal. The overall topology remains robust. That ancestor was already a cell with a DNA genome, a translation system, and a membrane. Everything that has followed is modification of that ancestral organization.

### Sexual Reproduction and Parthenogenesis

Sexual reproduction combines genomes from two parents and shuffles alleles by recombination. The process generates new genetic combinations every generation. Beneficial mutations that arise in different individuals can be united in a single descendant. Genetically diverse offspring are also more resistant to rapidly evolving parasites and pathogens. The advantage is known as the Red Queen effect.

The cost is a twofold reduction in reproductive rate: only females produce offspring, and mates must be located. Despite the cost, sex is the dominant mode among complex eukaryotes. The diversity benefit outweighs the cost under most natural conditions.

Parthenogenesis is development from an unfertilized egg. It eliminates the cost of sex. It is favored when mates are absent, when the environment is stable and the current genotype is already well adapted, or when rapid population growth is required. Many insects, some lizards, and numerous plants reproduce parthenogenetically for extended periods.

Most parthenogenetic lineages are short-lived on geological time-scales. Without recombination they accumulate deleterious mutations and cannot assemble new adaptive combinations when conditions change. Parthenogenesis therefore arises repeatedly but rarely persists. Sexual reproduction remains the prevailing solution to the problem of generating heritable variation in variable environments.

### Ethology and the Evolution of Behavior

Ethology is the study of animal behavior under natural conditions. Behavior, like morphology, has a genetic basis and evolves. Fixed action patterns are stereotyped sequences triggered by specific sign stimuli. They are innate. Learning modifies behavior within limits set by the genotype.

The evolution of behavior is studied by the comparative method and by measuring heritability and response to selection. Altruistic behavior that reduces the actor’s direct reproduction can spread if it increases the reproduction of genetic relatives. The condition is Hamilton’s rule: the cost to the actor is less than the benefit to the recipient weighted by relatedness. The rule accounts for the evolution of sterile castes in social insects and for many forms of parental care and cooperation.

Sexual selection produces traits that increase mating success even when they reduce survival. The peacock’s tail and the elaborate songs of birds are classic examples. Female choice and male–male competition are both documented. The same principles apply to human behavior to the extent that the relevant genetic variation and selective pressures exist. The extent is an empirical question, not a philosophical one.

### Ants, Termites and Bees

Ants, termites and the social bees and wasps are eusocial. Reproduction is restricted to one or a few individuals. The remaining members of the colony are sterile workers that raise siblings. The system has evolved independently many times. It is the most extreme form of social organization known in animals.

In the Hymenoptera (ants, bees and wasps) sex is determined by haplodiploidy. Females develop from fertilized eggs and are diploid. Males develop from unfertilized eggs and are haploid. Full sisters therefore share three-quarters of their genes. The relatedness asymmetry favors the evolution of sterile female workers that raise sisters rather than their own offspring. The genetic predisposition is not sufficient by itself. Ecological factors—defense of a nest, progressive provisioning of young, and the ability to dominate reproduction—are also required. Many haplodiploid species are not eusocial.

Termites are diploid. Both sexes work. Relatedness among siblings is the ordinary one-half. Eusociality in termites is associated with the need to care for a slowly developing brood inside a defended nest and with the advantage of a soldier caste. The genetic system differs from that of the Hymenoptera. The ecological outcome is similar.

Colony-level traits include division of labor, communication by pheromones, construction of complex nests, and, in some species, agriculture or slave-making. The sterile castes are altruistic at the individual level and cooperative at the colony level. The colonies function as superorganisms for many purposes. The underlying selective process remains kin selection acting on the genes that produce the sterile phenotypes.

### The Map That Contains Itself

A cell contains a genome. The genome contains the instructions for building the cell, including the machinery that reads the genome. The map contains the instructions for building the map-reader. The arrangement is ordinary. It is also the reason life can persist. Without the map the machinery cannot be rebuilt. Without the machinery the map cannot be read. Both are required. Both are copied.

The copying is imperfect. The imperfections are mutations. Most are harmful or neutral. A few are beneficial. The beneficial ones spread. The spread is evolution. The evolution has produced organisms that contain maps of themselves accurate enough to build the next generation. The accuracy is high. It is not perfect. The imperfection is the source of all subsequent change. The change includes the reader. The reader is still carrying a slightly imperfect copy of the map.

## <a id="ch_40"></a>40. Quantum Biology

Most biological processes are well described by classical chemistry. A few involve quantum effects that cannot be ignored.

Enzyme catalysis sometimes uses tunneling. In hydrogen-transfer reactions the proton or hydrogen atom can pass through the energy barrier rather than over it. The rate is higher than a classical calculation predicts. Kinetic isotope effects—the change in rate when hydrogen is replaced by deuterium—are larger than expected from mass alone and are consistent with tunneling. The effect is temperature-dependent in ways that match quantum models.

Photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes transfer energy from antenna pigments to the reaction center with high efficiency. Spectroscopic measurements show coherent oscillations in the energy transfer. The coherence persists for hundreds of femtoseconds at physiological temperatures. Whether the coherence improves the efficiency under natural conditions or is a side effect of the structure is still under study. The observation is established. The functional importance is not fully settled.

Avian magnetoreception is another candidate. Some migratory birds orient using the Earth’s magnetic field. One proposed mechanism is a radical-pair reaction in cryptochrome proteins in the eye. The yield of the reaction depends on the orientation of the radical pair relative to the magnetic field because of the interplay of electron spins. The mechanism is plausible and consistent with behavioral experiments. Direct proof that it is the sensor used by the bird is still incomplete.

Quantum effects in biology are real where they have been measured. They do not require that the organism maintain macroscopic coherence. They occur in specific reactions where the energy barriers, the timescales, and the isolation from the environment allow them. The majority of cellular chemistry remains classical. The exceptions show that evolution can use quantum mechanics when it is available.

### What Quantum Biology Does Not Show

The claims for quantum computation in the brain or for quantum-enhanced olfaction lack experimental support. The thermal environment of a cell destroys coherence on timescales far shorter than those required for such processes. Ordinary quantum chemistry—tunneling, zero-point energy, discrete spectra—is sufficient to explain the established cases. Exotic macroscopic quantum effects are not required.

The field therefore consists of a small set of confirmed tunneling and coherence phenomena embedded in an otherwise classical biochemical framework. The confirmed cases are interesting. They do not rewrite the foundations of biology.

### Quantum Effects in Genetics

Most genetic processes are classical. Base pairing, replication, transcription, and translation are described by ordinary chemistry. A few steps show quantum signatures that affect the outcome.

Proton tunneling contributes to some mutation rates. In DNA the hydrogen bonds that hold base pairs together can shift by tunneling. The tautomeric forms that result can mispair during replication. The rate is low. It is not zero. The contribution is measurable in some systems by comparing rates in ordinary water and in heavy water. The difference is consistent with a tunneling component. The bulk of mutations still arise from other causes: copying errors, chemical damage, and radiation. Tunneling is one channel among several.

Electron transfer in some repair enzymes and in photosynthetic reaction centers proceeds by tunneling. The distance dependence and the temperature dependence match quantum calculations. The proteins position the donors and acceptors so that the tunneling rate is useful. The positioning is the product of selection. The tunneling itself is a physical fact that selection has used.

The quantum contributions that have been demonstrated are local, specific, and already incorporated into the ordinary chemical account. They do not require a separate quantum genetics; they show that the chemistry of life includes the quantum mechanics of its atoms. The larger claim, that genetic information is held in macroscopic superposition, is taken up in the section on evolution.

### Adaptive Mutation and Quantum Coherence

In 1999 Johnjoe McFadden and Jim Al-Khalili proposed a quantum model for adaptive mutation. Adaptive mutation is the reported phenomenon in which certain mutations appear more frequently when they confer an advantage than when they are neutral. The classical expectation is that mutation rates are independent of utility. The observations, first described in bacteria under starvation, have been disputed. Some are explained by ordinary growth and selection on pre-existing variants. Others remain unresolved.

The quantum proposal begins with proton tunneling in DNA base pairs. A proton can occupy either of two positions. The two positions correspond to different base-pairing possibilities. The model treats the proton as remaining in a coherent superposition of the two positions for a biologically relevant time. Interaction with an environment that contains a usable substrate is argued to accelerate decoherence and thereby increase the rate at which the mutant state is realized. The estimated decoherence time in the model is on the order of seconds. That is long enough, in principle, for the proposed effect.

The proposal has not been confirmed. Direct measurements of coherence in DNA under cellular conditions have not shown the required superposition. Decoherence calculations that include more of the molecular environment yield shorter times. The adaptive-mutation experiments themselves have alternative classical explanations in many cases. The idea remains a possible mechanism for a disputed phenomenon. It is not an established modification of evolutionary theory.

McFadden and Al-Khalili later surveyed a wider set of quantum effects in biology: tunneling in enzymes, coherent energy transfer in photosynthesis, the radical-pair mechanism for magnetoreception, and a proposed vibration-assisted tunneling in olfaction. Some of these effects are measured. Their functional importance varies. The adaptive-mutation model is the most specific claim that quantum coherence could bias the generation of heritable variation. That claim is still open. The broader observation that quantum mechanics is part of the chemistry of life is not.

### Quantum Biology and Evolution

Evolution is a classical process at the scale of populations. Mutation, selection, drift, and recombination are described by ordinary population genetics. The underlying chemistry of mutation and catalysis includes quantum steps. Those steps do not change the structure of the evolutionary account. They change the rates and the channels through which variation appears.

Proton and electron tunneling contribute to mutation and to the work of repair enzymes, as the previous sections describe. The positioning is classical, the transfer step is quantum, and selection acts on the outcome, not on the mechanism.

Photosynthetic energy transfer and enzyme catalysis show coherent or tunneling contributions under physiological conditions. These processes affect the efficiency with which organisms capture energy and carry out metabolism. Efficiency is a selectable trait. Organisms that harness the quantum step more effectively leave more offspring, other things equal. The quantum step itself is not selected. The molecular architecture that makes the step available is selected. The distinction matters. Evolution does not need to “know” about quantum mechanics. It needs only to retain variants that work.

No established mechanism allows a cell to maintain a macroscopic superposition of genetic states and to collapse that superposition preferentially toward adaptive outcomes. The adaptive-mutation model remains a proposal. Decoherence in the cellular environment is rapid. The successful description of the origin and spread of adaptations continues to be the classical one: variation arises, most of it is neutral or deleterious, a fraction is advantageous, and selection increases the frequency of the advantageous fraction. Quantum mechanics is part of the physics that generates the variation and powers the metabolism. It is not a separate evolutionary force.

The practical consequence is modest and real. Calculations of mutation rates, of catalytic rates, and of energy-transfer efficiency are more accurate when the quantum channels are included. The evolutionary conclusions drawn from those rates do not change. The tree of life, the genetic code, and the history of adaptations remain the same. Quantum biology refines the chemistry. It does not rewrite the theory of evolution.

### How Birds Navigate

Migratory birds reach distant destinations without maps or instruments. They integrate several independent cues.

A magnetic compass is widespread. The leading candidate sensor is a light-dependent chemical reaction in the retina involving the protein cryptochrome. The reaction yields a directional signal relative to the Earth’s field. The compass is inclination-based in many species: it distinguishes poleward from equatorward rather than north from south.

Celestial cues supply a second reference. Diurnal migrants use the Sun’s azimuth, compensated by an internal circadian clock. Nocturnal migrants learn the rotation of the star field around the celestial pole while still in the nest. Both systems function under natural skies and fail under experimental disruption of the clock or of the stellar pattern.

Experienced birds also follow landmarks—coasts, rivers, mountain chains—and, in some species, olfactory gradients. Homing pigeons and certain seabirds deprived of smell are disoriented. The odor map is learned.

First-autumn juveniles often fly a genetically encoded direction for a genetically encoded duration. Only after the journey do they acquire a more detailed map. Adults can correct displacements and return to the normal route, showing that learned information supplements the innate program.

The systems are redundant. Birds switch among them when one is unavailable. No evidence indicates an internal calculation of absolute geographic position comparable to satellite navigation. Accuracy arises from the continuous cross-checking of simpler directional and landmark cues, together with social information from experienced companions in many species.

## <a id="ch_41"></a>41. The Human Genome

In 2001 two drafts of the human genome were published. In 2003 the project was declared complete, with reservations. In 2022 the last gaps, mostly difficult repetitive regions, were filled. We now have a continuous sequence of a human genome, a string of about three billion base pairs.

The string is not a blueprint in the way a blueprint specifies every board. It is closer to a recipe that assumes a cell already running. Genes, in the classical sense of protein-coding sequences, are a small minority of the total, on the order of one to two percent.

What the sequence gave biology was a reference. Variation could be compared to something. Common differences among people, single-letter changes and larger rearrangements, could be cataloged. Disease studies could ask which differences are more common in people with a condition than in people without it.

Reading the genome was the achievement of one generation. Writing it, in living people, is the argument of the next chapter.

Sequencing the genome was a technical achievement and a conceptual correction. The technical achievement was the reading of three billion base pairs with enough accuracy to be useful, first as drafts, then as a finished reference, then as a complete end-to-end sequence including the hard repetitive regions. The conceptual correction was the discovery that gene number did not measure complexity in any simple way. Humans have on the order of twenty thousand protein-coding genes. So do other animals. Some plants have more. Complexity, where it exists, is in the regulation, the splicing, the timing, and the networks, not in a longer list of parts.

Noncoding DNA is the majority of the sequence. Some of it is regulatory: switches that determine when and where a gene is used. Some of it is structural. Some of it is the remains of ancient viruses that inserted themselves and were inherited. Some of it may have no selected function. The fraction with function is disputed, and the dispute depends on what “function” is taken to mean. A sequence can affect a molecular measurement without affecting the organism’s success. The careful claim is that noncoding DNA is a mixture, not a wastebasket and not a hidden second genome of equal importance to the genes. Its importance is real and uneven.

Variation among people is the genome’s other lesson. Any two people differ at millions of sites. Most differences are common, small in effect, and shared across populations in different proportions. Some are rare and consequential in a single gene. The common differences are the raw material of polygenic scores and of adaptation. The rare ones are the raw material of many genetic diseases. Both kinds are inherited. Neither kind supports the older idea that human groups are discrete biological types. Human genetic variation is real, geographically patterned, and small compared with the variation inside any one population. The patterning is what migration and history produce. It is not a set of separate species.

The clinical use of the sequence has been most decisive for rare disease. A child with a severe, unexplained condition can have their genome, or their exome, sequenced and compared with their parents’. A new mutation in a known gene, or a pair of mutations in a recessive gene, can end a diagnostic search that once took years. Treatment does not always follow diagnosis. Sometimes it does. The diagnosis itself is a change in medicine.

For common disease the contribution is statistical. Genome-wide association studies find variants that are more common in people with a disease than in people without it. Each variant usually has a small effect. Together they can predict a fraction of the risk. The fraction is useful for research and, in some cases, for sorting people into higher and lower risk groups. It is not a personal prophecy. Environment, chance, and the limits of the studies intervene. Scores trained in one population often work less well in another, because the pattern of genetic correlation differs. Equity in the data is a scientific requirement, not only a social one.

The genome is a reference and a parts list. It is not a blueprint that specifies the finished body in detail. Development uses the list in a context: a fertilized egg, a womb, a sequence of signals, an environment. Read the list and you do not yet have the person. That limit is not a failure of the project. It is the next subject, and it is why genomics did not replace the rest of biology.

Privacy and ownership are the social edge of sequencing. A genome identifies a person and their relatives. It can reveal disease risk, ancestry, and, in some cases, information the person did not want. Databases that enable research also enable reidentification if they are careless. The scientific value of shared data is large. The harm of careless sharing is real. The balance is a governance problem sitting on top of a measurement revolution. The measurement will not slow down. The governance has to be built at the same speed.

Ancestry and identity should not be confused with the sequence. Genetic ancestry tests report similarities to reference populations. They are useful for genealogy and for the history of migrations. They do not assign a person to a race in any biological sense that withstands scrutiny, because human variation is continuous and overlapping. The tests measure real patterns. The social categories they are sometimes taken to support are coarser than the patterns. Keeping the measurement and the category apart is a service both to the science and to the people who use it.

Editing and sequencing together change what a variant means. A variant of unknown significance, found in a patient, can sometimes be tested in a cell or in an organoid to see whether it disrupts the gene’s function. The test turns a correlation into a mechanism. Mechanism is what makes a diagnosis solid and a therapy conceivable. The genome supplies the variant. The functional test supplies the interpretation. Neither alone is enough for the hardest cases. The combination is the direction of clinical genetics. It is slower than sequencing alone and more decisive.

### The Genome in Numbers

The human genome is the complete DNA sequence of a human cell. The haploid genome contains approximately 3.2 billion base pairs. About 1.5 percent codes for proteins. The remainder consists of introns, regulatory sequences, transposable elements, and other non-coding DNA. Roughly 20 000 protein-coding genes are present. Many genes produce multiple transcripts by alternative splicing.

The sequence was first completed in draft form in 2001 and in finished form in 2003. Subsequent projects have cataloged common variation. Any two unrelated individuals differ at about one site in a thousand. Most variants are single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Structural variants—insertions, deletions, inversions and copy-number changes—also contribute. The majority of variants are neutral or nearly neutral. A minority affect disease risk or drug response.

Genes are not uniformly distributed. Some chromosomal regions are gene-rich. Others are gene-poor. The mitochondrial genome is a separate circular molecule of 16 569 base pairs that is maternally inherited and encodes 13 proteins of the respiratory chain. Nuclear and mitochondrial genomes together constitute the hereditary material.

The genome is not a blueprint that specifies the organism in every detail. It is a parts list and a regulatory network whose output depends on cellular context, developmental history and environment. Sequencing has made that list available. Interpreting the regulatory logic remains incomplete.

### Human Genetics

Within the genome, variants matter in very different ways. Most are neutral, and a minority affect traits or disease risk.

Monogenic disorders are caused by variants in a single gene. Sickle-cell disease, cystic fibrosis, and Huntington’s disease are examples. The inheritance follows Mendelian ratios when the variant is fully penetrant. Many common diseases are polygenic. Height, blood pressure, and susceptibility to type 2 diabetes or schizophrenia are influenced by thousands of variants of small effect, plus environment. Polygenic scores sum the effects. They are predictive in populations similar to the ones in which they were derived and less predictive in others.

Genome-wide association studies scan hundreds of thousands of people for statistical links between variants and traits. The links identify regions. They do not by themselves prove causation. Functional studies are required. The same methods have mapped genes that affect drug response, a field called pharmacogenetics. A variant that is harmless in one context can determine whether a drug is effective or toxic.

Editing the human germline changes DNA that can be inherited. The 2018 birth of edited twins, discussed in the chapter on gene editing, had legal consequences: He Jiankui was convicted in China of illegal medical practice and imprisoned. Chinese regulations now prohibit clinical research that alters germ cells or embryos for reproduction. Somatic editing, which affects only the treated individual, is in clinical trials for several diseases. The distinction between somatic and germline alteration is the current regulatory boundary.

### Modern DNA Methods

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences. DNA ligase joins the ends. The combination allowed recombinant DNA in the 1970s. A gene from one organism could be inserted into a plasmid and propagated in bacteria. The technique produced insulin, growth hormone, and many other proteins.

The polymerase chain reaction amplifies a chosen segment of DNA exponentially. A pair of primers, a heat-stable polymerase, and thermal cycling generate millions of copies from a few molecules. Sequencing reads the order of bases. Sanger sequencing used chain-terminating nucleotides. Next-generation methods read millions of fragments in parallel. A human genome that once required years and hundreds of millions of dollars can now be sequenced in hours for hundreds of dollars.

CRISPR-Cas systems are adaptive immune mechanisms in bacteria. A guide RNA directs the Cas nuclease to a matching DNA sequence. The nuclease cuts. The cell repairs the break. Repair can disable the gene or, if a template is supplied, insert a new sequence. Base editors and prime editors change single bases or short stretches without double-strand breaks. The tools work in bacteria, plants, animals, and human cells. They are used in research, in agriculture, and in clinical trials for genetic disease.

Gene drives bias inheritance so that a chosen allele spreads through a population faster than Mendelian ratios allow. They have been demonstrated in insects in the laboratory. Their use outside containment is contested because the spread is designed to be difficult to reverse.

The methods are precise relative to earlier mutagenesis. They are not perfectly precise. Off-target cuts occur. Delivery to the right cells in a living organism remains difficult. The capability to read, write, and edit DNA at scale now exists. The limits are technical, regulatory, and ethical.

### Cloning

Cloning produces a genetic copy of an organism. In plants it is routine. Cuttings and tissue culture generate identical individuals. In animals the method is somatic-cell nuclear transfer. The nucleus of a somatic cell is placed in an enucleated egg. The reconstructed egg is stimulated to develop. The resulting animal has the nuclear genome of the donor.

Dolly the sheep was the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell. She was born in 1996. The success rate was low. Many reconstructed embryos failed. Those that developed often showed abnormalities in imprinting and in telomere length, which indicates that reprogramming of the somatic nucleus is incomplete. The genome of a differentiated cell evidently retains the information required to build an organism, but the process is neither routine nor free of epigenetic defects. Subsequent work produced cloned cattle, pigs, goats, cats, dogs, and other species. Efficiency has improved but remains far below natural reproduction.

In 2018 Chinese researchers produced the first cloned primates, two macaques, from fetal fibroblasts. A later rhesus monkey was cloned from fetal cells and required a non-cloned placenta. No healthy primate has been produced from an adult somatic cell. The reprogramming of an adult nucleus is incomplete in primates under current methods.

Reproductive cloning of humans has not been achieved. No verified human clone has been born. Therapeutic cloning, the production of embryonic stem cells genetically matched to a patient, has been performed in the laboratory. The embryos are not implanted. Most countries prohibit reproductive human cloning. A smaller number permit research on cloned human embryos under license. The technical barrier in primates remains high. The regulatory barrier is explicit.

## <a id="ch_42"></a>42. CRISPR and Gene Editing

Bacteria have been at war with viruses for billions of years. One of their defenses is a memory. They store snippets of viral DNA and use them to recognize the virus if it returns. A protein then cuts the viral genome. The system is called CRISPR.

In 2012 Jennifer Doudna, Emmanuelle Charpentier, and colleagues showed that the system could be aimed. A guide sequence could be designed, and the cutting protein, Cas9, would cut a chosen place in a chosen genome. Other laboratories reached the same capability at nearly the same time. Biology acquired an editor.

The editor is not magic. It cuts. The cell repairs the cut. The repair can disable a gene, or, if a template is supplied, sometimes insert a chosen sequence. Newer variants nick a single strand, or change one letter without a full break. The tools have multiplied. The principle remains: a sequence can be addressed.

In research, the effect has been a change of speed. Genes in mice, fish, crops, and cell lines can be altered in weeks rather than years. In medicine, the first wave of therapies edits cells outside the body and returns them, and the sickle-cell treatments described below are the leading example.

Editing embryos is a different act. In 2018 a researcher announced the birth of children whose genomes had been edited, ostensibly to reduce HIV risk. The experiment was widely condemned as premature, poorly justified, and a breach of norms that the field had stated. The condemnation was not a rejection of the tool. It was a rejection of using a tool, on people who cannot consent, before accuracy, necessity, and oversight were in place.

The line is worth keeping clear. Somatic editing changes a patient’s cells and ends with that patient. Germline editing changes descendants. Agriculture sits in a third category, and societies are already arguing it crop by crop. CRISPR did not create these distinctions. It made them urgent.

Gene editing is the point at which biology became, in a practical sense, a writing discipline as well as a reading one. The power is real. The gaps in delivery, specificity, and ethics are also real. A serious account refuses both the miracle story and the ban.

The tool is simple in outline and subtle in practice. A guide RNA matching a chosen sequence is supplied together with a cutting protein, usually Cas9 or a relative. The protein cuts where the guide matches. A quick-join repair often disrupts the gene. If a template is provided, the repair sometimes copies the template, inserting a chosen change. Base editors and prime editors, developed later, change letters with fewer double-strand breaks. The menu of editors has grown. Delivery remains the hard part.

Delivery is the difference between a result in a dish and a result in a patient. In a dish, the editor can be put into cells directly. In a body, it must reach the right cells, in the right tissue, in sufficient number, without damaging the rest. Viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, and direct injection are the current methods. Each has limits on cargo, on which tissues it reaches, and on immune response. Many of the first successes have been in blood, in the eye, and in the liver, where delivery is more tractable. Whole-body editing of arbitrary genes is not the present state. The map of what can be edited in a living person is, for now, a map of delivery as much as of genetics, and improving delivery would expand therapy more than improving the editor alone.

The sickle-cell treatments show both the power and the cost. Cells are taken from the patient, edited so that they produce fetal hemoglobin or so that a repressor of fetal hemoglobin is disabled, and returned after the remaining bone marrow is cleared. Patients have been freed from the crises of the disease. The procedure is intensive, expensive, and not without risk. It is also a proof that a genetic disease can be treated by editing the relevant cells. Other blood and immune disorders are following the same path.

Off-target cuts are the technical objection that has to be measured rather than assumed. An editor aimed at one sequence may cut similar sequences elsewhere. The rate depends on the guide, the editor, and the cell. It can be measured. It has been reduced by better design. It is not zero in every setting. For a therapy, the question is whether the residual rate is small compared with the benefit. For an embryo, the question is stricter, because every cell of the future person, and of their descendants if the change is inherited, carries the result.

Germline editing is the line most countries and most scientific bodies have treated as not yet permissible, outside tightly limited research that does not lead to a birth. The reasons are practical and ethical. Accuracy and long-term effects are not well enough known. The medical need is often addressable by other means, including selection of embryos in cases where that is accepted. The people affected cannot consent.

Agriculture is the third domain. Edited crops can resist disease, tolerate stress, or improve nutrition. Some jurisdictions treat certain edits, those that could have arisen by mutation, more like conventional breeding than like older transgenic methods. Others do not. The biological question and the regulatory question are different. The biological question is what change was made and what it does. The regulatory question is how a society chooses to label and approve it. A guide can state both and should not pretend they are the same question.

CRISPR did not invent the desire to change inheritance. It made the desire cheap and specific. The specificity is the advance. The cheapness is why the ethical and safety questions, which were once hypothetical, now have deadlines.

Somatic editing and enhancement should be distinguished. Treating a disease in a consenting patient’s cells is medicine. Editing an embryo for a trait that is not a disease, or editing a person for advantage rather than for treatment, is a different act. The line is argued. The existence of a difference between treatment and enhancement is clear even where the boundary is not. A therapy for sickle cell is not the same kind of decision as a speculative edit for muscle or for height. Keeping the difference visible is part of using the tool without confusing it with a general permission to redesign people.

Equity will determine whether the tool is a general advance or a narrow one. The first therapies are expensive. They require facilities. They will reach patients in rich health systems before they reach patients elsewhere, unless deliberate provision is made. The science does not make the provision. Institutions do. A chapter that celebrates the cure of sickle cell in a trial and omits the question of who receives it describes a result and not a change in the burden of the disease. Both belong in the account. The result is real. The burden shifts only when the result is delivered.

## <a id="ch_43"></a>43. Synthetic Biology

*If editing changes an existing text, synthetic biology asks whether the text can be written from scratch, or joined in combinations nature did not try.*

The field has several layers, from DNA synthesis at the bottom, through engineered pathways and minimal cells, to expanded genetic alphabets at the top.

The enabling change is the fall in the cost of reading and writing DNA. Sequencing now costs a tiny fraction of what it cost at the end of the Human Genome Project. Synthesis of genes, and of whole small genomes, is a commercial service. A design can be a file. The file can be ordered. The distance from idea to test has collapsed for any project that lives in a microbe or a cell line. That is the practical meaning of synthetic biology.

Pathway engineering is the workhorse. A cell has a metabolism. A pathway is a sequence of enzymatic steps from a starting material to a product. If the enzymes exist somewhere in nature, their genes can be moved into a production host, usually a yeast or a bacterium, and tuned. If they do not exist, they can sometimes be designed or evolved. The antimalarial precursor artemisinin, flavors, fragrances, and industrial chemicals have been made this way. The successes are real. So are the failures, which are less famous. A pathway that works in a flask can poison its host, or cost too much feedstock, or lose to an existing chemical process. The field is an industry as well as a science. Industries count costs.

Minimal cells test how much of a genome is required for life under comfortable laboratory conditions. A bacterial genome can be reduced, synthesized, and used to boot a cell. The reduced genome still contains genes of unknown function. Life, even pared down, is not yet a fully annotated machine. The result is a limit on our understanding and a tool for studying what the remaining genes do. It is not a cell built from first principles out of nonliving parts. That harder goal remains ahead.

Expanded alphabets and nonstandard amino acids show that the particular code we inherited is contingent. Cells have been made to use six-letter DNA and to incorporate amino acids that nature does not use. The purpose is usually a better protein for a particular job, or a cleaner biological system that cannot easily exchange genes with the wild. Containment by dependence on a synthetic nutrient is one proposed safety measure. It is a measure, not a guarantee. Evolution is patient.

Safety and misuse are part of the subject because the tools are widely available. Ordering a pathogen’s genome is restricted and screened by responsible suppliers. Not every supplier is responsible, and not every sequence reveals its purpose. The practical barriers to harm remain significant: expertise, equipment, delivery, and the fact that engineered organisms are often fragile. The barriers are lower than they were. Governance has been a mix of self-regulation, screening, and law. It will have to keep pace with cheaper synthesis and with automated design. The scientific opportunity and the governance problem grew from the same cause.

Synthetic biology’s place in a guide is as the writing side of the reading revolution. We can sequence life. We can, in increasing measure, specify changes and build new pathways. We cannot yet design a cell from scratch with the reliability of an engineer designing a bridge. The gap is the size of the remaining mystery of living systems. It is also a gap that narrows with each working pathway and each booted genome.

Automation is the next practical change. Design software, robotic liquid handling, and automated testing let a small team run a cycle of design, build, and measure that once required a large one. The cycle is the method. Faster cycles mean more of the design space can be searched. They also mean that the limits of understanding become clearer: a design that fails does so for a reason in the cell, and the reason is often a regulation, a toxicity, or a burden that the design did not include. Synthetic biology teaches the complexity of cells by trying to write them. The failures are data.

Biosafety levels and screening are the present controls. Laboratories are classified by the hazard of the organisms they handle. DNA synthesis companies screen orders against lists of dangerous sequences. The controls are imperfect and useful. They raise the cost and the visibility of misuse. They do not make misuse impossible. As synthesis moves into more hands and more automated settings, the controls have to move too. The alternative is a capability that grows faster than the practice of watching it. Watching is less exciting than designing. It is part of the same subject if the subject is to remain a public good.

Standards and parts registries are the attempt to make biology more like engineering. Catalogued parts, with measured behavior, can be combined with less surprise. The attempt has helped. Biology’s context dependence has limited it. A part that works in one strain, in one condition, may fail in another. The limit is not a reason to abandon standards. It is a reason to measure context as part of the standard. Synthetic biology matures as it records its failures of transfer and designs around them. Maturity looks like better annotation, not like the end of surprises.

The scientific point is quieter. Life is a material system. Its parts can be listed, synthesized, and recombined. The listing is incomplete. The recombination has already left the page and entered factories and clinics. The field is no longer young.

### Synthetic Biology: Definitions and Tools

Synthetic biology is the design and construction of new biological parts, devices and systems, and the redesign of existing natural systems for useful purposes. It applies engineering principles—standardization, modularity and abstraction—to molecular biology.

Standardized genetic parts (promoters, ribosome-binding sites, coding sequences, terminators) are assembled into circuits that perform logical operations, oscillate or produce defined outputs. Entire genomes have been synthesized and transplanted into recipient cells, producing viable organisms controlled by the synthetic genome. Minimal genomes that contain only the genes required for life under laboratory conditions have been constructed.

Applications include the production of pharmaceuticals, fuels and materials, the engineering of biosensors, and the exploration of the minimal requirements for cellular life. Risks include unintended ecological effects and the possibility of misuse. Containment strategies—auxotrophy, kill switches and physical isolation—are under development. The field demonstrates that the genetic code and cellular machinery can be treated as a programmable technology. It also reveals how much of cellular function remains incompletely understood.

## <a id="ch_44"></a>44. Life Through Deep Time

### The Fossil Record of Life

The fossil record is the sequence of preserved remains and traces of organisms in sedimentary rocks. It begins with chemical and morphological traces of microbial life 3.5–3.8 billion years ago. Multicellular organisms appear in abundance only in the Ediacaran, about 575 million years ago. The Cambrian explosion, beginning 540 million years ago, marks the rapid appearance of most major animal phyla that possess hard parts.

Subsequent radiations and extinctions are documented in increasing detail. The colonization of land by plants, arthropods and vertebrates occurs in the Palaeozoic. The end-Permian extinction eliminates more than 90 percent of marine species. The Mesozoic is dominated by dinosaurs and gymnosperms. The end-Cretaceous extinction removes the non-avian dinosaurs and many other groups. The Cenozoic radiation of mammals, birds and flowering plants follows.

Molecular clocks and phylogenetic trees calibrated by fossils recover the same broad sequence.
