Gaps exist—soft-bodied organisms are under-represented, and some intervals are poorly sampled—but the overall order of first appearances is robust. The record demonstrates that life has been continuously present for at least 3.5 billion years, that its complexity and diversity have increased, and that this increase has been repeatedly punctuated by mass extinctions and subsequent recoveries. It supplies the historical evidence for evolution.

### The Great Oxidation Event

The Great Oxidation Event was the first sustained rise of free oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere, occurring between approximately 2.4 and 2.1 billion years ago. Before the event the atmosphere and oceans were anoxic. Oxygen produced by cyanobacteria was consumed by reduced volcanic gases and by ferrous iron dissolved in seawater. When those sinks became saturated, oxygen accumulated.

The transition is recorded in the rock record. Detrital pyrite and uraninite, stable only under low oxygen, disappear. Red beds containing oxidized iron appear. Major banded-iron formation ceases. A pronounced positive carbon-isotope excursion indicates increased burial of organic carbon. Atmospheric oxygen rose from negligible levels to a few percent of the present concentration. The rise was permanent, although later fluctuations occurred.

The oxygenation transformed surface chemistry. It enabled aerobic respiration and thereby the higher energy yields required by large, active organisms. It also oxidized atmospheric methane, a potent greenhouse gas, and is implicated in the Huronian glaciation that followed. The event marks the point at which biological oxygen production permanently altered the planetary environment. All subsequent aerobic life depends on it.

### The Bacterium That Changed the Air

Two and a half billion years ago cyanobacteria began to produce oxygen as a waste product. The oxygen was absorbed by iron and by reduced gases. When those sinks were full, the oxygen accumulated. The atmosphere changed. The change killed most of the anaerobic organisms then alive. It also made aerobic respiration possible. Aerobic respiration yields far more energy per glucose molecule. The energy made larger bodies possible.

The rocks keep the record, as described above. The cyanobacteria did not plan the change. They excreted a gas. The gas altered the planet, and the alteration permitted the reader. Every breath taken since has depended on it. The reader is still dependent on the descendants of those bacteria, or on the chloroplasts that were once those bacteria. The dependence is total. It is not usually noticed.

### The Snowball Earth Hypothesis

The Snowball Earth hypothesis proposes that the planet was repeatedly covered by ice from pole to equator during the Neoproterozoic, roughly 720–635 million years ago. Two main glacial intervals—the Sturtian and the Marinoan—are recognized. Geological evidence includes glacial deposits at low palaeolatitudes, banded-iron formations that reappear after a billion-year absence, and cap carbonates that overlie the glacial strata, indicating rapid warming and high atmospheric carbon dioxide.

The proposed trigger is a runaway ice-albedo feedback. Once ice sheets reach a critical latitude, their reflectivity cools the planet further, driving the ice to the equator. Escape from the snowball state requires the accumulation of volcanic carbon dioxide to levels hundreds of times the present concentration. The resulting greenhouse warming melts the ice in a geologically short interval. The cap carbonates are the predicted chemical consequence of that deglaciation.

The hypothesis accounts for the unusual association of glacial deposits with indicators of low latitude and for the extreme carbon-isotope excursions of the Neoproterozoic. Alternative models invoke less complete ice cover—“slushball” states—with open equatorial oceans. Both versions remain under discussion. The episodes coincide with major changes in the carbon cycle and precede the appearance of the first large, complex organisms. Whether the glaciations directly facilitated that appearance is unresolved. The geological evidence for widespread, low-latitude ice is robust. The recovery shows in turn that the carbon-silicate cycle can restore habitable conditions even after global glaciation.

### The Cambrian Explosion

The Cambrian explosion is the relatively rapid appearance of most major animal phyla in the fossil record between about 540 and 520 million years ago. Preceding Ediacaran organisms are largely soft-bodied and of uncertain affinity. Cambrian strata contain arthropods, molluscs, brachiopods, echinoderms and early chordates, many with mineralized skeletons.

The suddenness is partly taphonomic. Hard parts preserve more readily than soft tissues. Molecular clocks nevertheless place the divergences of the major clades in the late Neoproterozoic, indicating that the explosion records both an increase in disparity and an improvement in preservability. Ecological drivers include the evolution of predation, the oxygenation of shelf seas, and developmental genetic innovations that permitted more complex body plans.

The explosion established the phylum-level architecture of animal life. Subsequent evolution has largely elaborated within those body plans. No comparable radiation of new phyla has occurred. The Cambrian event therefore marks the principal diversification of animal form.

### The Evolution of Plants

Plants originated from freshwater green algae. The closest living relatives are the charophytes. The transition to land required cuticles, stomata, and protected reproductive structures. The earliest fossil evidence of land plants is spores from the Ordovician, about 470 million years ago. Vascular tissue appears in the Silurian. By the Devonian, forests of lycophytes, ferns and progymnosperms existed.

Seeds evolved in the late Devonian. They freed reproduction from the requirement for free water and allowed colonization of drier habitats. Gymnosperms dominated the Mesozoic. Flowering plants (angiosperms) appear in the Early Cretaceous and radiate rapidly. Flowers and fruits coevolved with animal pollinators and dispersers. By the end of the Cretaceous, angiosperms were the most diverse plant group. They remain so today.

Photosynthetic efficiency, vascular architecture and reproductive strategy have been the principal axes of innovation. Polyploidy is common and has contributed to speciation. The same core genetic toolkit that patterns shoots and roots in mosses operates in flowering plants. The fossil record, comparative morphology and molecular phylogenies converge on a single origin of land plants and on the subsequent sequence of major innovations. Plants transformed the terrestrial surface, altered the atmosphere and created the habitats in which animals evolved.

### The Evolution of Animals

Animals are multicellular heterotrophs that develop from a blastula. Their closest unicellular relatives are the choanoflagellates. The earliest animal fossils are Ediacaran impressions, about 575 million years old. The Cambrian explosion, treated in its own section, brings most extant phyla into the record. Molecular clocks place the origin of the major clades somewhat earlier, in the late Neoproterozoic.

Bilaterians—animals with a single plane of symmetry and three germ layers—dominate the subsequent record. Two great branches exist: the protostomes (arthropods, molluscs, annelids and others) and the deuterostomes (echinoderms and chordates). Segmentation, jointed appendages, and a through-gut evolved independently in several lineages. The colonization of land by arthropods occurred in the Silurian–Devonian. Vertebrates followed in the Devonian. Tetrapods, amniotes and, later, endotherms each opened new ecological possibilities.

Mass extinctions repeatedly reset diversity. The end-Permian and end-Cretaceous events are the most severe. Recoveries produced the characteristic faunas of the following eras. Developmental genetics shows that the same Hox and other regulatory genes pattern the body axes of flies and mice. The morphological disparity of animals therefore rests on a conserved genetic toolkit deployed in different combinations. The fossil record, comparative anatomy and molecular phylogenies converge on a single origin of animals and on the subsequent branching order of the major phyla.

### Mass Extinctions

Mass extinctions are geologically brief intervals in which a large fraction of species disappear. Five major events are recognized in the Phanerozoic. The end-Ordovician, late Devonian, end-Permian, end-Triassic and end-Cretaceous extinctions each eliminated more than 70 percent of species in some estimates. The end-Permian is the most severe. Nine marine species in ten disappeared.

Causes differ. The end-Cretaceous coincides with the Chicxulub impact and with Deccan volcanism. The end-Permian coincides with the Siberian Traps eruptions and with evidence of ocean anoxia and warming. Other events are linked to glaciation, sea-level change or anoxia. In each case the extinction is rapid relative to background rates and is followed by a recovery interval of several million years.

Recoveries are not simple restorations. Surviving lineages radiate into vacated niches. The characteristic faunas of successive eras are the products of these resets. Mass extinctions demonstrate that external perturbations can override ordinary competitive and adaptive processes on a global scale. They are recurring features of the history of life.

### The End-Cretaceous Extinction

The end-Cretaceous extinction, 66 million years ago, eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs, marine reptiles, ammonites and a large fraction of other species. The event coincides with the impact of an asteroid approximately 10 km in diameter at Chicxulub, Mexico, and with the later stages of the Deccan Traps volcanism in India.

The impact excavated a crater 180 km wide, injected dust, soot and sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere, and generated a global heat pulse from re-entering ejecta. Sunlight was blocked for months to years. Photosynthesis collapsed. Acid rain and cooling followed. The volcanic eruptions released large volumes of carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide over a longer interval. Both perturbations are recorded in the sedimentary boundary layer that contains an iridium anomaly, shocked quartz and microspherules.

Survivors included birds, mammals, crocodilians and many marine invertebrates. Recovery of ecosystems required hundreds of thousands to millions of years. The extinction demonstrates that a single, geologically instantaneous event can remove dominant clades and reset the trajectory of terrestrial and marine life. The relative contributions of impact and volcanism remain debated. The coincidence of the impact with the extinction horizon is precise.

### Dinosaur Physiology and the Survivors

Non-avian dinosaurs were the dominant terrestrial vertebrates for more than 150 million years. Growth rates inferred from bone histology were rapid. Many species possessed feathers or filamentous integument. Metabolic rates were elevated relative to modern reptiles, although the precise degree of endothermy varied. The largest sauropods achieved masses exceeding 50 tonnes through a combination of efficient respiration, lightweight skeletons and high primary productivity.

Birds are the surviving dinosaur clade. They inherited feathers, a unidirectional respiratory system and, in most lineages, endothermy. The end-Cretaceous extinction removed all non-avian dinosaurs. Avian lineages that survived were small-bodied and capable of flight or of rapid terrestrial locomotion. Mammals, previously small and nocturnal, radiated into the vacated niches. The extinction therefore both terminated the dinosaur-dominated ecosystems and opened the ecological space in which modern birds and mammals diversified. The physiological traits that characterized dinosaurs did not disappear. They persist in birds.

### Other Dinosaur-Related Extinctions and Radiations

Dinosaurs originated in the Triassic after the end-Permian extinction had removed earlier dominant tetrapods. Their rise was gradual. They became ecologically dominant only in the Jurassic. Within the Mesozoic they experienced smaller extinction pulses, notably at the end of the Triassic and in the mid-Cretaceous, that pruned diversity but did not eliminate the group.

The end-Triassic extinction removed many competing archosaurs and is linked to the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. Dinosaurs expanded into the vacated niches. Mid-Cretaceous turnover affected marine reptiles and some dinosaur clades but left the major terrestrial groups intact. These earlier events illustrate that dinosaur dominance was not continuous or uniform. It was repeatedly shaped by extinction and recovery. The final, total removal of non-avian dinosaurs at the end of the Cretaceous was unique in its completeness. Prior perturbations had been survivable.

## <a id="ch_45"></a>45. Life at the Extremes

### Extremophiles

Extremophiles are organisms that grow under conditions lethal to most life. Thermophiles and hyperthermophiles live at temperatures above 60 °C and, in some cases, above 100 °C. Psychrophiles grow at temperatures below 15 °C and can remain metabolically active below 0 °C. Acidophiles and alkaliphiles tolerate pH values below 3 or above 9. Halophiles require high salt concentrations. Barophiles grow at pressures of hundreds of atmospheres.

The record holders are cultured or observed in hydrothermal vents, in polar ice, in acid mine drainage, in salt lakes, and in the deep subsurface. Their membranes, proteins, and nucleic acids are stabilized by adaptations that include increased ionic bonding, chaperone proteins, and compatible solutes. The adaptations are genetic. They demonstrate that the biochemical machinery of life can be adjusted to a wide range of physical conditions.

No organism is known to grow above approximately 122 °C or below approximately −20 °C in the presence of liquid water. No organism is known to grow at pressures above a few hundred megapascals or in the complete absence of liquid solvent. The limits are empirical. They mark the boundary of the known biosphere. They do not mark a fundamental chemical limit.

### Temperature Limits

The upper temperature limit for growth is set by the stability of membranes and proteins. Lipid bilayers become too fluid. Proteins denature. Hyperthermophiles raise the melting temperature of their proteins by increasing the number of ionic bonds and by compacting the hydrophobic core. They also use reverse gyrase to introduce positive supercoils into DNA, raising its melting point.

The lower limit is set by the availability of liquid water and by the kinetics of enzyme reactions. Psychrophiles produce enzymes with greater flexibility and membranes with a higher proportion of unsaturated lipids. Metabolic rates decline with temperature. Growth becomes immeasurably slow below about −20 °C even when liquid brine is present.

Laboratory experiments have extended the survival range. Spores and some vegetative cells remain viable after exposure to temperatures near absolute zero or above 150 °C for short periods. Survival is not growth. The window for sustained metabolism and reproduction is narrower. Outside the window, liquid water may exist but known biochemistry does not operate.

### Pressure Limits

Pressure affects volume. Reactions that decrease volume are favored at high pressure. Barophilic organisms adjust membrane fluidity and protein stability so that their enzymes continue to function at hundreds of atmospheres. The deepest cultured organisms come from the Mariana Trench, where the pressure is about 110 MPa.

At still higher pressures water freezes into high-pressure ice phases even at elevated temperatures. The availability of liquid solvent therefore declines. Laboratory studies have subjected microbes to pressures above 1 GPa. Survival occurs. Growth has not been demonstrated. The practical limit for active life appears to lie well below the pressures at which liquid water disappears.

Low pressure is equally restrictive. Below the triple point of water, liquid water is unstable. Organisms can survive desiccation as spores or in a dormant state. They cannot grow. The requirement for a liquid solvent therefore sets both an upper and a lower pressure bound once temperature is fixed. The bounds are observed on Earth and are expected to apply wherever the solvent is water.

### Other Physical Extremes

Radiation resistance is highest in organisms such as Deinococcus radiodurans. Multiple genome copies and efficient DNA-repair systems allow survival after doses of thousands of grays. The resistance is a byproduct of desiccation tolerance. It is not an adaptation to natural radiation levels on Earth. The same mechanisms would confer resistance to the radiation environments of Mars or of icy moons.

Desiccation tolerance allows survival for years or decades without liquid water. Trehalose and other compatible solutes stabilize membranes and proteins. Revival occurs when water returns. The strategy is common in arid soils and in the upper atmosphere. It does not permit growth in the absence of water.

High salinity, high metal concentrations, and low nutrient availability are tolerated by specialized organisms. In each case the adaptation is biochemical and genetic. The existence of these organisms expands the range of environments that must be considered potentially habitable. It does not remove the requirement for a liquid solvent, a free-energy source, and a mechanism of heredity. Those three requirements remain the practical boundary of the search for life.

### Worked Examples: Habitable Zones and Extremophiles

Example 1. A star has luminosity 0.25 L<sub>⊙</sub>. Where are the approximate inner and outer edges of its habitable zone?

The boundaries scale as √L. Inner edge ≈ 0.95 × 0.5 = 0.48 AU. Outer edge ≈ 1.7 × 0.5 = 0.85 AU.

Example 2. A hyperthermophile grows at 113 °C. By what factor is the thermal energy kT higher than at 20 °C?

T<sub>1</sub> = 386 K, T<sub>2</sub> = 293 K. Ratio = 1.32. The organism’s proteins remain folded despite the 32 percent increase in thermal energy.

Example 3. Pressure at the bottom of the Mariana Trench is 110 MPa. By what percentage is the volume of liquid water reduced relative to the surface (bulk modulus of water ≈ 2.2 GPa)?

Δ V/V = -P/B ≈ -0.05. Water is compressed by about 5 percent. Barophilic enzymes function under that compression.

The numbers fix the physical boundaries within which known life operates and the locations where similar boundaries might be crossed elsewhere.

## <a id="ch_46"></a>46. The Search for Life Elsewhere

### Habitable Zones

A habitable zone is the range of distances from a star at which a rocky planet can maintain liquid water on its surface. For a Sun-like star the zone lies roughly between 0.95 and 1.7 astronomical units. The inner edge is set by the runaway greenhouse and the outer edge by the maximum greenhouse. The boundaries depend on the stellar luminosity, the planetary albedo, and the greenhouse effect.

Liquid water is required only under the assumption that life is aqueous. Other solvents—ammonia, methane, or supercritical carbon dioxide—have been proposed. Each defines a different zone. The conventional zone remains the most conservative target because water is abundant and because terrestrial life demonstrates that aqueous chemistry works.

Tidal heating can extend habitability beyond the conventional zone. Moons of giant planets can maintain subsurface oceans even when the stellar flux is low. Europa, Enceladus, and Titan are examples in the Solar System. There the heat comes from tides, not from starlight. The chemistry may still be aqueous.

The concept of a habitable zone is a guide for observation. It is not a guarantee of life. Many planets inside the zone may be sterile. Planets outside the zone may harbor life in protected niches. The zone merely identifies the most accessible places to look. Occurrence-rate studies show that rocky planets inside it are common; whether any is inhabited is unknown.

### Biosignatures

A biosignature is an observable feature that is more readily produced by life than by abiotic processes. Atmospheric oxygen together with methane is a strong candidate. The two gases react and must be continuously replenished. On Earth the replenishment is biological. An abiotic source that maintains both at high abundance has not been demonstrated.

Surface pigments that absorb in characteristic bands, seasonal variations in gas concentrations, and the presence of complex organic molecules with a preferred chirality are additional candidates. None is unambiguous. False positives are possible. Oxygen can be produced by photodissociation of water on planets that have lost their hydrogen. Methane can be produced by serpentinization.

The search therefore requires multiple lines of evidence and a quantitative understanding of the abiotic background. Spectra of exoplanet atmospheres, surface imaging, and, eventually, in-situ sampling are the available methods. The absence of a biosignature does not prove the absence of life. It only raises the upper limit on the abundance or the productivity of any life that may be present.

### Life in the Solar System

Mars possessed liquid water on its surface for extended periods in the past. The evidence is valley networks, lake beds, and hydrated minerals. Present surface conditions are hostile. Subsurface aquifers or transient brines remain possible habitats. No definitive biosignature has been detected by the landers and rovers.

Europa and Enceladus hide oceans beneath their ice, in contact with rock and kept liquid by tidal heating; the next section weighs them as habitats.

Titan has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and surface lakes of liquid methane and ethane. Its chemistry is rich in organic compounds, but at about −180 °C any life there would need a different solvent and far slower reactions than life on Earth; whether such a biochemistry is possible is unknown.

Venus has a temperate cloud layer at about 50 km altitude. The droplets are acidic. The proposal that microbes could inhabit them is speculative. No supporting evidence exists. The surface itself is too hot for any known biochemistry.

The moons and planets of the outer Solar System remain the most accessible places where the question of extraterrestrial life can be tested by direct measurement.

### Icy Moons as Habitats

Of the icy moons described in [Chapter 25](#ch_25), Europa and Enceladus are the strongest candidates for present-day habitable environments beyond Earth. Both have liquid water in contact with rock, a supply of chemical energy from tides and hydrothermal reactions, and organic molecules. Ganymede’s ocean is probably sealed between layers of ice, and Callisto’s is less certain still. None has yielded a confirmed biosignature. Missions that sample the plumes or reach the ocean will test whether the chemistry has stayed abiotic or crossed into biology. NASA’s Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, reaches Jupiter in 2030, and ESA’s JUICE, launched in 2023, arrives the following year.

### Exoplanets and the Frequency of Life

As [Chapter 27](#ch_27) shows, rocky planets in the habitable zones of their stars are common, found around tens of percent of Sun-like stars. The raw material for life is therefore abundant.

The transition from habitability to inhabited status is unmeasured. The only known example is Earth. The time required for the origin of life on Earth is poorly constrained. It may have been short. It may have been rare. The subsequent evolution of complex, multicellular, and technological life took billions of years and may depend on contingent events.

Statistical arguments based on the single known case are weak. The absence of detected technosignatures within a few tens of light-years sets a weak upper limit on the abundance of technological civilizations. It does not constrain microbial life. The frequency of life remains an open empirical question. The answer will come from atmospheric spectroscopy of nearby exoplanets and from continued exploration of the Solar System.

### Exobiospheres

An exobiosphere is a biosphere on a planet or moon orbiting a star other than the Sun. None has been detected. The search proceeds by identifying habitable environments and then seeking biosignatures—observable features more readily produced by life than by abiotic processes.

Surface liquid water remains the most conservative target because it is the solvent of terrestrial life and because its presence can be inferred from orbital distance, albedo and atmospheric composition. Subsurface oceans maintained by tidal heating enlarge the target list to include moons of giant planets. The atmospheric and surface biosignatures under consideration are described in the preceding sections; each admits abiotic false positives, which is why multiple lines of evidence are required.

The statistical context is the occurrence-rate picture given earlier. A single detection would demonstrate that life is not unique to Earth. Non-detection in a large sample would place an upper limit on the abundance of biospheres that produce strong, global signatures. Present instruments can characterize the atmospheres of a few favorable targets. Future telescopes will enlarge the sample. The existence of exobiospheres remains an open empirical question whose answer will be obtained by observation, not by theory alone.

### Exobiology

Exobiology is the study of the origin, evolution and distribution of life beyond Earth. It encompasses the conditions required for life, the possible biochemistries that could satisfy those conditions, and the observational signatures that would reveal its presence.

The only known life is terrestrial. It is carbon-based, uses water as solvent, and employs nucleic acids and proteins. Laboratory experiments have shown that many of its building blocks form under abiotic conditions and that alternative solvents and backbones are chemically conceivable. No alternative system has been shown to replicate and evolve. The working definition of life used in exobiology therefore remains operational: a chemical system that maintains itself far from equilibrium, reproduces, and undergoes Darwinian evolution.

Within the Solar System the most accessible targets are Mars, Europa, Enceladus and Titan. Mars preserves evidence of past surface water. Europa and Enceladus possess subsurface oceans in contact with rock. Titan offers a methane-rich environment whose biochemistry, if any, would differ from Earth’s. Beyond the Solar System the targets are exoplanets and exomoons whose atmospheres or surfaces can be characterized. The search is limited by distance and by the ambiguity of biosignatures.

Exobiology does not assume that life is common. It asks what physical and chemical conditions permit life and how those conditions can be recognized at a distance. The answers are constrained by terrestrial biochemistry and by the universal laws of chemistry and thermodynamics. They will be settled by observation.

### The Drake Equation

The Drake equation estimates the number of communicative civilizations in the Galaxy. It is the product of the star-formation rate, the fraction of stars with planets, the number of habitable planets per star, the fraction that develop life, the fraction that develop intelligence, the fraction that develop technology, and the lifetime of the communicative phase. Most factors are unknown. The equation organizes the ignorance. It does not compute a number.

The only factors constrained by observation are the star-formation rate and the occurrence of planets. The remaining factors are speculative. The equation is therefore a framework for discussion, not a prediction. Its value lies in identifying which quantities must be measured. Those measurements are the program of astrobiology and of the search for technosignatures.

### Technosignatures

Technosignatures are observable evidence of technology. Radio transmissions, optical lasers, waste heat, atmospheric pollutants and artificial structures have been proposed. Searches for narrow-band radio signals have been conducted for decades. No confirmed signal has been found. The sensitivity and the sky coverage have increased. The parameter space remains large.

Waste-heat searches look for infrared excesses from Dyson spheres or from industrial activity. Atmospheric searches look for gases that are not produced by known abiotic or biological processes. Both are limited by the precision of present data. The absence of detections constrains the abundance of powerful, continuously radiating technologies within a few hundred light-years. It does not constrain intermittent or low-power technologies. The search continues.

### The Fermi Paradox

The Fermi paradox is the apparent contradiction between the expectation that technological civilizations should be common and the absence of evidence for them. The Galaxy contains hundreds of billions of stars. Many host planets. If even a small fraction develop technology and if that technology spreads, the Galaxy should have been visited or colonized many times. No unambiguous evidence of such activity exists.

Proposed resolutions include the rarity of life, the rarity of intelligence, the short lifetime of technological civilizations, the difficulty of interstellar travel, and the possibility that evidence exists but has not been recognized. None is established. The paradox is not a formal contradiction. It is a statement that the silence is surprising under certain assumptions. Those assumptions may be false. The observational upper limits on technosignatures within a few tens of light-years are still weak. The paradox will be resolved by better observations or by a clearer understanding of the evolutionary bottlenecks.

### Panspermia

Panspermia is the hypothesis that life or its precursors can be transferred between planets or between stellar systems. Lithopanspermia proposes transfer inside rocks ejected by impacts. The rocks must survive ejection, transit and entry. Laboratory experiments show that bacteria can survive the shock and the radiation for limited periods. The transfer of viable organisms between Mars and Earth is possible on dynamical grounds. It has not been demonstrated.

Interstellar panspermia faces greater obstacles. The transit times are millions of years. The radiation dose is lethal unless the organisms are deeply shielded. The hypothesis does not solve the origin of life. It relocates it. No evidence requires it. No evidence excludes it for the nearest planets. It remains an open possibility whose probability is low on present knowledge.

## <a id="ch_47"></a>47. Human Evolution

Human evolution is the phylogenetic history of the hominin lineage after its divergence from the chimpanzee lineage, approximately 6–7 million years ago. Early hominins were bipedal and small-brained. The genus Homo appears around 2.8 million years ago. Brain size increases thereafter. Stone tools appear by 3.3 million years ago. The Acheulean industry is associated with Homo erectus. Control of fire is documented by 1 million years ago.

Homo sapiens emerges in Africa around 300 000 years ago. Anatomically modern humans disperse out of Africa after 60 000 years ago. They interbreed with Neanderthals and Denisovans. Those archaic populations disappear. Genetic data show that non-African populations carry 1–2 percent Neanderthal ancestry. Some Oceanian populations carry additional Denisovan ancestry.

Cultural evolution accelerates. Symbolic behavior, complex tools and, later, agriculture and writing appear. Biological evolution continues but is now accompanied by rapid cultural and technological change. The fossil, archaeological and genetic records converge on an African origin of Homo sapiens and on subsequent global dispersal with limited archaic admixture.

The hominin fossil record now includes more than twenty named species. The sequence is not a single line. Multiple species coexisted for long intervals. Australopithecus and early Homo overlapped. Homo erectus persisted in Asia while other lineages evolved in Africa. Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo sapiens overlapped in time and interbred.

Genetic data calibrate the divergences. The sapiens–Neanderthal split is dated to approximately 600 000 years ago. The admixture events are detected by the excess sharing of derived alleles and by the length distribution of introgressed haplotypes.

Cultural evidence appears early: cut-marked bones, ochre use by 300 000 years ago, and symbolic artifacts after 100 000 years ago. The acceleration of cultural change after 50 000 years ago coincides with the global dispersal of Homo sapiens. Biological and cultural evolution have proceeded together since the origin of the genus. The genetic and fossil records are mutually consistent on the broad outline.

### Australopithecus and Early Hominins

The hominin lineage diverged from the chimpanzee lineage between 7 and 6 million years ago. The earliest well-sampled genus is Australopithecus, appearing around 4.2 million years ago. Australopithecus afarensis, known from East Africa, was bipedal yet retained arboreal adaptations. Brain size was only slightly larger than that of chimpanzees. Sexual dimorphism was pronounced.

Other species—Australopithecus africanus in South Africa, Australopithecus sediba, and the robust australopiths (Paranthropus)—show dietary and locomotor variation. Stone-tool use is documented by 3.3 million years ago, before the appearance of Homo. The australopiths demonstrate that bipedalism preceded significant brain enlargement. They occupy the morphological and temporal interval between earlier, poorly known hominins and the genus Homo. Their extinction coincides with the rise of early Homo and with environmental shifts toward more open habitats.

### Lucy and the Laetoli Footprints

Australopithecus afarensis is known from dozens of individuals, including the partial skeleton Lucy. The pelvis and knee are adapted for bipedalism. The arms and curved fingers retain arboreal capability. Sexual dimorphism is high. Brain size is 380–430 cm<sup>3</sup>. Footprints at Laetoli, dated to 3.6 million years ago, confirm bipedal gait with a human-like stride.

### Homo habilis

Homo habilis is the earliest widely recognized species of the genus Homo. Fossils from East Africa date between approximately 2.4 and 1.4 million years ago. Brain volume averages about 600 cm<sup>3</sup>, larger than australopiths yet smaller than later Homo. The face is less projecting. The hands show adaptations for precision gripping.

The species is associated with the Oldowan stone-tool industry—simple flakes and cores. Whether habilis itself made the tools is inferred from chronological and spatial coincidence. Body size remained small. Locomotion was fully bipedal. The taxonomic boundaries are debated. Some specimens may belong to Australopithecus or to a separate early Homo species. Regardless of the precise allocation, the fossils document the appearance of larger brains and systematic tool use in the hominin lineage by 2.4 million years ago.

### Tools and Bodies of Homo habilis

Homo habilis is associated with the Oldowan industry at multiple East African sites. The tools consist of flakes struck from cores. Use-wear studies show that the flakes were used to cut meat and plant material. Whether habilis itself made them is inferred rather than proved.

Body size estimates range from 30 to 50 kg. Limb proportions are more human-like than those of australopiths, yet the arms remain relatively long. Brain size varies from 500 to 700 cm<sup>3</sup>. The variation has led some workers to split the sample into more than one species. Whether the split is justified or whether the sample represents a single variable species remains debated.

### Homo erectus and the First Dispersals

Homo erectus appears in Africa around 1.9 million years ago. Brain size is substantially larger than in australopiths. Body proportions approach those of modern humans. The Acheulean stone-tool industry, characterized by hand-axes, is associated with the species. Control of fire is securely documented by 1 million years ago and may be older.

Homo erectus was the first hominin to leave Africa. Fossils and tools in Georgia, China and Indonesia date to between 1.8 and 1.6 million years ago. The dispersals demonstrate that a hominin with a larger brain, more efficient locomotion and improved technology could occupy a wide range of environments. Regional populations persisted for more than a million years. The species is the probable ancestor of both later African Homo and of the archaic Eurasian lineages that include Neanderthals and Denisovans.

### Homo heidelbergensis

Homo heidelbergensis is a Middle Pleistocene species known from Africa and Europe, dated between roughly 700 000 and 200 000 years ago. Brain size overlaps the modern human range, averaging 1 200 cm<sup>3</sup>. The species is associated with the later Acheulean industry and with the earliest evidence of constructed shelters and of hafted spears.

African populations of heidelbergensis are regarded by many researchers as the ancestors of Homo sapiens. European populations are regarded as the ancestors of Neanderthals. The species therefore occupies the last common ancestral position before the sapiens–Neanderthal divergence. Regional variation is considerable. Some authors prefer to split the sample into additional taxa. The fossils nevertheless document a hominin with a large brain, advanced tools and a wide geographic range in the Middle Pleistocene.

### The Schöningen Spears

The Schöningen spears, found in Germany and dated to about 300 000 years ago, are among the oldest wooden hunting weapons known. Their balance resembles that of modern javelins, which indicates planned hunting of large game and a long tradition of woodworking behind it.

They are usually attributed to Homo heidelbergensis, a species defined by a combination of archaic and derived traits: a prominent brow ridge, a brain within the modern range, and a link to the later Acheulean tool industry. The geographic split between African and European populations is supported by both morphology and the genetic divergence date of approximately 600 000 years ago, though some researchers prefer to assign the two samples to separate species.

### Neanderthals and Denisovans

Neanderthals occupied Europe and western Asia from approximately 400 000 to 40 000 years ago. They possessed large brains, robust skeletons and a Mousterian tool culture. They interbred with modern humans.

Denisovans are known primarily from DNA recovered from fragmentary remains in Siberia and from sediments. They contributed ancestry to modern Oceanian and some Asian populations. Both Neanderthals and Denisovans are sister groups to Homo sapiens within the genus Homo. Their extinction coincides with the arrival of modern humans in their respective ranges. The genetic legacy demonstrates that the replacement was not complete. Archaic admixture is a documented feature of recent human evolution.

Neanderthal genomes recovered from bones and from cave sediments show that the population was small and structured. Genetic diversity was lower than in modern humans. The low diversity is consistent with repeated bottlenecks. Adaptive alleles introgressed into modern humans include variants that affect skin and hair pigmentation and immune response. Some of the introgressed haplotypes are associated with increased risk of certain diseases. The net effect of the admixture was not uniformly beneficial.

Denisovan ancestry is highest in populations of New Guinea and Australia, reaching 4–6 percent. The introgressed segments include alleles that improve adaptation to high altitude in Tibetans. The source population of the Denisovan contribution appears to have been diverse. At least two distinct Denisovan lineages contributed. The genetic evidence therefore reveals a more complex history of archaic admixture than the fossil record alone had indicated.

### What Neanderthals Were Like

The Neanderthals of popular imagination were brutes. The Neanderthals of the evidence were something else. They lived through harsh glacial climates for hundreds of thousands of years, with stocky bodies suited to the cold. They hunted large animals and also ate shellfish, plants and, in some places, cooked plant foods. Starch grains and plant compounds preserved in the dental calculus of some individuals show a varied diet.

They made tools of great skill, including stone blades and composite tools in which a stone point was fixed to a handle with birch-bark tar, a glue that has to be made by controlled heating. In Bruniquel Cave in France, rings of broken stalagmites about 176 000 years old show that they went deep into dark caves and built there. Some groups wore ornaments made of eagle talons and marine shells. Whether they buried their dead on purpose remains debated, and so does the question of how far they used symbols.

The archaeologist Rebecca Wragg Sykes, in her book [*Kindred*](#bib_51), shows how much of this picture is recent, and how the older view was shaped by the first, poorly interpreted skeletons. The modern picture is of another human species with its own culture, not a failed draft of our own.

### Homo floresiensis

Homo floresiensis is a small-bodied hominin known from the island of Flores, Indonesia. Its skeletal remains date to between about 100 000 and 60 000 years ago, and its stone tools to as late as 50 000 years ago. Adult stature was about 1.1 m. Brain volume was approximately 400 cm<sup>3</sup>. Stone tools are associated with the remains.

The diminutive size has been interpreted as island dwarfism acting on an earlier Homo erectus population, or as the persistence of an even earlier, small-bodied lineage. Pathological explanations for the type specimen have been excluded by the discovery of additional individuals. The species demonstrates that hominins reached Wallacea and that isolated populations could evolve extreme body-size reduction. Its survival until at least 50 000 years ago means it overlapped in time with modern humans in the broader region. The phylogenetic placement remains uncertain.

Stone tools associated with the species are found in deposits that span hundreds of thousands of years. The tools are simple yet consistent. They indicate a stable technological tradition maintained by a small-bodied population.

The island setting supplies the selective context for dwarfism. Limited resources and the absence of large predators favor reduced body size in large mammals. The same process is documented in other island lineages. Whether floresiensis descended from Homo erectus or from an earlier, smaller-bodied migrant remains unresolved. The brain size of approximately 400 cm<sup>3</sup> is among the smallest known in the genus, about that of a chimpanzee. The combination of small brain, small body and persistent tool use shows that technological behavior is not strictly proportional to absolute brain volume.

### Homo naledi

Homo naledi is a hominin species known from the Rising Star cave system in South Africa. The remains of at least fifteen individuals have been recovered from the Dinaledi Chamber. The skeleton combines primitive and derived features. The shoulders, trunk and pelvis are australopith-like. The hands, feet and dentition are closer to later Homo. Brain volume is small, approximately 500 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Dating of the fossils yields an age between 335 000 and 236 000 years ago. The species therefore coexisted with early Homo sapiens in Africa. The location of the remains deep inside a cave system that lacks evidence of occupation has prompted the hypothesis that the bodies were deliberately placed there. Alternative explanations—natural trapping or water transport—have not been excluded. No associated stone tools or other cultural remains have been found in the chamber.

Homo naledi demonstrates that morphological diversity within Homo persisted into the later Middle Pleistocene. A small-brained species with a mosaic of primitive and derived traits lived alongside larger-brained hominins. Its phylogenetic position remains unresolved. It may represent a surviving lineage of early Homo or a convergent form. The fossils enlarge the known range of hominin variation in the period immediately preceding the appearance of anatomically modern humans.

### Brain-Size Discrepancy in Later Hominins

Brain size within the genus Homo was not uniform. By the later Middle Pleistocene, species with very different cranial capacities coexisted. Homo naledi, described above, had a brain volume of approximately 500 cm<sup>3</sup>. Contemporary early Homo sapiens and other archaic humans already had brains of 1 200–1 400 cm<sup>3</sup>. Earlier Homo erectus populations had averaged 800–1 100 cm<sup>3</sup> for more than a million years. Neanderthals and early modern humans later overlapped in the range 1 200–1 700 cm<sup>3</sup>.

The discrepancy demonstrates that encephalization was not a single, progressive trend shared by all lineages. Large brains are metabolically costly. A small-brained species could persist if its niche did not demand the same cognitive expenditure. The fossil record therefore contains both highly encephalized and persistently small-brained members of Homo until late in the Pleistocene. Brain size alone does not define the genus, nor does it increase monotonically through time. The variation is real and temporally overlapping.

### What Made Our Species Different

Homo sapiens appeared in Africa about 300 000 years ago, and the features that define us did not arrive together. A rounded braincase, a small face and a chin came gradually. Ochre was in use early, and shell beads and engraved patterns appear by about 100 000 to 75 000 years ago. Symbolic behavior, in other words, built up over a long time inside Africa before it spread.

The anthropologist Ian Tattersall has emphasized in [*Masters of the Planet*](#bib_43) how late and how sudden the full expression of symbolic thought seems to have been, compared with the anatomy that carried it. Yuval Noah Harari, in [*Sapiens*](#bib_22), argued that the decisive novelty was the ability to speak of things that do not exist, such as gods, nations and money, which allowed cooperation among thousands of strangers. The idea is vivid and widely discussed. It is a hypothesis about cognition that the bones cannot settle.

What is secure is that by 50 000 years ago people with fully modern minds lived on several continents, and that Australia had been reached by then or earlier. Over the following tens of thousands of years their descendants crossed the Arctic into the Americas and, much later, settled the islands of the Pacific. They did it with the same bodies we have, and there is no evidence that they differed biologically from us.

### The Origin of Language

Language is a species-specific human capacity. It combines a finite set of discrete units into an unbounded set of meaningful expressions. The capacity has a genetic basis. Mutations in the gene FOXP2 impair speech and language while sparing general intelligence. Comparative studies show that the human version of FOXP2 differs from the chimpanzee version by two amino acids. The functional consequences of those differences remain under investigation.

Anatomical prerequisites include a descended larynx, fine control of breathing, and expanded cortical areas for sequencing and semantics. None is sufficient by itself. The archaeological record supplies indirect evidence. Symbolic artifacts, complex tools and long-distance exchange appear sporadically after 100 000 years ago and become widespread after 50 000 years ago. These behaviors are widely regarded as requiring language. Direct fossil evidence of speech is absent.

The selective pressures that produced language are debated. Proposals include social coordination, teaching, and the negotiation of relationships in large groups. The capacity is universal among human populations and is acquired by children with minimal explicit instruction. It remains the clearest cognitive distinction between humans and other living primates.

### Cave Art and the Ice Age Mind

Some of the most striking evidence of the human mind is painted on cave walls. The Chauvet cave in France, with its lions, rhinoceroses and horses, was decorated more than 30 000 years ago. Lascaux, with its great bulls, is about 17 000 years old. Paintings on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi show that figurative art, including a scene with human-like figures and an animal, is at least 51 000 years old. Hand stencils appear on several continents. The Lion-Man ivory figure from Germany, carved about 40 000 years ago, joins a human body to a lion’s head.

What the images meant is not known. David Lewis-Williams argued in [*The Mind in the Cave*](#bib_30) that many of them came from altered states of consciousness, in which the nervous system produces patterns and visions that a community then interprets, and that the caves were places of ritual. The thesis explains some features, such as the recurrence of geometric signs, and is contested in others, and ethnographic analogy can only carry it so far.

Whatever their meaning, the paintings show skilled hands, a feeling for movement and a willingness to go far underground with torches. They also show that the capacity for imagined worlds, which sits at the center of the question of language, was present at least tens of thousands of years ago.

### After the Ice: Foragers and Early Farmers

The last ice age ended about 11 700 years ago, and in the warming that followed, human societies began to change. In the Levant, the Natufian people lived in permanent settlements before farming, buried their dead in cemeteries and gathered wild cereals with sickles. Residues in a cave near Haifa suggest that they brewed a beer-like drink some 13 000 years ago. At Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, around 11 500 years ago, hunter-gatherers raised monumental carved stone pillars before there were farms.

Steven Mithen, in [*After the Ice*](#bib_34), follows the world from the end of the glaciation to the first cities in a series of vivid scenes. David Graeber and David Wengrow argue in [*The Dawn of Everything*](#bib_19) that early societies were more varied and more experimental than the old story of a ladder from bands to tribes to states allows. They point to seasonal shifts in social organization and to deliberate choices about hierarchy. Archaeologists debate how much weight the evidence will bear.

The older picture of farming as a single invention, spreading from a Fertile Crescent, has not survived. Plants and animals were domesticated in several regions, at different speeds, by people who often kept foraging at the same time. The change was gradual, and not always an improvement in health, as the next section shows.

### Agriculture and the Neolithic Transition

Agriculture is the cultivation of domesticated plants and animals. It appeared independently in several regions after 12 000 years ago: the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and West Africa. The transition from foraging to farming was gradual. It involved the selective propagation of plants with non-shattering seed heads and of animals with reduced aggression.

Farming supported higher population densities. Permanent settlements, food surpluses and specialized crafts became possible. It also introduced new selective pressures. Diets narrowed. Infectious disease increased with crowding and with proximity to livestock. Skeletal evidence shows a decline in average stature and an increase in dental caries in early farming populations. Lactase persistence and amylase copy-number variation are genetic adaptations to agricultural diets.

The Neolithic transition is the demographic and ecological foundation of later urban societies. It is not a uniform improvement in health or leisure. It is a shift in subsistence that permitted larger populations and more complex social organization at the cost of new physiological stresses. The domesticated species and the human populations that depend on them have coevolved since.

### Horses, Wheels and the Spread of Languages

Most languages of Europe, Iran and northern India belong to one family, Indo-European, whose members are far more alike in basic words than chance would allow. Linguists reconstructed a common ancestor, with words for wheel, wagon and horse, before there was any genetic evidence of where its speakers lived. David Anthony’s [*The Horse, the Wheel, and Language*](#bib_1) argues that they were herders of the Pontic-Caspian steppe, north of the Black Sea and Caspian, about 5 000 years ago.

Ancient DNA has since given the idea a powerful support. Genomes from the Yamnaya culture of the steppe, from about 3300 to 2600 BCE, appear to have contributed a large share of the ancestry of people in northern and central Europe soon after. Wheeled wagons and herding on horseback, or at least with horses, made a mobile way of life possible.

Questions remain. Some scholars prefer an earlier, Anatolian origin linked to the spread of farming, and the dating of horse riding is argued. Language spreads for many reasons, not only by migration, and the match between genes and languages is never exact. Still, the case shows how archaeology, linguistics and genetics can be tested against one another.

# <a id="part_8"></a>Part VIII: The Human Body and Mind

*How a body is run and defended, how a brain works, and what we do not yet know about experience*

## <a id="ch_48"></a>48. The Human Body

The body is a system of organs that maintain conditions compatible with the life of its cells. Temperature, acidity, salt balance, and the supply of oxygen and fuel are held within narrow ranges. The holding is called homeostasis. It is active. It costs energy. When it fails, illness follows.

Food supplies the energy and the building materials. Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins are broken down by digestion into sugars, fatty acids, and amino acids, which are absorbed and distributed. Vitamins and minerals are required in smaller amounts, as the next section explains.

Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin in red blood cells. The same protein that makes blood red binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. Carbon dioxide is carried back, mostly dissolved. The heart pumps the blood. The lungs exchange the gases. The system is simple in outline and finely regulated in practice. Exercise, altitude, and disease all change the demands. The body adjusts the rate of breathing and the output of the heart to match.

Hormones are chemical signals carried in the blood, described in the next section. Together with the nervous system, they form the body’s two great communication networks.

The immune system tells self from non-self and attacks the latter; its workings are described below. Autoimmune diseases occur when the distinction fails and the system attacks the body’s own tissues, and allergies when it overreacts to a harmless substance.

Aging, infection, injury, and genetic error are the main ways the system fails. Medicine is the attempt to restore or replace the failed function. Surgery, drugs, hormones, and, increasingly, cells and genes are the tools. The body is not a machine in the simple sense. It is a living system that repairs itself until it cannot. Understanding the repair, and its limits, is the practical face of physiology.

### Vitamins, Hormones, and the Chemical Control of the Body

In the early twentieth century, diseases such as scurvy, beriberi, and rickets were traced to missing substances in the diet. The substances were named vitamins. They are required in small amounts. Some are cofactors for enzymes. Vitamin C is needed for the synthesis of collagen. The B vitamins are involved in energy metabolism. Vitamin D regulates calcium. Deficiency produces specific diseases. Excess of some vitamins also produces harm. The discovery converted nutrition from general advice about food into a chemistry of specific molecules.

Hormones are chemical signals produced by glands and carried in the blood. Insulin, from the pancreas, lowers blood sugar. Its absence or ineffectiveness produces diabetes. Thyroid hormone regulates metabolic rate. Adrenaline prepares the body for action. Sex hormones regulate reproduction. Growth hormone regulates growth. The endocrine system and the nervous system are the two main networks of control. They interact. Many signals are used by both.

Blood groups are determined by molecules on the surface of red cells. The ABO system and the Rh system are the best known. Transfusion requires matching. Mismatch can destroy the transfused cells. The groups are inherited in a Mendelian pattern. They are also useful as markers in genetics and in anthropology.

The chemical control of the body is precise. Concentrations are regulated by feedback. Too much of a hormone usually suppresses its own production. Too little stimulates it. The same logic appears in enzyme pathways and in gene regulation. The body is a set of chemical systems that maintain themselves by continuous adjustment. When the adjustment fails, disease follows. When the missing molecule can be supplied, as with insulin or a vitamin, the failure can often be corrected.

### Hormones and Their Hierarchies

Hormones are signaling molecules released into the blood. They act on distant targets that possess the appropriate receptors. Peptide hormones bind surface receptors and activate second-messenger cascades. Steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors that regulate transcription. The distinction determines speed and duration of effect.

The endocrine system is organized in hierarchies. The hypothalamus controls the pituitary. The pituitary controls peripheral glands. Negative feedback from the peripheral hormones stabilizes the set points. Disruption at any level produces disease. Diabetes mellitus is the failure of insulin signaling. Hypothyroidism is the failure of thyroid-hormone production. Both are correctable once the missing signal is supplied.

Local chemical signals—neurotransmitters, cytokines, growth factors—operate over shorter distances. They use the same receptor logic. The difference is range, not mechanism. Chemical control, whether endocrine or local, is the means by which cells coordinate activity without direct contact.

### The Circulation of the Blood and the Rise of Physiology

For centuries the heart was thought to heat the blood and the blood was thought to move back and forth in the vessels. The lungs were thought to cool it. The idea came from the Greeks and was refined by Galen in the second century. It lasted more than a thousand years.

In 1628 William Harvey published a different account. He measured the volume of blood the heart pumps. The quantity was far too large for the blood to be made and consumed continuously. It had to circulate. He traced the path from the right side of the heart to the lungs, back to the left side, out to the body, and back again. The valves in the veins allow flow only toward the heart. The capillaries that complete the circuit were seen later, with the microscope.

Harvey’s method was quantitative. He counted and measured. The conclusion followed from the numbers. Physiology, the study of function, began to replace anatomy alone. The same approach was later applied to respiration, digestion, and the nervous system.

The blood carries oxygen, bound to hemoglobin, and nutrients. It carries waste. It carries hormones. The heart is a pump. The vessels are a closed system. The pressure is maintained by the heart and regulated by the vessels. High blood pressure damages the vessels and the organs they supply. Low pressure fails to deliver oxygen. The whole arrangement is a closed loop under constant adjustment.

The same quantitative habit that established circulation established the rest of modern physiology. Measure the input. Measure the output. Find the path. The method is still the one used today.

### The Heart and Blood Pressure

The heart is a four-chambered pump in mammals and birds. The right side receives venous blood and sends it to the lungs. The left side receives oxygenated blood and sends it to the systemic circulation. Valves enforce one-way flow. The cardiac cycle consists of systole (contraction) and diastole (filling). Stroke volume times heart rate equals cardiac output. Typical resting output is 5 liters per minute. It can rise fivefold during exercise.

Blood pressure is the force exerted on arterial walls. Systolic pressure is the peak during ejection. Diastolic pressure is the minimum during filling. Mean arterial pressure is regulated by baroreceptors, the autonomic nervous system and the kidneys. Chronic elevation damages vessels and organs. The regulatory loops are negative feedback. They maintain pressure within a narrow range under ordinary conditions and adjust it when demand changes.

The same double circulation and pressure regulation operate, with variations in detail, across mammals and birds. They are the physiological basis of sustained high metabolic rates.

### Blood

Blood is a specialized connective tissue that circulates through the vascular system. It transports oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones and waste products. It also distributes heat and contributes to immune defense and hemostasis. In an adult human the volume is approximately five liters.

Plasma constitutes about 55 percent of the volume. It is an aqueous solution of proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen), electrolytes, nutrients and metabolic wastes. The remaining 45 percent is cellular. Erythrocytes (red cells) are anucleate in mammals. They contain hemoglobin and carry oxygen. Their biconcave shape maximizes surface area and flexibility. Leukocytes (white cells) comprise neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. They mediate innate and adaptive immunity. Platelets are cell fragments that initiate clotting.

Hemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively. The binding curve is sigmoid. Affinity is reduced by elevated carbon dioxide, lowered pH and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate—the Bohr effect—facilitating unloading in active tissues. Carbon dioxide is carried partly as dissolved gas, partly bound to hemoglobin, and mostly as bicarbonate after conversion by carbonic anhydrase in the red cell.

Hemostasis begins with vasoconstriction and platelet adhesion to exposed collagen. The coagulation cascade converts fibrinogen to fibrin, stabilizing the platelet plug. Anticoagulant pathways and fibrinolysis limit the clot to the site of injury. Disorders of any step produce thrombosis or bleeding.

Blood cells are produced in the bone marrow from hematopoietic stem cells. Erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and colony-stimulating factors regulate lineage output. The average lifespan of a human red cell is 120 days. Senescent cells are removed by macrophages in the spleen and liver. Iron from hemoglobin is recycled. The same fluid and cellular system operates, with variations in detail, throughout the vertebrates.

### The Immune System

The immune system distinguishes self from non-self and eliminates pathogens. Innate immunity is immediate and non-specific. Barriers, phagocytes, complement and inflammatory cytokines constitute the first response. Pattern-recognition receptors detect conserved microbial molecules and trigger the innate pathways.

Adaptive immunity is slower and specific. Lymphocytes carry receptors generated by somatic recombination. Each clone recognizes a different antigen. Clonal selection expands those clones that bind antigen. Helper T cells coordinate the response. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. B cells secrete antibodies. Memory cells persist after the pathogen is cleared and accelerate the response upon re-exposure.

Self-tolerance is established by deletion or inactivation of clones that recognize self antigens. Failure of tolerance produces autoimmune disease. The system is not perfect. Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. The host evolves countermeasures. The result is a continuous coevolutionary arms race. Vaccination exploits immunological memory by presenting antigen without causing disease. The same principles underlie both natural immunity and medical immunization.

## <a id="ch_49"></a>49. Disease, Microbes and Resistance

### Antibiotics and Resistance

Antibiotics are compounds that kill or inhibit bacteria at concentrations tolerable to the host. Most clinical antibiotics are natural products or their derivatives. They target cell-wall synthesis, protein synthesis, nucleic-acid synthesis or membrane integrity. The therapeutic window exists because these targets differ between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

Resistance arises by mutation or by acquisition of resistance genes. Mechanisms include enzymatic inactivation, target modification, efflux pumps and reduced permeability. Resistance genes are frequently carried on plasmids and transposons and spread by horizontal transfer. The same genes occur in environmental bacteria that have never encountered clinical antibiotics. Clinical use merely enriches pre-existing resistance, and multi-drug-resistant strains combine several mechanisms to survive more than one class of drug.

The rate of discovery of new antibiotic classes has slowed. Resistance continues to spread. The evolutionary process is ordinary natural selection acting on large bacterial populations with short generation times. Stewardship, combination therapy and the development of new agents are the available countermeasures. The underlying biology is the same biology that governs any host–parasite interaction.

### Vaccines and mRNA Medicine

A vaccine teaches the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the disease. The oldest vaccines used weakened or killed microbes. An mRNA vaccine instead supplies a set of instructions: a strand of messenger RNA, packaged in a droplet of fat, that tells a person’s own cells to make one harmless piece of the pathogen, such as the spike protein of a coronavirus. The cells make it for a few days, the immune system learns it, and the RNA is then broken down.

The enabling work was done over years by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who found in 2005 that modifying a building block of the RNA stops it from setting off alarm responses, and who received the Nobel Prize in 2023. Vaccines against COVID-19 were authorized in December 2020, within a year of the virus being sequenced. Early trials showed efficacy of about 95 percent against symptomatic disease. Because the instruction can be rewritten quickly, updates for new variants take weeks to design, and an mRNA vaccine against respiratory syncytial virus has also been approved.

Limits are real. Protection against infection fades over months, so boosters are needed. Side effects exist, nearly all mild and short-lived. The first products needed cold storage. Experimental mRNA treatments for cancer, which write a tumor’s own mutations into a personalized vaccine, are in trials, and whether they will work is not yet known.

### Pandemics and Emerging Infections

Most new infectious diseases of people come from animals. HIV passed from chimpanzees in Central Africa in the early twentieth century. The coronaviruses that caused SARS in 2002 and MERS in 2012 came through bats and, in turn, civet cats and camels. The influenza pandemic of 1918, probably the deadliest event in modern history, killed an estimated fifty million people, with estimates ranging from less than twenty million to more than ninety.

The cause of such events is ordinary evolution. Viruses mutate quickly, and when one finds a way into a new host and spreads efficiently, it has an enormous population in which to try variations. Crowding, travel, farming of animals and trade in wildlife increase the chances. The origin of SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19, remains debated, and the debate is a reminder of how limited the monitoring of animal pathogens still is.

Defences are known. Genomic sequencing of samples lets a new virus be identified within days and followed as it changes. Wastewater monitoring shows spread in a community before clinics are full. Vaccines and antivirals can be prepared in advance for related viruses. The hard part is not knowledge but funding that continues between emergencies, and the habit of acting early.

### Handwashing, Sanitation and the Victory over Infection

The greatest reduction in infectious disease in history came before the antibiotic. In 1847 the Hungarian physician Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that deaths from childbed fever were far higher in a ward served by doctors, who came from the autopsy room, than in a ward served by midwives. When he required handwashing in chlorinated water, deaths fell. His colleagues largely rejected the finding, since no theory yet explained it.

The germ theory supplied the explanation. Joseph Lister applied carbolic acid to wounds and instruments in the 1860s and brought surgical infection under control. Clean water, sewers, pasteurized milk, refrigerated food and vaccination followed, and in industrial countries mortality from infectious disease fell dramatically before most effective drugs existed.

The lesson is that prevention is often cheaper and more reliable than cure. It remains true in places without safe water, where diarrhoeal disease still kills many children, and it is true in hospitals, where simple hygiene reduces infections that antibiotics increasingly fail to cure.

### Antibiotics: Discovery and the Empty Pipeline

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mold had killed bacteria on a culture plate, and Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their colleagues turned penicillin into a drug in the early 1940s. The decades that followed were a golden age, with new classes of antibiotic found in soil microbes and then improved by chemistry. Mortality from bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis and wound infection fell sharply.

The pipeline has since thinned. Few entirely new classes have reached the clinic since the 1980s, partly because discovery is difficult and partly because a drug used briefly and held in reserve earns little for its makers. Resistance has meanwhile grown, so that infections once easily treated can now require drugs of last resort.

New approaches are under study. Bacteriophages, the viruses that infect bacteria, are used experimentally against resistant infections. Machine-learning systems have been used to search chemical libraries for compounds with antibacterial activity, and at least two new candidates found this way have shown promise in laboratory and animal tests. Whether any will become a drug is not yet known. What is clear is that stewardship, using drugs only when needed, is as important as discovery.

## <a id="ch_50"></a>50. The Microbiome

*You are not only your cells. You are an ecosystem.*

The gut alone holds trillions of bacteria, with fungi, viruses, and archaea in attendance. Skin, mouth, and lungs have their own communities. The genes in these microbes outnumber the genes in the human genome by a large factor. For a long time medicine treated this fact as contamination. It is closer to an organ.

The community helps digest what we cannot, trains the immune system, and produces molecules that enter the blood. Mice raised without microbes have abnormal immune systems and abnormal guts. Transfer the microbes, and some of the abnormalities change.

Antibiotics are the blunt history of the subject. They save lives and strip communities. The recovery is usually good and sometimes not. The long project is more precise: add the missing organism, feed the useful one, stop feeding the harmful one, and leave the rest alone. Microbiome science is past the stage of discovering that the organisms are there. It is at the stage of learning which ones matter, and when.

The community in the gut is the best studied because it is the largest and the most accessible. It is dominated by bacteria, with important contributions from archaea, fungi, and viruses that infect the bacteria. Its composition varies along the gut, between people, and within a person over time. Diet is the fastest lever. A change in fiber intake changes the community within days. Antibiotics change it within hours. Illness, travel, and drugs change it. A single sample is a snapshot, not a fate.

What the community does is specific, and specificity is the cure for hype. Some bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids, which feed the cells lining the colon and influence immune signaling. Some modify bile acids. Some synthesize vitamins. Some inactivate drugs, and some activate them. A cardiac drug, digoxin, is inactivated by a particular gut bacterium in some people, which changes the drug’s effect. That is a precise, actionable finding. “The microbiome affects health” is a slogan. A named organism, a named molecule, and a named host response is a result.

Fecal microbiota transplantation proved that a community can be a treatment. In recurrent C. difficile infection, the normal community has been damaged, often by antibiotics, and a pathogen occupies the niche. Transferring a healthy donor’s community restores resistance and cures most such patients. Defined consortia of cultured bacteria are being developed to do the same job more cleanly. The success is a proof of principle. It does not imply that transferring communities will cure unrelated diseases. Trials in other conditions have been mixed. The principle is real. The indications are narrow until shown otherwise.

Associations with obesity, diabetes, autism, depression, and autoimmune disease are widely reported and hard to interpret. People with these conditions often have different average communities. Diet, medication, and the disease itself can produce the difference. Establishing cause requires intervention or a mechanism, preferably both. Some mechanisms are emerging. Others will not emerge, because the association was a passenger. The field is in the stage where the passenger count is being reduced.

The hygiene observation belongs here. Populations with less exposure to diverse microbes in early life have more allergic and autoimmune disease. The observation is epidemiological. The mechanism is probably a matter of immune education: the developing immune system expects certain microbial signals and behaves differently without them. The practical implication is not a return to unmanaged infection. It is a more precise understanding of which exposures train the immune system and which only cause harm. That understanding is incomplete. It is far enough along to be part of pediatrics and of the design of future interventions.

The microbiome is an organ in the functional sense. It contributes to digestion, immunity, and drug response. It is not an organ in the anatomical sense, and it is not a second brain, despite the existence of real gut-brain signaling. Treating it as a partner rather than as dirt was the conceptual change. Treating it with the same demand for mechanism that the rest of medicine requires is the present task.

Diet is the intervention a person can actually control. Fiber feeds the bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids. A varied plant diet tends to support a more varied community. The tending is not a guarantee of any particular health outcome. It is a lever with evidence behind it, unlike many of the commercial tests that classify a person’s microbiome and sell a tailored cure. Most such tests are ahead of the evidence. The research is real. The retail interpretation is often not. The difference is the ordinary one between a field in progress and a market in a hurry.

Early life is when the community is assembled. Birth mode, feeding, antibiotics, and environment shape the first colonists. The assembly influences immune development. The influence is real in animal studies and supported in human epidemiology. It is not a script. Children differ. The practical implication is caution with unnecessary antibiotics in infancy and attention to the conditions of early feeding, not a rigid protocol sold as optimization. Assembly is a window. Windows are not machines.

Causality runs both ways. The community affects the host. The host’s diet, immune system, and drugs affect the community. Cross-sectional studies cannot sort the directions. Longitudinal studies and interventions can. The field has moved toward both. A result that includes a time course, or a transfer, or a metabolite traced from microbe to host effect, is a result that can support a direction. A result that is a single comparison of two groups is a result that cannot. Readers can apply the distinction themselves. It removes a large fraction of the overclaimed literature at a stroke.

## <a id="ch_51"></a>51. Precision Medicine

*Medicine spent a century learning the average patient. Precision medicine asks what differs in this one.*

Beyond cancer, precision is uneven. Rare-disease sequencing can end a diagnostic odyssey. Polygenic risk scores can, in some populations, identify people at high risk of heart disease who look ordinary by older measures. Wearable sensors and repeated blood tests promise a medicine of trajectories rather than annual snapshots. Most of that promise is still infrastructure.

mRNA medicine belongs in this chapter. The vaccines against COVID-19 demonstrated that a genetic instruction, packaged in lipid droplets, can be designed in days once a viral sequence is known, and manufactured as a platform rather than as a bespoke organism. The same platform is being aimed at other infections and at cancer antigens personal to a tumor. The demonstration was public and global. It is easy to forget how implausible it would have sounded in a science guide written in 1984.

Cancer is where precision has changed outcomes most clearly. A tumor is sequenced. A driver mutation is found. A drug aimed at the protein that mutation alters is given. In cancers with the right driver, the response can be rapid. Resistance almost always follows, because the tumor is a population of cells and selection applies. The next drug, or a combination, may answer the resistance for a time. The pattern has turned some diagnoses that were uniformly fatal into chronic or, in a minority of patients, curable diseases. It has left other cancers, without a usable driver or without a drug, where they were. Precision here means matching, not magic.

Immunotherapy is the other transformation. Checkpoint inhibitors remove a brake that tumors exploit. The immune system, once released, can clear cancers that had resisted everything else. It can also attack healthy tissue. Biomarkers, including the number of mutations in the tumor and the expression of certain proteins, predict response imperfectly. Cell therapies that engineer a patient’s own immune cells to recognize a cancer antigen have produced lasting remissions in some leukemias and lymphomas. They are complex to make and not yet general. The direction is clear. The immune system is a drug target and a drug.

Pharmacogenomics is quieter and already useful. Variants in genes that metabolize drugs change the dose a patient needs, or the risk of a severe reaction.
