Testing before prescribing is standard for some drugs and some ancestries where a dangerous variant is common. The principle extends further than the current testing. Implementation, not knowledge, is often the limit.

The limits are as important as the wins. Most common diseases are not single-gene diseases. A polygenic score can stratify risk and cannot yet dictate a unique treatment for each person. Data can accumulate without a decision attached. Cost can confine a therapy to the wealthy unless systems are built to do otherwise. Precision medicine earns its name when the extra information changes what is done and the change helps the patient. By that standard it has earned the name in parts of oncology, in rare disease, in drug safety, and in vaccines. It is still earning it everywhere else.

Data integration is the unfinished infrastructure. A patient’s genome, records, images, and wearable data are usually in different systems. Combining them safely and usefully is an engineering and a governance task. Where it has been done, rare-disease diagnosis has improved and research has accelerated. Where it has not, precision remains a set of separate tests. The science has outrun the plumbing. The plumbing is not glamorous. It is what turns a result in a paper into a result in a clinic.

Rare disease is where sequencing has already changed the standard of care. Many children with suspected genetic conditions now receive a sequencing test as part of diagnosis rather than as a last resort. The yield is substantial. A fraction of diagnoses lead to a change in treatment. A larger fraction lead to an end of uncertainty and to better counseling. The change is quiet compared with a new cancer drug. It is a change in what medicine considers ordinary. Ordinary sequencing for unexplained serious disease is the precision medicine that has most clearly arrived.

Prevention is the precision that scales. Identifying people at high genetic risk of heart disease, and treating the risk before the disease, changes outcomes for a population. The identification is imperfect. The treatment is often an ordinary drug. The combination is precision in the sense that the information selects who benefits most from an intervention that could not be given to everyone. This form of precision is less dramatic than a gene therapy and more consequential in total lives. A balanced account includes it. Drama is not the measure. Lives and years of health are.

## <a id="ch_52"></a>52. Aging and Longevity

*Aging is not a single disease. It is the rising risk of many diseases, and the slow loss of repair.*

Some of these mechanisms can be tested directly. Animals with altered single genes live substantially longer. Nutrient-sensing pathways, including those involving insulin and a regulator called mTOR, affect lifespan in yeast, worms, flies, and mice. Rapamycin, a drug that damps mTOR, extends life in mice. Whether it does so usefully in humans, at a dose that does not cost too much immunity, is not settled. Caloric restriction extends life in many species and has mixed, modest results in primates. Metformin, a diabetes drug, is under study for broader effects on aging. The studies are the right response. The marketing that leaps ahead of them is not.

Comparative biology is a source of clues. A mouse lives two or three years. A naked mole-rat of similar size lives decades and rarely develops cancer. A bowhead whale lives two centuries. Some of the difference is size and metabolic rate. Some of it is specific protections: better DNA repair, different immune strategies, membranes less prone to oxidation. The protections are genetic and, in principle, intelligible. They have not yet been copied into a therapy for humans. They show that lifespan is not a fixed law of biochemistry. It is a trait, and traits can differ.

Interventions in laboratory animals are the other source. Senolytic drugs, which clear cells that have stopped dividing but refuse to die and secrete inflammatory signals, improve health measures in old mice. Partial reprogramming with factors that can reset cell identity has reversed some age-related changes in animal tissues, with a risk of cancer or of loss of cell type that has to be managed. These results are why the field is active. They are results in animals, under controlled conditions, often with tradeoffs. Translation is the unsolved step.

Human evidence is slower and more important. Life expectancy rose mainly because fewer people died young. The maximum human lifespan has not shown a comparable rise. Centenarians exist and are studied. Their genetics and habits are informative and not yet a recipe. Caloric restriction and related diets improve some risk markers in people and have not been shown to extend maximum lifespan. Metformin, rapamycin, and other candidates are in trials aimed at healthspan. The trials are the correct next evidence. Marketing that precedes the trials is not evidence.

The practical conclusion is modest and still large. Some processes of aging are modifiable in animals. Some diseases of aging are already modifiable in people by ordinary medicine: blood pressure, lipids, smoking, vaccines, cancer screening. Further modification of the underlying processes is a research program with animal proof-of-concept and incomplete human proof. The goal that matches the evidence is more years of health, not a promise of indefinite life. Indefinite life is a speculation. Slower aging is a hypothesis with enough support to be worth testing carefully.

Inequality belongs in any honest chapter on longevity. Life expectancy differs by country, by income, and by access to ordinary medicine by amounts that dwarf the effect of any anti-aging supplement on the market. The largest available gains, globally, are still in infection control, in maternal care, in smoking reduction, and in the management of blood pressure and diabetes. Research on the biology of aging may add further gains. It does not replace the gains that public health already knows how to deliver. A reader should hold both projects in view. They are not rivals. They operate on different parts of the same curve.

Biomarkers of aging are an attempt to measure the process rather than the calendar. Epigenetic clocks, built from methylation patterns, predict mortality better than age alone in some studies. Other markers use proteins, inflammation, or physical function. None is yet a replacement for tracking actual disease and death in a trial. A clock that moves in response to an intervention is a hint. A trial that shows fewer heart attacks, or a longer life, is a result. The field is rich in hints and poorer in results of the second kind. The distinction should govern the headlines.

The tradeoff with cancer is structural. Mechanisms that allow cells to divide and repair also allow cells to divide when they should not. Mechanisms that suppress tumors, such as senescence and apoptosis, contribute to aging. An intervention that pushes on one side of the tradeoff must watch the other. Some of the most promising aging interventions are being studied with cancer surveillance built in. The surveillance is not a bureaucratic addition. It is a recognition of the biology. A longer life bought with a large increase in cancer would be a different kind of result. The field is looking for interventions that improve the whole, not only the marker.

## <a id="ch_53"></a>53. The Brain and Nervous System

The nervous system coordinates the body. It receives signals from the senses and from the internal organs. It sends signals to muscles and glands. It stores information and generates behavior.

The basic unit is the neuron. A neuron has a cell body, dendrites that receive signals, and an axon that carries signals away. The signal is an electrical impulse, the action potential. It is produced by the flow of ions across the membrane. Sodium and potassium are the main ions. The membrane is polarized at rest. When stimulated past a threshold, it depolarizes and the impulse travels. At the end of the axon the signal is usually passed to the next cell by a chemical neurotransmitter. Acetylcholine and many others are used. The synapse is the junction. Most drugs that affect the brain act at synapses.

The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. The peripheral nerves connect them to the rest of the body. The autonomic system controls involuntary functions—heart rate, digestion, pupil size—and has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions that often oppose each other.

The brain has major divisions. The brainstem controls basic life functions: breathing, heart rate, arousal. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance. The cerebrum is the largest part in humans. Its cortex is folded. The folds increase surface area. The cortex is divided into lobes. The frontal lobes are involved in planning, decision, and voluntary movement. The parietal lobes process touch and spatial information. The temporal lobes process hearing and aspects of memory. The occipital lobes process vision. The functions are specialized but interconnected. Damage to a region produces characteristic deficits.

The senses convert physical stimuli into nerve signals. The eye focuses light on the retina. Photoreceptors respond to light. The signals travel through the optic nerve to the brain. Color vision depends on three types of cones with different sensitivities. The ear converts sound waves into mechanical vibration and then into nerve signals in the cochlea. Balance is sensed by the vestibular organs in the inner ear. Taste and smell are chemical senses. Touch, temperature, and pain are sensed by receptors in the skin and elsewhere.

Reflexes are rapid, automatic responses. The knee-jerk reflex involves a sensory neuron, a motor neuron, and a synapse in the spinal cord. More complex behaviors involve the brain. Learning changes the strength of connections between neurons. Memory involves changes in synapses and, for long-term memory, changes in gene expression and structure.

Hormones interact with the nervous system. The hypothalamus links the two. It controls the pituitary, which controls other glands. Stress, growth, reproduction, and metabolism are regulated by both nerves and hormones. The brain is not separate from the body. It is the organ that integrates the signals and produces coordinated action. Its capacities—language, abstract thought, planning—are large. They are the product of the same cellular machinery that operates in every other tissue, arranged in a particular architecture.

### The Nervous System

The nervous system transmits and processes information by means of electrical and chemical signals. Neurons generate action potentials—brief, all-or-none reversals of membrane potential produced by voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels. The potential propagates along the axon without decrement. At chemical synapses the arriving action potential triggers calcium influx and vesicle release. Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell and opens or closes ion channels.

Synaptic strength is modifiable. Long-term potentiation and long-term depression are cellular correlates of learning. They depend on receptor trafficking, second-messenger cascades and, ultimately, changes in gene expression. Neural circuits implement sensation, motor control, homeostasis and, in larger brains, cognition. The same ionic mechanisms operate from jellyfish to humans.

Glia support, insulate and modulate neurons. Myelination increases conduction speed. The blood–brain barrier isolates the central nervous system from many blood-borne substances. Development of the nervous system requires precise axon guidance and activity-dependent refinement of connections. The adult brain retains limited plasticity. The principles of excitability, synaptic transmission and circuit computation are conserved across animals that possess nervous systems.

### The Human Brain

The human brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons and a comparable number of glial cells. The cerebral cortex, a folded sheet of gray matter a few millimeters thick, is disproportionately large relative to body size. It supports the expanded capacities for language, planning and abstract reasoning that distinguish humans.

The neurons work as described earlier. What differs is the scale and the architecture of the circuits. Long-range white-matter tracts connect distant cortical areas. Subcortical structures—thalamus, basal ganglia, cerebellum, brainstem—handle sensory relay, motor coordination, autonomic control and arousal. The connectome is the complete map of these pathways. It is still only partially known.

Development begins with a neural tube. Neurons are generated, migrate, and extend axons under genetic and activity-dependent guidance. Synaptic pruning in childhood and adolescence eliminates unused connections. Adult plasticity persists, most clearly in the hippocampus and in sensory and motor cortices after injury or training. The brain consumes about 20 percent of the body’s resting energy budget despite constituting 2 percent of its mass.

No single “center” implements cognition. Functions are distributed. Lesion, stimulation and imaging studies show that language, memory, attention and decision-making each recruit partially overlapping networks. The physical substrate is cellular and molecular. The relation between that substrate and subjective experience remains an open empirical question. The anatomy and physiology, however, are ordinary biology scaled to an unusual degree.

### What Neuroscience Knows

The brain is an organ of about eighty-six billion neurons, supported by a comparable population of glial cells, wired by connections that number in the tens of trillions. It is not a computer in any simple sense. It is the organ that makes computation, perception, memory, and movement out of cells.

The neuron is the signaling unit, and its signal is better understood than the system it belongs to. At rest, the inside of the cell is negative relative to the outside. Channels in the membrane, selective for particular ions, open and close. A sufficient input opens sodium channels, sodium enters, the voltage reverses briefly, and the reversal travels along the axon. At the synapse, the arrival of the pulse triggers the release of neurotransmitter. The receiving cell’s response depends on which transmitter and which receptor. Some inputs excite. Some inhibit. The cell sums them. Learning changes the strengths and the numbers of these connections. The summary is accurate and incomplete. Modulation, timing, and the identity of the cells matter as much as the bare on and off.

Maps of function came first from damage. Broca’s area and Wernicke’s area entered the vocabulary because injury there disrupted speech in different ways. The hippocampus entered the study of memory because a patient who lost both, in an operation for epilepsy, could not form new episodic memories and could still learn some skills. The cases were cruel and informative. Imaging later showed which regions are active, on average, during which tasks in healthy people. Activity is a correlation. It does not, by itself, prove that the region is necessary. Necessity is tested by disruption. Disruption in humans is limited to what disease, surgery, and careful noninvasive methods allow. In animals it can be precise.

Optogenetics made disruption precise in animals. A gene for a light-sensitive channel is inserted into chosen neurons. Light delivered to the tissue switches those neurons on or off. A behavior can be started or stopped by the switch. The method has linked particular cell types to fear, thirst, movement, and memory retrieval in mice. It is not a human therapy in any ordinary form. It is a research instrument that turned correlation into a stronger kind of evidence.

Recording has scaled. Arrays now listen to hundreds or thousands of neurons at once. The data are large. The interpretation is the bottleneck. A pattern of firing is not yet a content. Decoding work can predict, from the pattern, which stimulus was shown or which movement is about to occur, with imperfect accuracy. Prediction of that kind is evidence that the information is present in the recorded cells. It is not a reading of thought in the ordinary sense. The gap between a decoded variable and a subjective report remains.

Disease keeps the claims modest. Neurodegenerative diseases show that particular proteins, misfolded and spreading, can dismantle particular systems. Parkinson’s disease shows that replacing a missing chemical signal can restore movement for a time and does not restore the lost cells. Depression and schizophrenia show that the chemistry matters and that no single chemical account covers the patients. The brain is not one organ in the way the liver is one organ. It is many systems. A treatment that helps one system can leave the others untouched. That is a reason for precision and a reason against slogans.

The physical basis of thought is not in serious doubt among neuroscientists. Thought depends on the brain. Change the brain in particular ways and thought changes in particular ways. What remains open is the mapping: which patterns constitute which mental operations, how development wires the patterns, and how the patterns relate to conscious experience. The open questions are large. They sit on top of a base that is already physical, cellular, and, in increasing measure, testable.

Development is the part of neuroscience that a focus on the adult brain understates. The brain wires itself. Genes set the outline. Activity, before and after birth, refines the connections. Critical periods, taken up under plasticity below, show how much the plan depends on input. The wiring is not a readout of a fixed plan. It is a plan that expects input. That fact connects neuroscience to pediatrics, to education, and to the effects of early environment, without reducing any of those to a slogan about plasticity. Plasticity is real and bounded. The bounds are part of the science.

Memory is not a single store. Working memory holds a little information briefly. Episodic memory records events and depends heavily on the hippocampus for formation. Semantic memory holds facts and becomes partly independent of the hippocampus over time. Skill memory lives in other circuits. The distinctions are supported by patients who lose one and keep another. They matter for education, for dementia, and for the design of any interface that claims to match how people learn. A single word, memory, covers several systems. The systems fail separately and are studied separately.

Brain-computer interfaces are the applied edge. Electrodes decode intended movement and allow a paralyzed person to control a cursor or a robotic arm. The decoding is imperfect and improving. The clinical benefit, for some patients, is already real. The interface is not a reading of private thought in general. It is a reading of specific, trained signals related to a task. Keeping the specificity in view prevents both the understatement of a real assistive technology and the overstatement of a general mind-reading. The technology does what it is trained to do. That is enough to matter.

### Systems Neuroscience

Systems neuroscience examines how populations of neurons implement perception, action and cognition. Sensory systems transduce physical stimuli into spike trains. The retina compresses visual information. The cochlea performs a frequency decomposition. Thalamic nuclei relay and gate the resulting signals. Primary cortices extract features. Higher areas integrate them into object and scene representations.

Motor systems reverse the process. Premotor and motor cortices, the basal ganglia and the cerebellum plan and refine movements. The spinal cord executes patterned reflexes and locomotion. Feedback from proprioceptors continuously corrects the output. The same loops operate in skilled action and in simple withdrawal.

Cognitive functions—attention, working memory, decision-making—are distributed across fronto-parietal and temporal networks. The precise contribution of each area remains under investigation. The principles of receptive fields, population coding and recurrent dynamics are shared across systems. The implementation details differ. Systems neuroscience maps those details onto behavior.

Population coding is the representation of a variable by the joint activity of many neurons. In motor cortex, direction of reach is encoded by a population vector. In visual cortex, orientation is encoded by the relative firing of cells with different preferred orientations. The code is redundant and robust to the loss of individual cells.

Recurrent connectivity produces dynamics richer than feed-forward filtering. Attractor networks can store memories as stable states. Decision-making circuits integrate noisy evidence until a threshold is reached. Oscillations in the gamma and theta bands coordinate activity across areas and are modulated by attention and by behavioral state.

Learning alters synaptic weights. Spike-timing-dependent plasticity strengthens synapses when presynaptic spikes precede postsynaptic spikes and weakens them when the order is reversed. The rule is local yet capable of implementing reinforcement learning and unsupervised feature extraction when embedded in appropriate circuits. The same principles—population codes, recurrence and synaptic plasticity—operate from sensory periphery to prefrontal cortex. Their parameters differ. The computational repertoire is shared.

### Brain Plasticity

Brain plasticity is the capacity of neural circuits to change with experience. Synaptic strength is modified by long-term potentiation and long-term depression. Dendritic spines appear and disappear. Adult neurogenesis occurs in the hippocampus and olfactory bulb of many mammals. Cortical maps reorganize after injury or training. The changes are activity-dependent and are constrained by molecular brakes that increase with age.

Plasticity is highest in early life. Critical periods exist for vision, language and certain social behaviors. During these windows experience exerts a lasting effect. After the window closes the same experience has a smaller effect. The windows can be reopened to a limited degree by environmental enrichment, pharmacological intervention or intensive training. They do not remain open indefinitely.

Plasticity is not unlimited. Large lesions are not fully compensated. Skills acquired in adulthood rarely match the fluency of those acquired in childhood. The brain continues to adapt throughout life, yet the rate and extent of adaptation decline. Plasticity is the biological substrate of learning and recovery. It is also the reason that early experience has disproportionate consequences.

### Sleep and Memory Consolidation

Sleep is a regularly recurring state of reduced responsiveness and altered brain activity. It is universal among animals that possess nervous systems. During slow-wave sleep cortical neurons oscillate between up and down states. During rapid-eye-movement sleep the electroencephalogram resembles waking and most muscles are paralyzed.

Memory consolidation is one established function. Hippocampal replay during slow-wave sleep strengthens and reorganizes traces of recent experience. Synaptic homeostasis hypotheses propose that sleep renormalizes synaptic weights that have grown during waking, preserving the capacity for further learning. Neither account is complete. Both are supported by physiological and behavioral evidence.

Sleep deprivation impairs attention, working memory and metabolic regulation. Chronic restriction carries cumulative costs. The precise restorative processes remain incompletely identified. The universality of sleep and the severity of its disruption indicate that it is not optional. It is a biological requirement whose neural mechanisms are still being mapped.

### Memory Improvement

Memory improvement rests on established principles of encoding, consolidation and retrieval. Attention at the moment of encoding is required. Divided attention markedly reduces later recall. Elaborative encoding—relating new material to existing knowledge—produces stronger traces than rote repetition. The spacing effect is robust: distributed practice yields better long-term retention than massed practice. Retrieval practice (testing oneself) strengthens memory more than additional re-reading.

Sleep after learning enhances consolidation, particularly for declarative material. Aerobic exercise increases hippocampal volume and improves memory performance in adults. No pharmacological agent licensed for healthy individuals produces large, reliable gains. Mnemonic techniques (method of loci, peg systems) are effective for ordered lists because they supply distinctive retrieval cues. They do not expand general capacity.

The limits are biological. Working-memory span remains a few items. Long-term memory is vast but subject to interference and forgetting. Improvement comes from more effective use of ordinary mechanisms—attention, elaboration, spacing, retrieval and sleep—not from unlocking unused stores. The same principles apply across ages, with slower acquisition and greater benefit from spacing in older adults.

### Brain Exercises and Cognitive Training

Cognitive training comprises structured tasks intended to improve specific mental functions. Working-memory training produces reliable gains on the trained tasks and on closely related tests. Transfer to distant domains—fluid intelligence, everyday functioning, academic achievement—is small or absent in well-controlled studies. The pattern is consistent with improvement in task-specific strategies rather than in a general cognitive resource.

Commercial “brain-training” programs have not demonstrated broad benefits in independent replications. Physical exercise, particularly aerobic exercise, produces modest improvements in executive function and memory and is supported by physiological changes in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Learning a new skill (a language, a musical instrument) engages wider networks and is associated with measurable structural changes. The effects are domain-specific and require sustained practice.

No regimen reverses normal age-related decline or produces large gains in general intelligence in healthy adults. The brain adapts to the demands placed upon it. Those adaptations are real, local, and bounded by the same plasticity constraints that operate throughout life. Effective “exercise” is therefore the deliberate practice of the skill one wishes to improve, not a generic workout claimed to enhance all functions.

### Unused Brain Potential

The claim that humans use only 10 percent of their brains is false. Metabolic studies, lesion data and functional imaging show that virtually every region is active at some time. No large silent areas exist. Energy consumption is high and continuous. A brain that maintained 90 percent of its tissue in reserve would be biologically implausible.

What is true is that performance can be improved by training, that different tasks recruit different networks, and that injury can reveal latent capacities through reorganization. These facts do not imply a reservoir of unused tissue. They imply that existing circuits can be tuned and that alternative pathways can be strengthened. The limits are set by anatomy, by the molecular constraints on plasticity, and by the trade-offs inherent in any finite network.

Exceptional skills arise from extended deliberate practice acting on ordinary neural mechanisms, often aided by favorable genetics and early exposure. They do not arise from unlocking dormant regions. The brain is already fully engaged. Improvement comes from more efficient use of what is present, not from activating what is absent.

## <a id="ch_54"></a>54. Consciousness

Consciousness is the fact that there is something it is like to be you. A camera does not, so far as we know, have a point of view. You do. Explaining the point of view is the problem.

The easy problems, which are not easy, are the functional ones. How does the brain discriminate, integrate, report, and control? These can be studied. The hard problem, as the philosopher David Chalmers named it, is why any of that functioning is accompanied by experience. A complete diagram of the visual system would not, by itself, seem to explain why seeing red feels like something.

Science has not solved the hard problem. It has narrowed the easy ones.

Competing theories make different bets. Global workspace theories say a content becomes conscious when it is broadcast widely through the cortex for use by many systems. Integrated information theories say consciousness tracks a particular kind of internal causal structure, and try to quantify it. Higher-order theories say a state is conscious when the brain represents itself as being in that state. Predictive-processing accounts fold experience into the brain’s work of guessing the causes of its inputs. The theories are testable at the edges. None is established.

Two cautions follow. First, consciousness is not a license to ignore mechanism. Whatever experience is, in humans it depends on particular brain processes, and those processes can be disrupted in particular ways. Second, the unsolved problem is not evidence for a particular doctrine. It is evidence that the problem is unsolved. A guide written now should say so without embarrassment. The great guides of the twentieth century could not close this question either, and neither can this one.

A useful distinction separates access from experience. Access consciousness is the availability of information for report, for reasoning, and for the control of action. Experience is the felt quality that accompanies having the information. The two usually travel together in healthy people. They can be pulled apart in experiments and in clinical cases. A stimulus can influence behavior without being reportable. A patient can show brain responses consistent with awareness and be unable to move or speak. The distinction does not solve the hard problem. It makes the experimental subject less muddy.

Correlates of consciousness are the empirical foothold. When a subject reports seeing a stimulus, certain cortical patterns are present. When the same stimulus is presented but masked or missed, those patterns are absent or reduced, even though earlier sensory areas may still respond. The timing and the spread of activity matter. Each of the theories above makes predictions, and adversarial collaborations have begun to test them against the same experiments. That is the right method. It is too early to declare a winner.

Anesthesia and sleep are natural experiments. Under general anesthesia, report and the associated cortical patterns cease, and they return together. Different anesthetics act by different molecular routes and converge on similar network effects. Sleep stages show that behavior and experience can dissociate: in some stages people dream and in some they do not, and the brain signatures differ. Disorders of consciousness after injury show a spectrum from unresponsive wakefulness to states in which communication is possible through brain activity even when movement is not. These findings matter clinically. They also constrain theory. A theory of consciousness that cannot say why anesthesia abolishes it is incomplete.

The hard problem remains a problem about explanation, not about evidence that experience exists. Experience exists for the reader. The question is why any physical process should be accompanied by it, and whether a future theory will close the question or dissolve it. Some philosophers argue that the question is misconceived. Some neuroscientists argue that a sufficiently detailed account of access and of self-modeling will leave no further question that has an empirical grip. The argument is open. What is not open is the dependence of human experience on the brain. Damage, drugs, stimulation, and development all demonstrate the dependence. A theory that ignored them would not be a theory of this phenomenon.

Nonhuman consciousness is a related and unsettled question. Many animals have nervous systems that support learning, perception, and flexible behavior. Whether and where experience accompanies those capacities is inferred from anatomy, behavior, and, increasingly, from comparative neuroscience. The inference is not certainty. It is strong enough, for mammals and birds in particular, that welfare decisions already treat them as experiencing subjects. The guide’s claim is limited. Consciousness in humans is tied to measurable brain processes. Those processes have relatives in other animals. The hard problem is unsolved in every species, including ours.

The clinical stake keeps the subject from being only philosophical. Decisions about withdrawing care, about anesthesia, and about the treatment of infants and of nonhuman animals all assume something about the presence of experience. Better correlates make those decisions better informed. They do not make them automatic. A signature of awareness in an unresponsive patient changes what the family and the physicians know. It does not by itself say what should be done. The science improves the information. The decision remains a decision. Confusing the two helps neither.

Report is the usual measure and a limited one. Adults who can speak are the easiest subjects. Infants, nonhuman animals, and patients who cannot move require other measures: behavior, physiology, and neural signatures validated against report in those who can report. The extension is uncertain and necessary. A science of consciousness confined to verbal adults would miss most of the subjects who have nervous systems. The correlates established in adults are the bridge. Crossing the bridge carefully is the work. Refusing to cross it leaves the science narrower than the phenomenon.

The study of consciousness has attracted theories that outrun their tests. The corrective is the same as in any science. A theory must say what would count against it. Several current theories have begun to do so, and to be tested in shared experiments. The outcome of those experiments will retire some claims. It will not, by itself, solve the hard problem. Retiring claims is progress. A field that cannot retire claims is not yet a science. The presence of adversarial tests is a sign that this field is acquiring the habit. The habit matters more, at this stage, than any single theory’s success.

### What Consciousness Is

Consciousness is the subjective experience of being aware. It includes perceptual experiences, bodily sensations, emotions and the sense of self. The phenomenon is private. It is reported by language and inferred from behavior. No objective measurement captures the experience itself.

Neural correlates exist. Specific patterns of cortical activity, particularly in fronto-parietal networks and in posterior hot-zone regions, are reliably associated with reportable awareness. Disruption of those patterns by anaesthesia, seizures or lesions abolishes or fragments consciousness. The correlates identify necessary circuitry. They do not explain why the circuitry is accompanied by experience.

Theories differ. Global-workspace models propose that consciousness arises when information is broadcast widely across the brain. Integrated-information theories assign consciousness to systems that integrate information above a threshold. Higher-order theories require a representation of one’s own mental states. Predictive-processing accounts treat experience as the brain’s best hypothesis about the causes of sensory input. None is established. All attempt to relate the third-person facts of neuroscience to the first-person fact of experience.

The hard problem—why any physical process should give rise to subjective experience—remains unsolved. The easy problems—how the brain discriminates, integrates, reports and controls—are tractable and are being mapped. Consciousness is an evolved biological capacity whose neural basis is increasingly constrained by experiment and whose ultimate explanation is still open.

### The Hard Problem

The hard problem is the explanatory gap between physical processes and subjective experience. Neural correlates identify which processes are associated with awareness. They do not show why those processes are felt. Functional accounts explain what consciousness does—integrates information, enables report, guides behavior. They do not explain why the performance is accompanied by experience rather than occurring “in the dark.”

Proposed dissolutions include the claim that the gap is illusory once the functions are fully specified, and the claim that experience is a fundamental feature of certain information structures. Neither dissolution is widely accepted. Empirical progress continues on the correlates, on the effects of targeted disruption, and on the differences between conscious and unconscious processing. The metaphysical question remains open. The scientific constraint is that any solution must be consistent with the observed neural dependence and with the evolutionary continuity of nervous systems.

### Thought Experiments About the Self

[The Mind’s I](#bib_28), edited by Douglas Hofstadter and Daniel Dennett, collects stories and arguments that treat questions of mind as puzzles to be worked through. A classic is the teleporter. A machine scans you, destroys the original, and builds an exact copy elsewhere. Is the copy you, or someone who thinks so? Philosophers split. Derek Parfit argued that what matters is the continuity of memory and character, not which atoms are used.

Other puzzles press on different points. John Searle’s Chinese room imagines a person who follows rules to answer Chinese questions without understanding Chinese, and asks whether a program alone could understand anything. Thomas Nagel asked what it is like to be a bat, to show that a complete physical description of an echo-locating brain might leave out how it feels from the inside. Dennett’s own stories of a brain kept alive in a vat show how odd it becomes to say where one is.

None of the puzzles has a consensus answer. They are useful because they separate what science can settle from what it cannot. Experiments determine what brains do and what copies would preserve. They do not decide, by themselves, which of the competing meanings of the word *I* ought to survive.

## <a id="ch_55"></a>55. Minds That Are Not Ours

### Cetacean Brains and Cognition

Cetaceans possess large brains. The bottlenose dolphin brain weighs about 1.6 kg. The sperm-whale brain is the largest of any animal, exceeding 7 kg. Encephalization quotients for several dolphin species are second only to humans. The neocortex is extensively folded. A paralimbic lobe unique to cetaceans is present.

Behavioral evidence of complex cognition includes mirror self-recognition, comprehension of symbolic gestures and of word order in artificial languages, cooperative problem-solving, and socially transmitted foraging techniques, several of which are described in detail below.

The cognitive achievements are real. They do not imply human-like linguistic syntax or abstract reasoning of the same scope. Brain size and cortical folding indicate high processing capacity. The precise mapping of that capacity onto particular cognitive domains remains incomplete. Cetaceans demonstrate that large, complex brains and flexible behavior have evolved independently in a fully aquatic lineage.

### Dolphin and Whale Communication

Dolphins produce whistles and burst-pulse sounds. Signature whistles function as individual identifiers. Dolphins can copy the signature whistles of associates. The copies are used in reunions. No evidence demonstrates that the whistles possess combinatorial syntax comparable to human language. The repertoire is large and context-dependent.

Baleen whales produce low-frequency songs. Humpback songs are hierarchically structured and change progressively through a season. All males in a population converge on the current version. The songs function in mating advertisement. Sperm whales produce patterned clicks (codas) that differ among social groups and are culturally transmitted.

Communication in both groups is sophisticated and partly learned. It supports individual recognition, social cohesion and mating. It has not been shown to support displaced reference or open-ended productivity. The systems are adapted to the acoustic properties of water and to the social structures of the species. They illustrate the evolution of complex signaling without human language.

### Cetacean Social Structure and Culture

Many dolphin and whale species live in stable social groups. Bottlenose dolphins form fission–fusion societies with long-term alliances. Male alliances cooperate to consort females. The alliances can last decades. Killer-whale societies are matrilineal. Offspring remain with the mother for life. Vocal dialects and hunting techniques are transmitted within matrilines and differ among neighboring groups.

Cultural transmission is documented. Foraging specializations, migratory routes and vocal repertoires are learned and persist across generations. The transmission is social, not genetic. In killer whales the cultural differences are large enough that some populations are reproductively isolated by behavior. The same capacity for social learning underlies the rapid spread of novel behaviors when conditions change.

Cetacean culture demonstrates that cumulative social learning and stable traditions are not unique to primates. The content of the traditions is constrained by the species’ ecology and sensory modalities. The existence of the traditions shows that complex social knowledge can be maintained and transmitted in fully aquatic mammals.

### Self-Recognition and Culture in Dolphins and Orcas

Bottlenose dolphins pass the mirror-mark test. They use a mirror to investigate marks placed on parts of their bodies they cannot see directly. The behavior is interpreted as evidence of bodily self-awareness. The same species learn artificial gestural and acoustic languages in which word order changes meaning. They generalize the rules to novel combinations. The training demonstrates sensitivity to sequential structure. It does not demonstrate spontaneous productive syntax in the wild.

Wild sponge-using dolphins in Shark Bay carry marine sponges on their rostra while foraging. The behavior is transmitted primarily from mother to offspring and is almost exclusively female. Genetic data show that sponging is cultural, not a genetic polymorphism. Killer-whale populations specialize in distinct prey and techniques—beach-rubbing, wave-washing seals from ice, or carousel feeding on herring. The specializations are stable across generations and are accompanied by distinct vocal dialects. The cognitive requirements include social learning, motor imitation and long-term memory of techniques. The upper bound on abstract relational reasoning remains unquantified.

### Octopus Minds

The last common ancestor of humans and octopuses lived more than 500 million years ago and had, at most, a very simple nervous system. The octopus brain evolved independently, and it is large, with about half a billion neurons, comparable to a small dog. Two-thirds of those neurons sit in the arms, which can taste, touch and carry out some actions without instructions from the central brain.

Octopuses solve puzzles, unscrew jars, learn by watching, and carry coconut shells to use as shelters, one of the few examples of tool use among invertebrates. They recognize individual people, and some seem to play. Their lives are short, mostly one to three years, and they do not raise their young, so there is little opportunity for culture to be passed on.

The octopus matters philosophically because it is an intelligence that evolved on a separate path. Its body has no rigid skeleton, and its senses and its control of movement are organized in a different way from any vertebrate’s. If it is conscious, as many researchers suspect, then consciousness has evolved at least twice, in minds built from the same cellular materials and arranged very differently.

### Crows, Bees and Small Brains

Birds have no neocortex, yet crows and parrots rival apes in several tests of cognition. New Caledonian crows make hooked tools from twigs and leaves and pass the design from generation to generation. Scrub jays hide food and remember not only where but also whether another bird was watching, and move it if so. Some crows recognize individual human faces and remember them for years. Their pallium, which has a different layout from a mammal’s cortex, appears to carry out similar computations.

Even an insect brain with fewer than a million neurons can do surprising things. A honeybee returning to the hive performs a waggle dance whose angle and duration tell her nestmates the direction and distance of a flower patch. Bees can learn rules such as same and different, count small numbers, and in laboratory experiments have been trained to use symbols for quantity.

These results do not show that animals think as we do. They show that complex behavior does not need a large brain or a human kind of cortex, and that the brain is an organ whose design can differ widely and still solve similar problems.

### Do Animals Feel?

Whether an animal has experiences, and not only behavior, is the hardest question in this chapter. The evidence is indirect. Animals share with us the brain structures and chemicals that go with pain and emotion in humans, and they show avoidance, learning and trade-offs between pain and reward that go beyond reflex. For mammals and birds the case is strong.

In 2012 a group of neuroscientists meeting at Cambridge signed a declaration that the neurological basis of consciousness is not unique to humans, and that mammals, birds and octopuses share it. A 2024 New York declaration, signed by many researchers, went further and called for taking seriously the possibility of experience in fish, reptiles and some insects. The evidence for these groups is weaker, and many scientists remain cautious.

As with consciousness in general, the uncertainty runs in both directions. The cost of wrongly denying sentience to an animal that has it is greater than the cost of wrongly granting it, and that asymmetry has shaped welfare law in several countries. Science can supply the evidence. It cannot by itself decide how much weight a possible experience deserves.

# <a id="part_9"></a>Part IX: Earth, the Living Planet

*The ground, the air, the oceans, the web of life, and the energy that keeps a civilization running*

## <a id="ch_56"></a>56. The Structure of the Earth

The Earth is not a uniform ball. It has layers, and the layers were inferred before they were directly sampled.

The outermost layer is the crust, thin and rigid. Under the oceans it is typically 5 to 10 kilometers thick. Under the continents it is thicker, often 30 to 50 kilometers. Below the crust is the mantle, a thick layer of hot rock that extends to about 2,900 kilometers depth. The mantle is solid but, over long times, flows slowly. At the center is the core, divided into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, both made mostly of iron with some nickel and lighter elements. The inner core is solid because the pressure is high enough to keep iron solid despite the temperature.

The evidence for these layers came first from earthquake waves. P-waves and S-waves travel at different speeds and behave differently at boundaries. S-waves do not travel through liquid. Their absence in certain paths showed that the outer core is liquid. The speeds and reflections mapped the boundaries. Later, the composition was constrained by the density required to match the Earth’s total mass and by the chemistry of meteorites, which sample the material from which the planet formed.

The crust is not fixed. It is broken into plates that move. The idea of continental drift was proposed in detail by Alfred Wegener in 1912. He noted the fit of the continents, the match of fossils and rock formations across oceans, and evidence of past climates. The mechanism was missing, and the idea was resisted. In the 1960s, seafloor spreading and plate tectonics supplied the mechanism. New crust forms at mid-ocean ridges. Old crust sinks at trenches. Continents are carried with the plates. The Atlantic is widening. The Pacific is shrinking in places. Earthquakes and volcanoes concentrate at the boundaries.

The Earth’s magnetic field is generated by motion in the liquid outer core. The field reverses at irregular intervals. Those reversals are recorded in the seafloor as it forms, providing a tape of the spreading. The field also shields the surface from much of the solar wind. Without it, the atmosphere would be more vulnerable to stripping.

The age of the Earth is about 4.54 billion years, measured from the oldest meteorites and from the oldest terrestrial minerals. The oldest known crustal rocks are younger, because the surface has been recycled. Zircon crystals from Australia are more than 4.3 billion years old and show that continental crust and liquid water existed early.

Heat inside the Earth comes from leftover heat of formation and from radioactive decay. That heat drives the mantle’s slow convection, which drives the plates, and it supplies the energy for volcanoes and for the magnetic field. The surface we live on is the cool, thin skin of a planet that is still geologically active.

### Plate Tectonics

The Earth’s lithosphere is divided into rigid plates that move relative to one another. The motions are driven by mantle convection and by the sinking of cold oceanic lithosphere. Divergent boundaries produce mid-ocean ridges and new oceanic crust. Convergent boundaries produce subduction zones, volcanic arcs and mountain belts. Transform boundaries accommodate lateral slip.

The theory unifies continental drift, seafloor spreading and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes. Magnetic anomalies symmetric about ridge axes record reversals of the geomagnetic field and demonstrate that oceanic crust is created at ridges and destroyed at trenches. The oldest oceanic crust is about 180 million years old. Continental crust is older and is not systematically recycled.

Plate motions have rearranged the continents repeatedly. The assembly and breakup of supercontinents correlate with changes in sea level, climate and biological diversity. The same processes operate today. GPS measurements confirm the velocities predicted by magnetic anomalies and by earthquake slip vectors. Plate tectonics is the surface expression of the Earth’s internal heat engine.

### Geochemistry

Geochemistry is the study of the chemical composition of the Earth and of the processes that control the distribution of the elements. The bulk Earth is dominated by oxygen, silicon, magnesium and iron. Differentiation into core, mantle and crust partitioned the elements according to their chemical affinities. Siderophile elements concentrated in the core. Lithophile elements remained in the silicate Earth.

The long-term carbon cycle, described in the section on the carbon-silicate cycle, regulates atmospheric CO₂ on million-year timescales. Perturbations such as large igneous provinces or changes in weathering rates produce excursions recorded in the isotopic composition of sedimentary rocks.

Isotope systems (Rb–Sr, Sm–Nd, U–Pb, C, O, S) date events and trace sources. Fractionation between isotopes records temperature, biological processing and redox state. The same tools applied to meteorites and to other planets constrain the formation of the Solar System and the evolution of planetary surfaces. Geochemistry therefore links the atomic properties of the elements to the history of the planet.

### The Oxygen Cycle and the Rock Archive

The oxygen cycle is tightly linked to the carbon cycle. Photosynthesis produces O₂ and consumes CO₂. Respiration and weathering reverse the reactions. On geological timescales the burial of organic carbon and pyrite leaves a net excess of O₂. The Great Oxidation Event marks the point at which this excess became permanent. Subsequent fluctuations in atmospheric oxygen are recorded by redox-sensitive isotopes and by the presence or absence of particular mineral assemblages.

Large igneous provinces inject CO₂ faster than weathering can remove it, producing transient warming, while mountain building exposes fresh rock and so increases CO₂ consumption. The isotopic composition of marine carbonates records these imbalances, dates the events and quantifies the size of the perturbations. Geochemical cycles are therefore both regulators and archives of Earth’s surface environment.

### The Faint Young Sun Paradox

The early Sun was approximately 30 percent less luminous than today. A planet at 1 AU with Earth’s present atmosphere would have been frozen. Geological evidence shows liquid water as early as 4.4 billion years ago. The paradox is resolved by a stronger greenhouse effect. Higher concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane or both can maintain above-freezing temperatures.

The required concentrations are plausible. Weathering feedbacks regulate them. The solution is not unique. Cloud feedbacks or a lower albedo can contribute. The paradox demonstrates that the habitable zone is not fixed. It depends on atmospheric composition. The early Earth remained habitable because its atmosphere adjusted. The adjustment is a consequence of the carbon-silicate cycle and of biological influence after life appeared.

### The Carbon-Silicate Cycle

The carbon-silicate cycle is the long-term regulator of Earth’s climate. Volcanism releases CO₂. Weathering of silicate rocks consumes it. The weathering rate increases with temperature and with runoff. The feedback is negative. It stabilizes the climate on million-year timescales. Burial of carbonate and organic carbon removes carbon from the surface reservoirs. Subduction returns it to the mantle.

The cycle has operated for billions of years. It kept the surface temperature within the range that permits liquid water. Perturbations—large igneous provinces, changes in continental configuration—produce excursions. The excursions are temporary. The cycle restores balance. It is the principal reason Earth’s climate has remained habitable despite a brightening Sun and varying volcanic input.

## <a id="ch_57"></a>57. Climate Science

*Climate is weather averaged, and the average is moving.*

The energy balance can be stated simply. The Earth receives energy from the Sun, mostly in visible light. It emits energy to space as infrared radiation. If the energy in exceeds the energy out, the planet warms until the two balance again. Greenhouse gases intercept part of the outgoing infrared and return some of it downward. More greenhouse gas means a higher surface temperature at the new balance. This is physics measured in the laboratory and observed in the atmosphere. It is not a model. Svante Arrhenius calculated the effect of carbon dioxide in the 1890s, and the calculation has been refined, not repealed. Models are what you build when you want to know how much, how fast, and where.

Carbon dioxide is the dominant control over long periods because it stays in the air for centuries and because the oceans and rocks exchange it slowly. Methane is more potent per molecule and shorter-lived. Nitrous oxide and some industrial gases add smaller amounts. Water vapor is a strong greenhouse gas and a feedback rather than a driver: warmer air holds more of it, amplifying a warming started by the others. Aerosols from pollution cool the planet slightly by reflecting sunlight, and they are a reason the observed warming is not even larger. As aerosols are reduced for the sake of lungs, some masked warming can appear.

The rise in carbon dioxide from about 280 to about 420 parts per million is measured directly, in the modern record, and in ice cores for the preindustrial baseline. The isotopic composition of the added carbon matches fossil carbon, not volcanic carbon. Volcanoes emit carbon dioxide. Human activity currently emits on the order of a hundred times more. The source is not in serious doubt among the people who measure it.

The observed warming of about 1.2 degrees Celsius, with recent years higher, is measured by thermometers, by ocean buoys, and by satellites, after the known corrections for instrument changes and for urban effects. The corrections are a source of public confusion and a normal part of measurement. Independent analyses converge. The ocean’s heat content, which is the largest reservoir, has risen steadily. Ice has lost mass. Sea level has risen through thermal expansion and through the addition of meltwater. These are the fingerprints. They match the greenhouse account. They do not match a change in the Sun, which has not supplied the extra energy, or a rearrangement of heat without a net gain.

Models are tested by their ability to reproduce the past when given the past’s emissions, volcanic eruptions, and solar changes, and by their ability to fail when the human emissions are omitted. They pass the first and fail the second in the expected way. Their projections for the future depend on emissions. Continued high emissions lead to warming well above two degrees by late century. Rapid cuts lead to less. The range within any one emissions path comes mainly from clouds, from aerosols, and from the carbon cycle’s feedbacks. The range is a reason for humility about the exact number. It is not a reason for expecting no further warming.

Impacts are already measured. Heat waves are hotter and more frequent. Heavy rainfall is heavier in many regions, because warmer air holds more water. Drought risk rises in regions where evaporation increases more than rainfall. Sea level rise is accelerating slowly. Ecosystems are shifting toward the poles and uphill. None of this requires a model to notice. Attribution studies, which ask whether a particular event was made more likely by the warming, now regularly find that it was. The science of impacts is no longer only a forecast. It is a mixture of forecast and record.

The policy implication is separate from the physics and follows from it. Because carbon dioxide accumulates, the total emitted over time matters more than the rate in any one year. Because the ocean and the ice are slow, warming and sea level continue after emissions fall. Early reduction costs less total damage than late reduction, on the standard economic comparisons. Disagreement about the pace, the tools, and the fairness of reduction is a political disagreement. It does not reopen the energy balance.

Tipping points are the part of the subject that most exceeds a smooth projection. A tipping point is a threshold beyond which a system moves to a new state and does not easily return. Ice sheets, the Atlantic circulation, the Amazon forest, and permafrost carbon are the systems discussed. Some thresholds are better constrained than others. None is a reason to ignore the smooth projection, which already contains serious impacts. They are a reason to treat the smooth projection as a lower description of risk rather than as a complete one. The existence of thresholds is a property of the systems. Their exact locations are uncertain. Both facts belong in the account.

Carbon budgets translate the physics into a quantity a policy can use. For a given chance of staying below a temperature threshold, there is a remaining amount of carbon dioxide that can be emitted. The budgets are uncertain and usable. They say that continuing at the present rate exhausts a 1.5-degree budget quickly and a 2-degree budget over a longer, still limited, period. The exact year is less important than the direction. A budget is the kind of object this book has favored: a measurement converted into a constraint. Disagreement about how to meet the constraint is expected. Disagreement about whether the constraint exists is a disagreement with the measurement.

Adaptation and mitigation are both required by the lags. Mitigation reduces future warming. Adaptation reduces harm from warming already in train and from warming still to come. Cities, agriculture, and coasts can be adapted, at a cost, up to a point. The point depends on how much warming is allowed. Adaptation without mitigation eventually meets changes that are hard to adapt to. Mitigation without adaptation leaves people exposed to changes already locked in. The two are complements. Treating them as rivals is a rhetorical choice, not a scientific one. The science supplies the lags that make both necessary.

### Climate Science: Definitions and Methods

Climate science is the study of the long-term statistics of the atmosphere, ocean, cryosphere and land surface, and of the forcings that change those statistics.

Observational records include surface temperature series, satellite radiances, ocean heat content, ice-sheet mass balance and paleoclimate proxies. The instrumental record shows a global surface warming of approximately 1.2 °C since the late nineteenth century. The warming is larger over land than over ocean and larger in the Arctic than in the tropics. Attribution studies using climate models and observations assign the majority of the warming since 1950 to the increase in greenhouse gases from fossil-fuel combustion and land-use change.

Models solve the fluid equations on a rotating sphere together with radiation, convection and cloud parameterizations. Equilibrium climate sensitivity to a doubling of CO₂ lies between 2 °C and 5 °C, and regional changes in precipitation, extremes and sea level follow. The physical basis is established; the remaining uncertainties are quantitative.

### Paleoclimate, Feedbacks and Sea Level

Paleoclimate records extend the instrumental series. Ice cores provide continuous archives of temperature, greenhouse-gas concentrations and dust for the past 800 000 years. Ocean sediments and corals supply longer but less finely resolved records. These proxies show that CO₂ and temperature have varied together through the glacial cycles, with CO₂ lagging the initial orbital trigger and then amplifying it.

The carbon-cycle feedbacks are central. Warmer oceans hold less dissolved CO₂. Thawing permafrost and increased respiration release additional carbon. These positive feedbacks are already observable. Negative feedbacks—increased weathering, possible fertilization of marine productivity—operate on longer timescales. The net effect on century scales is positive.

Sea-level rise has two components: thermal expansion of seawater and the addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets. Both are under way. The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets contain enough ice to raise sea level by approximately 7 m and 58 m respectively if fully melted. Current mass-loss rates are accelerating. The committed rise from past emissions is already tens of centimeters. Future rise depends on emissions and on the still-uncertain dynamics of ice-sheet collapse.

### The Earth’s Atmosphere and Climate

The atmosphere is a thin gaseous envelope whose composition is maintained by geological and biological fluxes. Nitrogen and oxygen dominate. Trace gases—water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, ozone—control the radiative balance. Incoming solar radiation is partly reflected and partly absorbed. Outgoing long-wave radiation is trapped by greenhouse gases. The resulting surface temperature is approximately 33 K warmer than the effective radiating temperature.

Climate is the long-term statistics of weather. It varies on every timescale. Orbital (Milankovitch) cycles modulate the seasonal distribution of sunlight and pace the Pleistocene ice ages. Volcanic aerosols cool the surface for a few years. Changes in greenhouse-gas concentrations alter the energy budget for decades to millennia. The present rise in carbon dioxide is produced by fossil-fuel combustion and land-use change. It is occurring at a rate unprecedented in the ice-core record.

Feedbacks amplify or damp the response. Water vapor and snow–ice albedo are positive. Clouds and the carbon cycle contain both positive and negative terms. The atmosphere and ocean together redistribute heat. The same physical principles govern the climates of other planets that possess atmospheres.

## <a id="ch_58"></a>58. Ecology and the Living Planet

### Ecology

Ecology studies the distribution and abundance of organisms and the interactions that determine them. A population grows exponentially when resources are unlimited. Density-dependent factors—competition, predation, disease—slow growth as numbers rise. The logistic equation is the simplest model that incorporates a carrying capacity. Real populations fluctuate around that capacity under the influence of environmental variation and of interactions with other species.

Communities are sets of interacting populations. Competition, predation, mutualism and parasitism structure the set. Keystone species exert effects larger than their biomass would suggest. Removal of a keystone predator can allow prey to over-exploit primary producers and collapse the community. Energy enters most ecosystems through photosynthesis and is transferred with low efficiency—approximately 10 percent to each successive trophic level. Nutrients cycle. Energy does not.

Ecosystems are open. They exchange gases, water, organisms and energy with their surroundings. Succession follows disturbance. The trajectory depends on the remaining species pool, soil conditions and climate. Human activity now dominates many of these exchanges. The basic constraints of energy degradation, nutrient conservation and density dependence remain those of any ecological system.

### Food Webs and Energy Flow

Textbooks draw a food chain, with plants eaten by herbivores and herbivores by carnivores, but real ecosystems form webs. An animal feeds on many species and is eaten by many, and a large share of energy never passes through a living animal at all. In most ecosystems the biggest flow runs through dead material, as bacteria, fungi and invertebrates break down leaves, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

The structure of a web decides how disturbance spreads. When sea otters were hunted almost out of existence on the Pacific coast of North America, the sea urchins they ate multiplied and stripped the kelp forests bare, a trophic cascade. When otters returned, the kelp recovered. The effect works from the top down. In other systems the supply of nutrients at the bottom sets the limit, and the effect works from the bottom up.

Energy is lost at each step, mostly as heat, so food chains rarely have more than four or five levels, and the total mass of predators is far smaller than that of the plants that ultimately feed them. This is why large predators are rare and why they are vulnerable to any loss at the foundations of the web.

### Biomes: What Decides Where Life Lives

A biome is a large community of plants and animals shaped by climate. Two numbers explain most of the map: average temperature and annual rainfall. Warm and wet gives tropical rainforest, warm and dry gives desert, cool and wet gives temperate forest, and cold gives tundra and the boreal forest. The pattern is so regular that an ecologist can guess the vegetation of a region from a climate chart.

Soil, fire, grazing animals and altitude modify the pattern. Grasslands cover regions that could support forest, because fire and grazing keep trees out. A tall mountain compresses the sequence of biomes into a few kilometers of height, from forest at the base to bare rock at the summit.

The same logic makes the biomes sensitive to climate change. As the pattern of temperature and rainfall shifts, regions that suited one community begin to favor another, and species must move or adapt. Because trees move slowly and habitat is fragmented by roads and farms, the shift may be faster than many ecosystems can follow.

### Partnerships: Lichens, Coral and Mycorrhizae

Ecology is often presented as competition, but cooperation is just as common. A lichen is not a single organism. It is a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium living together, the fungus giving shelter and the partner supplying sugars from photosynthesis, and it can survive on bare rock where neither could live alone. A reef-building coral lives with algae in its tissues that supply most of its energy. When heat makes the algae leave, the coral bleaches.

Beneath the forest floor, most land plants, perhaps 80 percent of species, form partnerships with mycorrhizal fungi. The fungal threads reach far more soil than roots could, delivering water and minerals in return for sugars. Some fungi link several trees at once, and experiments show that carbon can pass through the network between neighboring plants. How much this matters to the plants is still debated, and early claims of a cooperative wood-wide web have been tempered by later studies.

These partnerships show that organisms are not self-contained units. Many of the mitochondria and chloroplasts discussed in the chapter on the cell began as partners, and the boundary between one organism and several partners can be a matter of definition.

### Metapopulations, Coevolution and Macroecology

Metapopulations are sets of local populations linked by dispersal. Local extinctions are balanced by recolonization. The persistence of the metapopulation depends on the rates of extinction and colonization and on the spatial arrangement of habitat patches. Habitat fragmentation increases extinction rates and decreases colonization rates. Both effects raise the risk of regional disappearance.

Coevolution is reciprocal evolutionary change in interacting species. Predators and prey, parasites and hosts, and mutualists all show evidence of coevolution. Arms races produce escalating defenses and counter-defenses. Mutualisms produce matching traits. The interactions are rarely pairwise. Most species interact with many others. The resulting networks are modular and nested. Their structure influences stability.

Macroecology examines statistical patterns across large spatial and temporal scales. Species-abundance distributions, species-area relationships and latitudinal diversity gradients are among the patterns. Proposed explanations include energetic constraints, historical contingency and neutral processes. No single explanation accounts for all patterns. The patterns themselves are robust. They constrain the possible dynamics of ecological communities.

## <a id="ch_59"></a>59. Biodiversity

Life has been pruned before. The fossil record holds several mass extinctions, the most famous of which ended the non-bird dinosaurs sixty-six million years ago. The present loss is different in cause and in speed. It is driven by a single species changing habitats, climates, and the movement of other species.

Biodiversity is not only a list of species. It is variation within species, and the workings of communities. A forest is not a set of trees. It is pollination, predation, decay, and soil. Remove a function and the list of remaining names misleads. Fisheries collapse when the large fish are gone even if the water still holds life. Soils fail when the community under them is simplified.

The background rate of extinction, inferred from the fossil record, is low. The documented rate for well-studied groups over the last few centuries is much higher. Amphibians, with their permeable skins and their dependence on both land and water, have suffered especially. Large mammals and birds have suffered where they were hunted or where their habitat was converted. Many invertebrates are declining in monitored places and unmonitored in most places. The phrase “sixth mass extinction” is a warning about trajectory, not a claim that the losses already equal the great fossil die-offs. The trajectory, if continued, points that way. It has not arrived.

Habitat loss is the largest present driver on land. Forests are cleared for crops and pasture. Wetlands are drained. Grasslands are plowed. Fragmentation leaves patches too small for species that need room. In the sea, fishing pressure and habitat damage from trawling and from coastal development play the corresponding role. Climate change adds a driver that habitat protection alone cannot cancel: a species may lose the climate it requires even inside a park. Exploitation, pollution, and invasive species add further pressure, dominant in some places and secondary in others.

The value of biodiversity is argued in several currencies. One is instrumental: pollination, fisheries, soil, and the chemical library of possible medicines. One is insurance: variety makes a system more likely to contain a member that can handle a new stress. One is scientific: each lineage is a history, and extinction deletes the history. One is ethical, and sits outside science. A guide can note that the first three are empirical claims with evidence behind them, and that the fourth is a judgment societies make. The empirical claims do not require the ethical one to be real. The ethical one does not require the empirical ones to be felt.

Successes show that decline is not a law. Species have recovered where hunting stopped and habitat returned. The bald eagle, the wolf in parts of its range, and various whales are examples, each with caveats. The ozone agreement shows that a global pollutant can be restricted when the science is clear and the substitutes exist. Protected areas work better when they are large, connected, and actually protected. Restoration works better when the driver has been reduced. These are design lessons, not consolations. They say that the outcome is sensitive to what people do.

The deeper tension is land. Food for eight billion people requires land or a large increase in yield per area, or both. Yield increases have spared land relative to what would otherwise have been needed. Further sparing, through yield, diet, and waste reduction, is the arithmetic of having both agriculture and wild habitat. The arithmetic can be done. It is not automatic. Biodiversity science is, at bottom, the measurement of what is being lost and of what the losses do, so that the arithmetic is not done in ignorance.

Extinction debt is a concept the numbers require. A habitat reduced below the size a species needs may still hold the species for a time. The loss appears later, when the remaining population fails to replace itself. Counts of species present today can therefore understate the effect of habitat loss already done. The debt is not a reason for despair about every damaged place. It is a reason to restore and to connect habitats sooner rather than later, while the species are still there to be saved. Lag cuts both ways. Damage can be slow to appear. Recovery can be real if the conditions are returned.

Invasive species are a driver that globalization amplified. Organisms moved by trade and travel encounter communities that have not adapted to them. Some fail. Some become problems. Islands have suffered most, because their species evolved without the new arrivals. Prevention is cheaper than removal. Removal works in some cases, especially on islands, and fails in others. The subject is a branch of ecology with a customs office. Treating it as either hopeless or trivial misreads the record, which contains both expensive failures and clear successes.

Genetic diversity within species is the part of biodiversity least visible and most useful. A species with little genetic variety is brittle. A species with a range of variants is more likely to contain one that tolerates a new disease or a new climate. Conservation that saves a species as a few individuals, without regard to variety, saves less than it appears to. Seed banks, captive breeding that manages relatedness, and protection of populations across a species’ range are the responses. The responses are technical. They follow from the same population genetics that explains evolution. Conservation is applied evolution, practiced in reverse, against a loss.

A guide’s job is not to preach. It is to state the mechanism. Extinction is permanent on human timescales. Evolution will fill gaps, over millions of years, with different creatures. The interval between is the interval in which we live. The species and the functions lost in that interval are a choice, in the limited sense that the drivers are human, even when no one intended the loss.

## <a id="ch_60"></a>60. Oceans and Ecosystems

*Most of the living surface of the planet is ocean. Most of that ocean is poorly visited.*

The sea is not a uniform bath. It is structured by light, temperature, and nutrients. Photosynthesis happens in the sunlit top. Below a few hundred meters, food falls or swims. The deep ocean is cold, dark, and inhabited. Hydrothermal vents support communities that run on chemical energy rather than sunlight, a reminder that life’s energy source is broader than the textbook diagram.

Currents move heat. The overturning circulation carries warm water north in the Atlantic and returns cold deep water south. A slowdown would shift climates around the basin. Whether a slowdown is under way, and how far it might go, is an active measurement problem, not a settled catastrophe. The measurement is worth doing because the circulation is a hinge.

The ocean’s practical importance is easy to understate because it is opaque. It is the largest carbon sink after the geological ones, a source of food for billions of people, and the driver of coastal weather. Studying it used to mean ships and nets. It now also means satellites, autonomous floats, and genetic surveys of seawater. The planet’s dominant habitat is finally being measured at something like the scale it occupies.

The ocean’s layers are set by density. Warm water sits on cold water. Fresh water sits on salt water. The boundaries between layers limit the upward mixing of nutrients and the downward mixing of oxygen. Most of the ocean’s productivity happens where nutrients reach the sunlit surface: in upwelling zones, in high latitudes in season, and near coasts. The open tropical ocean is often a desert by comparison, blue because it is empty. Productivity is not uniform, and fisheries follow the productive places.

The biological pump is the ocean’s way of moving carbon. Phytoplankton take up carbon dioxide. Some of the resulting organic matter sinks. A fraction reaches the deep sea and stays there for centuries. The pump is a part of the carbon cycle and a part of the climate system. Its strength depends on the plankton community, on nutrients, and on temperature. How it will change as the ocean warms and stratifies is a research question with a large lever attached.

Acidification is the chemical twin of warming. Dissolved carbon dioxide lowers pH and reduces the availability of the carbonate ions that many organisms use to build shells and skeletons. Corals, mollusks, and some plankton are the groups of concern. The effect is measurable in the water and in experiments. It is not uniform, because temperature, nutrients, and the organism’s biology modify it. Reefs under combined heat and acidity are the clearest warning. A reef can recover from a mild bleaching. Repeated severe bleaching, with slower calcification, is a different prospect.
