A child who calls a pony a big dog, or a man who uses the word *mother* for the second wife of his father, is stretching an old category to fit a new case. Every word, they say, is a bundle of such stretches, and thinking is the continual finding of likenesses beneath different surfaces.

Science supplies many examples. Rutherford’s picture of the atom as a miniature solar system, Kekulé’s dream of a snake biting its tail that gave him the benzene ring, and Einstein’s image of a person in a falling elevator all work by analogy. Their value lies in what they let a mind do next, and also in where they stop working: electrons do not follow planetary orbits, and the analogy has to be dropped at the right moment.

The thesis is a bold one, and cognitive scientists do not all accept its strongest form. It does fit a lesson that runs through this book. The strongest results in science are those whose analogy holds in detail, and the clearest explanations are those that say where the likeness ends.

### Formal Systems and Meaning

A formal system consists of a finite alphabet, a set of formation rules, a set of axioms and a set of inference rules. Theorems are the strings generated from the axioms by the rules. The system is purely syntactic. Meaning is assigned by an interpretation that maps strings to statements about some domain.

Gödel numbering shows that the syntax of a sufficiently rich system can be represented inside arithmetic. The system can therefore talk about its own proofs. Completeness holds for first-order logic: every logically valid formula is provable. It fails for arithmetic, as the incompleteness theorems demonstrate. Consistency and completeness cannot be simultaneously achieved for any system that includes elementary number theory.

The distinction between syntax and semantics is sharp inside the formal system. It is less sharp in natural language and in mental representation, where the same symbols carry both formal roles and interpreted content. The study of formal systems supplies the precise tools with which the limits of mechanical proof and the possibilities of self-reference are established. Those limits and possibilities are mathematical facts.

### A Puzzle in Meaningless Symbols

Douglas Hofstadter introduced a small game in [*Gödel, Escher, Bach*](#bib_25) to show how meaning relates to form. Strings are made from the letters M, I and U. You start with MI, and you may apply four rules: add a U to the end of a string that ends in I; double everything after the M; replace any III with U; delete any UU. Can you reach MU?

Try it, and you will wander through many strings and never arrive. The reason is found by stepping back from the rules to a property of every string. The number of I’s starts at one. Doubling changes it from n to 2n, and replacing III by U lowers it by three. Neither operation can turn a number that is not divisible by three into one that is, so zero I’s, as MU requires, is out of reach. The proof is outside the system, and that is its point.

The game is a miniature of a theme in the previous sections. A formal system is a set of rules on symbols, and it has no meaning until an interpretation is assigned. When the symbols are given the meaning of arithmetic, the rules acquire a content. The incompleteness theorems rest on this, and so does the question of how a mind, which is also a system of rules acting on symbols, can mean anything at all.

### Superrationality and the Prisoner’s Dilemma

Two prisoners are held apart. Each may stay silent or betray the other. Whatever the other does, betrayal pays better for the individual, yet if both betray they do worse than if both stay silent. This is the prisoner’s dilemma, the standard model of a situation in which the best choice for each person is bad for both. Many real tensions, between rivals, nations and herders sharing a pasture, have the same shape.

In 1980 Robert Axelrod invited experts to submit programs for a tournament of repeated dilemmas. The winner was the simplest entry, Tit for Tat: cooperate first, then do what the other did last time. It succeeded because it was nice, firm, forgiving and easy to understand. Axelrod’s later work showed how such strategies can arise in an evolving population, an idea that fits the biology of reciprocal cooperation.

Douglas Hofstadter, in a column collected in [*Metamagical Themas*](#bib_27), proposed a stronger argument. If rational players are truly alike, each should realize that whatever it decides the other will decide too, so both should cooperate. He called this superrationality. Most theorists find the reasoning too slippery, since the players are not guaranteed to be copies, but the column showed readers how a puzzle about choices becomes a puzzle about identity.

## <a id="ch_73"></a>73. Knowing, Doubting and Correcting

### On the Usefulness of Being Wrong

Science advances by being wrong in public and then correcting the error. The phlogiston theory of combustion was wrong. It nevertheless organized a large body of chemical observations and was replaced by a better account only after careful weighing showed that metals gain mass when they burn. The luminiferous aether was wrong. It nevertheless supplied the conceptual frame in which the Michelson–Morley experiment became decisive.

The pattern is general. A theory that is precise enough to be tested will eventually be tested. If it fails, the failure is informative. If it succeeds, the success is provisional. The provisional successes accumulate. They are the reason aircraft remain aloft, antibiotics cure infections, and GPS receivers know where they are. Each of those technologies rests on theories that have been wrong in detail and right enough in practice to be useful.

The same process applies to the chapters of this book. Some statements will be superseded. The supersession will not erase the parts that were already correct. It will merely draw the boundary between the two more accurately. Being wrong, provided the error is detectable, is a method. It is slower than being right, but it has the advantage of working.

### A Note on Certainty

The laws of physics are the most reliable statements human beings have so far managed to write down. They are still provisional. Newton’s law of gravitation was reliable enough to send men to the Moon and inaccurate enough to require replacement by general relativity. General relativity is reliable enough to operate the GPS network and incomplete enough to fail at the center of a black hole. The pattern is familiar. Each improvement removes an error and reveals a new boundary.

The practical response is not despair. It is the continued use of the best available description while noting where it ceases to apply. Aircraft do not fall out of the sky because quantum gravity is unfinished. Antibiotics do not stop working because the origin of life is unknown. The unfinished parts are interesting. They are not a reason to discard the finished ones. Certainty, in science, is a matter of degree and of domain. Both are larger than they were a century ago and smaller than a complete theory would make them.

### Many Levels of Description

A cup of coffee can be described as a collection of quantum fields, as a liquid with a temperature and a viscosity, or as something to drink before a meeting. Each description is correct in its own terms, and none is a rival to the others. Sean Carroll, in [*The Big Picture*](#bib_12), calls this attitude poetic naturalism: the world is made of one set of physical things, and there are many useful stories about them, each with its own vocabulary.

The levels are linked by what physicists call emergence. Temperature is not a property of a single molecule, yet it is perfectly real, because it summarizes the average motion of an enormous number of them. A table, a species, a market and a person are similar. They are patterns that are stable enough to be spoken of in their own right, though they consist of nothing but their parts.

Two cautions apply. The existence of a higher-level description does not break the laws below it. And a pattern being real at its own level does not make every story about it true. The test of a level is the same test used throughout this book: whether it lets us predict something and survives checking.

### On Experts

An expert is someone who has already made the mistakes you are about to make and has written them down. The writing is usually technical. It is nevertheless the shortest route past the mistakes. The alternative is to repeat them. Repeating them is slower and, in some fields, more expensive.

Expertise is not infallibility. Experts disagree. They also update. The disagreement is visible. The updating is visible. Both are preferable to the unanimity of people who have not examined the evidence. When an expert consensus exists and has survived repeated attempts to overturn it, the consensus is the least bad guide available. It can still be wrong. It is less likely to be wrong than an opinion formed without the same examination.

The chapters of this book rely on that consensus where it exists and note the disagreements where they remain. The reliance is provisional. It is also the reason the book can be shorter than the literature it summarizes.

### On the Persistence of Error

Error is not eliminated by the discovery that it is error. It is eliminated by the slower process of replacing the practices that embody it. The practice of bleeding patients survived the demonstration that it was harmful. The practice of denying continental drift survived the evidence that continents move. In both cases the evidence was available for decades before the practice changed.

The delay is not mysterious. Institutions, textbooks and habits have inertia. Individuals have reputations. Both resist revision. The resistance is eventually overcome when the cost of maintaining the error exceeds the cost of abandoning it. The overcoming is rarely graceful. It is nevertheless more reliable than the hope that error will vanish the moment it is pointed out. Pointing out is necessary. Replacement is what finishes the job.

### A Note on Progress

Progress in science is the replacement of a vague idea by a precise one, followed by the discovery that the precise idea is wrong in a smaller way. The smaller wrongness is an improvement. It is not a reason for celebration. It is a reason to continue.

The pattern is reliable. It is also slow. The slowness is not a defect of the method. It is a consequence of the requirement that the new idea must survive contact with observation. Contact with observation is frequently inconvenient. The inconvenience is the point. Ideas that cannot be inconvenienced are not scientific. They may be comforting. They are not progress.

### On the Retention of Obsolete Theories

Obsolete theories are not retained because they are true. They are retained because they are useful within a restricted domain, or because the cost of replacing them exceeds the cost of keeping them. Newtonian gravity is obsolete. It is also the reason spacecraft reach their destinations. The obsolescence is real. The usefulness is also real.

The retention is therefore not an error. It is a calculation. The calculation can be wrong. When it is wrong, the theory is eventually discarded. The discarding is rarely immediate. It occurs when a better calculation becomes available and when the institutions that teach the old calculation have been persuaded to teach the new one. The persuasion takes time. The time is measurable in textbooks.

## <a id="ch_74"></a>74. Future Challenges

*The unfinished list is not a secret. It is the table of contents of the journals.*

A challenge is not a reason for gloom. The list of a century ago included the nature of the stars, the structure of the gene, and the cause of infection. Those items moved from mystery to mechanism. The present list is what remains after that success. It is a larger list only because the horizon moved.

The challenges in fundamental physics are specific. Dark matter has been weighed and not identified. Dark energy has been measured and not explained. Quantum gravity has candidates and no experimental confirmation. The matter-antimatter imbalance has a size and no established mechanism. Neutrino masses have a range and an unsettled origin. Each of these is a place where a measurement could change the framework. The framework has survived a great many measurements. It is not immune to the next one.

In biology the challenges are equally specific. The origin of life lacks a demonstrated pathway. The cell is not fully mapped: many genes have functions that are partial or unknown, and the interactions are incompletely known. Development, the process that builds a body from an egg, is understood in outline in model organisms and not in anything like complete circuit detail. Consciousness is unsolved in the sense already discussed. Aging is a set of processes with partial interventions. Cancer is many diseases, some now treatable. Pandemic risk is permanent, because evolution is permanent, and preparedness is a choice. These are not vague frontiers. They are jobs with tools assigned to them.

Earth science faces a different kind of challenge: a system that can be measured and that is being changed while it is measured. The rate of ice-sheet loss, the stability of major circulations, the response of clouds, and the capacity of ecosystems to adapt or to fail are the uncertainties that dominate practical risk. They will be better known in twenty years. The emissions of those twenty years will already have been added. The challenge is scientific and temporal at once.

Technology’s challenges include the alignment and reliability of increasingly capable automated systems, the safe and equitable use of gene editing, the governance of surveillance that cheap computation makes possible, and the management of biological tools that are spreading as they cheapen. These are not purely technical. They have technical components. A system that cannot be understood by its operators, or a genetic change that cannot be confined, is a technical problem before it is a political one. The political one remains after the technical one is addressed.

The list is longer than a list from 1900 because the horizon moved. It is not longer because knowledge failed. The successes of the last century created new questions at a higher resolution. That is the ordinary progress of a science that works. A reader who finds the list daunting can equally find it a map of the interesting jobs. Both reactions fit the same facts.

Coordination is the meta-challenge. Several of the problems, climate, pandemic surveillance, the governance of powerful technologies, are shared. Shared problems require shared measurement and some degree of shared rule. The measurement is the scientific part. The rule is the political part. Science can supply the measurement and cannot supply the agreement. Pretending that the measurement settles the agreement leads to backlash. Pretending that disagreement about the agreement undermines the measurement leads to confusion. The two should be kept in their own columns. This book has tried to keep them so.

Some challenges are chosen and some are imposed. Dark matter is imposed: the measurements require an answer. A particular design of a technology is chosen: societies decide whether to build it. Treating chosen challenges as if they were laws of nature removes the responsibility for the choice. Treating imposed challenges as if they were optional delays the measurement. The list in this chapter mixes the two. Marking which is which is a useful habit. It keeps the sciences from being blamed for choices and keeps choices from being disguised as science.

Time scales differ, and the difference matters for action. A particle-physics experiment may take decades to build and run. A pandemic response has weeks. Climate policy has years to affect a trajectory that plays out over centuries. Treating every challenge as if it had the same urgency, or the same patience, misallocates effort. The sciences can say something about the time scales. They cannot rank the moral urgency. A reader who separates the time scale from the urgency will read both the science and the politics more clearly. The separation is a tool. It belongs with the other tools this book has offered.

## <a id="ch_75"></a>75. Possible Futures

*Prediction is the weakest chapter in any science guide. It is included because readers will make one anyway, and a disciplined guess is better than a mood.*

Some branches depend on choices. A world that builds nuclear plants, transmission lines, and renewable capacity looks different from a world that argues about them for another generation. A world that treats pandemic surveillance as infrastructure looks different from a world that rebuilds it after each outbreak. A world that develops machine intelligence inside serious constraints looks different from a world that does not.

Some forecasts are constrained by demographics and by physics. Population growth is slowing. Several large countries have fertility below replacement and will shrink unless offset by migration. Aging populations change the economics of health and of work. Climate warming will continue until net emissions are near zero, and sea level will continue longer. These are not speculations in the free sense. They are consequences of present measurements and of inertia.

Energy and computation have trajectories that are sturdy and not infinite. The cost of solar and wind electricity has fallen for decades and will meet limits of materials, land, and grid before it meets a limit of sunlight. The cost of computation has fallen for decades and will meet limits of energy and of the physics of switches. Both can continue to improve in usefulness after the raw curves flatten, through better design. Neither will improve without bound on the old curve. Plans that assume the old curve forever are plans that will be revised.

Biotechnology’s trajectory is toward cheaper reading and writing of genomes and toward more precise cell therapies. The consequences depend on regulation and on what is done with the tools. A world that uses them for therapies and for more productive crops looks different from a world that uses them for unconstrained ecological release or for enhancement that only the wealthy can buy. The tools do not select the world. Decisions do.

Machine intelligence is the forecast with the widest error bar. Current systems are capable and unreliable. Future systems may be more capable and more reliable, or the present limits may prove stubborn. The social effects of even the present systems are still being absorbed. A forecast that treats a particular level of capability as inevitable by a particular year is not a scientific claim. A forecast that the cheapening of cognitive tasks will matter is already confirmed.

Settlement beyond Earth, contact with another civilization, and radical extension of human lifespan are possible in the sense that no known law forbids them. They are not baseline. Contact in particular is a blank. The search has produced no confirmed signal. The silence constrains the density and the loudness of technological civilizations within our listening range. It does not decide whether any exist. The correct statement is ignorance, bounded by the search so far.

The useful attitude toward the future is the attitude this book has taken toward the present. Prefer the measurement. Name the uncertainty. Update when the measurement changes. Scenarios are tools for thinking. They are not findings. The laws in the earlier chapters will hold. The choices will determine which of the lawful futures is the one people inhabit.

Histories of prediction are humbling. Forecasts of flight, of nuclear power, of computing, and of space have been early, late, and wrong in detail even when right in outline. The outline that survives is usually the one tied to a cost curve or to a demographic fact. The detail that fails is usually a date or a social assumption. A reader can take the constrained outlines in this chapter more seriously than the speculative branches, and can take both less seriously than the measurements in the earlier chapters. The order of trust is the order of contact with evidence.

Branching is the honest picture. At each point where a cost curve, a regulation, or a discovery can go more than one way, the future forks. Some forks rejoin, because physics constrains them. Some diverge. A single narrative future is a storytelling convenience. It is not what the evidence supports. The evidence supports a set of trajectories, weighted by what is already in motion, and open where decisions have not been made. Holding the set, rather than adopting a favorite member of it, is the discipline this chapter recommends.

Agency is unevenly distributed and real. Most people cannot choose the outcome of a research program. Collectively, through institutions, people choose funding, regulation, and infrastructure. Those choices select among the lawful futures. The selection is not fine-grained. It is enough to bend trajectories. A passive reading of the future, in which technology arrives and society adapts, understates the selection. An inflated reading, in which any future can be chosen, understates the constraints. The middle is the accurate place. Constraints bind. Choices select. The future chapters of a later guide will record which selections were made.

## <a id="ch_76"></a>76. What Would Change in the Guides

The great one-volume guides to science of the twentieth century did a particular job. They told an educated reader what the sciences had established, in prose that did not sneer and did not flatter, and they separated fact from guess. A guide with the same job today would keep most of their structure. Mechanics, chemistry, the cell, evolution and the Solar System have not been repealed. It would replace chapters, and add chapters, where the world has changed under the book.

It would add chapters on subjects that had no stable form in the older books. CRISPR, because gene editing became cheap and specific. mRNA medicine, because a platform vaccine was designed from a sequence and deployed at global scale. The microbiome, because the microbial communities in and on the body moved from curiosity to organ. Gravitational waves, because they were detected and became a branch of astronomy. Exoplanets, because the census went from zero to thousands. Dark energy, because the acceleration was measured. Quantum information, because entanglement became a technology as well as a puzzle. Artificial intelligence, because learned systems became general tools. Climate science, because the warming and its cause became a detailed measurement. Synthetic biology, because genomes became files that can be ordered.

It would also rewrite chapters the older books already had. The universe chapter would gain a standard model, a precise age, and named tensions. The atom chapter would gain quarks, the Higgs boson, and a completed inventory of the Standard Model, with a clear statement of what the model does not contain. The gene, once a molecular discovery, is now a sequence that can be ordered, edited and interpreted in the clinic. The brain, once described anatomically, is now a system that can be recorded in large parts and perturbed cell by cell in animals, and the correlates of consciousness are separated from the unsolved hard problem. The periodic table is intact, and nanomaterials have been added to what the elements can be made to do.

The tone would change in places. Forecasts in the older books were sometimes early and sometimes late, so a later book would take more care with dates, and would say that a capability exists without saying when its consequences will arrive. Computers would be treated as scientific instruments, not curiosities. The unknown would be given more room, because the unknowns are sharper. Dark matter is a better mystery than the old question of whether other galaxies existed, because it is required by measurements already in hand. A sharp mystery is a sign that the subject has moved.

One more change is worth naming. The older guides were written by a single person who had read across the sciences and could present them in one voice. The sciences have since grown further apart in their techniques. A single voice is harder and more necessary: harder, because no one can be current at the frontier of every field, and more necessary, because the educated reader still needs the picture in one place, with the joints between fields visible. This book is an attempt at that place. It will be wrong in particulars. It will have succeeded if a reader finishes it knowing what is established, what is open, and how the two are told apart.

Updating is part of the form. A guide that cannot be revised is a monument; a guide revised whenever a result changes is a tool. The present book is dated by its figures, by its account of tensions, and by the state of technologies that move quickly. The dates are a feature. They tell a later reader what was known when the book was written, and they invite correction. A book about science that feared correction would have misunderstood its subject.

The aim is the aim of those guides: a single account, readable without a laboratory, of what an educated person should know about the world as the sciences currently describe it. Not a monument of certainty. A picture, dated, and open to correction. Actually.

### What Remains Open

The map is detailed and still unfinished. The identity of dark matter is unknown. We do not know why the cosmological constant is small. We do not know how the classical world emerges from the quantum wave function, or why there is a wave function at all. How life began, and whether it has begun elsewhere, is unknown. We do not know how the brain produces experience, or whether experience can be produced by anything other than a brain.

These are not small gaps. They are the places where the present theories stop. Filling any one of them would change the picture. Filling several would change it beyond recognition. The possibility is open. So is the possibility that some of the gaps are permanent, either because the information is lost or because the questions are malformed.

The practical consequence is modest. The parts of the map that are already drawn are sufficient to cure diseases, to build machines, to warn of asteroid impacts, and to measure the damage being done to the only biosphere we have yet found. They are also sufficient to show that those capabilities can be used in more than one way. The open questions are intellectually central. The closed ones are already consequential. Both deserve attention.

### A Final Observation

The universe has been expanding for 13.8 billion years. It will continue to expand for a period that is, on present evidence, much longer. During a brief interval near the middle of that history, a small number of its atoms became organized into readers of books about atoms. The organization is temporary. The books are optional. The fact that both exist at the same moment is the only reason this sentence can be written or read.

Nothing in the preceding chapters alters that contingency. They merely describe, as accurately as present knowledge allows, the conditions under which the contingency arose and the constraints it continues to face. The description is incomplete. It is still the best description we have. Whether it remains the best description depends on whether the temporary organization of atoms continues to prefer accurate maps to comforting ones. The preference is not guaranteed. It is, for the moment, observable.

### A Note on the Reader

The reader who has reached this point has already performed a non-trivial act. Several hundred pages of compressed technical prose have been traversed. Some of it will have been clear. Some of it will have required re-reading. Both outcomes are normal. Clarity in these subjects is usually the product of prior familiarity. The first encounter is rarely the clearest.

The re-reading, if undertaken, will be shorter. The map will be the same. The territory will not have changed. Only the reader’s location on the map will have shifted. That shift is the entire practical effect of the book. It is also the only effect the book can claim. The atoms continue their arrangements regardless. The reader, for a short interval, has a slightly more accurate description of those arrangements. The interval is finite. The description is provisional. Both limitations are acknowledged.

### A Remark on the Reader’s Patience

The reader who has continued to this point has demonstrated a tolerance for sentences that contain both numbers and qualifications. The tolerance is not universal. It is also not permanent. It can be exhausted by repetition, by obscurity, or by the suspicion that the author is enjoying the sound of his own caveats.

The suspicion is sometimes justified. The caveats are nevertheless required. The universe does not become simpler because a clearer sentence would be more agreeable. It becomes clearer when the sentence matches the evidence. The matching is the only service the book can offer. The service is limited. It is still the service that was requested.

# <a id="bm_epilogue"></a>Epilogue: Actually

The child who asks why the sky is blue deserves a real answer.

The sky is blue because molecules in the air scatter short wavelengths of sunlight more than long ones. The explanation uses electromagnetism, the size of atoms, and the spectrum of the Sun. It can be checked. It connects a glance upward to the same physics that runs in a laboratory.

That is the pattern of this book. A question that looks local becomes a question about laws. The laws turn out to be few, old in their operation, and still incomplete in our statement of them. The incompleteness is not a flaw in the telling. It is the present edge of the subject.

We know the age of the observable universe to a precision our ancestors could not have defined. We do not know what most of it is made of. We know the code of life and can edit it. We do not know how the code started. We can detect the collision of black holes across a billion light-years. We do not know how a brain produces a point of view. We can light a city with a panel of silicon. We have not yet arranged to do so without spending the climate we inherited.

None of these sentences cancels another. Holding established results and open problems in the same mind is the skill the sciences teach, more durable than any single result. The age of the universe and the identity of dark matter belong in the same head. So do the genetic code and the unsolved origin of life, and so do the detection of gravitational waves and the absence of a quantum theory of gravity. None of these pairs is a contradiction. Each is a measurement beside a gap. Prefer the measurement. Name the uncertainty. Update the book.

The child who asks why people age, or whether we are alone, deserves the same treatment the sciences try to give one another: a real answer where a real answer exists, a clear statement of the limit where it does not, and the willingness to replace the answer when the measurement requires it. That is the whole method. It has carried the picture this far, and it is the reason the picture can still change.

The method has a cost. It withholds comfort. It refuses to fill gaps with preferred stories. It asks the reader to carry uncertainty without treating uncertainty as a reason to discard what is known. The cost is the price of a picture that can be improved. Pictures that cannot be improved are not pictures of the world. They are decorations.

The world, as far as the picture reaches, is lawful, old, large, and incompletely mapped. We are a recent species on a small planet, able to read a surprising fraction of the map, and unable, so far, to read the rest. The fraction is the achievement. The rest is the work. Both are real.

The invitation at the end is the invitation at the beginning. Ask the question. Prefer the answer that meets the measurement. Keep the uncertainty that the measurement does not resolve. Replace the answer when a better measurement arrives. Nothing in the method requires a particular politics or a particular metaphysics beyond the willingness to let measurement correct belief, so people who disagree about everything else can share it in a laboratory, and the picture in this book can be taught across boundaries. The picture will be revised; the method of revision is the inheritance. A reader who keeps the method can do without this book. A reader who keeps the book and loses the method has kept the less important thing. Actually.

# <a id="bm_sources"></a>A Note on Sources

This book is an original account in the tradition of the classic one-volume science guides. Readers who want those predecessors will find them listed in the bibliography below.

Figures given here are the working values of current science, rounded for a general reader: a universe about 13.8 billion years old; ordinary matter near five percent of the cosmic budget, dark matter near twenty-seven, dark energy near sixty-eight; a human genome of about three billion base pairs; atmospheric carbon dioxide near 420 parts per million, against about 280 before industrial burning. Where a result is disputed, including the Hubble tension and the causes of aging, the dispute is named.

# <a id="bm_about"></a>About the Author

Lothar J. Musiol is a graduate of Munich University of Applied Sciences who spent more than forty years in the semiconductor industry, first at Germany’s largest company in the field, then at a string of American start-ups. He studied physics alongside all of it, seriously enough to know exactly how much he is simplifying. Dual citizenship, put to its most sensible use, lets him split his time between San Clemente, California, and Passau, Bavaria, where Austria begins at the garden fence. The household includes one married daughter, one grumpy Teacup Pomeranian named Gucci, and eleven chickens, listed in order of seniority rather than volume.

He writes to make complex ideas clearer and more engaging than most treatments manage, without ever pretending they are simpler than they actually are.
